units.la: VANTI interfit iuuentutem cum humanioribus studiis, & politiori literatura, vna etiam imbibere eminentiam illam cognitionis Christi, tu optimè nofti, Vir eximie, qui sæpiusculè solitus es prædicare sordete omnia ista humana, humanam prudentiam, industriam, erudition em, artes etiam ipsas & scientias, imò noxia esse & exitiosa, si à cognitione Christi separentur. Quo mihi videntur fœliciores, & non Deo tantùm, sed & Præceptoribus magis obligati, qui ab ijs ... cum Apostolo loquar, didicerur.
units.tr: How much it matters that young people, alongside the humanities and polished literature, should also drink in that outstanding knowledge of Christ, you know very well, distinguished sir, since you have often preached that all those human things (human prudence, industry, learning, the arts themselves and the sciences) are worthless, indeed harmful and deadly, if they are separated from the knowledge of Christ. Those seem to me the more fortunate, and bound not only to God but also more closely to their teachers, who ... (to speak with the Apostle) have learned.

units.la: 2 stum. Professus est iam olim Alexander magnus se Aristoteli, à quo puer formatus est, nō minus quàm patri Philippo debere, cùm ab hoc quidem viuendi, ab illo verò rectè viuendi accepisset initium. Tantam ille gratiam retulit præceptori suo, qui communibus naturæ nostræ tenebris inuolutus veram rectè viuendi rationem, nec ipse tenuit, nec alios docere potuit. Quanto maior referenda est gratia ijs Præceptoribus, qui ad genuinum rectè viuedi fontem Adolescentes reuocant, & ex verbo Dei informât in vera pietate & fide in Christum. Quo spectasse omnes beatæ memoriæ D. Rolloci labores ignorat nemo cui ipse notus fuit. Atque in hunc finem præter alios Scripturæ libros quos subinde discipulis suis prælegit, Epistolas Pauli ad Rom. & ad Galatas, in quibus plenius & clarius quàm in alia quaꝰ tota Scripturæ parte mysterium Christi revelatur, accuratissimè explica postremò adiecit Epistolam ad Hebræos, quæ eò tota tendit vt nos ad per-
units.tr: 2 ...stum. Alexander the Great long ago declared that he owed as much to Aristotle, by whom he had been educated as a boy, as to his father Philip, since from the one he had received the beginning of living, and from the other the beginning of living rightly. He repaid his teacher with such gratitude, though Aristotle, wrapped in the common darkness of our nature, neither possessed the true method of living rightly himself nor could teach it to others. How much greater thanks are owed to those teachers who lead young people back to the genuine source of right living and form them from the Word of God in true piety and faith in Christ! No one who knew him can be unaware that all the labours of the late Master Rollock, of blessed memory, aimed at this. To this end, among other books of Scripture which he read through with his pupils from time to time, he expounded with great care the Epistles of Paul to the Romans and to the Galatians, in which the mystery of Christ is revealed more fully and clearly than in any other part of Scripture. Last of all he added the Epistle to the Hebrews, which as a whole tends to this, that it might exhort us to perseverance

units.la: quaꝰ perseuerantiam & constatem professionem fidei in Christū adhortetur) eamq; hac,quæ nunc in lucem prodit. Analysi Logica illustrauit,qua mihi quidem videtur ita ad viuum Scriptoris mentem vbiq; expressisse,vt & à rudioribus paruo negotio intelligi possit, & peritioribus fontes aperiat,ex quibus vberes cœlestis doctrinæ riuos commodè possint diducere.Non sum nescius esse nonnullos qui hanc Scripturæ interpretādæ rationem improbent, quòd Spiritum sanctum in Scripturis loquentem ad artis Logicæ præceptiones alligare videatur. Atqui nos nullas sacrosanctæ Scripturæ ab arte vel scientia quacunque humana leges imponi,aut debere, aut posse arbitramur, sed Logicam duntaxat hac interpretandi ratione Scripturæ ancillam pedisequámque esse ostendimus. Cùm enim Theologiam omnium disciplinarum Dominam & moderatricem esse omnes iure agnoscamus, Logicæ famulitium cur ei denegemus? quamq; ea opem ad profana hominum scripta intelligenda confert, cur non eandé ad Prophetarum & Apostolorum scripta Θεοπνεύστα ministraret? Hac certè Analysin Logicam in nonnullis Pauli Epistolis iam ante à Rolloco felicitèr tentatam plus lucis attulisse quàm plerorumque prolixas commentationes, facilè iudicare possunt omnes, qui eam penitiùs introspexerunt & examinarunt: ex quibus multi sæpius professi sunt se non mediocrem fructum ex hoc scriptionis genere percepisse, eòque hortatores Rolloco fuerunt vt ad reliquas, quas adhuc nondum attigisset, Epistolas simili Analysi illustrandas manu admoueret: quod ab eo proculdubiò præstitum fuisset si Deus longioris ei vitæ vsuram concessisset. Ex horum numero facilè primum fuisse te, Vir eximie, nôrunt omnes quibus notum est quâ arcto amicitiæ vinculo D. Rolloco coniunctus fueris, quâque eum semper prosequutus sis beneuoleriâ. Quo solo nomine, si alia nulla subesset occasio, debeti tibi hoc opusculum nemo ibit inficias, sed alia longè maior & grauior accedit causa, Authoris ipsius suprema voluntas Testameto consignata, qua quicquid supererat operum ipsius sub tuo nomine exire voluit, & solennia haec dedicationis verba praefeferre, Gvlielmo Scoto In Perpetvvm Testimonivm Amicitiæ Nostræ Dedico Consecroqve. Accipe igitur hoc grati animi testimonium qualecunq; Analysin Logicam in Epistolam ad Hebraeos, simulq; breue tractatum de Iustificatione, quæ ideo placuit cum hac Analysi coiungere, quòd & propter breuitatè seorsim excudi non poterat, & ad quæstionem de Iustificatione hominis coram Deo determinanda doctrina de Christi sacerdotio, quæ in hac ad Hebraeos Epistola accuratissimè tractatur, singulare visum habeat, cùm illa ipsa oblatio & sacrificiū quod Sacerdos Christus Patri ad expiāda peccata nostra in cruce obtulit, sit vnica illa iustitia quā nobis Deus imputat, & propter quam nos è tribunali suo iustos esse pronunciat. Hanc autem Analysin cùm D.Rollocus,immatura morte præreptus,absoluere non posset, ne manca in lucem ederetur, eóque Ecclesiæ vsui (cui secùdùm Dei gloriam omnes suos labores vnicè semper cõsecrauerat) minus inseruiret, hanc mihi prouinciâ delegauit vt ei supremam manum imponerem.Quod onus,etsi (tenuitatis meæ mihi probè conscius) agnoscebam humeris meis impar esse,malui tamè in me suscipere, quâ in animi ingrati suspitionem apud eum incurrere,cui me omniū officiorum ratione obstrictum sentiebam. Dedi igitur operâ vt in tribus postremis capitibus (exceptis sex primis versibus capitis vndecimi) ad eam quæ Rolloco familiaris fuit, Analyseωs formam quàm fieri potuit proximè accederem. Quod si hic meus labor rerum diuinarum studiosis aliquam afferet vtilitatem, & tuo iudicio probabitur, satis amplum operę pretium me retulisse putabo. Vale in Domino. Idibus Aprilis 1605.
units.tr: and constant profession of faith in Christ. This he illustrated by the logical analysis, which now comes to light, and in which he seems to me to have expressed the mind of the writer so vividly throughout that it can be understood with little effort even by the less learned, and opens to the more skilled the sources from which they can conveniently draw off the rich streams of heavenly doctrine. I am aware that some disapprove of this method of interpreting Scripture, because it seems to bind the Holy Spirit, speaking in the Scriptures, to the precepts of the art of Logic. But we judge, and maintain, that no laws of human art or science whatever ought to be, or can be, imposed on holy Scripture; we have shown only that Logic, by this method of interpretation, is the handmaid and attendant of Scripture. For since we all rightly acknowledge that Theology is the mistress and governor of all the disciplines, why should we deny to her the service of Logic? And since Logic brings help for understanding the profane writings of men, why should it not likewise minister to the God-breathed [θεόπνευστα] writings of the Prophets and Apostles? That Rollock had already happily attempted this logical analysis in some Epistles of Paul, and that it has shed more light than the lengthy commentaries of most others, all can easily judge who have looked into it and examined it more deeply. Many of them have often confessed that they derived no small fruit from this kind of writing, and so they urged Rollock to apply the same analysis to the remaining Epistles, which he had not yet touched; and this he would undoubtedly have done had God granted him a longer span of life. That you, distinguished sir, were among the first of these, all those know who know how close the bond of friendship by which you were joined to Master Rollock was, and with what constant goodwill you always followed him. Even if there were no other occasion, no one will deny that I owe this little work to you on that ground alone; but a far greater and weightier cause also arises: the author's own final wish, sealed in his Testament, that whatever remained of his works should go forth under your name, and that they should bear these solemn words of dedication: To William Scott, in Perpetual Witness of Our Friendship, I dedicate and consecrate. Accept therefore this testimony of a grateful mind, such as it is: the Logical Analysis of the Epistle to the Hebrews, together with a brief treatise on Justification. I was pleased to join the latter to this Analysis, because on account of its brevity it could not be printed separately, and because the doctrine of Christ's priesthood, which is treated most carefully in this Epistle to the Hebrews, seems especially suited to settling the question of the justification of man before God; for that very offering and sacrifice which Christ the Priest offered to the Father on the cross to expiate our sins is that one righteousness which God imputes to us, and on account of which he pronounces us righteous from his judgment seat. Since Master Rollock, snatched away by an untimely death, could not complete this Analysis, and so that it would not be published unfinished and therefore be of less service to the Church (to which, after the glory of God, he had always devoted all his labours alone), he entrusted to me the task of putting the final hand to it. Although I, well aware of my own slightness, recognised that this burden was too heavy for my shoulders, I preferred to take it upon myself rather than incur the suspicion of an ungrateful mind with him, to whom I felt myself bound by every kind of obligation. I therefore took pains to approach as closely as I could, in the last three chapters (apart from the first six verses of the eleventh chapter), the form of analysis that was familiar to Rollock. If this my labour brings some usefulness to students of divine things, and is approved by your judgment, I shall think I have gained a sufficiently ample reward for my work. Farewell in the Lord. Ides of April, 1605.

units.tr: ON ROBERT ROLLOCK'S COMMENTARIES, enlarged by the revision of Henry Charteris.

units.la: VEndibili (Vetus est Verbum) suspendere Vino, Non opus est hedera: proba merx pracone reEmptore inuenict: qua cedro digna loquutus (mota Entheus assiduo Verbis limatus in Vsu Rollocus, Charitum flos, nostra & gloria gentis, Viturus Vel qua illeuit monumenta libellis (Perpetuum quibus est mihi fas sperare Virorum) Arte sua auctorem insignem satis edita laudant, Sint licet indicta, ingenio aut detrita minore.
units.tr: A good wine needs no bush, as the old saying goes. Sound merchandise finds its buyer without a herald. Rollock, the flower of the Graces and the glory of our nation, who spoke things worthy of cedar oil, inspired and polished by constant use of words, and who has been a model of fame in his little books (I may rightly hope these are lasting monuments of men), praises the author sufficiently distinguished by his art, though they be unspoken of, or worn away by a lesser talent.

units.la: Namque parem meritis tribuat si Gratia honorem, Si studium, aut Virtus, digna mercede beari Promereant, aurata foro tibi staret imago, Et caput auricomum, (fors qua tibi debita) Laurus Cingeret, ornaris qui publica commoda Vinus Ante alios, quantum stellas fulgore minores Cynthia praeradiat, (rumpantur Vt illa Codris) Quae scriptis, qua Voce, Deum quoque redditus albo Surpuit Vt mors sua orbi, caeloque locauit, Alternis patria faculam transmittis alumnis, Postuma inexhausta mansura & pignera mentis.
units.tr: For if Grace would grant an honour equal to his merits, if zeal or virtue deserved to be blessed with a fitting reward, a gilded statue would stand for you in the forum, and a golden laurel, which is your due, would crown your hair. You adorn the common good beyond others, as Cynthia outshines the stars that are less bright (let Codrus burst with envy). By your writings and by your voice you also restored God to the roll, and as your death snatched you from the world and placed you in heaven, you hand on the torch to pupils in turn for your country, a posthumous and inexhaustible pledge of your mind that will endure.

units.la: Qua licet imperfecta tibi sunt morte reliqua Supremam nec pasa manum, laudatur in illa Dimidiam tabula Venerem qua pinxit Apelles Extra omnes: & habent si quid praesagia Veri, Vt quondam Hippolytum superas reuocauit ad auras Diffeeptum, incolumemque suis Epidaurius Heros Restituit, mancis Charteri ita dextera chartis Paeonias porrexit opes, Vacuasque lacunas, Ne qua lacuna foret cera complevit eadem.
units.tr: Although what you left unfinished at your death was not touched by a final hand, it is praised in that state, just as Apelles' half-painted Venus on a panel is praised beyond all others. And if omens have any truth in them, as the Epidaurian hero once called Hippolytus back to the upper air, torn apart, and restored him unharmed to his own people, so Charteris' right hand offered healing powers to the maimed pages and filled the empty gaps with the same wax, lest any gap remain.

units.la: Sic memor officij Veteris, Veterisque magistri. Lampada qui extrema moriens sibi tradidit hora Effet Apollinei deinde Vt Pars maxima cætus, Magna opere in tato & parte memoratus haberet. Nec dubium parili fuerint si anale fla labore Quæ iam sparsa situ sordent carieque sepulta Fœlici purgata manu, quin Viuet Viterque Æternum, Vt meritus, chartis immortuus, auum.
units.tr: Thus he is mindful of the old duty and of the old master, who in his last hour, dying, handed the torch to him, so that he might be the greatest part of the Apollonian company and be remembered for his great work throughout. Nor is there doubt, if these scattered pages, now foul with mould and buried in decay, are cleansed by a fortunate hand, that both will live for ever, as they deserve, the one immortal in the pages, the other his forebear.

units.la: TVis auspiciis, Amice magne, Qui mancus, mutilus, lacer, iacebat, Orbatus citius suo parente Quàm lucem aspiceret liber misellus, Nunc sartus, nitidus, venustulúsque, Succo & Nectare, per Librariorum Prostat scrinia, tectus, integellus: Sic vt nec sycophantias malorum Omneis vnius æstimet vel assis. Absque te foret hic liber disertus (Certum μνημόσυνον tui sodalis, Qui solatiolum fuit Sophorum, Non horum modò, sed quot aut fuerunt, Aut posthac aliis erunt in annis) Depastus tineis malas tenebras Indignè incoleret tenebricosus. Perge vindicias tui clientis Sic postliminio parare Chartis, Famæ vt vindicias tibi clienti Laus postliminio parare pergat.
units.tr: Under your auspices, dear friend, this little book, which lay maimed, mutilated and torn, and was orphaned before it ever saw the light, now stands mended, bright and neat, pretty and whole, polished with juice and nectar, and is offered in the booksellers' shops, so that it does not value all the sycophantic slanders of the wicked at a single as. Without you this eloquent book would be a sure memorial [μνημόσυνον] of your friendship, a little solace to the wise, not only of these men but of all who have been or will be in later years. Eaten away by moths, it would have dwelt unworthily in dark obscurity. Go on defending your client's rights in this way, restoring them by right of return to the pages, so that the praise of his fame may go on restoring your client's claims to him.

units.la: IN hac epistola ad Hebræos, Author, quisquis ille fuerit, Hebræos hortatur vt eã doctrinam quam audiuerant constanter retineat. Epistola igitur exhortatoria est: Exhortationis propositio est, Retinete eam doctrinam quã accepistis, vel tenete prosessionem vestram. Eius multa afferuntur argumenta ad caput vltimum. Primum argumentum partim est à persona ministri, partim ab ipsa docendi ratione ac modo, sed praecipuè à persona ministri, Filij Dei per quē, non πολυτρόπως, sed vna eadem̄q; forma tradidit nobis vltimis hisce diebus salutis doctrinã. Hoc argumentum proponitur primis statim Epistolæ huius verbis, & concluditur initio capitis secundi. Ad huius argumenti amplificationem digreditur in magnificam descriptionem Filij Dei, qua quidem vult à nobis cōspici quanta sit illius persona dignitas, à verf. 2. ad finem capitis primi. Secundum argumentu est à certo Dei iudicio, quod sequetur neglectum professionis nostræ, vel doctrinæ tâ saluificæ,à vers.2.capitis secundi, ad posteriorem parte versus oStaui:vbi varia digressio est & multiplex occupatio, partim de Christi gloria, partim de ipsius passione ad finé capitis. Tertium argumentum coniunctu est & compositum, partim ex Prophetia siue Apostolatu, partim ex sacerdotio Christi. Hoc argumentum explicatur ab initio capitis tertij ad alteram partem versus sexti,& repetitur vers.14.&15.cap.quarti. Quartum argumentu est à beata nostra conditione,quod si teneamus professione domus Christi sumus,ab altera parte vers. 6. ad vers. 17. capitis tertij. Quintum argumentum est à priuatione cœlestis illius requietis, de qua loquitur Dauid Psal.95. Ad hoc argumentum transit in finé capitis tertij : habetur autem argumentum ipsum capite quarto ad alteram partę versus tertij. Quo loco egreditur ad ostendendu requie illam, de qua loquitur Dauid,diuersum esse,& à requie Sabbathi,& ab illa requie quâ popu-lus lus obtinuit per Iosua, cum collocaretur in terra Canaan, ad verf. II.Vbi est exhortationis conclusio cum argumento quinto repetito & confirmato, ad verf.14. Sextum argumentu est a Dei gratia & misericordia, versu ultimo capitis quarti. Capite quinto digreditur in confirmationem Pontificatus Christi in genere ad versum vndecimum, quo loco proponit de Melchisedeco dicendum, idque in eum finem vt demonstret Christu esse Pontificem secundum ordinem Melchisedec, hoc est, certum quenda ordine Pontificatus Christi. Veru a proposita hac de Melchisedeco doctrina digreditur, primu in reprehensione segnitiei & ruditatis Hebraeorum ad quos scribit, a versu 12. ad finem capitis, deinde in exhortatione, qua hortatur vt ferantur ad perfectione, adiecta graui denuntiatione in Apostatas, a verf. 1. cap. sexti ad verf. 9. vbi correctio est & mitigatio illius denunciationis ad verf. 11. quo loco speciali quadam exhortatio est ad perseuerandum in charitate & bonis operibus, ad alteram partem verf. 12. Atque hic redit ad exhortatione principalem, eiusq; argumentum affert septimu ab exemplo veterū & piorum Patrū, qui per fidem ac patientia obtinent promissam hæreditatem, ad posteriorem partem verf. 18. In altera parte verf. 18. est argumentū exhortationis ođauum, quod cursum eo corripuerimus vt spe propositam obtineamus. Capite septimo persequitur doctrinam de Melchisedeco propositam verf. 11. capitis quinti, & primum quidem Melchisedeci, vt erat typus Christi, descriptio est, cuius occasione de excellentia eius agit ad vers. 11. Vbi digressione facta probat mutatum esse sacerdotiū legale pariter & ministerium legale, ad versum 20. Ab eo loco agitur de ipso Christo, cuius typus erat Melchisedec, ciúsque præstantia & excellētia multis argumentis ostenditur, ad finem capitis noni. Capite autem decimo persequitur fusius quod cœperat ostendere versu 25. capitis 9. demonstrans Christum non sæpius offerendū, sed vnicam eius oblationem sufficere ad vers. 19. Quo loco reuertitur ad exhortationem principalem (à qua digressus fue-rat rat ab initio capitis septimi) eiusq; argumenta affert duo, nonum & decimum. Nonum est a libertate ingrediendi sacrariu cœleste: Decimum est a Præfecto domus Dei sive sacrarij in quod ingrediendu est. Hæc duo argumenta coniunguntur, a vrf. 19. ad verf. 26. Vndecimum argumetum est a pœna apostasiæ & defectionis a fide, a versu 26. ad versum 31. Duodecimu argumentum est a mercede fidei: Decimumtertium a vita æterna quam consequuntur perseuerantes in fide. Duo hæc argumenta habentur sub fine capitis decimi. Capite vndecimo toto digressio est in commendationem fidei. Capite duodecimo redit ad institutam exhortationem, cuius argumentum decimumquartum est verf. 1. a testibus, sive exemplis credentium qui perseuerarunt in fide. Decimumquintum est verf. 2. ab exemplo ipsius Christi: unde sumpta occasione exhortationem generalem, ad retinendam professionem, & constanter propositum nobis stadium decurrendum, præscriptis quasi specialibus quibusdam currendi legibus, illustrat, & ad patientiam in afflictionibus, ad præeundum alijs bono exemplo, ad pacem, ad sanctimoniâ, &c. tanquam speciales currendi modos adhortatur, à versu 3. ad versum 15. vbi est argumentum exhortationis decimumsextum, à iudicio quod sequetur eos qui Christum loquentem auersantur, ad versum 28. Quo versu decimumseptimum est argumentum, à participatione regni illius quod concuti non potest. Versu vltimo est argumetum exhortationis decimumoctauum, à natura Dei nostri qui ignis est consumens eos, consumpturus omnes qui non perseuerantes in fide ipsi non seruiunt iuxta ipsius placitum. Post exhortationem principalem capite vltimo doctrina est paranetica, qua hortatur ad officia quæ ad secundam præcipuè legis tabulam pertinent, ad versum 18. Vbi postquam Hebræis ad quos scribit preces pro se commendasset, Epistolam hanc precibus primum, deinde hortatione, postremò alijs aliquot varij argumenti sermonibus concludit.
units.tr: In this epistle to the Hebrews, the author, whoever he was, exhorts the Hebrews to hold firmly to the doctrine they had heard. The epistle is therefore hortatory, and the proposition of its exhortation is: "Hold fast to the doctrine you have received," or "hold fast your profession." Many arguments for this are set out through to the last chapter. The first argument is partly drawn from the person of the minister and partly from the manner and method of teaching itself, but chiefly from the person of the minister: the Son of God, through whom, not "in many ways" [polytropōs] but in one and the same form, he delivered to us the doctrine of salvation in these last days. This argument is stated in the very first words of the epistle and is concluded at the beginning of the second chapter. To amplify this argument, he turns to a magnificent description of the Son of God, by which he wishes us to see how great is the dignity of his person, from verse 2 of the first chapter to its end. The second argument is drawn from the certain judgment of God, which will follow the neglect of our profession, or of this doctrine so saving, from verse 2 of the second chapter to the latter part of the eighth verse. There is here a varied digression and a manifold occupation, partly concerning the glory of Christ and partly concerning his passion, to the end of the chapter. The third argument is joined and compound, drawn partly from the prophetic office or apostleship and partly from the priesthood of Christ. This argument is explained from the beginning of the third chapter to the second part of the sixth verse, and is repeated at verses 14 and 15 of the fourth chapter. The fourth argument is drawn from our blessed condition: if we hold fast our profession, we are the house of Christ; this is from the latter part of verse 6 to verse 17 of the third chapter. The fifth argument is drawn from the deprivation of that heavenly rest of which David speaks in Psalm 95. He passes to this argument at the end of the third chapter, and the argument itself is set out in the second part of the third verse of the fourth chapter. In that place he goes on to show that the rest of which David speaks is different both from the rest of the Sabbath and from that rest which the people obtained through Joshua when they were settled in the land of Canaan, down to verse 11. Here is the conclusion of the exhortation, with the fifth argument repeated and confirmed, to verse 14. The sixth argument is drawn from the grace and mercy of God, in the last verse of the fourth chapter. In the fifth chapter he turns to confirm the priesthood of Christ in general, down to verse 11, where he proposes that something must be said about Melchizedek, with the aim of showing that Christ is a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, that is, that there is a certain order of the priesthood of Christ. But from this proposed doctrine concerning Melchizedek he turns aside: first, into a rebuke of the sluggishness and dullness of the Hebrews to whom he writes, from verse 12 to the end of the chapter; then, into an exhortation by which he urges them to press on to perfection, with a grave threat added against apostates, from verse 1 of the sixth chapter to verse 9. Here there is a correction and softening of that threat, down to verse 11, where there is a particular exhortation to persevere in charity and good works, to the second part of verse 12. And here he returns to the principal exhortation and brings forward its seventh argument, from the example of the ancient and pious Fathers, who by faith and patience obtained the promised inheritance, to the latter part of verse 18. In the second part of verse 18 is the eighth argument of the exhortation, that we should run the race set before us so as to obtain the hope proposed to us. In the seventh chapter he pursues the doctrine concerning Melchizedek proposed in verse 11 of the fifth chapter, and first describes Melchizedek as a type of Christ; on the occasion of this he treats of his excellence, down to verse 11. Then, having made a digression, he proves that the legal priesthood and the legal ministry have been changed, down to verse 20. From that place he treats of Christ himself, of whom Melchizedek was the type, and his preeminence and excellence are shown by many arguments, to the end of the ninth chapter. In the tenth chapter he pursues more fully what he had begun to show in verse 25 of the ninth chapter, demonstrating that Christ is not to be offered often, but that his one offering is sufficient, down to verse 19. In this place he returns to the principal exhortation (from which he had digressed at the beginning of the seventh chapter) and brings forward two arguments, the ninth and the tenth. The ninth is from the freedom to enter the heavenly sanctuary; the tenth is from the Prefect of the house of God, or of the sanctuary into which we are to enter. These two arguments are joined, from verse 19 to verse 26. The eleventh argument is from the punishment of apostasy and defection from the faith, from verse 26 to verse 31. The twelfth argument is from the reward of faith; the thirteenth from the eternal life which those who persevere in faith obtain. These two arguments are found at the end of the tenth chapter. The whole of the eleventh chapter is a digression in commendation of faith. In the twelfth chapter he returns to the exhortation undertaken, whose fourteenth argument is, in verse 1, from the witnesses, or examples, of believers who persevered in faith. The fifteenth is, in verse 2, from the example of Christ himself; taking occasion from this, he illustrates the general exhortation to hold fast our profession and to run with constancy the course set before us, prescribing, as it were, certain special laws of running, and urges, as special modes of running, patience in afflictions, going before others with a good example, peace, holiness, and so on, from verse 3 to verse 15. Here is the sixteenth argument of the exhortation, drawn from the judgment that will follow those who turn away from Christ speaking to them, down to verse 28. In that verse is the seventeenth argument, from participation in that kingdom which cannot be shaken. In the last verse is the eighteenth argument of the exhortation, drawn from the nature of our God, who is a consuming fire, who will consume all those who do not persevere in faith and do not serve him according to his good pleasure. After the principal exhortation, the final chapter contains a paraenetic teaching, by which he urges the duties which pertain chiefly to the second table of the law, down to verse 18. Here, after commending to the Hebrews, to whom he writes, prayers on his own behalf, he concludes the epistle first with prayers, then with exhortation, and finally with several other discourses of various kinds.

units.la: ANALYSIS LOGICA IN EPISTOLAM Ad Hebræos.
units.tr: ANALYSIS LOGICA IN EPISTOLAM AD HEBRAEOS.

units.la: Argumentum Capitis Primi.
units.tr: Argument of the First Chapter.

units.la: Huius Capitis duæ sunt partes: Prima est propositio primi argumenti exhortationis hac epistola instituté,vt doctrinam quam acceperunt retineant verf. 1. Secunda est digressio in amplificationem propositi argumenti. Amplificatio est per descriptionem Filij Dei magnisicam,à versu 2.ad finem.
units.tr: This chapter has two parts. The first is the statement of the first argument of exhortation which this letter undertakes, namely that they should hold fast the doctrine they have received (v. 1). The second is a digression by way of amplifying the proposed argument. The amplification consists in a magnificent description of the Son of God, from verse 2 to the end.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: 1 Deus multis vicibus multisque modis olim loquutus Patribus per prophetas, vltimis diebus hisce loquutus est nobis per Filium.
units.tr: 1 God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spoke in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son.

units.la: EVS multis vicibus) Argumentum exhortationis primum verf. 1. proponitur, tum reliquo capite illustratur & amplificatur: Propositio argumenti est.Deus vltimis diebus hisce locutus est nobis per filium suum.Propositio argumenti non est simplex,sed tractata est per comparationem,vel dissimilem, vel minorem,doctrinæ traditæ Patribus.Comparatio igitur est,
units.tr: At sundry times) The first argument of the exhortation is set forth in verse 1, and is then illustrated and amplified in the rest of the chapter. The proposition of the argument is: God in these last days has spoken to us by his Son. This proposition is not simple but is handled by comparison, either of dissimilarity or of inferiority, with the doctrine delivered to the Fathers. The comparison, then, is this:

units.la: B
units.tr: B

units.la: Deus olim locutus est Patribus per Prophetas, vltimis diebus locutus est nobis per Filiu, Dif-similitudo(vt sic dicam) locutionis Dei maxime hîc consideranda est in Ministris: olim locutus est Patribus, per Prophetas tanquā miniftros, vltimis hisce diebus locutus est nobis, per Filium tanquā miniftrū. In personis igitur miniftris sermonis Dei, maxime posita est diffimilitudo, vel(fi lubet)imparitas. Verū ad dissimilitudine in personis addita est fecūdo loco diffimilitudo in forma loquendi, ac docendi. Deus locutus est Patribus πολυμερῶς, ἢ πολυτρόπως. Quibus verbis mihi videtur innui varietas Poli tię Ecclesiasticæ ac Diuinæ, quæ inde ab initio fuit, ætatibus Patrū, ad Christi vsque aduentū. Nā vt tacea species illas Politiæ diuinæ varias, politiam familiæ Patrum, deinde Politiā Ecclefiæ, quæ coepit esse quum populus in Ægypto collocatus est, profectò in politia primum familiæ, varia fuit οἰκονομία & dispensatio eorum quæ ad cultum Dei pertinent, & singulis ætatibus Patrum, aliquid in οἰκονομία vel mutatum est, vel auctum. Rursus fi ad politiam Ecclefiafticam descendamus, in ea quoque progressu temporis varia fuit οἰκονομία. Si lubet has voces in distincto sensu accipere, prima vox fignificabit multitudinem, & varietatem partium doctrinæ Patribus traditæ. Neque enim omnes doctrinæ de Deo partes, simul ac semel traditæ sunt, vna aliqua ætate: verum diuersis ætatibus Patrum, diuersæ partes doctrinæ sunt traditæ, & successu temporis doctrina de Deo augmetum cepit: Verbi gratia, Tempore Noachi cœpit auctior esse, quam fuit tempore Henochi: Deinde ætate Abrahami cœpit auctior esse quam fuit ætate Noachi: tum sub Isaaco cœpit auctior esse, quàm sub Abrahamo, &c. Vox autem altera πολυτρόπως ad doctrinæ propositæ formam pertinebit: Nam eadem doctrina, alia atque alia ætate, forma alia atque alia proposita est. In ἀπροσθέσει nihil expresse habetur, quod respondeat his vocibus, quas habemus expresse in πρὸτερον dissimilitudinis: Contrarium autem facile intelligi potest ex contrario, nempe quod Deus salutis doctrinam, non πολυμέρως, sed simul ac semel totam, non πολυτρόπως, sed una eademque constanti forma, tradiderit nobis vltimis hisce diebus, per Filium suum. Atque hactenus sic explicata est propositio argumenti primi comparata: Est autem argumentum partim quidem à persona ministri, partim verò ab ipsa docendi ratione ac modo, sed præcipuè à persona Ministri.
units.tr: God spoke in time past to the Fathers by the prophets; in these last days he has spoken to us by the Son. The dissimilarity (if I may so put it) in God's speaking is to be considered chiefly in the ministers: in time past he spoke to the Fathers through the prophets as ministers; in these last days he has spoken to us through the Son as minister. The dissimilarity, or (if you like) the inequality, therefore lies mainly in the persons who are the ministers of God's word. But to the dissimilarity in persons is added, in the second place, a dissimilarity in the form of speaking and teaching. God spoke to the Fathers polymerōs [πολυμερῶς] or polytropōs [πολυτρόπως]. By these words I think is hinted the variety of the divine and ecclesiastical polity, which has existed from the beginning, through the ages of the Fathers, down to the coming of Christ. For, to pass over the various forms of divine polity, the polity of the patriarchal family, and then the polity of the Church, which began when the people was settled in Egypt: certainly in the polity of the family first there was a varied oikonomia [οἰκονομία] and dispensation of those things that pertain to the worship of God, and in each age of the Fathers something in the oikonomia was either changed or increased. Again, if we descend to the ecclesiastical polity, in it too, as time went on, there was a varied oikonomia. If we wish to take these words in a distinct sense, the first word will signify the multiplicity and variety of the parts of doctrine delivered to the Fathers. For not all the parts of the doctrine concerning God were delivered at once and all together in one age; rather, in different ages of the Fathers different parts of doctrine were delivered, and as time went on the doctrine concerning God grew. For example: in the time of Noah it became fuller than it was in the time of Enoch; then in the age of Abraham it became fuller than it was in the age of Noah; then under Isaac it became fuller than under Abraham, and so on. The second word, polytropōs [πολυτρόπως], will pertain to the form of the doctrine proposed: for the same doctrine was set forth in one form in one age and in another form in another age. In the aprosthései [ἀπροσθέσει] nothing is expressly stated corresponding to these words which we have expressly in the first point of dissimilarity; but the contrary can easily be understood from the contrary, namely that God delivered to us in these last days, through his Son, the doctrine of salvation not polymerōs [πολυμέρως], in parts, but at once and all together, not polytropōs, in various forms, but in one and the same constant form. And so far the proposition of the first comparative argument has been explained. The argument is partly from the person of the minister, but partly from the very manner and mode of teaching; yet chiefly from the person of the minister.

units.la: 2 Quem constituit hæredem omnium: per quem etiam vndum condidit.
units.tr: 2 Whom he hath appointed heir of all things, by whom also he made the worlds;

units.la: 3 Qui quum sit splendor gloriæ, & charaster personæ illius, sustineátque omnia verbo illo suo potente purgatione peccatorum nostrorum per seipsum facta, sedit ad dextram maiestatis illius excelsissima.
units.tr: 3 Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high;

units.la: 4 Tanto præstantior factus Angelis, quanto excellentius præ illis sortitus est nomen.
units.tr: 4 Being made so much better than the angels, as he hath by inheritance obtained a more excellent name than they.

units.la: 5 Nam cui dixit Vnquam Angelorum, Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te? Ac rursum. Ego ero ei Pater, & ipse erit mihi Filius.
units.tr: 5 For unto which of the angels said he at any time, Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee? And again, I will be to him a Father, and he shall be to me a Son?

units.la: 6 Rursum autem quum inducit primogenitum in orbem terrarum, dicit, Et adorent eum omnes Angeli Dei.
units.tr: 6 And again, when he bringeth in the first begotten into the world, he saith, And let all the angels of God worship him.

units.la: 7 Et de Angelis quidem dicit, qui Angelos suos facit ventos, & Ministros suos, ignis flammam:
units.tr: 7 And of the angels he saith, Who maketh his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire.

units.la: 8 Ad filium autem, Thronus tuus, Deus in sæculum sæculi: virga recta, virga regni tui.
units.tr: 8 But unto the Son he saith, Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever: a sceptre of righteousness is the sceptre of thy kingdom.

units.la: 9 Dilexisti justitiam & odisti iniquitatem: propterea unxit te Deus, Deus tuus, oleo exultationis præ consortes tuos.
units.tr: 9 Thou hast loved righteousness, and hated iniquity; therefore God, even thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows.

units.la: 10 Et tu in initio Domine terram fundasti, & opera manuum tuarum sunt cæli.
units.tr: 10 And, Thou, Lord, in the beginning hast laid the foundation of the earth; and the heavens are the works of thine hands:

units.la: 11 Ipsi peribunt, tu autem permanes: & omnes ut vestimentum veterascent:
units.tr: 11 They shall perish; but thou remainest; and they all shall wax old as doth a garment;

units.la: 12 Ac velut amictum circumvolues eos, & mutabuntur: tu autem idem es, & anni tui non deficient.
units.tr: 12 And as a vesture shalt thou fold them up, and they shall be changed: but thou art the same, and thy years shall not fail.

units.la: 13 Ad quem autem Angelorum dixit Vnquam Sede ad dexteram meam, usque dum ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum.
units.tr: 13 But to which of the angels said he at any time, Sit on my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool?

units.la: 14 Nonne omnes sunt ministratores spiritus, qui ministerij causa mittuntur propter eos qui hæredes erunt salutis?
units.tr: 14 Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation?

units.la: Quem constituit) Ad amplificationem propositi argumenti primi, egreditur in magnificam def. descriptionem personae ministrae, Filij Dei, ex qua quidem descriptione vult à nobis confpici quanta sit eius personae dignitas: Describitur autem persona ministra, Dei Filius, ex argumentis, partim simplicibus, partim comparatis. Primum argumentum est ab haereditate ipsius amplissima à Patre ipsi data, vt qui sit Filius Patris vnigenitus: Nam si Filius est, haeres est necessario. Per quem) Secundum argumentum descriptionis est à mundi creatione, quae fuerat per Filium.
units.tr: Whom he hath appointed) To amplify the first argument proposed, he goes on to a magnificent def. description of the person of the minister, the Son of God. From this description he wishes us to see how great the dignity of that person is. The person of the Son of God is described by arguments, some simple and some comparative. The first argument is from his most ample inheritance, given him by the Father, since he is the only-begotten Son of the Father: for if he is a Son, he is necessarily an heir. By whom) The second argument of the description is from the creation of the world, which was made through the Son.

units.la: 3 Qui quum sit) Tertium est argumentum descriptionis, à gloriosa sessione ipsius ad dexteram Patris suhuic sessioni fundamenta substernuntur tria, primum est similitudo Filij cum Patre suo: Similitudo posita est in duobus, primum in eo quod sit splendor gloriae paternae, hoc est, gloriosae ipsius essentiae: haec similitudo, vel potius (vt sic dicam) identitas, est in subsistentia vna eademque. Deinde similitudo in eo posita est, quod sit character personae illius: haec similitudo est personae, qua Filius non tantum idem est cum Patre, quoad naturam & essentiam vnam eandemque, sed etiam quoad Personam filij Patri similis est, & refert quasi imaginem Patrem suum. Mysterium hoc similitudine e medio sumpta aliquo modo adumbrari posset, sic: Filius aliquis, qui non tantum natura sua, & essentia, idem sit quodam modo cum Patre, nempe paternae essentiae participatione,
units.tr: Who being) The third argument of the description is from his glorious session at the right hand of the Father. Three foundations are laid for this session. The first is the likeness of the Son to his Father. This likeness lies in two things. First, in that he is the brightness of the Father's glory, that is, of his glorious essence: this likeness, or rather (if I may so put it) identity, is in one and the same subsistence. Second, the likeness lies in this, that he is the character of that person: this likeness is of person, by which the Son is not only the same as the Father in nature and in one and the same essence, but is also like the Father in person, and bears, as it were, the image of his Father. This mystery might be somewhat shadowed forth by a likeness taken from among ourselves, thus: suppose some son who is not only the same in nature and essence as his father, namely by participation in the paternal essence,

units.la: sed etiam Patrem suum referat externis corporis lineamentis, quantitatibus, qualitatibus, vultu, voce, gestu: jam hic filius quod ad naturam dicitur imago essentiæ ac naturæ paternæ, quod vero ad externa corporis lineamenta, &c. dicetur imago personæ paternæ. Similiter res habet in Dei Filio, qui est Imago Patris, non tantum quoad naturam, & essentiam eandem, ac totam, sed etiam quoad personam, hoc est, vt sic dicam, illius vnius essentiæ lineamenta, vultum, vocem, gestum, hoc est, quoad ea quæ in Deo Patre incomprehensibilia sunt, & quæ necesse est mutuatitijs huiusmodi vocibus exprimere. Sustineatque) Secundum est fundamentum, quo nititur gloriosa illa sessio ad dextera m Patris, à conseruatione rerum omnium creatarum. Purgatione) Tertium est fundamentum à redemptione humani generis, quam vocat purgationem peccatorum nostrorum: Purgationem hanc ἐξ ἑαυτῶ per seipsum facta dicit, hoc est, per sui ipsius oblationem in cruce & perlauacrum, non externum aliquod, verum sui ipsius sanguinis: hoc enim purgationem per Christum factam mirificè commendat. Apostolus Philip. 2. 9. & deinceps, dicit Christum (ob hanc ipsam purgationem peccatorum nostrorum qua se exinaniuit) euectum esse ad summam sublimitatem, hoc est, ad dexteram Dei Patris: ergo & sine dubio hoc quoque fundamentum est quoddam, gloriosæ illius sessionis ad dexteram Patris.Sedit ad dexteram.) Ex fundamētis istis iā iaḋis, sequitur tertium illud argumentum descriptionis Filij Dei, à gloriosa ipsius sessione ad dexteram Patris.
units.tr: but also reproduces his father in outward bodily features, in stature, in qualities, in countenance, voice and gesture. Now this son, so far as nature is concerned, is called the image of his father's essence and nature; but so far as outward bodily features are concerned, etc., he is called the image of his father's person. Similarly the matter stands with the Son of God, who is the image of the Father not only in nature and in one whole and identical essence, but also in person; that is, if I may so put it, in the features, countenance, voice and gesture of that one essence, that is, in those things which in God the Father are incomprehensible and which we must express by borrowed words of this kind. Upholding) The second foundation on which that glorious session at the right hand of the Father rests is the preservation of all created things. Purging) The third foundation is from the redemption of the human race, which he calls the purging of our sins. He says this purging was made ex heautou [ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ], by himself, that is, by his own offering on the cross and by a washing not external but of his own blood: for this especially commends the purging made by Christ. The Apostle, Philippians 2:9 and following, says that Christ, on account of this very purging of our sins, by which he emptied himself, was exalted to the highest sublimity, that is, to the right hand of God the Father. Therefore without doubt this too is a foundation of that glorious session at the right hand of the Father. Sat down at the right hand.) From these foundations, now laid, follows that third argument of the description of the Son of God, from his glorious session at the right hand of the Father.

units.la: 4 Tanto præstantior)Nunc describitur Filius Dei comparatè, saḋa nimirum comparatione cum Angelis, qui creaturæ sunt præstantissimæ,& gloriosissimæ. Propositio comparationis hæc est: præstantior factus est Angelis: Ratio, excellentius sortitus est præ Angelis nomen: sensus enim huius versus est,quasi dicat, præstantior factus est Angelis, quia excellentius præijs nomen est sortitus. Verùm propositionem cum argumento suo inter se copulauit,per argumentum varium simulque proposuit. Nomen intelligo, honorificam appellationem,& mentionem Filij in scripturis, non vno in loco occurrentem cuiusmodi est nomen Filij Dei.
units.tr: 4 Tanto præstantior) Here the Son of God is described comparatively, namely by comparison with the Angels, who are the most excellent and most glorious of creatures. The proposition of the comparison is this: he has been made more excellent than the Angels. The reason is: he has obtained a more excellent name than the Angels. For the sense of this verse is, as if he said: he has been made more excellent than the Angels, because he has obtained a more excellent name than they. But he has joined the proposition and its argument together, and has set them forth at once in a varied way. By "name" I understand the honourable appellation and mention of the Son in the Scriptures, which occurs in more than one place, such as the name Son of God.

units.la: ς Nam dixit) Sequuntur testimonia,partim de Filio ipsiusque honorabili nomine in Scripturis sacris sese offerēre,partim de Angelis, ipsorúmq; ministerio:adducūtur autem omnia quæ sequuntur testimonia ad ostendendum id quod dictum est versu 4. Filium præ Angelis excellentius sortitum esse nomen, id est, honorabiliorem Filij in Scripturis sacris mentionem fieri,quàm Angelorum.
units.tr: 5 Nam dixit) There follow testimonies, some concerning the Son and his honourable name, which present themselves in the holy Scriptures, and some concerning the Angels and their ministry. All the testimonies that follow are adduced to show what was said in verse 4: that the Son has obtained a name more excellent than the Angels, that is, that a more honourable mention of the Son is made in the holy Scriptures than of the Angels.

units.la: Filius meus) Testimonium hoc primum est ex Psalmo 2. 7. Est autem de Filio Dei, in quo fit mentio ipsius vt Filij. Et rursum ) Secundum testimonium ex 1. Chron. 22. 10. Est autem de Filio, & in eo fit honorabilis mentio ipsius, vt Filij.
units.tr: Filius meus) This first testimony is from Psalm 2:7. It concerns the Son of God, and in it mention is made of him as Son. Et rursum) The second testimony is from 1 Chronicles 22:10. It concerns the Son, and in it an honourable mention of him is made as Son.

units.la: 6 Rursus autem) Tertium testimonium de Filio, ex Psa. 97. 7. In hoc testimonio fit mentio Filij, vt Dei adorandi, etiam ab ipsis Angelis
units.tr: 6 Rursus autem) The third testimony concerning the Son is from Psalm 97:7. In this testimony mention is made of the Son as God to be adored, even by the Angels themselves.

units.la: 7 Et de Angelis ) Quartum testimonium, ex Psal. 104. 4. Est autem de Angelis, & in eo fit mentio Angelorum, vt Ministrorum Dei velocissimorum, vt qui Spiritus sunt, & tanquam ignis flamma.
units.tr: 7 Et de Angelis) The fourth testimony is from Psalm 104:4. It concerns the Angels, and in it mention is made of the Angels as the swift ministers of God, since they are spirits and like a flame of fire.

units.la: 8 Ad Filium) Quintum testimonium, ex Psal 45. 7. Est autem de Filio, & in eo fit mentio Filij, vt gloriosi Regis, insidentis Throno suo, & manu tenentis sceptrum Regni sui.
units.tr: 8 Ad Filium) The fifth testimony is from Psalm 45:7. It concerns the Son, and in it mention is made of the Son as the glorious King, sitting on his throne and holding the sceptre of his kingdom.

units.la: 10 Et tu initio) Sextum testimonium ex Psal. 102. 26. Est autem de Filio: Eius mentio fit, vt Dei aeterni Creatoris omnium rerum.
units.tr: 10 Et tu initio) The sixth testimony is from Psalm 102:26. It concerns the Son, and mention is made of him as the eternal God and Creator of all things.

units.la: 13 Ad quem autem) Septimum testimonium, ex Psal. 110. 1. Est autem de Filio, & in eo fit mentio eius, vt Regis gloriosi sedentis ad dexteram Patris: tractatur per communicationem. Primum quaerit Apostolus, cuinam Angelorum vnquam fit hoc dictum quod sequitur? Responsio negata polt interrogationem intelligenda est, quasi dicat, nulli.
units.tr: 13 Ad quem autem) The seventh testimony is from Psalm 110:1. It concerns the Son, and in it mention is made of him as the glorious King sitting at the right hand of the Father; it is treated by way of communication. The Apostle first asks to which of the Angels this was ever said that follows. The answer, which is withheld after the question, is to be understood as if he said: to none.

units.la: 14 Nonne omnes) Ratio est negatae & intelligere responsionis, ab Angelorum conditione & functione: omnes sunt ministratores Spiritus, Qui ministerij) Definitio quædam est ministratorum Spiritūum,ex ijs quibus ministrant, nepe hæredibus salutis: Mittuntur enim minister-rij causa propter eos qui hæredes erunt salutis. Vel filubet, Ratio est, cur dixit ministratores Spiritus, ex fine missionis ipsorum: Mittuntur nim ministerij causa, idque propter hæredes salutis. Quare Angeli ministratores siue ministri dicuntur, respectu Dei cui ministrant, nō hominum, etsi ministrent Deo suo propter homines ipsorumque salutem. Hactenus itaque, adductis septem testimonijs, ostensa est illa propositio, quæ fuit suprà versu 4. Filium excellentius nomen sortitum præ Angelis. In Scripturis enim fit mentio Filij: primùm, vt Filij Dei: secundò, vt Dei adorandi: tertiò, vt Regis, cum Throno & sceptro: quartò vt Creatoris: quinto vt Regis sedentis ad dexteram Patris. Angelorum autem mentio fit vt Spiritum ministratorum. Nam quod nomen vocat, versu. 4. ego accipio illud non denominetantum Filij Dei, de quo in duobus primis testimonijs, sed etiam de alia quacunq; Christi appellatione & mentione: de qua in reliquis testimonijs
units.tr: 14 Nonne omnes) The reason for the negative answer, which is to be understood, is taken from the condition and function of the Angels: they are all ministering spirits. Qui ministerij) This is a definition of the ministering spirits from those to whom they minister, namely the heirs of salvation: for they are sent for the sake of ministry on account of those who will be heirs of salvation. Or, if you prefer, the reason why he called them ministering spirits is taken from the purpose of their being sent: they are sent for the sake of ministry, and that on account of the heirs of salvation. Hence the Angels are called ministering spirits or ministers with respect to God, to whom they minister, not to men, although they minister to their God on account of men and their salvation. So far, then, with the seven testimonies adduced, that proposition has been shown which was stated above in verse 4: that the Son has obtained a more excellent name than the Angels. For in the Scriptures mention is made of the Son: first, as Son of God; second, as God to be adored; third, as King, with throne and sceptre; fourth, as Creator; fifth, as King sitting at the right hand of the Father. But mention of the Angels is made as ministering spirits. For as to the word "name" in verse 4, I take it not only of the title Son of God, which is in the first two testimonies, but also of every other appellation and mention of Christ, which is in the remaining testimonies.

units.la: Argumentum Capitis secundi.
units.tr: Argument of the Second Chapter.

units.la: Huius Capitis tres sunt partes. Prima est. Conclusio principalis exhortationis, verf. 1. Deinde est secundum hortationis argumentum, tractatum & explicatum, averf. 1. ad postrema verba verf. 8 Vnde initium sumit tertia pars capitis, posita in varia digressione ac multiplici occupatione: quarum primæ duæ sunt de Christi gloria, ad versum vsque 10. reliquæ sunt de Christi passione, inde ad finem capitis.
units.tr: This chapter has three parts. The first is the principal conclusion of the exhortation, verse 1. Next is the second argument of the exhortation, treated and explained, from verse 1 to the last words of verse 8. From there the third part of the chapter takes its beginning, set in a varied digression and manifold occupation; of which the first two are concerning the glory of Christ, down to verse 10; the rest concern the passion of Christ, from there to the end of the chapter.

units.la: CAPVT. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: I Propterea oportet nos eo magis attendere ijs quæ audiuimus, nequando perfluamus.
units.tr: 1 Therefore we ought to pay all the closer attention to what we have heard, lest we drift away.

units.la: Propterea oportet ) Conclusio exhortationis post digressionem, quæ fuit inde à verf.2.Ca.1. Non infert simpliciter oportere nos attendere ijs quę audiuimus, sed comparate ait, eo magis attendere ijs quæ audiuimus; quasi dicat, Quo est Filius, per quem locutus est Deus hisce diebus vltimis, persona dignior ac gloriosior, eo magis oportet attendere ijs, quæ ex ipso audiuimus. Ergo conclusio hæc exhortationis infertur ex argumento illo, à persona Filij Dei, non nudè tantùm exposito, sed in digressione (vt audiuimus) amplificato. Porrò attendere ijs quę audita sunt, nihil est aliud quàm id quod dicitur postea, retinere professionem, hoc est, doctrinam Christi jam perceptam, quod quidem quid aliud est, quàm perseuerare in fide ad finem vsque? Nequando ) Quo pertineat & spectet illa attentio docet: eo autem spectat, ne quando effluamus, hoc est, ne quo tempore ea quæ audita sunt nobis effluant. Metaphora est à vasis quæ perfluunt, ac non continent infusum liquorem.Sententia igitur est: Attendite, & in hoc incumbite summa diligentia, vt contineatis & retineatis ea quæ audiuistis.
units.tr: Therefore we ought) This is the conclusion of the exhortation, following the digression that began at verse 2 of chapter 1. He does not simply infer that we ought to attend to what we have heard, but draws a comparison: we ought to pay all the closer attention to what we have heard. It is as if he said: the more worthy and glorious the person through whom God has spoken in these last days, the more we ought to attend to what we have heard from him. So this conclusion of the exhortation is drawn from the argument about the person of the Son of God, not merely stated but amplified in the digression (as we have heard). Moreover, to attend to what has been heard is nothing other than what is said afterwards, namely to hold fast the profession, that is, the doctrine of Christ already received; and what is that but to persevere in the faith to the end? Lest we drift away) The text teaches what this attentiveness aims at: it aims at not drifting away, that is, at not letting what we have heard slip from us at any time. The metaphor is taken from vessels that leak and do not hold the liquid poured into them. The sense, therefore, is: pay attention, and apply yourselves with the greatest diligence, so that you may hold and retain what you have heard.

units.la: 2 Etenim si per Angelos dictus sermo fuit firmus, omnisque transgressio & contumacia iustam mercedis retributionem retulit.
units.tr: 2 For if the word spoken through angels was firm, and every transgression and disobedience received a just recompense of reward.

units.la: 3 Quomodo nos effugiemus si tantam neglexerimus salutem? quæ quum primum enarrari cæperit per ipsum Dominum ab iis qui ipsum audierant fuit nobis confirmata.
units.tr: 3 How shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation? which, having at first begun to be spoken through the Lord himself, was confirmed to us by those who heard him.

units.la: 4 Testimonium illis præente Deo & signis & prodigiis, Variisque Virtutibus & Spiritus sanctí distributionibus pro sua Voluntate.
units.tr: 4 God also bearing witness with them, both by signs and wonders, and by various powers and distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his own will.

units.la: 5 Non enim Angelis subiecit mundum illum suturum de quo loquimur.
units.tr: 5 For he did not subject to angels the world to come, of which we speak.

units.la: 6 Testatus est autem quidam alicubi, dicens, Quid est homo, vt memor sis eius, aut filius hominis, vt eum respicias?
units.tr: 6 But one has testified somewhere, saying, What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you visit him?

units.la: 7 Fecisti eum paulo super inferiorem Angelis: gloria & honore coronasti eum, & constituisti eum super opera manuum tuarum.
units.tr: 7 You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honour, and set him over the works of your hands.

units.la: 8 Omnia subiecisti sub pedibus eius: Enimuero in hoc quod ei subiecit omnia nihil omisit quod non sit ei subiectum.
units.tr: 8 You have put all things under his feet. For in that he subjected all things to him, he left nothing that is not subject to him.

units.la: 2 Etenim si per) Secundum argumentum exhortationis, à certo Dei iudicio quod sequitur neglectum professionis nostræ, vel doctrinæ tá saluificæ. Non effugiemus, inquit, si tantam neglexerimus salutem, id est, salutarem doctrinam. Ergo in ea perseuerate. Antecedens illustratum est comparatione minorum.Si doctrina per Angelos ministrata, hoc est, si doctrina Legis(nam per Angelos fuit ministrata. Galat. 3.19.) firma fuit,hoc est,ut sequentia verba exponunt,si nemo Legis per Angelos datę,transgressionem impunè tulit, quanto magis non effugiemus si tantam neglexerimus salutem? Omnisque transfsio)Hęc est epexegesis verbi proximi: nam ideò sermo Legis, qui datus est per Angelos, firmus fuit, quia omnis transgressio illius sermonis, & contumacia, justam mercedis retributionem retulit: sermo enim firmus est qui non impunè violatur.
units.tr: 2 For if the word through) This is the second argument of the exhortation, drawn from the certain judgment of God that follows the neglect of our profession, or of this most saving doctrine. We shall not escape, he says, if we neglect so great a salvation, that is, the saving doctrine. Therefore persevere in it. The antecedent is illustrated by an argument from the less to the greater. If the doctrine ministered through angels, that is, the doctrine of the Law (for it was ministered through angels, Gal. 3.19), was firm, that is, as the following words explain, if no one who transgressed the Law given through angels went unpunished, how much more shall we not escape if we neglect so great a salvation? And every transgression) This is an explanation of the immediately preceding word. For the word of the Law, which was given through angels, was firm because every transgression and disobedience of that word received a just recompense of reward; for a word is firm when it is not violated with impunity.

units.la: 3 Quaquum primum) Argumenti secundi, quod proximè præcedentibus verbis conclusum est, amplificatio inserta per parenthesin videtur, ab hoc loco, ad versum vsque quintum.Conclusio argumenti fuit, Nos non effugiemus judicium, si tantam neglexerimus salutem,hoc est, salutis doctrinam. Amplificatio, siue ratio est,a ministerio Apostolorum: quasi dicat,Salutis hæc doctrina, præterquam quod per ipsum Dominum primum cœpit enarrari, etiā ab Apostolis qui cum Domino versati sunt, ipsum viderunt,ipsum audiuerunt, & (vt est 1. Ioan.1.1.) manibus suis ipsum contrectarūt, ab Apostolis, inquam, tanquam testibus fide dignissimis,nobis est confirmata:Ergo vel hac etiam de causa, & propter hoc ipsum ministerium Apostolorum, non effugiemus judicium, si tantam neglexerimus salutem. Nota igitur, quò plures sunt testes doctrinæ à Christo primùm traditæ, eò gravius futurum est judicium nostrum, si eam doctrinam contempserimus. Sic ergo paucis verbis accipe summam verf. 2, & 3. quibus tractatur secundum argumentum propositæ exhortationis. Argumentum est à judicio Dei hoc modo. Nō effugiemus, si doctrinam salutis, quæ per Filium Dei tradita est, neglexerimus. Ergo non est negligenda aut contemnenda. Antecedentis ratio est à minori. Nō effugerunt qui doctrinam Legis, per Angelos traditam contempserunt. Ergo quanto magis non effigient, qui doctrinam salutis per Dei Filium traditam neglexerint. Hujus conclusionis amplificatio est, præsertim etiam quum per Apostolos Domini doctrina, hæc salutis fit confirmata.
units.tr: 3 For which, as soon as) The amplification of the second argument, which has just been concluded in the preceding words, seems to be inserted by way of parenthesis, from this place to the fifth verse. The conclusion of the argument was: we shall not escape judgment if we neglect so great a salvation, that is, the doctrine of salvation. The amplification, or reason, is taken from the ministry of the Apostles, as if he said: this doctrine of salvation, besides having first begun to be spoken through the Lord himself, has also been confirmed to us by the Apostles, who were with the Lord, saw him, heard him, and (as 1 John 1.1 says) handled him with their hands; by the Apostles, I say, as most trustworthy witnesses. Therefore, for this very reason, and on account of this very ministry of the Apostles, we shall not escape judgment if we neglect so great a salvation. Note, then, that the more witnesses there are to a doctrine first delivered by Christ, the heavier our judgment will be if we despise that doctrine. Thus, in a few words, take the sum of verses 2 and 3, in which the second argument of the proposed exhortation is treated. The argument is from the judgment of God, in this way: we shall not escape if we neglect the doctrine of salvation delivered through the Son of God. Therefore it must not be neglected or despised. The reasoning of the antecedent is from the lesser: those who despised the doctrine of the Law delivered through angels did not escape. Therefore how much more will they not escape who neglect the doctrine of salvation delivered through the Son of God. The amplification of this conclusion is that the doctrine of salvation has been confirmed all the more, especially since it has been confirmed through the Apostles of the Lord.

units.la: 4 Testimonium illis) Commendatio est Ministerij Apostolorum, à testimoniis divinis, quibus ipsorum vocatio extraordinaria confirmata est & exornata. Testimonia divina sunt, signa, prodigia, variæ virtutes, ac distributiones Spiritus sancti, quibus testimoniis & donis extraordinarijs testari voluit mundo Dominus Apostolos ita illuminatos & gubernatos fuisse, ut in doctrina cœlesti tradenda errare nullo modo potuerint. Commendatio hæc ministerij Apostoloci eò quoque referetur quò ipsum eorum minisferium referebatur,nempe ad docendum id quod dixit, contemptores doctrinæ salutis non effugiturosjudicium.
units.tr: 4 God also bearing witness) This is a commendation of the ministry of the Apostles, drawn from the divine testimonies by which their extraordinary calling was confirmed and adorned. The divine testimonies are signs, wonders, various powers, and the distributions of the Holy Spirit; by these testimonies and extraordinary gifts the Lord willed to bear witness to the world that the Apostles had been so enlightened and governed that they could in no way err in delivering the heavenly doctrine. This commendation of the Apostolic ministry also refers to the same end to which their ministry itself was directed, namely, to teach what he has said: that the despisers of the doctrine of salvation will not escape judgment.

units.la: 5 Non enim) Hactenus digressiuncula fuit in amplificationem propositi argumenti secundi: Nunc redire videtur ad confi mandam consecutionem illam quæ fuit à minori ad majus Contemptores doctrinæ Legis per Angelos traditæ non effugerunt, ergo quanto magis non effugiemus nos,si doctrinam Filij Dei contempserimus. Ratio sequelæ est à gloria Christi præ Angelis, quæ in eo sita est, quod non Angelis, sed Christo subjecit Deus mundum illum futurum. De quo) Hæc verba docent per mundum futurum nihil aliud intelligi, quàm tantam illam salutem, de qua dixit supra, vers.
units.tr: 5 For he did not) Hitherto there has been a little digression to amplify the second argument proposed. Now he seems to return to confirm that inference from the less to the greater: the despisers of the doctrine delivered through angels under the Law did not escape; therefore how much more shall we not escape if we despise the doctrine of the Son of God. The reason for the inference is drawn from the glory of Christ above the angels, which consists in this: God did not subject to angels, but to Christ, the world to come. Of which) These words teach that by the world to come nothing else is meant than that great salvation of which he spoke above, in verse 3. For the kingdom of God, or the world to come, consists in righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit, and finally in eternal salvation (Rom. 14.17).

units.la: 3.Nam regnum Dei, sive mundus futurus,situs est in justitia,pace,gaudio per Spiritu sanctum, denique salute æterna. Rom.14.17.

6 Testatus est autem) Dignitatem & gloriam Christi præ Angelis,confirmat testimonio Dauidis.Testimonium hoc est, ex Psalmo 8.5. In hoc testimonio Dauidis citato,primùm est pro positio dignitatis hominis, sive naturæ humanæ in Christo(nam de eo præcipuè accipienda sunt verba Prophetæ) propositio, inquam, dignitatis cum admiratione quadam. Oritur autem admiratio,ex consideratione, partim vilitatis naturæ humanæ, partim dignitatis illius, in qua tamen natura nostra inChristo est euecta.
units.tr: 6 But one has testified) He confirms the dignity and glory of Christ above the angels by the testimony of David. This testimony is taken from Psalm 8.5. In this quoted testimony of David, there is first a statement of the dignity of man, or of human nature in Christ (for the words of the Prophet are to be understood chiefly of him): a statement, I say, of dignity, with a certain wonder. The wonder arises from the consideration partly of the lowliness of human nature, and partly of that dignity to which our nature has nevertheless been raised in Christ.

units.la: 7 Fecisti
units.tr: 7 You made

units.la: 7 Fetifti eum) Hoc versu, & principio fequentis versus, est propositæ dignitatis naturæ humanæ explicatio:Primùm verba hæc adducta sunt per occupationem:At Christus homo factus est Angelis inferior, nempe quum factus est obediens Patri,vsque ad mortem,mortem autem crucis?Respondet primùm concessione,paulisper quidem factum Christum,Angelis inferiorem: deinde correctione, paulò post tamen Christum gloria & honore coronatum:Tum illa gloria in quam est euectus declaratur ex rebus creatis, super quas omnes Christus est constitutus Dominus, & Rex, & quæ sub pedibus Christi omnes sunt subiectæ,
units.tr: 7 You made him) In this verse, and the beginning of the following verse, there is an explanation of the stated dignity of human nature. First, these words are adduced by way of an objection: but Christ, made man, was lower than the angels, namely when he was made obedient to the Father, even unto death, the death of the cross. He answers first by concession: indeed, Christ was made for a little while lower than the angels; then by correction: yet shortly afterwards Christ was crowned with glory and honour. Then that glory to which he has been raised is declared from the created things over which Christ has been set as Lord and King, and which are all made subject under the feet of Christ.

units.la: 8 Enimuerò) Author colligit ex proximis Dauidis verbis,consectarium quoddam: nempe quòd nihil plane omissum sit à Patre, quod non sit Christo subiectum.Consectarium hoc infertur ex nota vniuersi generis qua creaturæ subiectæ Christo circumscriptæ sunt à Propheta: Nam si omnia subjecit, ergo nihil est non subiectum. Consectarium hoc continet summam testimonij adductì:nam ex eo hoc discimus, quàm late pateat Christi dominium, ad omnes nimirum creaturas, nulla plane excepta.
units.tr: 8 Moreover) The author draws from the immediately preceding words of David a certain corollary: namely, that nothing whatever has been left out by the Father that is not subject to Christ. This corollary is inferred from the note of the whole class of creatures, by which the creatures subject to Christ are circumscribed by the Prophet: for if he subjected all things, then nothing is not subject. This corollary contains the sum of the testimony adduced; for from it we learn how widely the dominion of Christ extends, namely to all creatures, none at all excepted.

units.la: At nunc nondum videmus ei omnia esse subiecta.
units.tr: But now we do not yet see all things subjected to him.

units.la: 9 Sed Iesum illum cernimus gloria & honore coronatum, qui paulisper fuit inferior Angelis factus, propter mortis perpessionem: Vt beneficio Dei pro omnibus mortem gustaret.
units.tr: 9 But we see Jesus, crowned with glory and honour, who was made a little lower than the angels because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for all.

units.la: 10 Decebat enim Ꝥ ipse propter quem sunt hæc omnia, & per quem sunt hæc omnia, multos filios in gloriam adducendo, principe salutis ipsorum per afflictiones consecraret.
units.tr: 10 For it became him, for whom are all things and by whom are all things, in bringing many sons to glory, to make the captain of their salvation perfect through afflictions.

units.la: 11 Nam & qui sanctificat & qui sanctificantur, ex uno sunt omnes : quam ob causam non erubescit ipsos vocare fratres.
units.tr: 11 For both he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all of one; for which cause he is not ashamed to call them brethren.

units.la: 12 Dicens, Annunciabo nomen tuum fratribus meis, in medio Ecclesia tibi hymnos canam.
units.tr: 12 Saying, I will declare thy name unto my brethren; in the midst of the church will I sing praise unto thee.

units.la: 13 Et rursum, Ego fretus ero ipso. Et iterum, Ecce ego & pueri quos mihi dedit Deus.
units.tr: 13 And again, I will put my trust in him. And again, Behold I and the children whom God hath given me.

units.la: 14 Quoniam igitur pueri participes sunt carnis & sanguinis, ipsos, ipse quoq; cõsimiliter particeps factus est eorundem, Ut per mortem abolearet eum qui mortis imperium habet, hoc est, Diabolum.
units.tr: 14 Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil.

units.la: 15 Et liberos redderet quotquot metu mortis, per omnem vitam obnoxij erant seruituti.
units.tr: 15 And deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage.

units.la: 16 Non enim videlicet Angelos assumpsit, sed semen Abrahæ assumpsit.
units.tr: 16 For verily he took not on him the nature of angels; but he took on him the seed of Abraham.

units.la: 17 Unde debuit per omnia fratribus similis fieri, Ut misericors esset & fidelis Pontifex in iis quæ apud Deum agenda forent, ad expiandum peccata populi.
units.tr: 17 Wherefore in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make reconciliation for the sins of the people.

units.la: 18 Nam ex eo quod perpessus fuit quum tentatus est, potest & iis qui tentantur succurrere.
units.tr: 18 For in that he himself hath suffered, being tempted, he is able also to succour them that are tempted.

units.la: Ut nunc nondum) Reliquo capite toto varia est digressio, & multiplex occupatio, prima est aduersus confestarium proximum, quod collectum lectum est ex verbis Dauidis: Atqui, dici potuit ab aliquo, nondum videmus illi subiecta esse omnia? Respondet Author, primum concessione, id quidem ita esse. Intelligit autem nondum Christo subiecta esse omnia, respectu membrorum Christi, quorum quidem respectu nondum plane subiecta sunt Christo, mors, peccatum, Diabolus.
units.tr: Now not yet) The rest of the chapter contains a varied digression and several topics. The first is directed against the immediately preceding conclusion, which was drawn from David's words: someone might say, "But can it be said that we do not yet see all things subjected to him?" The author answers, first by conceding that it is indeed so. He means that all things are not yet subjected to Christ with respect to the members of Christ, for with respect to them death, sin and the devil are not yet fully subjected to Christ.

units.la: 9 Sed Iesum illum) Respónsionis altera pars, per correctionem. At, inquit, ipse Iesus in se consideratus, & vt caput est membrorum suorum gloria, & honore coronatus est, hoc est, dominium obtinuit in omnes res, & in se iam plane vicit mortem, peccatum, Diabolum, sibique ea subiecit. Qui paulisper) Altera videtur occupatio esse, cuius occasio arrepta est ex testimonio Dauidis: quasi dicat quis, Atqui, teste Propheta, certè paulispèr fuit inferior Angelis factus. Illud quidem concedit, simulque causam subiectionis, & finem exponit, Causa subiectionis illius, qua ad tempus factus est inferior Angelis, fuit mortis perpessio: Nam subiectio, siue (vt sic dicam) inferioritas Christi, in mortis perpessione maximè posita est. Vt beneficio) Hic finis est, cur in morte factus sit inferior Angelis, est autem vt nos à morte liberaret: ergo finis fumusnos, nostráque salus. Simul causa cur pro nobis mortuus sit addita est, Dei beneficium, siue Dei gratia: nam hoc ex Dei gratia fuit, & in Dei beneficijs numerandum est imprimis, quod Christus nostram vicem in morte sua suppleuit, quum nobis alioqui necessario moriendum fuerit.
units.tr: 9 But Jesus) The second part of the answer, by way of correction. But, he says, Jesus himself, considered in himself and as the head, is crowned with glory and honour for his members; that is, he has obtained dominion over all things, and in himself has already fully conquered death, sin and the devil, and has subjected them to himself. Who was made a little lower) This seems to be another topic, whose occasion is taken from David's testimony, as if someone said: "But, according to the prophet, he was certainly made a little lower than the angels." He grants this, and at the same time sets out the cause and the purpose of that subjection. The cause of that subjection, by which for a time he was made lower than the angels, was the suffering of death; for his subjection, or (so to speak) his inferiority, lies chiefly in the suffering of death. That by the favour) This is the purpose of his being made lower than the angels in death: it was to free us from death. So the purpose is our good and our salvation. At the same time the cause of his dying for us is added: the favour or grace of God. For this came from God's grace, and is to be counted first among God's benefits, that Christ supplied our place in his death, whereas otherwise we would necessarily have had to die.

units.la: 10 Decebat enim) Ratio cur pro nobis omnibus Christus mortuus fit, per occupationem: Estque hæc occupatio tertia. Annon potuit Deus alia ratione feruare humanum genus, quàm morte Christi Filij fui? Respondet à decoro, fiue ex eo quod Deum facere decuit. Decebat Deum, vt in gloriam adduceret multos filios, Principem salutis ipsorum per afflictiones consecrare. Propter quem) Periphrasis quædam Dei est, quæ (vt videtur) rationem continet, cur Deum decebat sic facere: Est autem à jure & potestate Dei, quæ innuitur ex eo, quod propter ipsum, & per ipsum sunt hæc omnia, hoc est, quod ipse fit, & finis, & fons atque author horum omnium. Hinc sequitur, eum jure quodam suo potuisse de his omnibus statuere pro arbitratu suo.
units.tr: 10 For it became him) The reason why Christ died for all of us is given by way of a further topic, and this is the third. Could God not have preserved the human race by some other means than the death of his Son? He answers from fitness, that is, from what it became God to do. It became God to bring many sons to glory and to consecrate the captain of their salvation through afflictions. For whom) This is a certain periphrasis of God, which (as it seems) contains the reason why it became God to act thus. It rests on the right and power of God, which is hinted at in the words that all things are for him and through him: that is, he is the end, the source and the author of all these things. From this it follows that by a certain right of his own he could decide about all these things as he pleased.

units.la: 11 Nam (ꝯ qui) Quarta occupatio. At diceret quis: Qui potuit pati Filius Dei, vel qui potuit consecrari per afflictiones? Respondet, Et qui sanctificat, & qui sanctificantur ex vno sunt omnes, hoc est, ex vna & communi natura, & (vt sic dicam) materia patibili, fiueperpef fionibus obnoxia: Carnem & sanguinem vocat postea hoc capite versu 14. Est igitur hæc ratio per occupationem, cur Deus consecrauerit per afflictiones Principem salutis noftre
units.tr: 11 For both) The fourth topic. But someone might ask: how could the Son of God suffer, or how could he be consecrated through afflictions? He answers: both he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all of one, that is, of one and the same nature, and (so to speak) of passible matter, subject to sufferings. Later in this chapter, at verse 14, he calls this flesh and blood. This, then, is the reasoning, by way of digression, why God consecrated the captain of our salvation through afflictions.

units.la: Quam ob causam) Ex testimonio ipsius Christi, qui vocat eos qui sanctificantur fratrum nomine, confirmat, & Christum sanctificantem, & nos qui sanctificamur, ex una & communi natura ac materia esse.
units.tr: For which cause) From the testimony of Christ himself, who calls those who are sanctified by the name of brethren, he confirms that both Christ, who sanctifies, and we, who are sanctified, are of one nature and one matter.
