units.la: 12 Dicens; Testimonium Christi confirmat ex Scripturis, primum ex Psalmo 22.13.
units.tr: 12 Saying) He confirms Christ's testimony from the Scriptures, first from Psalm 22.13.

units.la: 13 Et rursum) Secunda Scriptura est Psal. 18. 3. vbi Christus loquitur ut homo & frater noster: in ipsum fiducia in Deum hominis est propria: & creaturae. Et iterum) Tertia Scriptura est Esaiae 8.18.
units.tr: 13 And again) The second Scripture is Psalm 18.3, where Christ speaks as a man and our brother: trust in God in him is proper to man and creature. And again) The third Scripture is Isaiah 8.18.

units.la: 14 Quoniam igitur. Ex proximis Esaiae verbis colligit quod instituit, nempe Christum participem esse carnis & sanguinis, siue Christum nobiscum unius esse naturae. Hoc autem syllogismo infert, institutum. Christus dicit: Ecce ego & pueri, h. e. associat le pueris: Atqui pueri participes sunt carnis & sanguinis, Ergo ipse Christus quoque similiter particeps factus est eorundem. Sententia propositionis est in testimonio Esaiae: Assumptio cum conclusione est in prima parte huius versus. Vt per mortem) Conclusionem illustrat ex fine suo: finis autem triplex ex his & sequentibus verbis elici potest: Primus finis est, ut moreretur; Sequitur hic finis ex proxima conclusione primum & proxime: Nam si ejusdem naturae nobiscum factus est, potuit mori potuit: atque ob id pfum factus est ejusdem naturae vt moreretur. Est igitur haec principalis conclusio quam instituit hoc loco ostendendam, nempe Christum per afflictiones & mortem consecratum. ) Secundus finis est, abolitio Diaboli, sequitur priorem: Nam ideo mortuus est ut aboleret Diabolum, Primum est Diaboli quaedam periphrasis,& circumscriptio: deinde, ne forte ex circumscriptione ignoraretur, est ipsius expressa nominatio: Nam nomina rerum saepe sunt notiora nobis ipsarum descriptionibus.
units.tr: 14 Forasmuch then) From the nearby words of Isaiah he draws what he has set out, namely that Christ is a partaker of flesh and blood, that is, that Christ is of one nature with us. He infers this by a syllogism. Christ says: "Behold I and the children", that is, he joins himself to the children. But the children are partakers of flesh and blood. Therefore Christ himself likewise became a partaker of the same. The content of the major premise is in Isaiah's testimony; the assumption, with the conclusion, is in the first part of this verse. That through death) He illustrates the conclusion from its purpose, and the purpose can be drawn threefold from these and the following words. The first purpose is that he should die. This follows first and most immediately from the nearest conclusion: for if he was made of the same nature as we are, he could die, and for this reason he was made of the same nature, in order to die. This, then, is the principal conclusion he has set out to show here: that Christ was consecrated through afflictions and death. The second purpose is the abolition of the devil, which follows from the first: for he died in order to destroy the devil. The first is a certain periphrasis and circumlocution of the devil; then, lest the circumlocution leave it unclear, there is his express naming. For the names of things are often better known to us than their descriptions.

units.la: Et liberos) Tertius finis, qui sequitur ex secundo: Liberatio nostri: qui autem liberantur, describuntur ex servitute cui obnoxij erat per omnem vitam, hoc est, ex servili sua conditione, quiam quidem ostendit, ex illo mortis metu, tanquam causa quadam sua: nam qui metuunt mortem, illi servi sunt, ac servili sunt conditione, non autem ingenui, neque filij, & metuere iram Domini servile est ac servi arguit.
units.tr: And deliver) The third purpose, which follows from the second, is our liberation. Those who are set free are described by the servitude to which they were subject all their life, that is, by their servile condition, which he shows from the fear of death as a cause of it. For those who fear death are slaves and in a servile condition, not free-born and not sons; and to fear the wrath of the Lord is servile and marks a slave.

units.la: Non enim videlicet) Liberationem de qua dixit proxime, & quae per Christum est, deinceps ostendit ex tribus fundamentis, quorum primum est natura humana, vel semen Abrahae assumptum a Christo: hoc fundamentum illustrat ex diversis, seu per remotionem natu & Angelicae, ut potest quae inepta sit ad hoc opus liberationis nostrae.
units.tr: For verily) He next shows the liberation of which he spoke just before, and which comes through Christ, from three foundations. The first is human nature, or the seed of Abraham assumed by Christ. He illustrates this foundation by contrast, or by removing the angelic nature, as unfit for this work of our liberation.

units.la: Unde debuit) Alterum fundamentum ex superiori collectum, similitudo nimirum Christi & nostri, nofti, in qualitatibus & perpessionibus, eiusdē & cómunis naturæ.Vt misericors,) Tertium fundamentum ex proximo. Ex qualitatibus & infirmitatibus communibus euasit Christus misericors & fidelis Pontifex apud Deum. Inijs quæ) Pontificatus Christi quædam declaratio subjeƈta est. Declaratio hæc primũ est à rebus subjeƈtis, in quibus cernitur Christi Pontificatus: Cernitur enim in ijs quæ apud Deum agenda sunt: Deinde declaratio est à Pontificatus fine, qui est ad expiandum peccata populi.
units.tr: Wherefore it behoved) The second foundation is drawn from what has gone before: the likeness of Christ and ours in qualities and sufferings, since we are of the same and common nature. That he might be merciful) The third foundation follows from the next. From common qualities and infirmities Christ became a merciful and faithful high priest before God. In things which) A certain declaration of Christ's priesthood is subjoined. This declaration is given first from the things in which Christ's priesthood is seen: it is seen in what is to be done before God. Then the declaration is from the end of the priesthood, which is to make atonement for the sins of the people.

units.la: 18 Nam ex eo) Ostendit ideò Christum sactum similem fratribus per omnia, vt esset misericors, hoc est, ostendit tertium fundamentum sequi ex secundo, ideò misericordem esse & fidelem Pontificem, quòd fratribus similis factus sit per omnia: ostendit, inquam, hoc ex certa quadam specie communium afflictionum, nempe tentationibus; ex eo, inquit, quòd perpessus est tentationes Diaboli Christus euasit misericors erga tentatos similiter: Hinc sequitur factum eum similem fratribus in omnibus afflictionibus, vt misericors esset erga quoquunque modo afflictos: illustratio est generis à certa quadam sui specie.
units.tr: 18 For from that which: he shows that Christ was therefore made like his brothers in all things, so that he might be merciful, that is, he shows that the third ground follows from the second: that he is a merciful and faithful High Priest because he was made like his brothers in all things. He shows this, I say, from a certain specific kind of common afflictions, namely temptations: "from that," he says, "because Christ suffered the temptations of the Devil, he became merciful toward those similarly tempted." From this it follows that he was made like his brothers in all afflictions, so that he would be merciful toward those afflicted in any way whatsoever: it is an illustration of the genus from a certain one of its species.

units.la: Argumentum Capitis tertij.
units.tr: Argument of the Third Chapter.

units.la: Hoc capite primum habemus argumentum exhortationis tertium, ad alteram vsque partem versus 6. quo loco habemus argumentum exhortationis quartum, ad versum vsque 4. hinc sequitur conclusio exhorta ionis, ad versum vsque 14. a versu 14. repetitio fit argumenti quarti, ad versum 17. a quo versu est transitio ad argumentum exhortationis quintum, ad finem vsque capitis,
units.tr: In this chapter we have first the third argument of exhortation, up to the second part of verse 6; there we have the fourth argument of exhortation, up to verse 4. From this follows the conclusion of the exhortation, up to verse 14. From verse 14 there is a repetition of the fourth argument, up to verse 17; from which verse there is a transition to the fifth argument of exhortation, to the end of the chapter.

units.la: CAPVT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: 1. Vnde fratres sancti vocationis coelestes participes, considerate Apostolum & Pontificem profefsionis nostrae Christum Iesum.
units.tr: 1. Wherefore, holy brethren, partakers of the heavenly calling, consider the Apostle and High Priest of our profession, Christ Jesus.

units.la: 2. Fidelem et qui ipsum constituit: vt & Moses fidelis fuit in tota domo ipsius.
units.tr: 2. Who was faithful to him that appointed him, as Moses also was faithful in all his house.

units.la: 3 Tanto namque ampliore gloria prae Mose hic dignus est habitus, quanto maiorem habet honorem is qui construxit domum quam domus ipsa.
units.tr: 3 For this man was counted worthy of more glory than Moses, by so much as he who hath builded the house hath more honour than the house.

units.la: 4 Omnis enim domus construitur ab aliquo: qui vero condidit omnia haec est Deus.
units.tr: 4 For every house is builded by some man; but he that built all things is God.

units.la: 5 Et Moses quidem fidelis fuit in tota domo ipsius, vt famulus, ad testificanda quae post erant dicenda.
units.tr: 5 And Moses verily was faithful in all his house, as a servant, for a testimony of those things which were to be spoken after;

units.la: 6 & Christus, vt filius, domui suae praesit.
units.tr: 6 But Christ as a son over his own house.

units.la: Vnde fratres) Nunc Apostolus reuersus ad institutum, primum affert argumentum exhortationis tertium: est autem argumentum hoc conjunctum, partim ex Prophetia seu Apostolatu, partim ex Sacerdotio Christi habemus Iesum Christum Apostolum & Pontificem professionis nostrae: ergo teneamus professionem sessionem, vt concludit postea cap. 4. verf. 14. Argumentum hoc tertium inferre videtur, ex ijs quae ab initio hujus epistolae dicta sunt, ac priorem quidem ejus partem ex his quae dicta sunt de Christi prophetia & ministerio, posteriorem ex his quae dicta sunt proxime, postrema nimirum parte capitis secundi, de Christi passione siue functione sacerdotali: passus enim est Christus, vt Secerdos & Pontifex. Sensus ergo hujus loci est: Quum Christum habeatis, & ministrum doctrinae quam prositemini, & Sacerdotem, suo sacrificio ac sanguine sancientem ratamque facientem eam ipsam doctrinam (Christus enim ratum facit suo sanguine Novum Testamentum) considerate eum diligenter, & tenete professionem veltram; in verbo enim considerandi comprehensa est conclusio exhortationis. Vocationis) Definitio quaedam est Sanctorum quos dixit: Nam ij sancti sunt, qui participes facti sunt vocationis coelestis, hoc est, qui vocati sunt ad coelestia. Nam quos vocauit eos justificauit, quos justificauit eos glorificauit. Rom. 8. 30.
units.tr: Wherefore, brethren) Now the Apostle, returning to his subject, first brings forward the third argument of exhortation. This argument is compound: partly from his prophetic office or apostleship, and partly from the priesthood of Christ. We have Jesus Christ, the Apostle and High Priest of our profession; therefore let us hold fast our profession, as he concludes later in chapter 4, verse 14. This third argument seems to be drawn from what has been said at the beginning of this epistle, the first part from what has been said of Christ's prophetic office and ministry, the latter from what has just been said, namely in the last part of chapter 2, about Christ's passion or priestly function. For Christ suffered as Priest and High Priest. The sense of this passage is therefore this: since you have Christ, both the minister of the doctrine you profess and the Priest who by his sacrifice and blood ratifies and confirms that very doctrine (for Christ confirms the New Testament by his blood), consider him diligently and hold fast your profession. For the conclusion of the exhortation is contained in the word "consider." Vocationis) This is a definition of the holy ones he has named. For those are holy who have been made partakers of the heavenly calling, that is, who have been called to heavenly things. For whom he called, them he also justified; whom he justified, them he also glorified. Rom. 8. 30.

units.la: 2 Fidelem ei) Amplificatio est argumenti proximi, a fidelitate (vt sic dicam) Christi in officio suo, tam Apostolico siue Propheti-co, quam sacerdotali. Qui ipsum constituit Periphrasis est Dei Patris, qui filium constituit Apostolum & Pontificem, hoc est, vocauit ad illa munera obeunda. De hac vocatione Filij, vide postea Cap. 5. versu 5. Fidelitas Christi respicit vocantem, vel eum qui ipsum vocauit, hoc est, Deum Patrem: vt fidelitas cujusque in officio eum respicit à quo vocatus est ad officium quodcunque sic obeundum: Nam illi reddenda ratio est præftiti officij. Vt & Moses) Fidelitatem Christi in officio suo illustrat similitudine Mosis, ac fidelitatis ipsius: Moses enim typus quidam fuit Christi, & magna fuit ipsius authoritas in Dei populo.
units.tr: 2 Faithful to him) This is an amplification of the preceding argument, drawn from the faithfulness (so to speak) of Christ in his office, both apostolic or prophetic and priestly. Who appointed him) This is a periphrasis for God the Father, who appointed the Son Apostle and High Priest, that is, called him to perform those offices. On this calling of the Son, see later chapter 5, verse 5. The faithfulness of Christ looks to the one who calls, or to him who called him, that is, God the Father, just as the faithfulness of anyone in an office looks to the one by whom he was called to that office, for he must give an account of the office so performed to him. As Moses also) He illustrates the faithfulness of Christ in his office by the likeness of Moses and of Moses' faithfulness, for Moses was in some sense a type of Christ, and his authority among the people of God was great.

units.la: 3 Tanto namque Occupatio est, ergo eodem loco habes Christum quò Moses fuit, & Mosi duntaxat parem facis? Respondet Apostolus, Mose esse digniorem Christum, ac refponfionem hanc confirmat: Particula enim ista nam que, præfupponit primùm objectionem, deinde refponfionem, quasi dicat objicienti paritatem illam Christi & Mosis: Christus præftantior est Mose tanto, quanto major est is qui construxit domum, quàm domus ipsa: est itaque hæc ratio prima cur Christus ampliore gloria præ Mose dignus fit habitus, à conditione vtriusque, & Christi, & Mosis. Christus est conftruator domus, & ipse opifex, Moses est domus, vel pars domus constructæ à Christo: Has conditiones comparat in impari: Qui conditione sua impares sunt, profecto necesse est eos pariter impares esse in gloria: imparibus enim debetur impar gloria. Si luber, bet, redige rationem in hanc formam. Constructor domus & domus ipsa sunt impares honore & gloria, siue majorem habet honorem constructor domus, quàm domus ipsa: At Christus est qui construxit domum: Moses est domus ipsa, & Christi quasi fabrica: Ergo Christus ampliore gloria præ Mose dignus est habitus. Hujus syllogismi propositio & conclusio, composita sunt in enunciato quod vim habet connexi, assumptio vt manifesta subticetur.
units.tr: 3 For this man) This is an occupatio, an anticipated objection. Do you, then, place Christ in the same position as Moses, and make him merely equal to Moses? The Apostle answers that Christ is worthier than Moses, and he confirms this answer. The particle "for" (namque) presupposes first the objection and then the answer, as if he said to the objector that there is that equality between Christ and Moses: Christ is more excellent than Moses by as much as he who built the house is greater than the house itself. This is therefore the first reason why Christ is counted worthy of greater glory than Moses, drawn from the condition of both, of Christ and of Moses. Christ is the builder of the house and himself the craftsman; Moses is the house, or a part of the house built by Christ. He compares these conditions as unequal. Those who are unequal in their condition must certainly be unequal in glory too, for unequal glory is due to unequal persons. If you wish, reduce the reasoning to this form: the builder of a house and the house itself are unequal in honour and glory, or the builder of the house has more honour than the house itself. But Christ is he who built the house; Moses is the house itself, and as it were the workmanship of Christ. Therefore Christ has been counted worthy of greater glory than Moses. The proposition and conclusion of this syllogism are combined in a statement which has the force of a conditional, and the assumption is left out as being obvious.

units.la: 4 Omnis enim domus) Priorem assumptionis partem, nempe eam quæ est de Christo, confirmat ab ipso genere. Omnis domus construitur ab aliquo: At Ecclesia est domus; Ergo construitur ab aliquo. Ab alio autem quàmà Deo construi non potest: hoc enim est quod dicit (Porrò qui condidit omnia hæc Deus est) Ergo Deus est ejus conditor: At Christus est Deus, vt vidimus primo capite, Ergo Christus est ejus conditor.
units.tr: 4 For every house) He confirms the first part of the assumption, namely the part concerning Christ, from the general principle itself. Every house is built by someone. But the Church is a house. Therefore it is built by someone. It cannot, however, be built by anyone other than God, for this is what he says: "But he who built all things is God." Therefore God is its builder. But Christ is God, as we saw in the first chapter. Therefore Christ is its builder.

units.la: 5 Et Moses) Altera ratio intelleƈtæ responsionis, etiam ab impari conditione Mosis & Christi. Moses in domo Dei fuit fidelis quidem, sed vt famulus. At Christus vt filius domui suæ præest. Hinc sequitur ampliore gloria præ Mose Christum dignum esse habitum; siue Christum & Mosen impares esse in gloria. Domo ipsius) hoc est, Dei, & quæ ad Deum speƈtat proprie, non ad Mosen: famulus enim
units.tr: 5 And Moses) This is a second reason for the answer given, also drawn from the unequal condition of Moses and Christ. Moses was indeed faithful in the house of God, but as a servant. But Christ rules over his own house as a son. From this it follows that Christ has been counted worthy of greater glory than Moses, or that Christ and Moses are unequal in glory. In his house) that is, of God, and what properly belongs to God, not to Moses, for a servant is not the lord of the household.

units.la: non est Dominus familiæ : Moses autem in Ecclesia tantum famulus fuit: In Ecclesia enim nullum est vllius dominium, nisi solius Dei & Christi, sed duntaxat, famulitium. Ad testificanda) Vsus famulitij Moßs in domo Dei, Constitutus enim fuit famulus ad testificandum, & id quidem obscurè, quæ postea dicenda erant aperte, de Christo ipsiusq; dominio.
units.tr: Moses, however, was only a servant in the Church, for in the Church no one has lordship except God alone and Christ, but only servitude. For a testimony) This is the use of Moses' servanthood in the house of God. For he was appointed a servant to bear witness, and indeed obscurely, to those things which were afterwards to be declared openly, concerning Christ and his lordship.

units.la: 6 At Christus) Apodosis comparationis minorum : Christus domui suæ præest vt filius: filius ex aduerso respondet famulo : filij enim & famuli longè alia atque alia conditio est in familia.Suæ)hoc quod dicit suæ, αὐτῷ, respondet illi quod dictum est de Mose ipsius, αὐτῷ: Nam Christus vt filius & hæres præest domui, non quidem alienæ, sed suæ.
units.tr: 6 But Christ) This is the apodosis of the comparison of the lesser: Christ rules over his own house as a son. The son in contrast answers to the servant, for the condition of a son and of a servant in a household is very different. His own) What he says, "his own" (αὐτῷ), answers to what was said of Moses, "his" (αὐτοῦ), for Christ rules the house as son and heir, not indeed of another's house, but of his own.

units.la: Cuius domus sumus nos, si fiduciam & spem illam de qua gloriamur, ad finem usque firmam tenuerimus.
units.tr: Whose house are we, if we hold fast the confidence and the rejoicing of the hope firm unto the end.

units.la: Cuius domus ) Vocabuli domus interpretatio quædam est, & ad nos applicatio quasi dicat: domum Filij intelligo nos omnes credentes. Atque hic incipit argumentum exhortationis quartum, in hanc formam, Si fiduciam & spem illam de qua gloriamur, ad finem vsque tenuerimus, hoc est, si tenuerimus professionem, domus Filij sumus. Ergo teneamus prosessionem. Argumentum est à beata nostra conditione: beatitas enim nostra in eo posita est, vt simus domus Filij. Postea versu 14. eandem dem conditionem exprimit verbo μετοχῆς hoc est, participationis Christi, & communionis cum Christo: μετοχοί, inquit, γεγόνα μεν τῦ χρι-στῦ. Si fiduciam] παῤῥησίαν græcè dicitur, hac voce significatur propriè audacia, qua fit vt compareamus coram Tribunali Dei ludicis Vide 1. Ioannis 3. 21. Hoc quod sequitur in textu καυχήμα gloriatio, effectum est παῤῥησίας & spei: Nam gloriamur sub spe gloriæ Dei. Rom. 5. ve. f.2. Porrò his verbis fiduciæ & gloriationis significatur doctrina illa qua hæc ministrantur: & in his tanquam effectis intelliguntur cusæ fusæ, fides & spes: παῤῥησία enim est fidei, καύχημα vero spei.
units.tr: Whose house) This is a kind of interpretation of the word "house," and an application to ourselves, as if he said: by the house of the Son I mean all of us who believe. And here begins the fourth argument of exhortation, in this form: If we hold fast the confidence and the rejoicing of hope to the end, that is, if we hold fast our profession, we are the house of the Son. Therefore let us hold fast our profession. The argument is drawn from our blessed condition, for our blessedness consists in this, that we are the house of the Son. Later, in verse 14, he expresses the same condition by the word "partakers" (μέτοχοι), that is, of the participation in Christ and communion with Christ: "We have become partakers of Christ" (μέτοχοι γεγόναμεν τοῦ Χριστοῦ). "The confidence" is in Greek παῤῥησίαν [parrhēsian], a word which properly signifies boldness, by which we come to stand before the judgment seat of God the Judge. See 1 John 3. 21. What follows in the text, καύχημα [kauchēma], "rejoicing," is the effect of confidence and hope, for we rejoice in the hope of the glory of God. Rom. 5. 2. Moreover, by these words of confidence and rejoicing is signified that doctrine by which these things are ministered, and in these as effects are understood the causes, faith and hope, for παῤῥησία [parrhēsia] belongs to faith, and καύχημα [kauchēma] to hope.

units.la: 7 Quapropter sicut dicit Spiritus ille sanctus, Hodie si vocem eius audieritis.
units.tr: 7 Wherefore, as the Holy Spirit says, Today if you will hear his voice,

units.la: 8 Ne obdurate corda vestra, sicut in exacerbatione, in die tentationis illius in deserto.
units.tr: 8 Harden not your hearts, as in the provocation, in the day of temptation in the wilderness.

units.la: 9 Vbi tentauerunt me patres vestri, probauerunt me, & viderunt opera mea quadraginta annis.
units.tr: 9 When your fathers tempted me, proved me, and saw my works for forty years.

units.la: 10 Quapropter infensus fui nationi istì: & dixi, semper errant corde, neque cognouerunt vias meas.
units.tr: 10 Wherefore I was grieved with that generation, and said, They always err in heart, and have not known my ways.

units.la: 11 Itaque iurauì in ira mea, Si introibunt in requiem meam.
units.tr: 11 So I swore in my wrath, If they shall enter into my rest.

units.la: 12 Videte fratres, ne quando sit in illo vestrum cor malum & infidele deficiendo a Deo viuo.
units.tr: 12 Take heed, brethren, lest there be in any of you an evil and unbelieving heart, in falling away from the living God.

units.la: 13 Sed exhortamini alij alios quotidie, quoad appellatur dies hodiernus, ne quis ex vobis induretur tur fraude peccati.
units.tr: 13 But exhort one another daily, while it is called Today, lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.

units.la: Quapropter) Conclusio est exhortationis principalis, amplificata simili comparatione exhortationis illius, qua Spiritus sanctus olim per Dauidem populum Israeliticum hortatus est. Psal. 95. 7. Protasis praecedit quinque versibus. Apodosis fiue redditio sequitur duobus versibus sequentibus. Sententia comparatę conclusionis haec est, quasi dicat, quamobrem quemadmodum Spiritus sanctus per Dauidem hortatus est aliquando populum Israeliticum, ne indurararet cor suum, ita ego admoneo, nequando fit in vllo vestrum cor malum & infidele. Hodie) Propositio hortationis Spiritus sancti, ad populum Israeliticum.
units.tr: Wherefore) This is the conclusion of the principal exhortation, enlarged by a comparison with that exhortation by which the Holy Spirit once exhorted the Israelite people through David (Ps. 95. 7). The protasis precedes, in five verses; the apodosis, or response, follows in the two verses after. The sense of the comparison and the conclusion is this: as if he said, therefore, just as the Holy Spirit once exhorted the Israelite people through David not to harden their heart, so I admonish that there be not in any of you an evil and unbelieving heart. Today) the proposition of the Holy Spirit's exhortation to the Israelite people.

units.la: 8 Sicut in) Declaratio propositionis, per comparationem indurationis ac rebellionis, quae jam olim fuit populi.
units.tr: 8 As in) the explanation of the proposition, by way of comparison with the hardening and rebellion which were already of old the people's.

units.la: 9 Vbi tentauerunt) Tentationum ac rebellionum populi in deserto declaratio & enarratio. Et viderunt) Exaggeratio facti ipsorum, ex eo quod tot annos Dei opera mirifica in deserto viderint.
units.tr: 9 Where your fathers tempted) an explanation and narration of the temptations and rebellions of the people in the wilderness. And saw) an exaggeration of their deed, from the fact that they saw God's wonderful works in the wilderness for so many years.

units.la: 10 Quapropter) Narrat iram Dei, propter tentationem populi. Et dixi) Irae subiungit comminationem ex ira profectam: in qua primum habemus causam judicij, errorem populi & ignorantiam: deinde judicium ipsum: Iudicium est: Non introibunt in requiem meam: confirmatum est adhibito iure iurando.
units.tr: 10 Wherefore) He recounts God's wrath on account of the people's temptation. And I said) To the wrath he adds a threat arising from that wrath, in which we have first the cause of the judgment, the people's error and ignorance; then the judgment itself: the judgment is, They shall not enter my rest, confirmed by the addition of an oath.

units.la: 12 Videte) Apodosis siue redditio coparationis,quasi dicat:sicut olim dixit Spiritus sanctus &c.ita ego nunc dico vobis, videte fratres nequando, &c. Dehortatur autem ab apostasia, hortatur vero ad perseuerantiam. Cor malum) Quid sit cor malum sequens verbum exponit, est enim cor infidele: infidelitas autem cordis defectione à Deo ostenditur: Nam infidelis est,qui deficit à Deo viuo.
units.tr: 12 Take heed) The apodosis, or response, of the comparison, as if he said: just as the Holy Spirit once spoke, etc., so now I say to you, brethren, take heed lest, etc. He dissuades from apostasy, and urges perseverance. An evil heart) The following word explains what an evil heart is: it is an unbelieving heart. Unbelief of the heart, moreover, is shown by falling away from God; for he is unbelieving who falls away from the living God.

units.la: 14 Christi enim participes facti sumus, si modo principium illud quo subsistentamur, firmum tenuerimus ad finem usque:
units.tr: 14 For we have become partakers of Christ, if indeed we hold firm the beginning of our confidence to the end,

units.la: 15 Interim dum dicitur, Hodie si vocem eius audieritis, ne obdurate corda vestra, vt in exacerbatione.
units.tr: 15 While it is said, Today if you will hear his voice, harden not your hearts, as in the provocation.

units.la: 16 Nam quidam quum audissent, exacerbarunt Dominum : non omnes tamen qui exierant ex Ægypto per Mosen.
units.tr: 16 For some, when they had heard, provoked him; yet not all who had come out of Egypt through Moses.

units.la: Christi enim) Repetitur argumentum exhortationis quartum post conclusionem:Nam participatio Christi, vel Christi participes fieri nihil est aliud reipsa, quàm esse eius domus qui enim domus est Christi, Christus in ipso inhabitat. In quo autem Christus habitat, is coniunctus est cum Christo: quare argumentum est à κοινωνία, siue communione cum Christo.Principium)Quid intelligat nomine principij substantiae,ipse sequenti versu edocet: est autem obedientia fidei, in qua habemus subsistentiam quasi nostram. Porrò sensus est: Si fir-
units.tr: For we have become partakers) The argument of exhortation is repeated a fourth time after the conclusion. For participation in Christ, or becoming partakers of Christ, is in fact nothing other than being his house; for he who is the house of Christ has Christ dwelling in him. And he in whom Christ dwells is joined with Christ; so the argument is drawn from communion [κοινωνία], that is, fellowship with Christ. Beginning) What he means by the word beginning, that is, substance, he himself teaches in the following verse: it is the obedience of faith, in which we have our substance, as it were, as our own. Moreover, the sense is: if we hold firm

units.la: {y} Principium] ... mam 'enuemus professione nostram Christi fiidi sumus participes.
units.tr: {y} Beginning] ... [the rest of this line is corrupt in the scan] ... our confession of hope, we shall be partakers of Christ.

units.la: 15 Intelligimus autem dictum) hoc est, quasi dicat, principium intelligo illud, quod olim dixit Spiritus sanctus per Dauidem, hodie si vocem &c.
units.tr: 15 But we understand the saying) that is, as if he said: by the beginning I understand that which the Holy Spirit once said through David, Today if you will hear his voice, etc.

units.la: 16 Nam quidam) Declaratio est exacerbationis illius de qua proxime dixit, per occupationem: Objici enim potuit, An omnes exacerbauerunt Dominum? Responderet à quibusdam hoc factum, non ab omnibus qui exierant ex Ægypto.
units.tr: 16 For some) This is an explanation of the provocation of which he spoke just before, anticipated: for it could be objected, Did all provoke the Lord? He answers that this was done by some, not by all who had come out of Egypt.

units.la: 17 Quibus autem infestus fuit quadraginta annis? nonne iis qui peccauerant, quorum corpora conciderunt in deserto?
units.tr: 17 But with whom was he grieved for forty years? Was it not with those who had sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness?

units.la: 18 Quibus autem iurauit non ingressuros in requiem suam nisi iis qui non obedierant.
units.tr: 18 And to whom did he swear that they should not enter into his rest, but to those who did not obey?

units.la: 19 Et videmus non potuisse ingredi propter incredulitatem.
units.tr: 19 And we see that they could not enter because of unbelief.

units.la: Quibus autem) Sternit sibi viam ad argumentum exhortationis quintum: sumptum autem est (vt videbimus) ex eo, quod destituentur illa requie. Si non retineatis professionem, metuendum est ne frustremini illa requie, de qua dictum est à Dauide: Ergo retinete professionem. Illustratum est antecedens hoc tribus his postremis versibus capitis tertij. Est autem illustratio à simili exemplo infidelium Israelitarum, quod tractatur διαλογισμῷ interrogatione & responsione. Sensus huius versus est si ornatum rhetoricum rejiciamus) Ira infinsus fuit Deus tot annis ijs qui peccauerant,ac proinde eorum corpora in deserto ceciderunt.
units.tr: But to whom) He prepares the way for the fifth argument of exhortation, taken (as we shall see) from the fact that they were deprived of that rest. If we do not hold fast our confession, we must fear lest we be frustrated of that rest of which David spoke; therefore hold fast your confession. The preceding point is illustrated by these three final verses of chapter three, and the illustration is drawn from the similar example of the unbelieving Israelites, treated by way of a dialogue [διαλογισμῷ], by question and answer. The sense of this verse, if we set aside the rhetorical ornament, is: God was angry for so many years with those who had sinned, and therefore their bodies fell in the wilderness.

units.la: 18 Quibus autem) Sensus est, Iurauit non ingressuros in requiem suam eos Israelitarum qui non obedierant. Summa vtriusque versus huc redit. Illi Israelitarum qui à Deo defecerunt non ingressi sunt in requiem ipsius. Vnde sequitur, & nos, fi defecerimus à fide & prosessione nostra, non ingressuros esse in requie. Notandum duas has interrogationes, priorem quae est versu 17. posteriorem quae est versu 18. respondere duobus verbis quorum mentio fit in testimonio illo Dauidis supra citato, nempe Iuraui in ira mea.
units.tr: 18 But to whom) The sense is: he swore that the Israelites who had not obeyed should not enter into his rest. The sum of both verses comes to this: those of the Israelites who fell away from God did not enter into his rest. Whence it follows: if we too fall away from faith and our confession, we shall not enter into rest. It should be noted that these two questions, the former in verse 17 and the latter in verse 18, answer to two words which are mentioned in that testimony of David cited above, namely I swore in my wrath.

units.la: 19 Et videmus) Confirmatio illorum quae dixit duobus versibus proximè praecedentibus, ab ipsa experientia & euentu rei: quasi dicat, Re ipsa videmus eorum quae dicta sunt euentum & experientiam: videmus, inquam, non potuisse ingredi in requiem Israelitas, propter incredulitatem, iuxta illud Dei iusiurandum, quod iurauit in ira sua.
units.tr: 19 And we see) A confirmation of what he said in the two verses immediately preceding, from experience itself and the outcome of the matter: as if he said, we see in fact the outcome and experience of what has been said; we see, I say, that the Israelites could not enter into rest because of unbelief, according to that oath of God which he swore in his wrath.

units.la: Argumentum Capitis quarti.
units.tr: Argument of the Fourth Chapter.

units.la: Hoc capite habemus argumentum exhortationis quintum, ad postremam partem versus tertij, Inde diGREssio est, ad versum 11. Versu 11. redit ad principalem conclusionem, cumque repetit argumentum quintum, ipsumque illustrat ac confirmat, ad versum 14. quo loco ad conclusionem principalem redit, ipsamque repetit, simulque argumentum conclusionis tertium, à Christi pontificatu, ad versum vltimum. Verfa denique vltimo repetita est eadem conclusio, & exhortatio, eíque adjeƈtum argumentum exhortationis sextum.
units.tr: In this chapter we have the fifth argument of exhortation, from the last part of verse 3, the digression running from there to verse 11. At verse 11 he returns to the principal conclusion, and repeats the fifth argument, illustrating and confirming it, down to verse 14; at that point he returns to the principal conclusion and repeats it, together with the third argument of the conclusion, drawn from Christ's priesthood, down to the last verse. Finally, in the last verse the same conclusion and exhortation are repeated, and the sixth argument of exhortation is added to them.

units.la: CAPVT IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER 4.

units.la: 1 Metuamus igitur nequando derelicta promissione introeundi in requiem eius, videatur aliquis ex vobis fuisse frustratus.
units.tr: 1 Let us fear, therefore, lest, the promise of entering into his rest being left, any of you should seem to have been frustrated.

units.la: 2 Etenim nobis Euangelizatum est, sicut & illis, at non profuit illis auditus sermo, vt qui fide contemperatus non fuerit ipsis qui audierant.
units.tr: 2 For we have had the gospel preached to us, as well as to them; but the word they heard did not profit them, because it was not mixed with faith in those who heard it.

units.la: 3 Itroimus enim in requiem nos qui credidimus, sicut dixit, itaque iuraui in ira mea, si ingressuri sunt in requiem meam:
units.tr: 3 For we who have believed enter into rest, as he said: "As I swore in my wrath, if they shall enter into my rest."

units.la: Metuamus igitur) Ex simili illo exemplo judiciorum Dei in Israelitas, quod tractatum est tribus versibus postremis capitis tertij, concludit similiter nos, si non retinuerimus prosessionem, non ingressuros in requiem Domini. Ex quo sequitur instituta exhortatio. Ergo retinete professionem. Obseruatum est supra istud esse argumentum exhortationis quintum, a priuatione illius cœlestis requietis, de qua Dauid in Psalmo suo locutus est. Derelicta) His verbis infidelitatem circumscribit. Nam infidelitas siue Apostasia & defeƈtio, cernitur in derelictione promissionis Dei de requie æterna.Fuisse Frustratus)Nempe promissa illa requie. Qui enim non primum credit in promissionem beneficij, profeƈto is non consequitur beneficium, primum ergo credendum promissioni, ut deinde re promissa fruamur.
units.tr: Let us fear, therefore) From that similar example of God's judgments on the Israelites, which was treated in the last three verses of chapter 3, he similarly concludes that we, if we do not hold fast our profession, shall not enter into the Lord's rest. From this follows the exhortation set forth: therefore hold fast your profession. It has been observed above that this is the fifth argument of exhortation, drawn from the deprivation of that heavenly rest of which David spoke in his psalm. Left) By these words he circumscribes unbelief. For unbelief, or apostasy and defection, is seen in the abandoning of God's promise of eternal rest. Frustrated) Namely, of that promised rest. For whoever does not first believe the promise of a benefit certainly does not obtain the benefit. We must therefore first believe the promise, so that afterwards we may enjoy the thing promised.

units.la: Etenim nobis) Probat consecutionem praecedentem, quae fuit à simili exemplo judicij Dei in Israelitas contumaces, ad similem conditionem futuram eorum qui in regno Christi sunt, si similiter atque illi defecerint ab eo. Est autem probatio à simili beneficij Evangelij communicatione, ex qua colligitur necessario similitudo in judiciis, in hanc formam: Nobis Evangelizatum est sicut & illis: atqui non profuit illis auditus sermo Evangelij, ut qui increduli fuerint, hoc est, non sunt ingressi in requiem illam, neque consecuti sunt beneficium in verbo promissum: Ergo & nos similiter, si increduli fuerimus, nullum fructum ex audito verbo percipiemus.
units.tr: For we have had) He proves the preceding inference, which rested on a similar example of God's judgment against the stubborn Israelites, to the similar future condition of those who are in the kingdom of Christ, if they likewise fall away from him as those did. The proof is from the similarity of the communication of the benefit of the gospel, from which similarity in judgments is necessarily inferred, in this form: We have had the gospel preached just as they did; but the word of the gospel did not profit them, since they were unbelieving, that is, they did not enter that rest and did not obtain the benefit promised in the word. Therefore we too, likewise, if we are unbelieving, shall receive no fruit from the word we hear.

units.la: At non profuit) Propositio antecessit in proximis verbis, haec est assumptio syllogismi. Ut qui) Ratio assumptionis ab incredulitate Israelitarum. Auditus sermo tum permisceri fidei dicitur, cum fide apprehenditur. Metaphora est à potiore, quae proprie admisceri solet. Conclusio syllogismi non est expressa. Caeterum haec est syllogismi forma, si libet eum breviis conficere: Nobis est Evangelizatum similiter atque illis. Ergo quemadmodum illi non credentes, non sunt ingressi requiem promissam, ita nos quoque deficientes à fide, non introibimus in requiem promissam. At Author subsumpsit priorem compa-
units.tr: But it did not profit) The major premise went before in the preceding words; this is the minor premise of the syllogism. Since they) The reason for the minor premise is taken from the unbelief of the Israelites. The heard word is said to be mixed with faith when it is apprehended by faith. This is a metaphor drawn from the more worthy thing, which is properly what is usually mixed. The conclusion of the syllogism is not expressed. Otherwise, if one wishes to make the syllogism briefer, it takes this form: We have had the gospel preached in the same way as they did. Therefore, just as they, not believing, did not enter the promised rest, so we also, if we fall away from faith, will not enter the promised rest. But the author has assumed the first part of the comparison so that he might conclude the latter from it, since both parts of the conclusion were to be concluded together, linked; for it is a proof of the consequence of a compound proposition.

units.la: [illegible, ~3 letters] rationis partem, vt posteriorem ex ea concluderet, cùm vtraque pars conclusionis simul nexa concludenda fuerit: est enim probatio sequelæ propositionis compositæ.
units.tr: [illegible, about three letters] part of the comparison, so that he might conclude the latter from it, since both parts of the conclusion were to be concluded together, linked; for it is a proof of the consequence of a compound proposition.

units.la: Introimus enim) Probat quod dixit proximè, nihil profuisse illis auditum sermonem, quod non crediderint, hoc est, non ingressos fuisse in requiem propter incredulitatem: probat, inquam, ex eo quod ij demum qui crediderunt, introeunt in requiem, hoc modo. Nos (inquit) qui credimus, & non alij introimus in requiem: Ergo illi qui non crediderunt, non poterant introire in requiem. Contrariorum enim contraria sunt consequentia. Est argumentum à pari consecutione in contrarijs. Sicut dixit) Requiem hanc de qua loquitur exponit & declarat testimonio illo Dauidis, superiore capite citato, verf. 11. Significat enim se non aliam requiem proximis verbis intelligere, quàm illam cuius mentio facta est in illo Dauidis testimonio, quo dictum est, Itaque juraui in ira mea, &c. Hoc igitur loco digressio est ad ostendendum Sabbatismum populo Dei proprium.
units.tr: For we who believe) He proves what he said just before, that the word heard profited them nothing because they did not believe, that is, they did not enter into rest on account of unbelief. He proves this, I say, from the fact that only those who believed enter into rest, in this way: We (he says) who believe, and not others, enter into rest. Therefore those who did not believe could not enter into rest. For contraries have contrary consequences. It is an argument from a like consequence in contraries. As he said) He explains and declares the rest of which he speaks by that testimony of David cited in the previous chapter, verse 11. For he means that by the words that follow he understands no other rest than the one mentioned in that testimony of David, where it was said: "So I swore in my wrath," and so on. Therefore this place is a digression, to show the sabbatism proper to the people of God.

units.la: —Licet operibus à iactis fundamentis mundi perfectis.
units.tr: —Although the works were finished from the foundation of the world.

units.la: Ita enim dixit quodam in loco de septimo die, Et requieuit Deus die septimo ab omnibus operibus suis.
units.tr: For he has spoken thus somewhere of the seventh day: "And God rested on the seventh day from all his works."

units.la: Et hic rursum, Si introibunt in requiem meam 6 Quia igitur reliquum est Ʋt alij introeant in eam, & quibus prius annunciatum fuit non introierunt propter incredulitatem.
units.tr: And here again: "If they shall enter into my rest." 6 Since therefore it remains that others should enter into it, and those to whom it was first announced did not enter because of unbelief.

units.la: 7 Rursum quendam præsinit diem, Hodie apud Davidem dicens, tanto post tempore (prout dictum est) Hodie si Ʋocem eius audieritis, ne obdurate corda Ʋestra.
units.tr: 7 Again he fixes a certain day, saying through David, after so long a time (as has been said): "Today, if you hear his voice, harden not your hearts."

units.la: 8 Nam si eos Iesus in requie collocasset, nequaquam de alio posthac die loquutus suisset.
units.tr: 8 For if Jesus had settled them in rest, he would never afterwards have spoken of another day.

units.la: 9 Itaque reliquus est aliquis sabbatismus populo Dei.
units.tr: 9 Therefore there remains a certain sabbatism for the people of God.

units.la: 10 Nam qui ingressus est in requiem ipsius, requieuit & ipse ab operibus suis, quemadmodum à suis Deus.
units.tr: 10 For he who has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works, as God did from his.

units.la: Licet operibus) Hoc adjectum est per occupationem, dici enim potuit, Cum requies illa diei Sabbathini fuerit jam inde à condito mundo, populusque eo die perpetuò requiescere consueuerit: cur dictum est à Domino per Danidem, itaque juraui, &c. hoc est, cur jurauit Dominus, exclusurum se populum à requie, quasi non antea vnquam requieuerit? Huic objectioni occurrit Author, quasi dicat: Iurauit Dominus non ingressurum cotumacem populū in requiem suam, licet etiam in Sabbatho requieuit. His verbis habemus periphrāsin diei sabbathini, ex ipsius caussa. Caussa autem est à perfectione operū Dei in initio, quum creauit omnia sex diebus, septimo autē die requiescit ab operib. suis. Ergo sensus est: Licet opera Dei fuerint perfecta ab initio, ac proinde fuit requies Sabbathi: Nam perfectio operum Dei importat requiem Sabbathi.
units.tr: Although from his works) This is added by way of anticipation. For it could be said: since that rest of the sabbath day has existed from the founding of the world, and the people have customarily rested on that day perpetually, why did the Lord say through David, "So I swore," and so on; that is, why did the Lord swear that he would exclude the people from rest, as if they had never rested before? The author meets this objection, as if he were saying: the Lord swore that he would not admit the stubborn people into his rest, although he too rested on the Sabbath. In these words we have a periphrasis of the sabbath day, drawn from its cause. The cause, however, is the perfection of God's works at the beginning, when he created all things in six days and rested from his works on the seventh day. Therefore the sense is: although God's works were perfect from the beginning, and so there was the rest of the Sabbath; for the perfection of God's works implies the rest of the Sabbath.

units.la: 4 Ita enim dixit) Probat hanc requiem Sabbathi ab illa superiori diuersam esse, ex diuersis de hac & illa testimonijs. Nam de hac requie diei Sabbathini, hoc est testimonium quod habetur. Gen. 2.2. De requie autem illa superiori diuersum quoddam est testimonium quod habetur. Psal. 95. 11. Nempe si introibunt, &c. Ex his diuersis testimonijs, innuit diuersam esse requiem diei Sabbathini, ab ea cuius meminit Dauid in Psalmo suo.
units.tr: 4 So he said) He proves that this sabbath rest is different from that earlier rest, from the different testimonies concerning each. For concerning this sabbath rest of the sabbath day there is the testimony found at Gen. 2.2. But concerning that earlier rest there is a different testimony, found at Ps. 95.11, namely "If they shall enter," and so on. From these different testimonies he indicates that the sabbath rest is different from the rest of which David spoke in his psalm.

units.la: 6 Quia igitur) Ex proxime adducto testimonio colligit tanquam consectarium quoddam, oportuisse praefiniri nouum quendam diem quasi Sabbathi & requietis, diuersum ab illo die siue tempore, quo oblata est requies veteri illi ac rebelli populo: hunc vocat hodiernum diem. Colligit autem consectarium hoc in hunc modum, quasi dicat, Ex hoc testimonio Dauidis sequitur populum illum veterem & rebellem non ingressum esse in requiem Domini cuius meminit Dauid, nam jurejurando sunt exclusi. Hinc rursus sequitur nouum quendam diem praefiniendum fuisse. Necessitas hujus sequelae haec est, Oportuit certe aliquos introire in requiem illam promissam. Unde sequitur, quum illi rebelles non introierint, oportuisse nouum diem requietis aliis ingressu-ris
units.tr: 6 Since therefore) From the testimony just adduced he draws, as a kind of corollary, that a new day had to be fixed beforehand, a kind of Sabbath and rest, different from that day or time in which rest was offered to that old and rebellious people. This he calls "today." He draws this corollary in the following way, as if he were saying: from this testimony of David it follows that that old and rebellious people did not enter into the Lord's rest of which David spoke, for they were excluded by oath. Hence again it follows that a new day had to be fixed beforehand. The necessity of this sequence is this: some certainly had to enter that promised rest. Whence it follows that, since those rebels did not enter, a new day of rest had to be fixed for those who were to enter

units.la: Note: the marginal and reference text is not reliably legible in this scan. ris præfiniri.Hodie si vocem) Diem hunc, ex verbis Domini apud Dauidem, hodie vel hodiernum diem nominat. Hodierni diei nomine intelligit totum illud tempus quantucunque, quo offertur gratia in Christo Iesu. Tempus hoc gratiæ metimur primo Christi aduentu, tanquam termino a quo, & secundo Christi aduentu, tanquam termino ad quem Prout dictum) Repetit testimonium hoc Dauidis, in quo nominatur tempus hoc hodierni diei.
units.tr: ris to be fixed beforehand. Today, if you hear his voice) He names this day, from the words of the Lord in David, "today" or "the present day." By the name of today he understands the whole period, however long, during which grace is offered in Christ Jesus. We measure this time of grace from the first coming of Christ, as its starting point, to the second coming of Christ, as its end point. As it was said) He repeats this testimony of David, in which this time of "today" is named.

units.la: 8 Nam si eos) Per occupationem docet hunc diem præfinitum non intelligendum esse de illo tempore quo Iesus siue Iehofchua collocauit populum in requie, vel requiescere fecit in terra Canaan: Objici enim potuit, Annon est hic dies ille dies quo Iehofchua in requie collocauit populum Dei? Respondet, demonstratque hodiernum hunc diem non intelligendum esse de die illo requietis populi in terra Canaan: Nam post illam populi requiem, Dominus per Dauidem de alio posthac die locutus fuit: Ergo non est hic intelligendus ille dies, quo collocatus est populus, ac requieuit in terra Canaan. Nisi mauis hanc esse huius loci analysin. Prius docuit, requiem illam de qua locutus est Dominus apud Dauidem, aliam atque diuersam esse a requie diei sabbathini, supra verf. 4.5. Inde digressio fuit, qua ex testimonio Dauidis, collegit præfinitum esse a Domino quædam nouum requietis diem. Imò præfiniri eum oportuisse. Nunc verf. 8. reddit ad institutum, docetque illam requiem (de qua apud Dauidem) diuersam esse à requie populi, in terra Canaan. Objici potuit. Annon illa requies, de requie populi in terra Canaan accipienda est? Refponfio negata intelligenda est, cujus hic ratio est reddita. Argumentum sumptum est ab ipso tempore & die de quo locutus est Dominus apud Dauidem. Locutus autem est de alio die, quàm illo quo per Iehofchuam populus collocatus est in requie terræ Canaan, & de die illo, qui illam requiem multo post tempore insecutus est. Argumentatio est in hanc formam. Si Iehofchua eos in requie collocaffet, five, quod idem est, Si hæc quæ est apud Dauidem requies, ea effet quæ fuit populi in terra Canaan, duce Iehofchua, profecto de alio posthac tempore non fuisset locutus Dominus. At de alio posthac tempore ac die locutus est, Ergo hæc requies quæ invenitur apud Dauidem, non intelligenda est de illa populi requie in terra Canaan. In requie) Nempe illa cœlesti ac vera, de qua Dominus apud Dauidem. Hanc κατ' ἐξοχὴν requietis nomine appellat, nam ea demum vera est requies.
units.tr: 8 For if) By way of anticipation he teaches that this fixed day is not to be understood of that time when Jesus, that is Joshua, settled the people in rest, or made them rest in the land of Canaan. For it could be objected: is not this the day on which Joshua settled the people of God in rest? He answers, and shows that this today is not to be understood of that day of the people's rest in the land of Canaan; for after that rest of the people, the Lord spoke through David of another day afterwards. Therefore that day on which the people was settled and rested in the land of Canaan is not to be understood here. Unless you prefer this to be the analysis of this place. First he taught that the rest of which the Lord spoke through David is other and different from the rest of the sabbath day, above verses 4 and 5. Then came the digression, in which from David's testimony he gathered that a new day of rest had been fixed beforehand by the Lord; indeed, that it had to be fixed. Now in verse 8 he returns to his purpose and teaches that that rest (of which David speaks) is different from the rest of the people in the land of Canaan. It could be objected: should that rest not be understood as the rest of the people in the land of Canaan? The answer is to be understood as a denial, and its reason is given here. The argument is taken from the very time and day of which the Lord spoke through David. He spoke, however, of another day than that on which the people was settled in rest under Joshua in the land of Canaan, and of a day which followed that rest a long time afterwards. The argument runs in this form: if Joshua had settled them in rest, or, what is the same, if this rest which is found in David were that of the people in the land of Canaan under Joshua's leadership, then surely the Lord would not have spoken of another time afterwards. But he did speak of another time and day afterwards. Therefore this rest which is found in David is not to be understood of that rest of the people in the land of Canaan. In rest) Namely, that heavenly and true rest of which the Lord speaks through David. He calls it by the name of rest par excellence [κατ' ἐξοχὴν], for that alone is the true rest.

units.la: 9 Itaque reliquus) Conclusio qua infertur ex his quæ dicta sunt. verf. 4. 5. tu ex proximo versu, requiem aliquam populo Dei reliquam esse, & quidem illis verbis Domini apud Dauidem intelligendam. Postquàm enim primum peroccupationem docuit aliam esse illam requiem cuius meminit Dauid, à requie diei sabbathi, deinde docuit aliam esse à terrena illa requie populi in terra Canaan: hoc versu demum concludit, reliquum esse populo Dei suum quendam sabbatismum, hoc est, requiem, cujus meminit Dominus apud Dauidem. Nota igitur toto hoc loco mentionem fieri triplicis requietis, primò requietis diei sabbathi, secundò requietis populi in terra Canaan, tertiò requietis populi Dei in cœlis: Cujus quidem postremæ duæ illæ priores vmbræ ac figuræ fuerant. Hanc postremam sic collegit ex remotione duarum præcedentium: Dominus apud Dauidem non locutus est de requie diei sabbathi, non locutus est de requie in terra Canaan: Ergo oportet reliquam esse aliquam requiem populo Dei, cujus meminit Dominus apud Dauidem.
units.tr: 9 Therefore a remaining) This is the conclusion drawn from what has been said in verses 4 and 5, and from the preceding verse: that some rest remains for the people of God, to be understood from those words of the Lord spoken through David. For after he first showed that the rest David speaks of is other than the rest of the Sabbath day, and then that it is other than the earthly rest of the people in the land of Canaan, he finally concludes in this verse that a certain Sabbath-keeping, that is, a rest, of which the Lord spoke through David, remains for the people of God. Note therefore that the whole passage makes mention of three rests: first, the rest of the Sabbath day; second, the rest of the people in the land of Canaan; third, the rest of the people of God in heaven. Of these, the last two were shadows and figures of the last. He infers this last rest from the removal of the two preceding ones: the Lord did not speak through David of the rest of the Sabbath day, nor of the rest in the land of Canaan; therefore some rest must remain for the people of God, of which the Lord spoke through David.

units.la: 10 Nam qui) Sabbatismum hunc populo Dei reliquum, ostendit ex sabbatismi quadam definitione, hoc modo: Sabbatismus est quo quis requiescit ab operibus suis (illustratur assumptio similitudine requietis & cessationis ipsius Dei) ergo reliquus est populo Dei aliquis sabbatismus, siquidem hæc fit sabbatismi definitio ac ratio nempe cessatio ab operibus. In requiem ipsius ) Alludit ad verba Domini apud Dauidem, quibus dixit; Si ingressuri sunt in requiem meam. Porrò requiem Domini intelligit illam pacem & gloriam Dei immensam a
units.tr: 10 For he who) He shows that this Sabbath-keeping remains for the people of God from a certain definition of Sabbath-keeping, in this way: a Sabbath-keeping is that in which someone rests from his works (the assumption is illustrated by the likeness of the rest and cessation of God himself). Therefore some Sabbath-keeping remains for the people of God, since this is the definition and principle of Sabbath-keeping, namely cessation from works. Into his rest) He alludes to the words of the Lord through David, by which he said: "If they shall enter into my rest." Moreover, by the rest of the Lord he means that peace and immeasurable glory of God

units.la: { } Ioan. ... ineffabilem, cujus Deus suos facit participes. Hactenus igitur digressio fuit inde à postrema parte ver. 3. in qua tantum videtur laborare in exponendo verū sensum illius requietis, cujus fit mentio apud Dauidem. Psal. 95. 11. Itaque exclusis duabus acceptionibus non veris ac genuinis, tertiam acceptionem requietis, cujus ibi mentio facta est, veram ac genuinam tandem conclusit verf. 9. Hanc autem indicauit quum dixit, sabbatismum aliquem populo Dei reliquum: His enim verbis significat coelestem ac spiritualem requiem: Ac si dixisset: itaq; reliquum est, vt nomine requietis (cujus mentio fit apud Dauidem) intelligamus coelestem quandam ac spiritualem requiem, qua tandem fruentur populus Dei.
units.tr: { } John ... ineffable, of which God makes his own people partakers. Thus far, then, the digression runs from the last part of verse 3, in which he seems to labour only in explaining the true sense of that rest which is mentioned through David (Ps. 95:11). So, having excluded the two acceptations which are not true and genuine, he finally concludes, in verse 9, the third acceptation of rest, of which mention is made there, as the true and genuine one. He indicated this when he said: "a certain Sabbath-keeping remains for the people of God." For by these words he signifies a heavenly and spiritual rest. As if he had said: therefore it remains that, under the name of rest (of which mention is made through David), we understand a certain heavenly and spiritual rest, which the people of God will at last enjoy.

units.la: II Studeamus igitur ingredi in illam requiem, ne quis in idem incidat contumacia exemplum.
units.tr: 11 Let us therefore strive to enter into that rest, lest anyone fall into the same example of disobedience.

units.la: 12 Viuus est enim sermo Dei & efficax & penetrantior quouis gladio ancipiti, ac pertingit vsque ad diuisionem animae simul ac spiritus, compagumq; & medullarum, & dijudicat cogitationes & conceptiones cordis.
units.tr: 12 For the word of God is living and effective and sharper than any two-edged sword, and it reaches even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and it judges the thoughts and intentions of the heart.

units.la: 13 Nec est vlla res creata quae non manifesta sit in conspectu ipsius: imo omnia sunt nuda & patentia oculis eius, qui cum nobis est negotium.
units.tr: 13 Nor is there any created thing that is not manifest in his sight; indeed, all things are naked and open to the eyes of him with whom we have to do.

units.la: Studeamus igitur) Conclusio est exhortationis: Porrò eadem est sententia cum illa, quae fuit primò versu hujus capitis. Sensus enim est Teneamus professionem nostram: tenendo enim professionem, studemus, ingredi in requiem. Ne quis in) Cum conclusione repetitur argumentum quintum, illustratum simili exemplo contumaciæ populi veteris: est autem à Dei judicio, quo frustrabimur ac priuabimur illa æterna requie, ad exemplum illius populi contumacis ac increduli: idem exemplum hoc loco est, idem judicium propter contu- maciam.
units.tr: Let us therefore strive) This is the conclusion of the exhortation; moreover, its sense is the same as that of the first verse of this chapter. For the meaning is: let us hold fast our profession; for by holding to the profession we strive to enter into rest. Lest anyone) With the conclusion the fifth argument is repeated, illustrated by the similar example of the disobedience of the ancient people. It concerns God's judgment, by which we shall be frustrated and deprived of that eternal rest, after the example of that disobedient and unbelieving people. The example is the same here, and so is the judgment, on account of disobedience.

units.la: 12 Viuus est enim) Probat pœnam contumaciæ, ex efficacia verbi Dei contempti à contumacibus: Primùm autem est efficaciæ verbi diuini propositio: viuus est (inquit) sermo Dei, hoc est ( vt verbum sequens exponit,) efficax ad vtrumque, siue seruandum, siue perdendum, licet posterius hoc per accidens fiat. Tum proposita verbi efficacia declaratur, primùm comparatè, facta cum gladio ancipiti comparatione: Deinde simpliciter, ex effectis suis. Efsecta verbi partim sunt in animo hominis, partim in corpore: In animo autem rursus dupliciter operatur verbum, vel enim operatur in crassiore animi parte, quam ψυχὴν vocant: vel in puriore, quam spiritum & mentem appellant. Paulus ad Ephef. 4. 23. spiritum mentis vocat. Verbum itaque Dei dicit efficax esse ad diuidendum, non modò crassiorem animi partem, in qua sunt affectus, sed etiam puriorem illā mentem siue spiritum. Effectum verbi diuini in corpore duplex est, primùm in exteriori corpore, quod intelligit compag̃m, nomine: Deinde in interiori corpore, quod intelligit medullarum nomine. His verbis igitur significat Author, nihil esse in homine, nihil in animo hominis, nihil in corpore hominis, siue crassu, siue purum, siue externum, siue internum, ad quod non pertingat verbum Dei, & quod non diuidat. Et diudicat) Haec verba adijcit, ad exponendam proximam allegoriam: Nam quod dixit de diuisione animae, spiritus, compagum, medullarum, illud nunc proprie effert, dum dicit verbum Dei dijudicare cogitationes, ac conceptiones cordis.
units.tr: 12 For the word) He proves the punishment of disobedience from the efficacy of the word of God, when it is despised by the disobedient. First comes the proposition concerning the efficacy of the divine word: "the word of God is living" (he says), that is (as the following word explains) effective for both, whether for saving or for destroying, although the latter happens only incidentally. Then the efficacy of the word, once proposed, is declared: first comparatively, by the comparison with a two-edged sword; then simply, from its effects. The effects of the word are partly in the mind of man, partly in the body. Now in the mind the word works in two ways: either it works in the grosser part of the mind, which they call psyche [ψυχήν], or in the purer part, which they call spirit and mind. Paul, in Ephesians 4:23, calls it the spirit of the mind. So the word of God, he says, is effective in dividing not only the grosser part of the mind, in which the affections are, but also that purer mind or spirit. The effect of the divine word in the body is twofold: first in the outer body, which he names by the term joints; then in the inner body, which he names by the term marrow. By these words, therefore, the author signifies that there is nothing in man, nothing in the mind of man, nothing in the body of man, whether gross or pure, external or internal, to which the word of God does not reach and which it does not divide. And judges) He adds these words to explain the preceding allegory. For what he said about the division of soul, spirit, joints and marrow, he now states plainly, when he says that the word of God judges the thoughts and intentions of the heart.

units.la: 13 Nec est illa) Sermonem transfert a verbo Dei, ad ipsum verbi Authorem Christum, & a Christo ipsiusque perspicacia ac prouidentia, & Christi quasi oculis, quos nihil quatumuis abditu & abscondituq potest effugere, argumentatur quodam modo a verbi ipsius efficaciam. Nam si oculus ejus omnia penetrat ac peruidet, profecto verbum ipsius efficax esse necesse est.
units.tr: 13 Nor is there) He transfers the discourse from the word of God to Christ himself, the author of the word; and from Christ, his penetration and providence, and Christ's eyes, as it were, which no matter how hidden and concealed a thing is, cannot escape, he argues in a certain way for the efficacy of the word itself. For if his eye penetrates and sees through all things, his word must surely be effective.

units.la: 14 Habentes igitur Pontificem magnum qui penetrauit caelos, Iesum Filium Dei, teneamus hanc professionem.
units.tr: 14 Having therefore a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast this profession.

units.la: 15 Non enim habemus Pontificem qui non potest affici sensu infirmitatum nostrarum: Sed tentatum in omnibus similiter, absque peccato.
units.tr: 15 For we do not have a high priest who cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities, but one tempted in all things likewise, apart from sin.

units.la: Habentes igitur Repetita exhortationis conclusio, vna cum argumento tertio, a Christo pontificatu, non solum Pontificem vocat, sed magnum addit Epitheti hujus occasio arrepta videtur ex loco proximo, in quo prædicta est Christi sapientia ac summa perspicacitas in omnibus rebus peruidedis. Hinc enim non tantum Pontificem, sed magnum Pontificem prædicat. Qui penetrauit) Magnū Pontifice ex eo declarat, quod cœlos penetrarit, h.e. cœleste illud sacrarium, cujus typus erat illud terrenum sacrarium, in quod solitus est ingredi Pontifex terrenus. Iesum Filium) Pontificem ex nomine suo designat, & ex petitione Filij Dei commendat.
units.tr: Having therefore) The conclusion of the exhortation is repeated, together with the third argument, drawn from Christ's priesthood. He calls him not only high priest but adds "great" to the title; the occasion for this epithet seems to have been taken from the nearby passage, in which Christ's wisdom and supreme penetration in seeing all things is set forth. For this reason he proclaims him not merely high priest but great high priest. Who has passed through) He shows that he is a great high priest from the fact that he has passed through the heavens, that is, that heavenly sanctuary, of which the earthly sanctuary, into which the earthly high priest was accustomed to enter, was a type. Jesus the Son) He designates him as high priest by his name, and commends him by the title Son of God.

units.la: 15 Non enim) Amplificatio coclusionis proximæ, à Pontificis Christi qualitate sive conditione, nempe συμπαθείᾳ quod afficiatur sensu infirmitatum nostratum: hoc autem innuit qui dicit, tentatum eum in omnibus similiter absque peccato. In antecedente enim causa consequentes effectu intelligendum est. Illustrata autem est hæc Christi συμπαθείᾳ, per remotionem cötrarię ἀπὸ θείας quasi dicat, non est ἀπαθὴς, sed συμπαθής.
units.tr: 15 For) An amplification of the preceding conclusion, drawn from the quality or condition of Christ as high priest, namely that he is sympathetic [συμπαθείᾳ] to the feeling of our infirmities. He hints at this when he says that he was tempted in all things likewise, apart from sin. For in the antecedent cause the consequent effect is to be understood. This sympathy of Christ is illustrated by the removal of the contrary, from apathy [ἀπὸ θείας, read ἀπαθείας], as if he said: he is not apathetic [ἀπαθὴς] but sympathetic [συμπαθής].

units.la: 16 Accedamus igitur cum fiducia ad Throni gratiæ, ut consequamur misericordiam, & gratiam inueniamus ad opportunum auxilium.
units.tr: 16 Let us therefore draw near with confidence to the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy and find grace for timely help.

units.la: Accedamus igitur) Post amplificationem repetita est conclusio principalis, alia quidem verbis à superiori, sed reipsa eadem. Nomen fiduciæ vsurpatum est supra cap. 3. verf. 6. vbi conclusit & dixit, Si fiduciam & spem illam de qua gloriamur, ad finem usque firmam retinuerimus. rimus. Eodem sensu concludit nunc, accedendum esse cum fiducia ad thronum gratiæ:Nam tenere firmum fiduciam,& accedere cum fiducia ad thronum gratiæ, idem sunt reipsa. Vt consequamur ) Sumdet accedsum hunc ad thronum gratiæ, ab vsu, & fructu suo: ita enim fiet vt misericordiam & gratiam consequamur, à throno enim gratiæ proficisci gratiam oportet, & ad eum peruenire, qui ad thronum gratiæ accedit. Estque hoc argumentum exhortationis sextum à Dei gratia & misericordia.
units.tr: Let us therefore draw near) After the amplification the principal conclusion is repeated, in words different from the earlier ones, but in substance the same. The word confidence was used above in chapter 3, verse 6, where he concluded and said: "if we hold firm the confidence and hope of which we boast to the end." In the same sense he now concludes that we must draw near with confidence to the throne of grace; for to hold firmly to confidence and to draw near with confidence to the throne of grace are in fact the same thing. That we may obtain) He takes this approach to the throne of grace from its use and fruit: for in this way we obtain mercy and grace; grace must indeed proceed from the throne of grace, and it must be reached by him who comes to the throne of grace. This is the sixth argument of the exhortation, drawn from God's grace and mercy.

units.la: Argumentum Capitis quinti.
units.tr: Argument of the Fifth Chapter.

units.la: Hoc capite primum est digressio ab instituta exhortatione in confirmationem Pontificatus Christi in genere, ad versum vsque 1ᵛ.quo loco proponit de Melchisedeco dicendum. Idque in eum finem, vt conspiciatur Christum esse pontificem secundum ordinem Melchisedec. Quare, vt superiore capitis parte probauit Christum Pontificem esse in genere: Itaque versu 11. aggreditur addemonstrandum Christum Pontificem esse secundum ordinem Melchisedec, hoc est, certum quendam ordinem Pontificatus Christi, versu 12. à proposita illa de Melchisedeco doctrina digreditur in reprehensionem segnitiei & ruditatis Hebræorum, ad quos scribit ad finem usque capitis.
units.tr: In this chapter the author first digresses from the exhortation he had set out, to confirm the priesthood of Christ in general, as far as verse 10, where he announces that he is to speak of Melchizedek. He does this with the aim that it may be seen that Christ is a priest according to the order of Melchizedek. Accordingly, as in the first part of the chapter he proved that Christ is a priest in general, so in verse 11 he sets about demonstrating that Christ is a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, that is, according to a certain order of Christ's priesthood. In verse 12 he turns aside from this doctrine concerning Melchizedek into a rebuke of the sluggishness and dullness of the Hebrews, to whom he writes, and continues to the end of the chapter.

units.la: CAPUT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: 1 Nam omnis Pontifex ex hominibus assumitur, & pro hominibus constituitur in iis quæ apud Deum Deum agenda sunt, ut offerat donaria & victimas pro peccatis:
units.tr: 1 For every high priest is taken from among men, and is appointed for men in the things pertaining to God, that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins:

units.la: 2 Qui quantum satis est possit miserari vicem ignorantium & aberrantium: quod & ipse circum datus sit infirmitate:
units.tr: 2 Who can have compassion, as far as is sufficient, on the ignorant and those who go astray, since he himself is also beset with weakness.

units.la: 3 Et propter hanc debeat, sicut pro populo, ita & pro seipso offerre victimam pro peccatis.
units.tr: 3 And because of this he ought, as for the people, so also for himself, to offer a sacrifice for sins.

units.la: 4 Neque sibi ipsi quisquam sumit hunc honorem, sed qui vocatur a Deo, sicut & Aaron.
units.tr: 4 Nor does anyone take this honour to himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was.

units.la: 5 Ita & Christus, non sibi hunc honorem tribuit ut fieret Pontifex, sed is qui dixerat ei, Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te.
units.tr: 5 So also Christ did not glorify himself to become high priest, but he who said to him, You are my Son, today I have begotten you.

units.la: 6 Sicut & alibi dicit. Tu es Sacerdos in aeternum, secundum ordinem Melchisedec.
units.tr: 6 As he also says elsewhere, You are a priest for ever, after the order of Melchizedek.

units.la: 7 Qui in diebus carnis suae, quum deprecationes & supplicationes apud eum qui poterat ipsum servare a morte, cum clamore valido & lacrymis obtulisset, & exauditus esset ex metu.
units.tr: 7 Who, in the days of his flesh, when he had offered up prayers and supplications, with strong crying and tears, to him who was able to save him from death, and was heard because of his fear.

units.la: 8 Quamvis filius esset, tamen ex iis quae passus est didicit obedientiam.
units.tr: 8 Although he was a Son, yet he learned obedience from the things that he suffered.

units.la: 9 Et consecratus, factus est Author salutis aeternae omnibus qui ipsi auscultant:
units.tr: 9 And having been made perfect, he became the author of eternal salvation to all who obey him,

units.la: 10 Cognominatus a Deo Pontifex secundum ordinem Melchisedec.
units.tr: 10 Being named by God a high priest after the order of Melchizedek.

units.la: Nam omnis) Digreditur in declarationem Pontificatus Christi. Primum autem probat eum Pontificem esse in genere, instituta comparatione cum veteribus illis Pontificibus. Particula Nam, referri debet ad versum 14. capitis superioris: Docet enim Christum vere Pontificem esse: quod fuit argumentum exhortationis tertium, repetitum verf. 14. superioris capitis. Et sensus est quasi dicat: Quod dixi eum Pontificem esse, id apparet verum ex comparatione Christi cum Legali Pontifice. Introducitur autem haec ratio per occupationem. Quaeri enim potuit, An merito Christum Pontificem dixerit illo versu citato? Nunc itaque probat per comparationem fidam cum Legali Pontifice, Christum Pontificem esse. Est autem comparatio in tribus, quae primum proposita sunt in Legali Pontifice, primis quatuor versibus. Deinde accommodantur ad Christum, ad versum vsque 11. Hoc itaque versu est prima proprietas Pontificis in genere. Pontifex omnis ex hominibus assumitur, & pro hominibus constituitur in iis, quae apud Deum sunt agenda. Ut offerat) Finis est Pontificis assumpti & constituti, nempe oblatio donariorum & victimarum pro peccatis, hoc est, omnis oblatio in genere rerum quarumcunque, sive vitae expertium, ut erant donaria, sive viuentium, ut erant victimae.
units.tr: For every) He turns to the explanation of Christ's priesthood. First, he proves that he is a priest in general, by setting up a comparison with those old priests. The particle For ought to be referred to verse 14 of the previous chapter. For it teaches that Christ is truly a priest; this was the third argument of the exhortation, repeated in verse 14 of the previous chapter. The sense is, as if he were saying: what I said, that he is a priest, appears true from the comparison of Christ with the priest under the Law. This reasoning is introduced by way of anticipation. For it could be asked, Did he rightly call Christ a priest in that verse cited? So now he proves, by a faithful comparison with the priest under the Law, that Christ is a priest. The comparison consists of three points, which are first set out in the priest under the Law, in the first four verses. Then they are applied to Christ, down to verse 11. So in this verse is the first property of the priest in general: every priest is taken from among men, and is appointed for men in the things that pertain to God. That he may offer) This is the purpose of the priest who is taken and appointed, namely the offering of gifts and sacrifices for sins, that is, every offering in general of whatever things, whether those without life, as gifts were, or living things, as sacrifices were.

units.la: 2 Qui quantum satis) Secunda proprietas Pontificis in genere, in qua fit comparatio: Est autem συμπαθεια qua afficitur sensu miseriae ignorantium & aberrantium: Quod & ipse) Sympathiae ratio petita a simili infirmitate ipsius Pontificis, qua tanquam veste circundatus est & circumseptus, hoc est, omni ex parte obnoxius.
units.tr: 2 Who can have compassion) The second property of the priest in general, in which the comparison is made. It is sympathy [συμπάθεια], by which he is affected with a sense of the misery of the ignorant and those who go astray. Since he himself) The reason for sympathy is drawn from the like weakness of the priest himself, by which he is, as it were, clothed and surrounded, that is, liable to it on every side.

units.la: { } Cf. note in margin; partially illegible. noxius est ijsdem naturæ incommodis ac vitijs (Et ipse) Particula (Et)nota vel similitudinem, vel paritatem, quasi dicat, quod pariter ipse.
units.tr: { } Cf. note in margin; partially illegible. He is liable to the same disadvantages and faults of nature (and he himself). The particle (and) marks either a likeness or an equality, as if he were saying that he himself likewise.

units.la: 3 Et propter) Infirmitatem Pontificis parem arguit, ex eo quod pariter pro peccatis populi & suijpsius, debeat victimam offerre.
units.tr: 3 And because of this) He argues that the weakness of the priest is equal, from the fact that he must likewise offer a sacrifice for the sins of the people and of himself.

units.la: 4 Neque sibi ipsi) Tertia proprietas Pontificis, in qua fit comparatio cum Christo Pontifice: Est autem vocatio Dei, quòd non sumit sibijpsi hunc honorem, sed ad eum vocatus est à Deo. Illustratum est speciali exemplo Aaronis qui à Deo vocatus est.
units.tr: 4 Nor does anyone) The third property of the priest, in which the comparison with Christ the priest is made. It is the calling of God: he does not take this honour to himself, but is called to it by God. This is illustrated by the special example of Aaron, who was called by God.

units.la: 5 Ita & Christus) Hactenus fuit comparationis protasis, siue propositio, continens tres proprietates, in quibus fit comparatio: Sequitur nunc apodosis redditio siue accommodatio similitudinis. Accommodatur enim & applicantur Christo superiores proprietates Pontificis, sed καθ' ὑςτερών. Primum enim applicatur tertia & vltima Pontificis proprietas. Christus vocatus est à Deo Patre. Sed ut qui) Periphrasis est Dei Patris, quasi dicat: Sed Deus Pater tribuit ei hunc honorem.
