Confirmat autem attributum à Patre hunc honorem, duobus testimonijs, priore ex Psalmo 2. 7. posteriore ex Psal. 110. 4.
units.tr: 5 So also Christ) Up to this point is the protasis, or proposition, of the comparison, containing three properties in which the comparison is made. Now follows the apodosis, or the rendering and application of the likeness. For the higher properties of the priest are applied and fitted to Christ, but kath' hysteron [καθ' ὕστερον], in reverse order. For first the third and last property of the priest is applied: Christ was called by God the Father. But he who) This is a periphrasis for God the Father, as if he were saying: but God the Father gave him this honour. He confirms that this honour was bestowed by the Father by two testimonies, the first from Psalm 2:7, the second from Psalm 110:4.

units.la: 7 Qui in dieb us) Applicat ad Christum secundam Pontificis proprietatem, nempe sensum infirmitatum nostrarum, & ευμπαθῆσαι hanc enim videtur innuere, dum dicit; Filium in diebus carnis luæ exijs quæ passus est didicisse obedientiam. Nam ex caussa intelligi potest efsectum: passio autem Christi caussa est, sensus vero infirmitatum nostrarum effectum est. In diebus carnis) Hoc est, in tempore infirmitatis suæ. Nam Christus crucifixus fuit ex infirmitate. 2. Cor. 3. 14. Carnis ergo nomine metonymicos infirmitatem intelligit. Quum deprecationes) Hic videtur inserta quædam definitio dierum carnis, siue temporis infirmitatis Christi. Sumpta est autem partim ex deprecationibus & supplicationibus, cum clamore valido, & lachrymis Patri suo oblatis, partim ex effecto deprecationum & supplicationum, nempe deprecationum acceptatione. Qui poterat) Periphrasis est Dei Patris, quā etiam designatur fundamentum super quo exitructæ sunt quasi preces Christi, & fides per quam precatus est: nempe Dei Patris omnipotentia, qua potuit ipsum à morte seruare. Hac Dei potentia nitebatur fides Abrahami, quo tempore sub ipsè contra spem credidit. Rom. 4. 21. Cum clamore) Modus est ac gestus precantis, quo significantur preces intensissimæ, & quàm maximè feriæ ac vehementes. Sic dicitur Christus precatus esse quū in horto esset, cum sudore, qui erat quasi grumi sanguinis in terram descendentes. Luc. 22. 44. Et exauditus) Hoc est effectum deprecationum Christi, quo significatur Christum exauditum à Patre, & liberatum ab illo metu quem habuit ex horroribus qui magis magisq; impendebant. Neque enim tantum perturbatus fuit dum esset in horto, præsenti sensu diuinæ iræ in nostra peccata, sed etiam grauissimo metu iræ futuræ. De hac liberatione Christi leges nonnihil apud Lucam 22. 42. 43. vbi spostquam dixit Christus, Pater si vis, transfer poculum hoc à me) habemus visum esse ipsi Angelum è cœlo corroborantem eum
units.tr: 7 Who in the days) He applies to Christ the second property of the priest, namely the sense of our infirmities, and to sympathise [συμπαθῆσαι]. For this he seems to suggest, when he says that the Son learned obedience in the days of his flesh from the things that he suffered. For the cause can be understood from the effect: the passion of Christ is the cause, but the sense of our infirmities is the effect. In the days of his flesh) That is, in the time of his weakness. For Christ was crucified out of weakness (2 Cor. 13:4). So by the name of flesh he understands, by metonymy, weakness. When he had offered) Here a certain definition of the days of the flesh, or the time of Christ's weakness, seems to be inserted. It is taken partly from the prayers and supplications, with strong crying and tears, offered to his Father, and partly from the effect of the prayers and supplications, namely the acceptance of the prayers. To him who was able) This is a periphrasis for God the Father, by which is also indicated the foundation on which Christ's prayers were, as it were, built, and the faith by which he prayed: namely the omnipotence of God the Father, by which he was able to save him from death. Abraham's faith rested on this power of God, when he believed against hope (Rom. 4:21). With strong crying) This is the manner and gesture of one praying, by which are signified prayers most intense, and as vehement and fervent as possible. So Christ is said to have prayed when he was in the garden, with sweat which was like drops of blood falling to the ground (Luke 22:44). And was heard) This is the effect of Christ's prayers, by which is signified that Christ was heard by the Father, and freed from that fear which he had of the horrors that pressed upon him more and more. For he was not only troubled while he was in the garden, from the present sense of divine wrath against our sins, but also from the most grievous fear of the wrath to come. Something about this deliverance of Christ may be read in Luke 22:42, 43, where, after Christ had said, Father, if you are willing, take this cup from me, we find that an angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him.

units.la: 8 Quamuis Filius) Hactenus definitio fuit dierum carnis in parenthesi quadam, quæ interpellata est justa sententia. Nam hæc conjungenda sunt cum iis, quæ dicta sunt principio versus præcedentis, in hunc modum: Qui in diebus carnis suæ quamuis Filius esset &c. Porrò his verbis est passionis Christi amplificatio, à persona Filij Dei. Didicit) Hoc est effectum passionis. Sensus est: Reipsa expertus est quid sit obedire Deo & irato Patri propter peccata nostra: nimirum expertus est non satis fieri offenso Deo, nisi, vt Paulus loquitur (Philip. 2. 8.) obedientia quæ est ad mortem vsque, & eam quidem ignominiosissimam & maximè execrabilem, vtpote crucis mortem. Didicit quidem hoc Filius, sed non inuitus, verùm summa voluntate: secus obedientia Filij non fuisset pro peccatis nostris satisfactio. Quare Galat. 1. 4. dicitur Filius dedille semetipsum pro peccatis nostris.
units.tr: 8 Although he was a Son) Up to this point there has been a definition of the days of the flesh in a certain parenthesis, which has interrupted the proper sense. For these words must be joined with what was said at the beginning of the preceding verse, in this way: who, in the days of his flesh, although he was a Son, etc. Moreover, by these words the passion of Christ is amplified, from the person of the Son of God. He learned) That is, the effect of the passion. The sense is: he truly experienced what it is to obey God, and to obey the angry Father because of our sins. Namely, he experienced that the offended God was not satisfied unless, as Paul says (Phil. 2:8), there was obedience even to death, and that the most ignominious and most accursed death, namely the death of the cross. The Son indeed learned this, but not unwillingly, rather with the greatest willingness; otherwise the obedience of the Son would not have been a satisfaction for our sins. Therefore in Galatians 1:4 it is said that the Son gave himself for our sins.

units.la: E
units.tr: E

units.la: 9 Et consecratus ) Passionem illam Christi acobedientiam commendat ex effectu suo: Hincenim factus est Christus Author salutis æternæ, non tantum ( vt dicit Apostolus ad Philip. 2. 9. (obedientiam ipsius secuta est exaltatio in summam sublimitatem, sed etiam salus nostra æterna. Porrò consecratio hæc ( interprete ipso Apostolo supra 2. 10. ) per afflictiones, adeoque per mortem ipsam fuit. Nam Christus per crucem & mortem consecratus fuit ad munus illud sacerdotale, & ad hoc vt Princeps & Author euaderet salutis nostræ.
units.tr: 9 And having been made perfect) He commends that passion of Christ, and his obedience, from its effect. For from this Christ became the author of eternal salvation, not only (as the Apostle says in Phil. 2:9) was his obedience followed by exaltation to the highest sublimity, but also by our eternal salvation. Moreover, this consecration (the Apostle himself explaining it above, 2:10) was through afflictions, and so through death itself. For Christ was consecrated through the cross and death to that priestly office, and to this end, that he might become the Prince and Author of our salvation.

units.la: Omnibus qui ) Notanda est vniuersi generis restrictio. Christus quidem factus est Seruator omnibus, sed cum hac restrictione, credentibus. Atque hæc ipsa fidei restrictio intelligenda est in generalibus illis sententijs quæ passim occurrunt in Euangelio : vt cum dicitur, omnibus promitti vitam æterna, intellige credentibus.
units.tr: Note the restriction of the whole class. Christ was indeed made Saviour to all, but with this restriction: to believers. This restriction of faith must be understood in those general statements that occur everywhere in the Gospel: when it is said that eternal life is promised to all, understand "to believers."

units.la: 10 Cognominatus a Deo ) Probat salutis Authorem factum Christum, à cognomine illo Pontificis diuinitus ipsi attributo. Confirmatio igitur est à Dei ipsius testimonio. Secundum ordinem) Restringit Pontificatum Christi ad certam speciem, siue certum ordinem: nempe non quidem Aaronis, sed Melchisedeci: quo significat cognominatum Christum Pontificem, non temporarium, sed æternum.
units.tr: 10 Named by God: He proves that Christ was made the author of salvation from that title of high priest divinely given to him. The confirmation is therefore from God's own testimony. According to the order: He restricts the priesthood of Christ to a certain kind, or a certain order, namely not that of Aaron but that of Melchizedek. By this he signifies that Christ was named high priest not for a time but for ever.

units.la: 11 De quo nobis multa sunt dicenda, eaque difsicilia explicatu :quandoquidem segnes factiestis auribus.
units.tr: 11 Of whom we have much to say, and things hard to explain, since you have become sluggish in hearing.

units.la: De quo nobis) Hactenus comparatione Christi Pontificis cum Pontifice Legali docuit Pontificem esse Christum. Comparatio fuit in tribus proprietatibus quae in Pontifice omni requiruntur. Ex his duas tantum in apodosi comparationis Christo applicauit: Primam enim proprietatem, nempe quod ex hominibus assumitur omnis Pontifex, non applicatam Christo reliquit, ut quae satis de ipso intelligi possit. Nam de hoc non ambigitur, Christum ex hominibus assumptum, & pro hominibus constitutum esse. Nunc, ut supra ostendit Pontificem esse Christum, docet Pontificem esse secundum ordinem Melchisedeci, hoc est, ostendit Pontificatus ipsius speciem. Primum proponit de Melchisedeco dicenda multa, & ea quidem difficilia: Eo pertinent nimirum haec quae dicuntur de Melchisedeco omnia, ut melius conspiciatur Christum Pontificem esse secundum ordinem Melchisedeci. Quandoquidem segnes) Ratio est cur proponit de Melchisedeco dicendum. Est autem ab Hebraeorum ad quos scribit segnitie & ruditate. Atque hic, etsi proposuerit de Melchisedecodicendum, tamen transitum sibi facit ad reprehensionem Hebraeorum, quam prosequitur ab hoc loco ad caput usque septimum. Quare necesse est dicamus Apostololum ab instituto suo digredi, abductum quidem culpa, nempe ignauia & ruditate ipsorum Hebræorum.
units.tr: Of whom we have: Up to this point, by comparing Christ the high priest with the priest of the law, he has taught that Christ is the high priest. The comparison rested on three properties required in every high priest. Of these he applied only two to Christ in the second part of the comparison. The first property, namely that every high priest is taken from among men, he left unapplied to Christ, since it can be sufficiently understood of him. For there is no doubt that Christ was taken from among men and appointed for men. Now, as above he showed that Christ is the high priest, he teaches that he is a priest according to the order of Melchizedek; that is, he shows the kind of his priesthood. First he sets out that many things must be said about Melchizedek, and those difficult ones. To this belongs everything that is said about Melchizedek, so that it may be better seen that Christ is high priest according to the order of Melchizedek. Since you have become sluggish: this is the reason why he proposes to speak about Melchizedek. It is due to the sluggishness and dullness of the Hebrews to whom he writes. Here, although he has proposed to speak about Melchizedek, he nevertheless turns aside to rebuke the Hebrews, a rebuke he pursues from this place to the end of the seventh chapter. Wherefore we must say that the Apostle departs from his plan, drawn aside indeed by fault, namely the laziness and dullness of the Hebrews themselves.

units.la: 12. Vos enim quos oportuit pro temporis ratione doctores esse, rursum opus est docere quæ sint elementa initij eloquiorum Dei: factique ejus, quibus lacte sit opus, & non solido cibo.
units.tr: 12 For you, who ought by now to be teachers, again need someone to teach you the elements of the beginning of God's oracles; you have come to need milk, not solid food.

units.la: 13 Enim vero cui cum lacte res est, is rudis est sermonis iustitiæ: (infans enim est)
units.tr: 13 For everyone who partakes of milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, for he is an infant.

units.la: 14. Sed adultorum est solidus cibus, eorum videlicet qui propter habitum sensus habent exercitatos ad discretionem boni ac mali.
units.tr: 14 But solid food belongs to adults, that is, to those who, by reason of practice, have their senses trained to discern good and evil.

units.la: Vos enim) Proposita est segnities eorum in proxima ratione. His autem verbis est propositionis illius argumentum, à genere doctrinæ quo ipsis est opus, nempe elementari, & catechetica siue puerili. Quos oportuit) Exaggerat necessitatem hanc doctrinæ elementaris, qua ipsis opus est, ex eo quod pro temporis ratione oportuit esse, hoc est, ex ea ipsorum conditione, quam tempus tam diuturnu postulabat, nempe ut doctores essent, non autem discipuli erudiendi in ipsis primis elementis Religionis Christianæ. Factique ejus) Illustrat rationem propositionis, quam exaggerauit definitione & interpretatione quadam: Nisi mauis rationem hic reddi cur sit ijs opus elementari doctrina, ab ipsorum conditione, nempe infantia. Nam his verbis est infantis periphrasis. Infans enim est cui lacte est opus, & non solido cibo:
units.tr: For you: Their sluggishness has been set out in the immediately preceding reason. These words give the argument for that statement, drawn from the kind of teaching they need, namely elementary, catechetical or childish teaching. Who ought: He heightens the necessity of this elementary teaching which they need, from the fact that, given the length of time, they ought by now to be teachers. That is, he argues from their condition, which so long a time demanded, namely that they should be teachers and not pupils to be taught the very first elements of the Christian religion. And the elements of his: He illustrates the reason for the statement, which he heightened by a certain definition and interpretation. Unless you prefer that the reason be given here for why they need elementary teaching, drawn from their condition, namely infancy. For in these words there is a periphrasis of "infant": an infant is one who needs milk and not solid food.

units.la: 13 Enimuero cui) Probat infantiam eorum& ruditatem definitione quadam infantis:Infans est,cui res est cum late. Vobis opus est late. Ergo vos estis infantes. Is rudis) Dicendum fuisse videtur, Is infans est. Sed infantiæ esse‑ štum posuit, nempe ruditatem, pro ipsa infan‑ tia, ac fi dixisset, Infans est, ac proinde rudis. Sed hanc ruditatem applicauit non ad eos qui re vera infantes sunt,sed ad Hebræos qui in re‑ ligione quodam modo infantes erant,dixitque rudis est sermonis iustitiæ.
units.tr: 13 For whoever has to do with milk: He proves their infancy and roughness by a certain definition of an infant: an infant is one who has to do with milk. You need milk; therefore you are infants. Is unskilled: It seems he should have said "is an infant." But he put roughness, namely unskilfulness, in place of infancy itself, as if he had said "he is an infant, and therefore unskilled." He applied this roughness not to those who are truly infants, but to the Hebrews, who in religion were in a way infants, and he said "unskilled in the word of righteousness."

units.la: 14 Sed adultorum) Illustratio proximæ propo‑fitionis & rationis à contraria definitione adulti, quasi dicat, Adulti sunt contra quibus res est cum solido cibo. Eorum videlicet) Definitionis proximæ quasi definitio quædam est, ac si dicat, dum dico adultos esse quibus opus est solido cibo, nihil aliud volo, quàm adultos esse eos qui propter habitum sensus habent exercitatos. Adulti igitur sunt, primum qui habent habitum crebra exercitatione comparatum, deinde qui beneficio habitus habet sen‑ sus (hoc est, facultates animi) expeditos ad judi‑ candum de bono & malo, habitus enim expedi‑ tam facultatem in agendo significat.
units.tr: 14 But solid food belongs to adults: This illustrates the immediately preceding statement and reason by the contrary definition of an adult, as if he said: adults are those who have to do with solid food. Namely: the immediately preceding statement is, as it were, a definition, as if he said: when I say that adults are those who need solid food, I mean nothing other than that adults are those who, through habit of sense, have been trained. Adults therefore are, first, those who have a habit acquired by frequent exercise; then, those who by the benefit of that habit have their senses (that is, the faculties of the mind) made ready for judging good and evil. For habit signifies a ready faculty in acting.

units.la: Argumentum Capitis sexti.
units.tr: The Argument of the Sixth Chapter.

units.la: Hoc toto capite digressio est ab eo, de quo dicedum instituit verf.11. Cap.5. nepe de Melchisedeco. Inchoata autem digressio fuit, capitis 5. vers. 12. In hac digressione quæ est hoc capite, argumenti magna est varietas. Primum exhortatio est tribus primis versibus, ad hoc vt feruntur ad perfeƈtionem, confirmata graui denunciatione in Apostatas, ad versum vsque nonum. Tum correƈtio & mitigatio quædam est illius denunciationis, inde ad vers. 11. Hinc sequitur specialis quædam exhortatio ad perseuerandum in charitate & bonis operibus, ad alteram vsque partem vers. 12. Vbi per occasionem redit ad principalem, exhortationem quæ est ad perseuerantiam in fide, eiusque argumentum adducit septimum, in quo amplificando persistit, ad versum vsque 18 eiusque partem alteram, vbi ex nono & octauo argumento principalem concludit denuò exhortationem. Versu denique 19. discedit a principali exhortatione, paulatimque transit ad id quod dicendum de Melchisedeco proposuit. cap. 5. vers. 11.
units.tr: This whole chapter is a digression from the subject that he had set out to discuss at verse 11 of chapter 5, namely Melchisedec. The digression began at chapter 5, verse 12. In this digression, which occupies this chapter, there is great variety of argument. First, there is an exhortation in the first three verses, that they be carried on to perfection, confirmed by a grave denunciation against apostates, extending to verse 9. Then comes a certain correction and softening of that denunciation, extending to verse 11. Hence follows a particular exhortation to persevere in love and good works, down to the second part of verse 12. There, by way of occasion, he returns to the principal exhortation, to perseverance in faith, and adduces as its argument the seventh, which he continues to develop up to verse 18 and its second part; there, from the ninth and eighth arguments, he again concludes the principal exhortation. Finally, at verse 19 he departs from the principal exhortation and gradually passes over to what he proposed to say about Melchisedec, chapter 5, verse 11.

units.la: CAPVT. VI.
units.tr: Chapter 6

units.la: I Quapropter omisso qui in Christo rudes inchoat sermone, ad perfeƈtionem feramur: non iacentes rursum fundamentum resipiscentia ab operibus mortuis & fidei in Deum.
units.tr: 1 Therefore, leaving aside the teaching that begins with the basics of Christ, let us be carried on to perfection, not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith toward God.

units.la: 2 Baptismatum doƈtrina, ac manuum impositionis & resurreƈtionis mortuorum, & iudicij æterni.
units.tr: 2 The doctrine of baptisms, of the laying on of hands, of the resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment.

units.la: 3 Atque id faciemus, si quidem permiserit Deus.
units.tr: 3 And this we will do, if God permits.

units.la: 4 Impossibile est enim eos qui semel fuerint illuminati, gustauerintque donum cœleste, & participes factifuerint Spiritus sancti,
units.tr: 4 For it is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, and have tasted the heavenly gift, and have become partakers of the Holy Spirit,

units.la: 5 Gustauerintque bonum Dei Verbum, ac Virtutes futuri seculi;
units.tr: 5 And have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come,

units.la: 6 Si prolabantur, denuo renouari ad refipiscentiam, vt qui rursum crucifigant sibimetipsis filium Dei, & ad ignominiam exponant.
units.tr: 6 If they fall away, to be renewed again to repentance, since they crucify again the Son of God to themselves and expose him to shame.

units.la: 7 Nam terra quae imbrem sapius infe venientem combiberit, & progenuerit herbam accommodam ijs per quos excolitur, recipit benedictionem a Deo.
units.tr: 7 For the earth that has drunk in the rain that often falls upon it, and brings forth herbage fit for those by whom it is tilled, receives blessing from God.

units.la: 8 At quae profert spinas & tribulos, reproba est, & maledictione proxima: cuius exitus tendit ad exustionem.
units.tr: 8 But the land that bears thorns and thistles is rejected, and near to a curse, whose end is burning.

units.la: Quapropter omissò) Pergit in digressione coepta in fine superioris capitis. Atque vt superius reprehendit ipsorum ruditatem & infantiam: Ita hic hortatur ad hoc vt ferantur ad perfectionem, hoc est, ad perfectam de Christo doctrinam. Propositio exhortationis est his verbis, in prima parte huius versus: Cujus sensus est. Omissis rudimentis Religionis Christianae; feramini ad doctrinam persectiorem.Non iacientes) Declaratio est illius doctrinae, quam dixit rudes in Christo inchoare, h. e. doctrinae elementaris: est autem ex partibus illius doctrinae. Sunt autem partes doctrinae elementaris & fundamentalis, 1. Doctrina refipiscentiae ab operibus mortuis. 2. Doctrina fidei in Deu. 3. Doctrina baptismatum. 4. Doctrina impositionis manuum. 5. Doctrina resurrectionis mortuorum. 6. Doctrina judicij aeterni. Haec enim atque aliae ejusmodi sunt partes doctrinae elementaris ac catecheticae. Ex his colligere licet, tepore Apostolorum fuisse catechistas ac κατηχούμενος, denique catechetica doctrina.
units.tr: Therefore, leaving aside) He continues the digression begun at the end of the previous chapter. Just as above he rebuked their rudeness and infancy, so here he urges them to be carried on to perfection, that is, to the perfect doctrine concerning Christ. The exhortation is set forth in the first part of this verse. Its sense is: leaving aside the rudiments of the Christian religion, be carried on to the more perfect doctrine. Not laying) This explains the doctrine that he said they begin in Christ as rude beginners, that is, the elementary doctrine. It consists of the following parts. The parts of the elementary and fundamental doctrine are: (1) the doctrine of repentance from dead works; (2) the doctrine of faith toward God; (3) the doctrine of baptisms; (4) the doctrine of the laying on of hands; (5) the doctrine of the resurrection of the dead; (6) the doctrine of eternal judgment. These, and others of this kind, are the parts of elementary and catechetical doctrine. From these it can be gathered that in the time of the Apostles there were catechists and catechumens [κατηχούμενος], in short, catechetical teaching.

units.la: 3 Atque id faciemus)Hoc est, feremur ad persectionem, non jacentes rursum fundamentum &c. si Deo ita fueritvisum, sine cujus voluntate ac nutu nihil possumus. Ergo hoc versu propositam exhortationem quodammodo corrigit, ac restringit diuina permissione.
units.tr: 3 And this we will do) That is, we shall be carried on to perfection, not laying again the foundation, and so on, if God shall so will, without whose will and nod we can do nothing. So in this verse he in some measure corrects and restricts the exhortation proposed, by the divine permission.

units.la: 4 Nam fieri.) Argumetum est exhortationis a grauissimo Dei judicio in eos, qui postquam instructi sunt sermone illo qui in Christo rudes inchoat, non feruntur ad perfectionem, sed pro labuntur: h.e. (vt vno verbo dicam) in Apostatas: Est autem judicium aduersus istos denunciatum, refipiscentiae (vt sic dicam) impossibilitas. Condrtionem istorum, quę antecedit ἀποστασίαν his partibus explicat. Qui semel fuerint) Prima pars conditionis est mentis illuminatio. Gustaverintque) Secunda pars est cordis quidam gustus ac sensus, sed superficiarius duntaxat. Et participes) Tertia pars est participatio ipsius Spiritus sancti, qui est author & effector praecedentium partium ac beneficiorum Dei. Gustaverintque) Quarta pars est participatio causae instrumentalis praecedentium beneficiorum. Est autem Dei verbum, per quod Spiritus sanctus operatur, & mentis illuminationem, & cordis sensum. Ac virtutes) Quinta pars: degustatio quaedam virtutum, & (vt sic dicam) potentiarum, quas in futuro seculo plene ne percipiemus. Significat autem inchoationem futuræ beatitatis per gustum quendam virtutum futuri seculi. Nam & Apostatæ degustant illam vitam beatam ante apostasiam, verùm(vt sic dicam ) superficialiter. Gustus enim hîc atque sensus non est in profundo, aut inimo cordis, sed tantum(vt sic dicam)in summa cute ac superficie. Nam verbum Dei siue verbi semen quod committitur cordibus Apostatarum, & hypocritarum,comparatur semini quod cadit inter seminandum in petrosa loca, quæ non habent multam terram, verùm terræ quandam superficiem, cui subest petra. Semen quod cadit in loca petrosa, exoritur quidem statim, ac emergit supra terram,quia non agit radices deorsum: Sole autem exorto, subitanea illa herba exarescit : ita semen verbi quod cadit in cor Apostatæ, quasi petrosum, & superficiariam duntaxat terram habens, exoritur,ac statim quidem exoritur,verùm illa quasi seges & herba. statim exarescet, quia non egit radices penitus in profundo cordis, & ager cordis non est bonus & honestus.
units.tr: 4 For it is impossible.) This is an argument for the exhortation from the most grave judgment of God against those who, after they have been instructed in that word which begins the rudiments in Christ, are not carried on to perfection but fall away; that is, to put it in one word, into apostates. The judgment declared against such people is the impossibility of repentance, so to speak. He explains the conditions of these people, which precede the apostasy [ἀποστασίαν], in these parts. Who have once been) The first part of the condition is the illumination of the mind. And have tasted) The second part is a certain taste and perception of the heart, but only superficial. And have become partakers) The third part is participation in the Holy Spirit himself, who is the author and effector of the preceding parts and of God's benefits. And have tasted) The fourth part is participation in the instrumental cause of the preceding benefits. This is the word of God, through which the Holy Spirit works both the illumination of the mind and the perception of the heart. And the powers) The fifth part is a certain tasting of the powers, and, so to speak, of the abilities, which we shall fully receive in the age to come. He signifies that it is the beginning of future blessedness through a certain taste of the powers of the age to come. For apostates too taste that blessed life before their apostasy, but, so to speak, superficially. For the taste and perception here is not in the depth or innermost part of the heart, but only, so to speak, on the topmost skin and surface. For the word of God, or the seed of the word, which is committed to the hearts of apostates and hypocrites, is compared to the seed that falls, while sowing, on rocky places, which do not have much soil, but a certain surface of soil, under which lies rock. The seed that falls on rocky places springs up at once as it emerges above the earth, because it does not send its roots downward; but when the sun rises, that sudden herb withers. So the seed of the word that falls into the heart of an apostate, being rocky and having only a superficial soil, springs up, and indeed springs up at once; but that crop and herb will wither at once, because it has not put its roots down into the depth of the heart, and the field of the heart is not good and honest.

units.la: 6 Si prolabantur) Hæc est altera pars descriptionis Apostatarum, ab eorum lapsu ac defectione, vnde & Apostatæ nominantur : Nam hoc loco posita est pro Apostatis ipsorum descriptio : primùm à conditione eorum ante lapsum,quæ quatuor vel quinque partibus explicata fuit.Deinde à lapsu ipso.Vt denuo) Hoc est judicium in Apostatas denunciatum,finalis(vt vocant)impœnitentia:Nam Deus peccatum in Spiritum sanctum, cujusmodi est Apostatarum, specialiter plectit finali hac impœnitentia.Vt quirurfum) Ratio finalis impœnitentiæ, vel impoffibilitatis refipiiscentiæ, abipforum fa&o:rursum (inquit) crucifigunt fibimetipfis Filium Dei:Tum hoc quid sibi velit, verbis fequentibus exponitur: ad ignominiam eum exponunt.Eodem sensu Heb.10.29.dicit eos concul-care Filium Dei, & sanguinem fœderis(per quem fuerant sanctificati) profanum ducere: quo quidem facto non minus ignominiæ exponitur Christus, quàm expositus est ignominiæ quum à Iudæis est crucifixus.
units.tr: 6 If they fall away) This is the second part of the description of apostates, taken from their lapse and defection, whence they are also called apostates. For here their description is set forth for apostates: first from their condition before the lapse, which was explained in four or five parts, and then from the lapse itself. To be renewed again) That is, the judgment declared against apostates: final, as they call it, impenitence. For God specially punishes the sin against the Holy Spirit, of which apostates are guilty, with this final impenitence. Since they crucify) This is the reason for final impenitence, or the impossibility of repentance, taken from their own deed: since they crucify again, he says, the Son of God to themselves. What this means is explained in the following words: they expose him to shame. In the same sense, Heb. 10.29, he says that they trample underfoot the Son of God and count the blood of the covenant (by which they had been sanctified) as unclean. By this deed Christ is exposed to no less shame than he was exposed to shame when he was crucified by the Jews.

units.la: 7 Nam terra) Iudicium hoc denunciatum illustrat similitudine terræ, quæ cùm sæpiùs imbrem in fe venientem combiberit, attamen nihil profert præter spinas & tribulos: quemadmodum,inquit,hujusmodi terra reproba est & maledictioni affinis; Ita Apostatæ quijam sæpiùs imbrem verbi diuini in fe venientem combiberunt, & tamen nullum fructum bonum proferunt, sed prolabuntur, reprobi sunt & maledictioni affines h. e.desperata est eorum conuersio & salus. Iudicium in terram reprobam illustratur dissimili benedictione terræ bonæ, quæ progenerat herbam accommodam ijs à quibus excolitur.Protafis diffimilitudinis est verf. 7. Apodosis de terra reproba est versu sequenti.
units.tr: 7 For the earth) He illustrates the judgment declared by the likeness of the earth, which, though it has often drunk in the rain that comes upon it, yet brings forth nothing but thorns and thistles. As such land, he says, is rejected and near to a curse, so apostates, who have often drunk in the rain of the divine word that came upon them, and yet bring forth no good fruit, but fall away, are rejected and near to a curse; that is, their conversion and salvation is despaired of. The judgment on the rejected land is illustrated by the contrasting blessing of the good land, which brings forth herbage fit for those by whom it is tilled. The protasis of the comparison is in verse 7; the apodosis, that the land is rejected, is in the following verse.

units.la: 8 At qua profert) Nempe postquam imbrem fcpius in se venientem combiberit. Cuius exitus) Declaratio maledictionis, cujus proximè meminit. Nam in eo sita est maledictio terræ sterilis & infructuosæ, vt tandem comburatur.
units.tr: 8 But that which) Namely, after it has often drunk in the rain that falls upon it. Whose end) An explanation of the curse he mentioned just before. For the curse of barren and unfruitful land lies in this, that at last it is burned.

units.la: 9 Sed persuasimus nobis de Tobis, dilectii, istis meliora, & cum salute coniunctâ, etiamsi ita loquamur.
units.tr: 9 But we are persuaded of better things concerning you, beloved, and things that accompany salvation, even though we speak in this way.

units.la: 10 Non enim iniustus est Deus, vt obliuiscatur operis Iestri & laboriosæ charitatis quam exhibuistis ipsius nomini, vt qui ministrauerit sanctis & ministretis.
units.tr: 10 For God is not unjust, so as to forget your work and the labour of love that you have shown toward his name, in that you have ministered to the saints and still minister.

units.la: Sed persuasimus) Secunda pars capitis. Correctio & mitigatio quædam proximi judicij aduersus Apostatas denunciati, per occupationis quandam speciem. Hebræi enim ad quos scribit hæc quæ dixit in Apostatas in se dicta accipere potuerunt. Ideò Apostolus tempestiuè occurrit, dicitque; etiamsi ita loquamur, nempè de Apostatis, tamen persuasimus nobis de vobis meliora &c. Nota semper occurrendum esse piorum offensioni, quoties aliquid quod grauius est denunciatur in impios. Et cum salute) Quæ proximè dixit meliora, ea definit quodammodo, vocatque cum salute conjuncta, vel ad salutem pertinentia, nam ea demùm verè bona sunt quæ salutem afferunt.
units.tr: But we are persuaded) The second part of the chapter. It is a certain correction and softening of the imminent judgment declared against apostates, by a kind of pre-emptive stroke. For the Hebrews to whom he writes could take what he said against apostates as said against themselves. Therefore the Apostle meets the point in good time and says: even though we speak thus, namely of apostates, yet we are persuaded of better things concerning you, and so on. Note that the offence of the godly must always be met whenever something more severe is declared against the impious. And things that accompany) He somewhat defines the better things he has just mentioned, calling them things accompanying salvation, or pertaining to salvation; for those things are truly good which bring salvation.

units.la: 10 Non enim iniustus) Argumentum est persuasionis illius (quam dixit) Apostoli, ab operibus eorum bonis. Ac si sic argumentaretur: Opera vestra bona sunt: Ergo persuasimus nobis de vobis meliora. Nam opera bona confirmant, & nobisipsis, & alijs qui opera bona nostra intuentur, Dei gratiam erga nos, ac salutem nostram. Philip. 1. 6. Persuasum habens hoc ipsum fore, vt qui coepit in vobis opus bonū, perficiat vsq; ad diem Iesu Christi. Et laboriose) Definitio quaedam est operis eorum cujus meminit: definit autem illud ex charitate, tanquā fonte & principio suo; & Dei nomine siue gloria, tanquā fine suo. Nam illud demum est opus vere bonum, quod profeƈtū à charitate cordis interna, dirigitur in gloria nominis Dei. Ʇt qui ministrauerit) Nunc adducit in medium speciale illud opus eorum ex charitate profeƈtum, & exhibitum Dei nomini. Est autem quod ministrauerint sanƈtis; atque etiamnum ijs ministrant. Nam quum bonum opus dicatur fieri erga omnes, tum maxime id meretur boni operis nomen, quod fit erga sanƈtos, hoc est, domesticos fidei. Dum tempus habemus, simus benefici erga omnes, maxime vero erga domesticos fidei. Galat. 6. 10. Ministerium hoc eorum non tantum praeteritum dicit, sed etiam praesens. Perseuerantiam itaque innuit in bene agendo. Ergo tum maxime persuademus nobis bene fore bonis, quum videmus eos in bono perse-
units.tr: 10 For God is not unjust) This is an argument for that persuasion of the Apostle which he mentioned, drawn from their good works. It is as if he argued thus: your works are good; therefore we are persuaded of better things concerning you. For good works confirm both ourselves and others who look upon our good works in God's grace toward us and our salvation. Phil. 1.6: being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will carry it on until the day of Jesus Christ. And the labour) This is a certain definition of the work he mentioned: he defines it by love, as its source and origin, and by the name, or glory, of God, as its end. For that is truly a good work which, issuing from inward love of the heart, is directed to the glory of God's name. As those who have ministered) Now he brings forward that particular work of theirs, which issued from love and was shown to God's name. It is that they have ministered to the saints, and still minister to them. For although a good work is said to be done toward all, yet that deserves the name of a good work most of all which is done toward the saints, that is, the household of faith. While we have time, let us do good to all, but especially to the household of faith (Gal. 6.10). He says that their ministry is not only past but also present. Thus he indicates perseverance in doing good. Therefore we are most persuaded that all will be well with them when we see them persevering in the good

units.la: Obs. Pour sons de notre strat cles intellectus; des strats perseuerare, non tantum bene coepisse. Nam enim iniustus) Ratio est cur sequatur ex operibus eorum bonis, bona eorum conditioimpotentium futura, quam ipse sibi persuasam esse dixit: Est autem sumpta à iusta Dei natura, Deus iustus est. Ergo quum vos fitis bene operati, persuadeo mihi Deum daturum vobis illis meliora, & cum salute conjuncta. Iustitia haec Dei distributiua est, vt vocant, de qua lege Rom. 2. 6. & deinceps & 2. Thess. 1. 6. 7. Nota principium ac fundamentum primum omnis boni quod ad nos vsque peruenit, esse in ipsius Dei natura iusta, veraci, potenti, sapienti, misericordi &c. Quoties ergo analysis fiue resolutio alicujus boni fit in suas causas, non prius conquiescendum est, quam veniatur ad primam illam & summam causam, Dei ipsius naturam: Et fides, ac perfuasio nostra (vt videre est hoc ipso loco) vt sit firma & stabilis, necesse est nitatur Dei naturae tanquam primo suo fundamento. Quamobrem ad hoc vt sit fides in nobis solida ac firma, ante omnia debemus scrutari beneficio Spiritus ipsius Dei profunditates, vt deprehendamus aliquousque naturam illam infinitam, & incomprehensibilem. Obiici potest: videtur hoc loco meritum operum posse colligi: Nam, inquit, Deus esset iniustus si non compensaret bona opera; quare sequitur Deum obligatum esse ad compensandum bona opera, nisi malit iustitiae suae re-
units.tr: Obs. Note the sense of our understanding here: the author means that they must persevere, not merely have begun well. For if he were unjust: this is the reason why it follows from their good works that their good conditions will be those of the powerless, which he says he is himself persuaded of. This is taken from the just nature of God: God is just. Therefore, since you have acted well, I am persuaded that God will give you better things, joined with salvation. This justice of God is called distributive, and on it see Romans 2:6 ff. and 2 Thessalonians 1:6-7. Note that the first principle and foundation of every good that reaches us is in the very nature of God, who is just, true, powerful, wise, merciful, and so on. Therefore, whenever the analysis or resolution of any good is made into its causes, we must not rest until we arrive at that first and highest cause, the very nature of God. And our faith and persuasion (as is evident in this very place) must rest, if they are to be firm and stable, upon the nature of God as their first foundation. Wherefore, if faith in us is to be solid and firm, we must above all, by the gift of God's own Spirit, search out the depths, so that we may grasp in some measure that infinite and incomprehensible nature. It may be objected that merit of works seems to be inferred here: for, it says, God would be unjust if he did not reward good works; therefore it follows that God is bound to reward good works, unless he prefers to renounce his own justice.

units.la: {y} ... nunciare: vbi autem obligatio siue debitum, ibi meritum est, quamobrem bona opera nostra merentur. Respondeo paucis: Dei justitia quidem postulat vt bona opera Spiritus Sancti (nam de his loquitur) compensentur: sed hoc fit non ratione ipsorum operum, etiā sanctissimorum, cum in ijs perpetuò sit aliqua imperfectio, sed ratione meriti Christi fide apprehensi à persona ea quæ bene operata est. Quoties ergo legimus in Scriptura de mercede siue compensatione, vel bonorum operum personæ, vel personæ ipsius quæ bene operatur, toties in mentem nobis venire debet Christus, ipsiusque meritum, ad quod mercedis siue compensationis nomen proprie est relatum. Nam eæ omnes improprie locutiones sunt, in quibus merces vitæ æternæ, vel omnino gratia Dei refertur, vel ad opera personæ, vel ad personam ipsam operantem. In his enim omnibus Metonymia aliqua est, qua ex effectis causa significatur.
units.tr: {y} ... to renounce. But where there is obligation or debt, there is merit; therefore our good works merit. I answer briefly: God's justice indeed requires that the good works of the Holy Spirit (for he is speaking of these) be rewarded; but this happens not on account of the works themselves, even the most holy, since there is always some imperfection in them, but on account of the merit of Christ, apprehended by faith by the person who has done good. Therefore, whenever we read in Scripture of a reward or recompense, whether of good works or of the person who does good, Christ and his merit should come to mind, to which the name of reward or recompense is properly referred. For all those expressions are improper, in which the reward of eternal life, or grace of God, is referred either to the works of the person or to the person himself who works. In all these there is a certain metonymy, by which the cause is signified by its effects.

units.la: 11 Cupimus autem vt vnusquisque uestrum idem ostendat studium ad plenam spei persuasionem ad finem usque.
units.tr: 11 Now we desire that each one of you show the same diligence toward the full assurance of hope until the end.

units.la: 12 Vt ne sitis segnes:
units.tr: 12 That you be not slothful:

units.la: Cupimus autem) Tertia pars capitis: arrepta occasione ex proximo loco, adhortatur ad perseverantiam in bonis operibus, siue studium bonorum operum: simulque dehortatur à segnitie, quæ contraria est studio bonorum operum. Non tantum omnes promiscue adhortatur ad illud studium, sed singillatim singulos. Durationem hujus studij dicit esse oporteread finem vsque. Non enim coronatur nisi qui perseuerauerit ad finem.Effectu hujus studij tradit <bl>πληροφορίαν</bl> spei: Certitudo enim spei nostrae, qua speramus assecuturos nos vitam æternam, confirmatur nobis hoc ipso, quod sentimus in nobis studium bonorum operum. Vnde 2. Pet.1.10. Studete vocationem & electionem vestram firmam efficere, hæc enim fi feceritis nunquam impingetis.Nō prætereundum est silentio quod studium dicat, nempe bonorum operum,non nudè bona opera, quo verbo innuit non valere opus, alioqui in fe bonum,nisi ex ferio aliquo studio, & animi proposito existat. Velle enim prius esse debet,quàm perficere,& Deus dat suis prius velle quàm perficere. Deus enim is est qui efficit in vobis,& vt velitis, & vt efficiatis Philipp.2. verf.13.
units.tr: "We desire" is the third part of the chapter: having seized the occasion from the preceding place, he exhorts to perseverance in good works, or zeal for good works, and at the same time dissuades from sloth, which is contrary to zeal for good works. He exhorts not only all people in general to that zeal, but each one individually. He says that the duration of this zeal ought to last to the end, for only the one who has persevered to the end is crowned. He states that the effect of this zeal is <bl>fulness of assurance [πληροφορίαν]</bl> of hope: for the certainty of our hope, by which we hope to obtain eternal life, is confirmed to us by this very thing, that we feel in ourselves a zeal for good works. Hence 2 Pet. 1:10: "Labour to make your calling and election sure; for if you do these things you will never fall." We must not pass over in silence that he says zeal, namely for good works, not simply good works; by which word he implies that a work is of no value, unless in itself good, it arises from some earnest zeal and purpose of mind. For willing must come before performing, and God gives his own people to will before they perform. For it is God who works in you both to will and to do, Phil. 2:13.

units.la: 12 Vtne fitis) Hic dehortatur à segnitie, quæ studio bonorum operum contraria est.
units.tr: 12 That you be not) Here he dissuades from sloth, which is contrary to zeal for good works.

units.la: sed imitatores eorum qui per fidem ac patientiam obtinent promissam hæreditatem.
units.tr: but followers of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises.

units.la: 13 Deus enim pollicitus Abrahæ, quum non posset per quenquam maiorem iurare, iurauit per seipsum:
units.tr: 13 For when God made promise to Abraham, because he could swear by no greater, he swore by himself,

units.la: 14 Dicens, Certè benedicens benedicam tibi & multiplicans multiplicabo.
units.tr: 14 Saying, Surely blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply you.

units.la: 15 Atque ita quum patienter expectassFet, assequutus est promissum.
units.tr: 15 And so, after he had patiently endured, he obtained the promise.

units.la: 16 Nam homines quidem per cum iurant qui sit maior, atque ijdem omnis controversia finis est iusiurandum ad confirmationem adhibitum.
units.tr: 16 For men verily swear by the greater, and an oath for confirmation is to them an end of all strife is used, ...

units.la: 17 Quain re Deus volens ex abundanti haeredibus promissionis ostendere immutabilitatem consilij sui, fideiussit iureiurando.
units.tr: 17 Wherefore God, willing more abundantly to show to the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, confirmed it by an oath.

units.la: 18 Vt per duas res immutabiles in quibus fieri non potest vt mentitus sit Deus, validam consolationem habeamus nos, qui cursum eo corripuimus vt spem propositam obtineamus.
units.tr: 18 That by two immutable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation, who have fled for refuge to lay hold on the hope set before us.

units.la: Sed imitatores eorum) Haec quarta pars est capitis: in qua videtur redire ad principalem conclusionem siue exhortationem, qua hortatur ad perseuerantiam in fide. Nam dum patientiam cum fide conjungit perseuerantiam in fide subindicat, siue fidem quae manet duratque sub omni tentatione & afflictione. Nam graecum verbum est ὑπομονή, quod idem est quod ὑπομονή. Argumentum quo hortatur ad fidem & patientiam, sumptum est ab exemplo veterum, & priorum patrum. Est autem hoc argumentum principalis exhortationis septimum. Obtinent) Commendatio est exempli siue facti Patrum, hoc est, fidei & patientiae eorum, a fructu illo fidei & patientiae suae, quem tandem perceperunt. Commendatio haec ideo addita est, vt exemplum Patrum Hebraeos magis moueat. Promissam hæreditatem vocat, quia prius est verbo promissa quàm reipsa data: idque ideo vt prius ipsi glorificarent Deum credendo in verbum promissionis ipsius, quàm rem promissam acciperent, mittèrenturque in ejus possessionem.
units.tr: "Followers of those": this is the fourth part of the chapter, in which he seems to return to the main conclusion or exhortation, by which he urges perseverance in faith. For while he joins patience with faith, he hints at perseverance in faith, that is, faith which remains and endures under every temptation and affliction. For the Greek word is ὑπομονή [hypomonē], which means the same as patience. The argument by which he urges faith and patience is taken from the example of the ancients and earlier fathers. This argument is the seventh of the principal exhortation. "Obtain": this is a commendation of the example or deed of the Fathers, that is, of their faith and patience, from the fruit of that faith and patience which at last they received. This commendation is added so that the example of the Fathers may move the Hebrews more. He calls it the promised inheritance because it was promised by word before it was actually given, so that they might first glorify God by believing the word of his promise, before they received the promised thing and were sent into its possession.

units.la: 13 Deus enim pollicitus) Transitio est ad speciale exemplum Abrahæ, & fidei ac patientiæ ipsius, quo quidem exemplo Abrahæ speciali illustrat quod in genere dictum est de fide ac patientia veterum ac piorum Patrum. Hoc itaque versu proponit Deum pollicitum fuisse Abrahæ, adhibito jurejurando, atque eo quidem facto, non per alium, sed per seipsum. Quia non potest) Ratio cur Deus per seipsum juraverit ἀπὸ τῶν ἀδυνάτων; ab impossibili, quia non potuit per quenquam majorem jurare. Quoties enim Iurisiurandi necessitas est, per majorem jurandum est, si modò sit major aliquis, non autem per parem vel inferiorem. At Deo, quum non sit major, necesse est jurare per seipsum. Caussa autem cur per majorem jurandum est, si modò major aliquis sit, hæc est: quia oportet major sit ejus authoritas, quem testem & vindicem appellamus dum juramus, quàm est nostra ipsorum qui juramus, hoc est, oportet ejus fides ac veracitas indubitata sit, & is sit oportet quo nititur omnis veritas.
units.tr: 13 "For God, having promised" is a transition to the special example of Abraham, and of his faith and patience, by which special example he illustrates what was said in general about the faith and patience of the ancient and godly Fathers. In this verse, then, he sets forth that God made a promise to Abraham, with the addition of an oath, and that this was done not through another but through himself. "Because he could not": the reason why God swore by himself, ἀπὸ τῶν ἀδυνάτων [from the impossible]; because he could swear by no greater. For whenever there is necessity of an oath, one must swear by a greater, if indeed there is someone greater, and not by an equal or an inferior. But since God has no one greater, he must swear by himself. The cause why one must swear by a greater, if indeed someone greater exists, is this: the authority of him whom we call as witness and avenger when we swear must be greater than that of us who swear; that is, his faith and truthfulness must be beyond doubt, and he must be that on which all truth rests.

units.la: 14 Dicens certè Postquàm proposuit Deum, cùm pollicitus est Abrahæ, jurasse per seipsum,promissionem illam Dei jurejurando confirmatam in medium affert: Verba hæc petita sunt ex Genef. cap. 22. vers. 17. verba quidem (fateor) non habent expressm aliquod Deijusiurandum: verum ex verbo præcedente in quo dictum est, Deum per seipsum jurasse, constat fuisse ipsius aliquod jusiurandum. Apostolus fortasse hoc Dei jusiurandum ipso loco expressit per particulam ἐπʼ ἐμοῦ hoc est, juxta phrasin Hebraicam, cumulatissimè benedicam. His autem verbis promissio feminis illius benedictionis, h.e. capitis Christi, Abrahamo est facta.
units.tr: 14 "Saying, Surely": after he has set forth that God, when he made promise to Abraham, swore by himself, he brings forward in the midst that promise of God confirmed by an oath. These words are taken from Gen. 22:17. The words indeed (I admit) do not expressly contain any oath of God; but from the preceding word, in which it is said that God swore by himself, it is clear that there was some oath of his. The apostle perhaps expressed this oath of God in that place by the particle ἐπʼ ἐμοῦ [by myself], that is, according to the Hebrew idiom, "I will bless you abundantly." By these words the promise was made to Abraham of that blessing of the seed, that is, of the head, Christ.

units.la: 15 Atque ita cum)Hic habemus speciale illud exemplum fidei & patientiæ Abrahæ: Ac si dixisset, Abraham ex sanctis Patribus vnus, patienter credidit & expectauit promissionis Dei complementum. Effectus est) Hæc est commendatio spei & patientiæ Abrahami, ex euentu siue effectu suo, nempe promissionis complemento, cuiusmodi commendatio fuit supra vers.12.
units.tr: 15 And so when) Here we have that special example of the faith and patience of Abraham, as if he had said: Abraham, one of the holy Fathers, believed patiently and waited for the fulfilment of God's promise. He obtained) This is the commendation of Abraham's hope and patience from its outcome or effect, namely the fulfilment of the promise. It is the same kind of commendation as at verse 12 above.

units.la: 16 Nam homines) Redit ad Dei illam promissionem jureiurando confirmatam, eamque à simili illustrat: similitudo autem sumpta est ab agenda ratione illa, quæ hominibus vsitata est in siniendis controuersiis suis. Similitudinis protasis est hoc versu; ac si dixisset: Homines quidem jurant ad confirmandam promissionem à se factam. Per eum iurant)
units.tr: 16 For men) He returns to God's promise, confirmed by an oath, and illustrates it by a comparison. The comparison is drawn from the practice customary among men in settling their disputes. The protasis of the comparison is in this verse, as if he had said: Men indeed swear to confirm a promise made by themselves. They swear by one)

units.la: Amplificatio est protasçeos, à modo quo jurant homines; Iurant per eum qui ipsis major est, nempe & essentia siue natura sua, & autoritate siue dignitate: Nam jurare non oportet homines, nisi per majorem, non authoritate modò & dignitate, sed & natura & essentia. Vnde jurare per hominem non licet, ne eum quidem qui in authoritate est, & supra nos eminet, vel hac ratione, quòd natura & essentia non fit superior, licet authoritate & dignitate emineat. Non etiam satis est vt is per quem jurat homo, & natura siue essentia sua, & dignitate siue authoritate major sit, nisi etiam is per naturam mentiri non possit, hoc est, immutabilis sit natura cujusmodi est solus Deus. Quamobrem ne per Angelum quidem licet homini jurare, quanquam is, & natura, & dignitate, hominé sit superior. Christum hominem excipio, qui caput est omnis imperij ac potestatis. Colossen. cap. 2. verf. 10. Atque ijdem omnis. Hic finis est cur homines dum promittunt jusiurandum simul adhibent; nempè vt omnis controuersiæ finis sit, jam adhibito ad promissionem, siue omnino verbum, iureiurando. Nota igitur, Non iurandum nisi in iudicio, & coram iudice aliquo, idque eo fine vt decidantur controuersiæ. Nota etiam ex his verbis, legitimam esse iudicij illam formam, qua iureiurando finiuntur controuersiæ.
units.tr: This is an amplification of the protasis, drawn from the manner in which men swear. They swear by one who is greater than themselves, both in his essence or nature and in his authority or dignity. For men ought not to swear except by one greater, not only in authority and dignity but also in nature and essence. Hence it is not lawful to swear by a man, not even by one who holds authority and stands above us, for the reason that in nature and essence he is not superior, though he excels in authority and dignity. Nor is it enough that the one by whom a man swears be greater both in nature or essence and in dignity or authority, unless he is also one who cannot lie by nature, that is, one whose nature is unchangeable, as is the nature of God alone. For this reason it is not lawful even to swear by an angel, although he is superior to man both in nature and in dignity. I make an exception for Christ as man, who is the head of every rule and power. Colossians cap. 2. vers. 10. And so this is the end for which men, when they make a promise, at the same time add an oath: namely, so that every dispute may be ended by the oath now added to the promise, or indeed the whole matter settled by it. Note, therefore, that one must swear only in a court, and before some judge, and for the purpose of ending disputes. Note also from these words that this form of judicial procedure, by which disputes are ended by an oath, is lawful.

units.la: {y} Colossen. cap. 2. verf. 10.
units.tr: {y} Colossians cap. 2. vers. 10.

units.la: 17 Qua inre) Similitudinis apodosis ad si dixisset, Sic & Deus fidejussit iureiurando, hoc est, iurauit vt confirmaret fidam à se promissionem; Volens ex abundanti) His verbis habes consilium Dei, siue finem quem respexit in iurando, hunc nempe vt offenderet immutabilitatem consilij sui, ac per consequens immutabilitatem promissionis, quae ex aeterno illo consilio profecta est. In antecedente enim consequens intelligendum est. Nam hoc notandum est, nihil Deum promisisse, vel omnino locutum esse, quod non prius in aeterno illo consilio suo deliberatum & conclusum fuit Rom. 8. 18. dicit vocari nos ex proposito ipsius. Ergo verbum illud quo nos vocat in tempore, ante tempora saecularia conclusum fuit in aeterno illo Dei consilio. Est & his verbis modus, quo fidejussit Deus iureiurando. Modus autem est ex abundantia: Abundantia opponitur necessitas, nimirum quae simplex est, & quae Deum respicit. Nam si Deum respicias, quum ipsius nuda promissio firma sit ac immutabilis, nulla necessitas est cur ad promissionem addatur iusiurandum. Necessitas autem est κατα τι & respectu nostri, quibus nuda promissio non sufficit, qua sumus per naturam incredulitate & infirmitate. Eadem est ratio Sacramentorum quae est iurisiurandi. Nam & ijs non indiget Dei verbum, per se quidem firmum & immutabile, verum ex Dei miserimisericordia, propter infirmitatem nostram, ex abundanti verbo Dei sunt addita. Verbi autem ipsius & promissionum Dei simplex est necessitas. Haeredibus) Hi sunt in quorum gratiam, & promittit Deus, & jurat: nempe hæredes vitæ æternæ. Nota igitur, promissiones Dei, licet quoad prædicationem earum ad omnes etiam reprobos sese extendant, tamen quoad efficaciam non pertinere nisi ad electos Dei. (Fideiussit iureiurando) Verbum græcum ἐμεσίτευσεν, quod significat interponere iusjurandum, siue jurisiurandi interpositione uti dum promissio sit: Nam iusiurandum est quasi Mediator inter Deum promittentem, & homines credentes, quod ideo interuenit, ut homines Deo promittenti magis credant.
units.tr: 17 Wherefore) The apodosis of the comparison answers to "as if he had said": So also God gave surety by an oath, that is, he swore in order to confirm the promise made by himself. Desiring abundantly) In these words you have God's counsel, or the purpose he had in view in swearing, namely that he might show the immutability of his counsel and, consequently, the immutability of the promise, which proceeded from that eternal counsel. For the consequent is to be understood in the antecedent. Note that God has promised nothing, or spoken at all, that was not first deliberated and determined in that eternal counsel of his. Romans 8:18 says that we are called according to his purpose. Therefore the word by which he calls us in time was determined in that eternal counsel of God before the ages of time. This phrase also states the manner in which God gave surety by an oath. The manner is "abundantly". Abundance is opposed to necessity, which is the simple necessity that regards God. For if you look at God, since his bare promise is firm and unchangeable, there is no necessity for an oath to be added to the promise. Necessity, however, is in some respect [κατα τι] and with regard to us, to whom a bare promise is not sufficient, since by nature we are prone to unbelief and weakness. The reason for the sacraments is the same as that for the oath. For God's word does not need them either, since it is firm and unchangeable in itself; but out of God's great mercy, on account of our weakness, they have been added abundantly to the word of God. The word itself and the promises of God have only a simple necessity. To the heirs) These are the ones for whose benefit God both promises and swears, namely the heirs of eternal life. Note, therefore, that although God's promises extend to all, even to the reprobate, as regards their proclamation, nevertheless as regards their efficacy they pertain only to the elect of God. (He gave surety by an oath) The Greek word emesiteusen means to interpose an oath, or to use the interposition of an oath while a promise is being made. For the oath is as it were a mediator between God promising and men believing, and it intervenes so that men may believe God's promise more firmly.

units.la: Vt per duas) Superiùs finis fuit cur fidejusserat Deus iureiurando, hoc est, iusiurandum promissioni suæ adhibuerit. Nunc hoc versu finis est cui & promiserit & iurauerit, nempe vt validam consolationem habeamus per duas res immutabiles, nempe promissionem Dei primùm, quæ suapte natura immutabilis est; Deinde per jusiurandum Dei, quod similiter immutabile est. Tria sunt hic immutabilia: Consilium Dei versu præcedenti; promissio Dei, & jusiurandum Dei hoc versu. His tribus nititur fides & consolatio nostra, licet hoc versu meminerit tantùm duarum rerum, nempe promissionis & jurisiurandi In quibus fieri) Ratio est cur posititis illis duabus rebus immutabilibus, necesse est vt validam habeamus consolationem. Sensus horum verborum est, quod postquam Deus promisit simul & iurauit, fieri non potest vt mentiatur, hoc est, non praestet quod promisit simul & iurauit: Is enim dicitur mentiri, qui quod promisit se facturum, quod etiam iurauit, id non praestat. Validam consolationem) Sub valida consolatione quae effectum est, intelligenda venit hoc loco πληροφορία fidei, hoc est, certa fidei perfuasio, quae causa est consolationis validae. Nomine enim consolationis intelligo pacem illam quae est erga Deum, & quae superat omnem intellectum, & quam Apostolus Rom. 5. 1. ex fide tanquam causa sua deducit: Iustificati igitur ex fide pacem habemus erga Deum. Consolationem igitur iam validam necesse est antegrediatur fides firma. Hic vnicus locus sufficit ad conuincendam aduersariorum illam doctrinam, qua tradunt oportere nos dubitare de salute nostra ac vita aeterna. Nam dubitationis doctrinam tradere, quid quaeso aliud est quam docere, tam promissionem Dei, quam ipsius iurandum mutabile esse, adeoque etiam ipsum Dei consilium aeternum, ex quo ista sunt, mutabile esse. Quod si haec tria mutabilia sint, Annon oportet ipsum Deum esse mutabilem? quae summa est in Deum blasphemia: Quod si robiciant, jiciant, firmam istam fidem & consolationem validam non accipiendam de singulis fidelibus, sed indefinite de Ecclesia Dei ;. Refpondeo exemplum hoc Abrahami, hoc est, certi cuiufdam & singularis hominis, cujus paulo ante fa&a est mentio, & cui Deus promisit simul & iurauit, in eundem hunc finem, vt validam haberet consolationem : exemplum, inquam, hoc Abrahami fatis fupe{que arguere; quod, & promittat, & iuret Deus, in gratiam vniuscuiusque fidelis, vt is nominatim firmam habeat fidem & validam consolationem. Nos qui currum ) Periphrasis quædam est & descriptio eorum, ad quos pertinet valida ista consolatio, de qua locutus est proxime, & ad quos etiam pertinent duæ illæ res immutabiles, quibus valida ista consolatio nititur. Sunt nimirum ij qui currum eo corripuerunt, vt spem propositam obtineant, hoc est, qui ingressi sunt hoc studium Christiani cursoris, & in currendo durant ac perseuerant. Atque hic reuertitur Apostolus ad principalem exhortationem, qua ad perfeuerantiam in fide & professione adhortatur. Hujus autem exhortationis argumentum est hoc loco oftauum. Ex his nota: Non nisi ad eos qui student perseuerare in fide & professione pertinere consolationem validam.
units.tr: That by two) Above, the purpose for which God gave surety by an oath was stated, that is, why he applied an oath to his promise. Now in this verse the end is stated for which he both promised and swore: namely, that we may have strong consolation through two immutable things: first, God's promise, which is immutable by its very nature; and second, God's oath, which is likewise immutable. There are three immutable things here: God's counsel in the preceding verse, God's promise, and God's oath in this verse. Our faith and consolation rest on these three, although in this verse he mentions only two things, namely the promise and the oath. In which it is impossible) This is the reason why, since these two immutable things are set, we must have strong consolation. The sense of these words is that, since God has both promised and sworn, it is impossible for him to lie, that is, to fail to perform what he promised and also swore to do. For he is said to lie who does not perform what he promised he would do and also swore to do. Strong consolation) By the strong consolation which is the effect here is to be understood the fullness of assurance [πληροφορία] of faith, that is, the certain persuasion of faith, which is the cause of strong consolation. By consolation I understand that peace which is toward God, which surpasses all understanding, and which the Apostle in Romans 5:1 derives from faith as its cause: Being justified by faith, we have peace toward God. Therefore firm faith must go before strong consolation. This one passage is sufficient to refute the doctrine of our opponents, who teach that we ought to doubt our salvation and eternal life. For what else is it, I ask, to teach doubt than to teach that God's promise and his oath are both changeable, and hence also his eternal counsel, from which these things come, is changeable? And if these three things are changeable, must not God himself be changeable? This is the greatest blasphemy against God. But if they object that this firm faith and strong consolation are not to be taken of each believer individually, but indefinitely of the Church of God, I reply that the example of Abraham, that is, of a certain and particular man, mentioned a little before, and to whom God both promised and swore for this same end, that he might have strong consolation, is enough to prove, I say, that God both promises and swears for the sake of each believer, so that each one by name may have firm faith and strong consolation. We who have fled for refuge) This is a kind of periphrasis and description of those to whom this strong consolation belongs, of whom he spoke just now, and to whom also those two immutable things belong, on which this strong consolation rests. They are, namely, those who have taken hold of the course so as to obtain the hope set before them, that is, who have entered upon this study of the Christian runner and persist and persevere in the running. Here the Apostle returns to his principal exhortation, by which he urges perseverance in faith and profession. The argument of this exhortation is the eighth argument in this passage. From this note: strong consolation pertains only to those who strive to persevere in faith and profession.

units.la: 19 Quam velut anima anchoram habemus tutam ac firmam, & ingredientem vsque in ea quæ sunt intra velum.
units.tr: 19 Which we have as a sure and firm anchor of the soul, and which enters even within the veil.

units.la: 20 Quo pracurfor pro nobis ingressus est Iesus, secundum ordinem Melchisedec, Pontifex factus in aeternum.
units.tr: 20 Where the forerunner Jesus has entered on our behalf, according to the order of Melchizedek, made a high priest for ever.

units.la: Quam velut) Digreditur ab instituta exhortatione in definitionem quandam spei, cujus proxime meminit. Genus in definitione metaphoricum est, id quod indicat particula ista (velut) Est enim spes, in qua fidem intelligo (Nam fides & spes in Scripturis indifferenter solent accipi) Est, inquam fides, siue spes, quasi anchora animæ nostræ tanquam nauis. Est enim ea natura sua instabilis & fluctuans, ac circumferetur quouis vento vel leuissimo. Eph. 4. 14.
units.tr: Which as) He departs from the exhortation he had set out, into a certain definition of hope, of which he has just made mention. The genus in the definition is metaphorical, as the particle "as" indicates. For hope, by which I understand faith (for faith and hope are commonly taken interchangeably in Scripture), is, I say, faith or hope, as an anchor of our soul, as of a ship. For by its nature it is unstable and tossed about, and is carried round by every wind, even the lightest. Eph. 4. 14.

units.la: Tutam ac firmam) Differentiæ fidei ac spei sequuntur: Prima est, quòd anchora sit tuta, nempe ab omni iniuria & tentationum infultu. Secunda est quod Anchora sit firma, hoc est, firmiter fundata, & fixa, hæc prioris caussa est. Et ingredientem) Hæc tertia est quasi differentia in definitione spei, à loco illo in quem ingreditur, nempe cœlis ipsis, imò supremo & intimo cœlo, siue loco qui est longè supra omnes cœlos. Ephes. 4. 10. Cujus quidem loci sacrarium illud siue sanctum sanctorum veteris Tabernaculi, typus quidam fuit Sacrarium enim siue sanctum sanctorum, velo distinctum erat à sancto quod vocant, siue Tabernaculo exteriori.
units.tr: Sure and firm) The differences between faith and hope follow. The first is that the anchor is sure, namely from every injury and from the assault of temptations. The second is that the anchor is firm, that is, firmly grounded and fixed; this is the cause of the first. And entering) This is the third difference, as it were, in the definition of hope, drawn from the place into which it enters, namely the heavens themselves, indeed the highest and innermost heaven, or the place which is far above all the heavens. Eph. 4. 10. And that place, the sanctuary or holy of holies of the old Tabernacle, was in a certain way a type of it. For the sanctuary, or holy of holies, was separated by the veil from what they call the holy place, or the outer Tabernacle.

units.la: 20 Quo pracursor) Ratio quædam est cur fides siue spes nostra ingrediatur vsque in sacrarium : sumpta est ab Iesu Christo, ejusque tanquam praecursoris in coelos ingressu, eoque pro nobis, nempe vt pararet nobis in coeliis locum. Ioan. 1. 41. secundum ordinem) Definitio quaedam Christi adjecta est ab ejus Pontificatu, & certi cujusdam generis Pontificatu. Ergo in hac definitione Christi, Pontifex est quasi genus. Ordo Melchisedec, & aeternitas Pontificatus ipsius, quasi differentiae, quibus distinguitur Pontificatus Christi a Pontificatu Aaronis. Atque hic quidem redit ad doctrinam illa de Melchisedeco Pontifice propositam supra cap. 5. vers. 11. quo loco de Melchisedeco multa dicenda proposituit. Ab eo enim loco, in hunc usque locum perpetua fuit digressio ab eo de quo ibi dicendum instituit.
units.tr: 20 Where the forerunner) There is a certain reason why our faith or hope enters even into the sanctuary; it is taken from Jesus Christ and from his entry into the heavens as forerunner, and so on our behalf, namely that he might prepare a place for us in the heavens. John 1. 41. According to the order) A certain definition of Christ is added from his priesthood, and from a certain kind of priesthood. So in this definition of Christ, "high priest" is as it were the genus. The order of Melchizedek and the eternity of his priesthood are as it were the differences by which the priesthood of Christ is distinguished from the priesthood of Aaron. And indeed here he returns to the doctrine about the priest Melchizedek proposed above in chapter 5, verse 11, where he proposed to say many things about Melchizedek. For from that place to this one there has been a continuous digression from that which he had there set out to discuss.

units.la: Argumentum Capitis septimi.
units.tr: The argument of the seventh chapter.

units.la: Primum hoc capite agitur de Melchisedeco, Christi Pontificis typo. Ac primum quidem ejus est descriptio, ad vers. 4. Deinde praestantia ejus probatur ad vers. 11. Secundo hoc capite probat mutatum esse sacerdotium legale, pariter & Ministerium legale, ad vers. 10. Postremo de Iesu agit, cujus typus erat Melchisedec, eiusque praestantiam prae Leviticis sacerdotibus, probat ad finem usque capitis.
units.tr: In the first place, in this chapter, Melchizedek is treated, the type of Christ the High Priest. First, his description is given, up to verse 4. Then his excellence is proved, to verse 11. Secondly, in this chapter he proves that the Levitical priesthood has been changed, and likewise the Levitical ministry, to verse 10. Lastly, he deals with Jesus, of whom Melchizedek was a type, and proves his excellence above the Levitical priests, to the end of the chapter.

units.la: CAPVT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: 1 Nam hic Melchisedec Rex erat Salem. Pontifex Dei altissimi, qui occurrit Abraha revertenti a caede regum & benedixit ei,
units.tr: 1 For this Melchisedec was king of Salem, priest of the most high God, who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him,

units.la: 2 Cui & decimas ex omnibus impartitus est Abraham :qui primum quidem ex interpretatione dicitur rex iustitia : deinde Vere etiam rex Salem: quod est Rex pacis.
units.tr: 2 to whom also he gave a tenth of all, Abraham who is first, by interpretation, called king of righteousness; then truly also king of Salem, which is king of peace.

units.la: 3 Sine Patre, sine Matre, sine genere : nec initium dierum, neque Vita finem habens : sed assimilatus Filio Dei, manet Sacerdos in perpetuum.
units.tr: 3 Without father, without mother, without descent; having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like to the Son of God, he remains a priest for ever.

units.la: 4 Spectate Vero quantus hic fuerit, cui etiam decimas spoliorum dederit Abraham Patriarcha.
units.tr: 4 Behold how great this man was, to whom even Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth of the spoils.

units.la: 5 Et ij quidem qui sunt ex filijs Leui Sacerdotio fungentes, præceptum habent decimarum accipiendarum a populo secundum Legem, hoc est a fratribus suis, licet egressis ex lumbis Abraha.
units.tr: 5 And indeed those of the sons of Levi who discharge the priesthood have a commandment, according to the Law, to take tithes from the people, that is, from their brethren, although they have come forth from the loins of Abraham.

units.la: 6 Is Vero cuius genus ad illos non refertur, decimas accepit ab Abraham, & habenti promissiones benedixit.
units.tr: 6 But he whose lineage is not traced back to them took tithes from Abraham and blessed him who had the promises.

units.la: 7 Porro sine Vlla controuersia id quod minus est ab eo quod maius est benedicitur.
units.tr: 7 Moreover, beyond all dispute, the lesser is blessed by the greater.

units.la: 8 Atque hic quidem homines qui moriuntur, decimas accipiunt : illic autem is de quo testatum est quod Viuat.
units.tr: 8 And here indeed mortal men receive tithes, but there one of whom it is witnessed that he lives.

units.la: 9 Et (Vt ita loquar) in Abraham decimatus est etiam ipse Leui, qui decimas solet accipere.
units.tr: 9 And (so to speak) Levi himself, who is wont to receive tithes, was tithed in Abraham.

units.la: 10 Nam is adhuc in lumbis patris erat, quum occurreret Abraha Melchisedec.
units.tr: 10 For he was still in the loins of his father when Melchisedec met Abraham.

units.la: Nam hic Melchisedec ) Redit ad id quod de Melchisedeco dicendum proposuit cap.5. vers. 11. Nam inde à versu 12. illius capitis, digressus ligressus est ad hunc vsque locum, Hic igi‐ur propositam ibi de Melchisedeco doctri‐ nam persequi instituit. Primùm autem hoc capite est Melchisedeci descriptio: describi‐tur autem vt typus erat Christi, ac proinde omnes descriptionis partes de Melchisedeco typicè accipiendæ sunt : de Christo autem verè ac proprie intelligendæ. Rex erat Sa‐ lem) Descriptionis pars prima ab officio Re‐ gio, quo Christum illum Regem adumbra‐ uit. Pontifex) Secunda descriptionis pars ab officio Sacerdotali, quo etiam Christum il‐ lum Pontificem figurauit. Altissimi ) Hoc Dei epithetum & adjunctum commendat of‐ ficium. Nam quo Deus excellentior , eò di‐ gnior ejus Pontifex est. Qui occurrit ) Ter‐tia descriptionis pars, à certa quadam functio‐ne officij & muneris Regij: Occurrit Abra‐ hæ reuertenti à cæde regum , proferens pa‐ nem & vinum , non offerens sacrificium , vt volunt aduersarij. Atque hoc factum Regis fuit, non Pontificis. Vide de hoc Genes. 14. vers. 18. Et benedixit ei) Quarta descriptio‐ nis pars, à functione officij sacerdotalis. Nam Pontificis est & Sacerdotis benedicere. Si loquamur proprie solus Deus & Christus be‐ nedicit : homines autem olim benedixerunt vt Christi quidam typi. Nunc autem post ad‐ uentum Christi ipsius, qui corpus est, homines benedicunt, non vt typi, sed vt serui & ministri ejus,ipsius nomine.
units.tr: For this Melchisedec) He returns to what he proposed to say about Melchisedec in chapter 5, verse 11. For from verse 12 of that chapter he had digressed as far as this place; here therefore he sets out to pursue the doctrine about Melchisedec proposed there. First, in this chapter, comes the description of Melchisedec, and he is described as a type of Christ; therefore all parts of the description are to be taken typically of Melchisedec, but understood truly and properly of Christ. King of Salem) The first part of the description is from the kingly office, by which he foreshadowed Christ as King. Priest) The second part of the description is from the priestly office, by which he also prefigured Christ as Priest. Of the Most High) This epithet of God and this addition commend the office. For the more excellent God is, the more worthy his priest. Who met) The third part of the description is from a certain function of the kingly office and duty: he met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings, bringing out bread and wine, not offering a sacrifice, as the adversaries maintain. And this was an act of a king, not of a priest. See on this Genesis 14, verse 18. And blessed him) The fourth part of the description is from the function of the priestly office. For it belongs to a priest and a sacrificer to bless. Properly speaking, God alone and Christ bless; men, however, formerly blessed as certain types of Christ. Now, however, after the coming of Christ himself, who is the body, men bless, not as types but as his servants and ministers, in his name.

units.la: Cui & decimas) Quinta descriptionis pars, à persolutis eiab Abrahamo spoliorum decimis, quo facto Abraham eum Dei Pontificem, & Christi venturi typum agnouit. Ex omnibus)Nempe spoliis:nihil enim spoliorum illorum fuit quod non est decimatum; ad hoc vt essetintegra & perfecta illa decimarum oblatio. Ex hoc loco videri potest decimarum perfolutionem aliquo modo naturalem esse: Nam tum nulla decimis lata fuit Lex ceremonialis. Decimae enim proprie & primum ad Deum ipsum pertinebant. Oblationes autem quaecunque debentur Deo, vt sacrificiorum & aliarum rerum, principium suum habent aliquo modo à natura ipsa, & hominum conscientia. Qui primum quidem) Sexta descriptionis pars, à notatione & definitione nominum quae habuit Melchisedec: vocatus enim primum est Melchisedec, hoc est, Rex Iustitiae, deinde Melchi Salem, hoc est, Rex pacis. Vtroque hoc nomine figurauit Christum, qui proprie appellatur & Rex Iustitiae, nempe illius aeternae & per fidem imputatae: & Rex pacis, quae fidei fructus est, & iustitiae per fidem imputatae: Iustificati enim per fidem pacem habemus erga Deum. Rom. 5.1.
