units.tr: To whom also he gave tithes) The fifth part of the description is from the tithes of the spoils paid to him by Abraham, by which deed Abraham recognised him as God's priest and a type of the Christ who was to come. Of all) Namely of the spoils; for none of those spoils was left untithed, so that the offering of tithes might be whole and complete. From this place it can be seen that the payment of tithes is in some way natural, for no ceremonial law concerning tithes had yet been given. Tithes properly and primarily belonged to God himself. Offerings of whatever kind owed to God, such as sacrifices and other things, have their origin in some way in nature itself and in the conscience of men. Who first indeed) The sixth part of the description is from the interpretation and definition of the names which Melchisedec had: he is called first Melchisedec, that is, King of Righteousness, and then Melchi Salem, that is, King of Peace. By both names he foreshadowed Christ, who is properly called both King of Righteousness, namely of that eternal righteousness imputed through faith, and King of Peace, which is the fruit of faith and of the righteousness imputed through faith: for being justified by faith we have peace with God. Romans 5:1.

units.la: 5 Sine Patre) Septima descriptionis pars, ex eo quod expers fuerat omnis cognationis, & consanguinitatis naturalis & terrenae, ad morem rem em aliorum hominum, Hoc argumentum exlicatur tribus membris. Primum est quod ine Patre fuerat: Secundum quod fine matre: Tertiu quod omnino fine genere & γενεαλογία extiterit. Genef. 14. vnde hæc deprompta sunt, nō habentur ista totidem verbis, sed quia illic nulla fit mentio Patris, Matris,& omninò generis Melchifedeci, ideò silentium illud Mosis, vel potiùs Spiritus fanéti eo in loco, sic interpretatur Apostolus hoc loco, ac fi expresse fuisset scriptum, Melchifedecum, neque Patrem, neque Matrem, neq; genus habuisse. Nam certum est, Mosem ideo non meminisse, vel Patris, vel Matris, vel omninò generis Melchifedeci; quia is erat Christi venturi typus, & Deus voluit ignorari Melchifedeci & Patrem, & Matrem, & omninò genus, vt ab hominibus pro typo Christi haberetur.Quamobrem nimis temerè mihi videntur facere qui inuito quasi Deo,Patrem,Matrem,& omninò genus Melchifedeci volunt cognoscere. Vtut est, hæc proprie in Christum competunt, qui ἀπάτωρ fuit quâ homo, conceptus nimirùm per Spiritū sanctum: ἀμήτωρ fuit quâ Deus, vtpote Dei Filius ab æterno genitus: Licèt etiam sint qui dicant, quâ homo eum ἀμήτορα fuisse, quia mater ejus Virgo erat, ideóque proprie non dicenda mater: Denique fine genere, cognatione, & consanguinitate ista naturali fuit quâ Deus, & Dei Filius. Videtur Paulus 2. Cor. 5.
units.tr: 5 Without father) The seventh part of the description is from his being free of all natural and earthly kinship and blood-relationship, as other men are. This argument is unfolded in three members. The first is that he was without father; the second, that he was without mother; the third, that he was altogether without descent and genealogy. Where these things are drawn from Genesis 14, they are not stated in so many words; but because there is no mention there of Melchisedec's father, mother, or descent at all, the Apostle here interprets that silence of Moses, or rather of the Holy Spirit, in that place, as if it had been expressly written that Melchisedec had neither father, nor mother, nor descent. For it is certain that Moses made no mention of Melchisedec's father, or mother, or descent at all, because he was a type of the Christ who was to come, and God willed that Melchisedec's father, mother and descent should be unknown, so that he might be taken by men for a type of Christ. Wherefore those seem to me to act too rashly who, as if against God's will, want to know Melchisedec's father, mother and descent. However that may be, these things properly apply to Christ: as man he was ἀπάτωρ (without father), conceived, namely, by the Holy Spirit; as God he was ἀμήτωρ (without mother), being the Son of God begotten from eternity. Although there are also those who say that as man he was ἀμήτωρ, because his mother was a virgin and therefore should not properly be called a mother. Finally, he was without descent, kinship and natural blood-relationship as God and as the Son of God. Paul seems, in 2 Corinthians 5, to profess that he would know Christ henceforth without these things, without father, mother and all descent, when he says: "Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer. For in Christ those old things, even those in which this human kinship lies, have now passed away, and all things have become new."

units.la: 16. profiteri se Christum sine his, Patre, Matre omninoque genere, in posterum cogniturum, cum dicit: Quod si etiam nouimus Christum secundum carnem, nunc tamen non amplius nouimus. Nam in Christo illa vetera, etiam in quibus est cognatio ista humana, jam praeterierunt, & noua facta iunt omnia. Nec initium dierum) Victima descriptionis pars, ab eius aeternitate, quam ex eo colligit Apostolus, quod in illo Genesisloco nulla mentio fiat, vel ortus, vel mortis Melchisedeci. De Melchisedeco quidem hoc dictum est typice, de Christo autem vere & proprie accipiendum. Nam is vere aeternus est, quum Deus sit ab aeterno in aeternum, & Pontifex etiam in aeternum, non tantum qua Deus est, sed etiam qua homo. Fortasse non male accipienda sunt, quae hoc loco dicuntur de Christo, non tam habita ratione naturarum ejus, quam officij, hoc est, Pontificatus ejus. Ut enim Pontifex est, neque genus habet, neque principium, neque finem. Ideo hic dictum est, eum manere Sacerdotem in perpetuum. Sed assimilatus) Cauflam innuit aeternitatis siue perpetuitatis hujus Melchisedeci, ex eo quod typus fuerit Christi, ac proinde assimilatus fuerit ei.
units.tr: 16. Paul seems to profess that he would know Christ henceforth without these, without father, mother and all descent. Nor beginning of days) The eighth part of the description is from his eternity, which the Apostle infers from the fact that in that passage of Genesis no mention is made of either the birth or the death of Melchisedec. This was said of Melchisedec typically, but is to be understood of Christ truly and properly. For he is truly eternal, since he is God from eternity to eternity, and priest for ever, not only as God but also as man. Perhaps what is said here of Christ may rightly be taken not so much with regard to his natures as to his office, that is, his priesthood. For as Priest he has neither descent, nor beginning, nor end; therefore it is said here that he remains a priest for ever. But made like) He indicates the cause of this eternity or perpetuity of Melchisedec: he was a type of Christ and therefore was made like him.

units.la: 14 Spectatae Vero) Occasione descriptionis proximae, de excellentia Melchisedeci, agit Apostolus. Propositio excellentiae est cum praefatiuncula quadam, qua attentionem conciliat.Spectate, inquit, Propositionis sententia est, ac si dixisset, Melchisedec ipse magnus fuit & excellens. Cui etiam decimas) Argumenta excellentiae ipsius omnia ex proxima descriptione sunt desumpta. Quorum primum hoc est, a decimis spoliorum Melchisedeco persolutis, etiam ab ipso Abrahamo Patriarcha. Epitheton hoc Patriarchae amplificat honorem hunc ab Abrahamo delatum Melchisedeco.
units.tr: 14 Behold, indeed) On the occasion of the preceding description, the Apostle treats of the excellence of Melchisedec. The statement of his excellence comes with a little introductory word that wins attention: "Behold," he says. The sense of the proposition is as if he had said, Melchisedec himself was great and excellent. To whom also he gave a tenth) All the arguments for his excellence are drawn from the preceding description. The first of these is that Abraham the patriarch himself paid tithes of the spoils to Melchisedec. This epithet of patriarch magnifies the honour which Abraham bestowed on Melchisedec.

units.la: 5 Et ij quidem) Haec quoque altera est amplificatio facti illius Abrahami; a dissimili comparatione decimarum quas accepit Melchisedec, & decimarum quas accipiunt sacerdotes Leuitici. Leuitici sacerdotes accipiunt decimas suas a populo, h.e. a fratribus suis, idque ex Legis Dei praescripto. At vero Melchisedec decimas accepit ab ipso Abrahamo. Protasis est hoc versu : apodosis sequenti. Qui sunt) Periphrasis est sacerdotum Leviticorum. Praeceptum habent) Ratio est cur accipiant decimas, a Dei mandato. Hoc est a) Definitio quaedam populi a fraterna illa conjunctione quam habent Leuitae cum populo : quasi dicat, Leuitae accipiunt decimas ab iis qui sunt ex communi secum stirpe. Licet egressis ex lumbis) Amplificatio quaedam est facti hujus populi, sive fratrum, ac si dicat: Licet egressi sint ex lumbis Abrahae, quemadmodum & ipsi Leuitae, tamen persoluunt ex praescripto Legis Dei Leuiticis sacerdotibus decimas, tanquam ipsis maioribus: Maior enim cui persoluuntur decimæ, quàm is qui persoluit eas. Nota Deum & ipsius verbum dispares efficere eos qui alioqui sunt pares. Quis te discernit, inquit Paulus? quid autem habes quod non acceperis? 1. Corinth. 4. 7. Cuius genus) hoc est, qui non est ex stirpe Leuitica. Et habenti) Secundum est excellentiæ Melchisedeci argumentum, à functione illa officij sacerdotalis, in benedicendo, de qua suprain descriptione. Factum autem hoc Melchisedeci in benedicendo exaggerat à conditione Abrahami. Is enim erat Abraham ad quem promissiones Dei pertinebant.
units.tr: 5 And indeed those of the sons of Levi) This is a second amplification of that deed of Abraham, drawn from the unlike comparison between the tithes received by Melchisedec and the tithes received by the Levitical priests. The Levitical priests receive their tithes from the people, that is, from their brothers, and this by the prescription of God's Law. But Melchisedec received tithes from Abraham himself. The protasis is in this verse, and the apodosis in the following one. Who are) This is a periphrasis for the Levitical priests. Have a commandment) This gives the reason why they receive tithes: by God's command. That is, of) A certain definition of the people, taken from the brotherly bond which the Levites have with the people, as if he said: the Levites receive tithes from those who are of the same stock as themselves. Although they have come out of the loins) This is an amplification of the deed of this people, or of the brothers, as if he said: although they have come out of the loins of Abraham, just as the Levites themselves have, nevertheless they pay tithes to the Levitical priests, according to the prescription of God's Law, as to their elders; for the one to whom tithes are paid is greater than the one who pays them. Note that God and his Word make unequal those who are otherwise equal. "Who makes you to differ?" says Paul. "What have you that you did not receive?" 1 Corinthians 4:7. Whose genealogy) that is, one who is not of the Levitical stock. And had the promises) This is the second argument for the excellence of Melchisedec, drawn from that function of the priestly office, namely blessing, which was described above. Moreover, this deed of Melchisedec in blessing is magnified by the condition of Abraham, for he was the one to whom God's promises belonged.

units.la: 7 Porrò sine) Ex eo quòd Melchisedec benedixerit Abrahæ, concludit Melchisedecum Abrahamo excellentiorem, in hanc formam. Id quod minus est ab eo quod majus est benedicitur. At à Melchisedeco benedictus est Abraham. Ergo Melchisedec Abrahamo major est.
units.tr: 7 And without any contradiction) From the fact that Melchisedec blessed Abraham, he concludes that Melchisedec is greater than Abraham, in this form: what is less is blessed by what is greater. But Abraham was blessed by Melchisedec. Therefore Melchisedec is greater than Abraham.

units.la: 8 Atque hic quidem) Tertium argumentum excellentiæ Melchisedeci sacerdotis, ab ipsius æternitate. Illustratum autem est ex dissimili comparatione sacerdotum Leuiticorum, qui moriuntur omnes. Sacerdotum Leuiticorum hoc loco periphrasis quædam est, & descriptio, ex decimis quas accipiunt, vt & Melchisedeci ab acceptis decimis circumscriptio est. De quo testatum) Probat eum in æternum viuere, ex testimonio Scripturæ, quæ nullum verbum habet de ejus morte. Genef. 14. Cùm igitur Scriptura silentio prætereat ejus mortè, idque dedita opera, ad hoc vt esset typus Christi, sequitur igitur eū viuere & manere in æternū. Nota differimé inter Pontificé Leuitici ordinis, & Pontificem hujus ordinis in quo erat Melchisedec. Leuitici ordinis Pontifices, qui totidem erant typi venturi Christi, varij erant, aliisque aliis tempore succedebant. At verò hujus ordinis in quo erat Melchisedec, vnicus tantum numero fuit Pontifex. Vnicum autem oportuit esse, quia æternus fuit, nec initium dierum, nec vitæ finem habens.
units.tr: 8 And here indeed) This is the third argument for the excellence of Melchisedec the priest, drawn from his eternity. It is illustrated by the unlike comparison with the Levitical priests, who all die. In this place the Levitical priests are described by a certain periphrasis, from the tithes they receive, just as Melchisedec is described by his receiving of tithes. Of whom it is testified) He proves that he lives for ever from the testimony of Scripture, which says nothing of his death (Genesis 14). Since Scripture therefore passes over his death in silence, and that deliberately, so that he might be a type of Christ, it follows that he lives and remains for ever. Note the difference between the priest of the Levitical order and the priest of that order to which Melchisedec belonged. The priests of the Levitical order, who were all types of the coming Christ, were many, and they succeeded one another in turn. But in that order to which Melchisedec belonged there was only one priest in number. And he had to be one, because he was eternal, having neither beginning of days nor end of life.

units.la: 9 Et Ἡ ) Argumentum excellentiæ Melchisedeci quartum, ex eo quod non tantum ab Abrahamo decimas acceperit Melchisedec, sed etiam in Abrahamo ab ipso Leui, qui patet erat Leuiticorum omnium sacerdotum. Ex quo sequitur, Melchisedecum excellentem quendam fuisse viru, & sacerdotibus Leuiticis omnibus excellentiorem.
units.tr: 9 And, as it were, Levi himself: this is the fourth argument for the excellence of Melchisedec, namely that Melchisedec received tithes not only from Abraham but also, in Abraham, from Levi himself, who was the father of all the Levitical priests. From this it follows that Melchisedec was a certain excellent man, and more excellent than all the Levitical priests.

units.la: 10 Nam si adhuc) Probat in Abrahamo decimatum esse Leui, ex eo quod Leuitum nondum genitus fuerit in lumbis Abrahæ, quum Melchisedec decimas ab Abrahamo accepit, quo tempore Melchisedec Abrahamo redeunti à cæde Regum occurrit. Nota ex hoc, factum parentis pariter esse factum feminis
units.tr: 10 For if it were yet: He proves that Levi paid tithes in Abraham, because Levi had not yet been begotten in the loins of Abraham when Melchisedec received tithes from Abraham, at the time when Melchisedec met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings. Note from this that the deed of the parent is likewise the deed of the offspring, while the offspring is in the parent's loins, when the parent himself does something.

units.la: G quod est in ipsius lumbis, tum cum ipse facit aliquid. Hoc modo factum Abrahami pariter fuit factum Leui nondum geniti, & Leuiticorum omnium sacerdotum, qui cum Patre suo Leui pariter in lumbis erant Abrahae cum decimas dedit Melchisedeco, Hoc modo etiam primum illud Adami peccatum, fuit pariter nostrum omnium, qui tum in ejus lumbis fuimus quum ipse peccauit. Ideo Apostolus Rom. 5. 12. in Adamo dicit nos omnes peccasse: peccatum autem Adami in nos deriuatum est, & ratione naturae corruptionis, & ratione reatus actualis ipsius peccati, & desectionis.
units.tr: In this way the deed of Abraham was equally the deed of Levi, not yet born, and of all the Levitical priests, who together with their father Levi were in the loins of Abraham when he gave tithes to Melchisedec. In this way also the first sin of Adam was equally the sin of all of us, who were in his loins when he himself sinned. Therefore the Apostle says in Rom. 5. 12 that all of us sinned in Adam: the sin of Adam has passed down to us both by reason of the corruption of nature and by reason of the actual guilt of the sin itself and of the defection.

units.la: 11 Porro si consummatio per Leuiticum Sacerdo- tium erat (nam sub hoc fancita Lex est populo) quid amplius erat opus alium exoriri Sacerdotem secun- dum ordinem Melchisedec, nec secundum ordinem Aaronis dici?
units.tr: 11 Moreover, if perfection was through the Levitical priesthood (for under it the Law was given to the people), what further need was there for another priest to arise according to the order of Melchisedec, and not to be called according to the order of Aaron?

units.la: 12 Mutato enim Sacerdotio, necesse est & Legis quoque mutatio fiat.
units.tr: 12 For when the priesthood is changed, there is of necessity a change also of the law.

units.la: 13 Nam is de quo haec dicuntur, ad aliam tribum pertinet, de qua nullus attendit altari.
units.tr: 13 For he of whom these things are said belongs to another tribe, from which no one has attended at the altar.

units.la: 14 Palam est enim e tribu Iuda exortum esse Dominum nostrum: cui tribui nihil de Sacerdotio loquutus est Moses.
units.tr: 14 For it is plain that our Lord sprang out of the tribe of Judah, to which tribe Moses said nothing concerning the priesthood.

units.la: 15 Idque etiam magis patet ex eo quod ad instar Melchisedec exoritur Sacerdos alius:
units.tr: 15 And this is even more evident from the fact that another priest arises after the likeness of Melchisedec,

units.la: 16 Qui non ex Lege, cuius mandatum sit carnale, sed ex virtute indissolubilis vitae.
units.tr: 16 who is not made according to the law of a carnal commandment, but according to the power of an indissoluble life.

units.la: 17 Testificatur enim.
units.tr: 17 For it is testified:

units.la: f alius est sacerdos
units.tr: another priest

units.la: 17 Testificatur enim ad hunc modum, Tu es Sacerdos in æternum, secundùm ordinem Melchisedec.
units.tr: 17 For it is testified in this way: You are a priest for ever, according to the order of Melchisedec.

units.la: 18 Nam mandatum præcedens abrogatur propter ipsius imbecillitatem & inutilitatem.
units.tr: 18 For the preceding commandment is set aside because of its weakness and unprofitableness.

units.la: 19 Nihil enim sanctificauit Lex: sed superintroducta spes melior, per quam appropinquamus Deo.
units.tr: 19 For the Law made nothing perfect; but a better hope is introduced, through which we draw near to God.

units.la: Porro si) Occupatio est: obijci enim potuit ab Hebræis siue Iudæis, ad ea quæ dicti sunt proximè de Melchisedeco, ejusque excellentia ac præstantia. Esto, sit Melchisedec, sit nouus sacerdos, qui non est secundùm ordinem Leui: sit quoque hæc quam dicis noui sacerdotis præstantia: Attamen per Leuiticum sacerdotium fuit perfectio & sanctificatio. Respondet negatiuè: Non fuit per Leuiticum sacerdotium perfectio siue sanctificatio. Objectio simul & responsio negata ista suppressa est. Negatæ autem responsionis ratio in contextu est expressa. Si perfectio siue sanctificatio per Leuiticum sacerdotium erat, quid amplius erat opus alium exoriri sacerdotem, secundùm ordinem Melchisedech? &c. At alius exortus est sacerdos, qui est secundùm ordinem Melchisedec (Christum intelligit, cujus typus erat Melchisedec, Ergo consummatio siue sanctifi-catio non erat per Leuiticum sacerdotium. De negata hac conclusione lege cap.10. vers.
units.tr: And if) This is an objection: for the Hebrews or Jews could raise an objection to what was said just before about Melchisedec and his excellence and pre-eminence. Granted, let Melchisedec be, let him be a new priest who is not according to the order of Levi; let this pre-eminence of the new priest which you mention also be granted. Nevertheless, perfection and sanctification came through the Levitical priesthood. The Apostle answers in the negative: perfection or sanctification did not come through the Levitical priesthood. The objection and the denied response are both left unexpressed here, but the reason for the denied response is expressed in the context: if perfection or sanctification came through the Levitical priesthood, what further need was there for another priest to arise according to the order of Melchisedec? And so on. But another priest has arisen who is according to the order of Melchisedec (he means Christ, of whom Melchisedec was a type). Therefore perfection or sanctification did not come through the Levitical priesthood. For this denied conclusion see chapter 10, verse 1.

units.la: 1. Nota finem religionis siue cultus Dei à Deo præscripti esse, vt homo fit perfectus & consummatus. Hunc finem Scripturæ sacræ esse tradit Apostolus 2. Timoth. 3. 17. ut perfectus sit homo Dei, inquit, ad omne opus bonum perfecte instructus. Perfectionem istam pono in ijs benedictionibus Dei in Christo, quæ ad alteram vitam spectant, in vocatione efficaci, in justificatione, in sanctificatione. Nam sub hac sancta) Amplificatio est quædam ejus, quod dixit de consummatione quæ est per Leuiticum sacerdotium, per occupationis quandam speciem inserta. Est autem amplificatio à Lege, siue ministerio Legali, quod sancitum est populo sub hoc sacerdotio Leuitico. Ex quo videtur sequi consummationem esse oportere per Leuiticum sacerdotium. Quid enim est quod sanctificat, si non ministerium hoc Legale? Notandum est hoc loco, neque sacerdotium illud Leuiticum, neque Legem sub hoc sacerdotio sancitam populo (ceremonialem intelligo) ijs quidquam profuisse ad perfectionem siue sanctificationem, qui seorsim umbras à corpore acceperunt. Nam hoc loco Apostolus typos illos Legales seorsim sumit à rebus ipsis quas figurabant, eosque etiam rebus figuratis opponit. Sic autem constituti, nullam vim habent ad hominem perficiendum siue sanctificadum. Typos autem sic accepit Apostolus ex hypothesi & sensu Iudæorum, qui typos seorsim à rebus figuratis sumpserunt, & in umbris quasi religionem Deique cultum posuerunt.
units.tr: Note that the end of religion, or of the worship of God prescribed by God, is that man may be made perfect and complete. The Apostle teaches that this is the end of Holy Scripture, 2 Timothy 3:17: that the man of God may be perfect, he says, thoroughly furnished unto every good work. I place this perfection in those blessings of God in Christ which look to the life to come: in effectual calling, in justification, in sanctification. For under this holy) This is a certain amplification of what he said about the perfection which is through the Levitical priesthood, inserted by way of a kind of objection. The amplification is drawn from the Law, or the legal ministry, which was given to the people under this Levitical priesthood. From this it seems to follow that perfection ought to be through the Levitical priesthood. For what is there that sanctifies, if not this legal ministry? It must be noted here that neither that Levitical priesthood nor the Law given to the people under this priesthood (I mean the ceremonial law) profited anything for perfection or sanctification to those who received the shadows apart from the body. For in this place the Apostle takes those legal types apart from the things themselves which they foreshadowed, and he also sets them against the things foreshadowed. Thus constituted, they have no power to perfect or sanctify a man. The Apostle took the types in this way from the hypothesis and sense of the Jews, who took the types apart from the things foreshadowed, and placed religion and the worship of God, as it were, in the shadows.

units.la: 12 Mutato igitur ) Altera occupatio est. Esto hoc ( inquit Iudæus aliquis ) mutatus fit sacerdos, & translatus e tribu vna in tribum alteram: at vero non inde sequitur legis quoque, hoc est, ministerij Legalis mutationem fieri. Annon enim (dixerit) sub nouo Sacerdote, qui fit ex altera tribu, potest manere vetus illud legis ministerium, & jam olim præscripta illa colendi Deum ratio? Respondet Apoftolus, translato sacerdotio necessario mutari quoque Legem, fiue ministerium Legale totum.
units.tr: 12 For the priesthood being changed) This is the second objection. Granted, says some Jew, that the priest is changed and transferred from one tribe to another. It does not follow from this that the law also, that is, the Levitical ministry, is changed. For could not (he might say) the old ministry of the law remain under the new priest, who comes from another tribe, along with the mode of worshipping God that was prescribed long ago? The Apostle replies that when the priesthood is transferred, the law too must necessarily be changed, that is, the whole Levitical ministry.

units.la: 13 Nam is de quo) Sequelam fiue connexionem proximam confirmat: idque hoc argumento. Primum a natura & conditione illius tribus ad quam translatum est sacerdotium. Is, inquit, de quo hæc dicuntur, hoc est, is qui factus est nouus sacerdos, per ea verba Dei Patris, quæ habentur Pfal. 110. verf. 4. (Iuravit Iehouach. Tu es Sacerdos &c.) is, inquam, ad eam tribum pertinet, de qua nullus vnquam attendit altari, h. e. de qua nullus vnquam obijt aliquam partem ministerij Legalis, quod positum est in sacrificijs, alijsque id genus ceremonijs. Sequitur ergo, translato sacerdotio neceffario totius ministerij legalis mutationem fieri.
units.tr: 13 For he of whom these things are said) He confirms the immediate sequence or connection, and does so with an argument drawn first from the nature and condition of the tribe to which the priesthood has been transferred. He of whom these things are said, he says, that is, he who has been made the new priest, through the words of God the Father in Psalm 110:4 (The LORD has sworn, Thou art a priest, etc.), belongs, I say, to a tribe from which no one ever attended the altar, that is, from which no one ever performed any part of the Levitical ministry, which consists in sacrifices and other such ceremonies. It follows, therefore, that when the priesthood is transferred, a change of the whole Levitical ministry must necessarily take place.

units.la: 14 Palam est) Probatur antecedens enthymematis proximi. Nouus hic sacerdos, vt manifeftò constat, exortus est e tribu Iuda. At tribus Iudæ respectu nihil de sacerdotio locutus est Moses, hoc est (vt dixit supra) de Tribu Iuda nullus attendit altari,neque à Mose cuiquam ex hac tribu impositum est hoc munus sacerdotij.Ergo nouus hic sacerdos ad eam tribum pertinet de qua nullus attendit altari.Nota hîc Mosem in Lege sua nihil præcripfiffe de hoc sacerdotio quod est fecundùm ordinem Melchifedeci. Tradidit multa(fateor) de ordine sacerdotij Aaronici: at huius ordinis non meminit, neque eius leges præscripsit. De hoc autem ordine habes Psalmo 110. Tradit Moses(fateor)historiam Melchifedeci. Genef. 14. 18. 19. 20. Quo loco eum ex effectis facerdotem fuisse ostendit, verùm de hoc sacerdotij ordine nullas leges præscripsit, id quod fecit de ordine sacerdotij Aaronici.
units.tr: 14 For it is plain) The antecedent of the preceding enthymeme is proved. This new priest, as is manifestly clear, has arisen from the tribe of Judah. But Moses said nothing about priesthood with respect to the tribe of Judah; that is (as he said above), no one from the tribe of Judah has attended the altar, and Moses never assigned this office of priesthood to anyone from that tribe. Therefore this new priest belongs to the tribe from which no one has attended the altar. Notice here that Moses, in his law, prescribed nothing about this priesthood, which is according to the order of Melchizedek. He does indeed (I grant) set out many things about the order of the Aaronic priesthood, but he makes no mention of this order and prescribes no laws for it. You have it concerning this order in Psalm 110. Moses (I grant) does record the history of Melchizedek in Genesis 14:18-20, where he shows him to have been a priest from the facts of the case, but he prescribed no laws for this order of priesthood, as he did for the order of the Aaronic priesthood.

units.la: 15 Idque etiam magis) Secundum argumentum quo probat sequelam illam; Quod mutato sacerdotio necesse fit legis quoq; mutatio nem fieri. Hoc argumentum sumptum est à natura & conditione ordinis illius ex quo est hic nouus sacerdos,nempe Christus. Hic sacerdos est ex ordine Melchifedeci exortus, non ex lege factus sacerdos, sed ex vi indissolubilis vitæ. Ergo mutato sacerdotio necesse est vt Legis quoq; mutatio fiat: quid enim huic sacerdoti,qui non est ex lege factus,cum ministerio illo legali?Nota rursus nullam esse legem Mofaicam de hoc sacerdote, qui est fecundùm ordinem Melchifedec. Cuius mandatum) Legis quædam descriptio est, qua arguit ex lege non factum fuisse eum Sacerdotem : Legis enim mandatum est carnale, h. e. de rebus caducis & eununidis, quae carnis nomine in Scripturis significantur. Sed ex Vi) Legi opponit vim indissolubilis vitae, tanquam veram causam qua factus est hic sacerdos: Per vim autem indissolubilis vitae, intelligit efficaciam illam verbi, & iurisiurandi Dei, quae est ad vitam quae nunquam dissoluitur, hoc est, ad durationem sempiternam. Ex hac enim vi durat Pontificatus Christi in aeternum.
units.tr: 15 And this even more) This is the second argument by which he proves that sequence: that when the priesthood is changed, the law must also necessarily be changed. This argument is drawn from the nature and condition of that order from which this new priest comes, namely Christ. This priest has arisen according to the order of Melchizedek; he has been made a priest not by the law but by the power of an indissoluble life. Therefore, when the priesthood is changed, the law must necessarily be changed too: for what has this priest, who was not made by the law, to do with that legal ministry? Notice again that there is no Mosaic law about this priest, who is according to the order of Melchizedek. Who has been made a priest not according to the law of a fleshly commandment) This is a description of the law, by which he shows that Christ was not made priest by the law. For the commandment of the law is fleshly, that is, concerned with perishable and frail things, which in Scripture are signified by the name of flesh. But by the power of an indissoluble life) He sets against the law the power of an indissoluble life as the true cause by which this priest was made. By the power of an indissoluble life he means that efficacy of the word and oath of God which is directed to a life that is never dissolved, that is, to an everlasting duration. For by this power the priesthood of Christ endures for ever.

units.la: 17 Testificatur enim ad hunc) Probat veram hanc causam sacerdotij Christi, sive Christum factum esse sacerdotem ex vi indissolubilis vitae, a testimonio ipsius Dei in Scripturis, in quibus Pater sic Filium suum alloquitur : Tu es Sacerdos in aeternum secundum ordinem Melchisedec. Atque haec verba Patris ad Filium, habent vim indissolubilis vitae. Ergo factus est sacerdos ex vi indissolubilis vitae. Vide Psal. 110.
units.tr: 17 For it is witnessed of him) He proves that this is the true cause of Christ's priesthood, namely that Christ was made priest by the power of an indissoluble life, from the testimony of God himself in Scripture, where the Father addresses his Son thus: Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek. And these words of the Father to the Son have the power of an indissoluble life. Therefore he was made priest by the power of an indissoluble life. See Psalm 110.

units.la: 18 Nam mandatum) Hactenus primum fuit argumentum, quo probata est Legis sive Ministerij legalis mutatio: Sumptum fuit a translatione sacerdotij: In eo immoratus est ad hunc usque versum. Hic igitur habemus secundum eiusdem rei argumentum, sumptum a minsterij Legalis inefficacitate, sive impotentia & inutilitate. Ministerium illud Legale nullis viribus praeditum est, & inutile est, nempe ad sanctificationem.Ergo abrogatur.
units.tr: 18 For there is a setting aside) So far the first argument has been the proof that the law, or the legal ministry, is changed. It was drawn from the transfer of the priesthood, and he has dwelt on it up to this verse. Here, then, we have a second argument for the same matter, drawn from the inefficacy, or powerlessness and uselessness, of the legal ministry. That legal ministry has no power and is useless, namely for sanctification. Therefore it is abrogated.

units.la: 19 Nihil enim) Ratio cur nullis fit viribus praeditum & inutile mandatum, ab effecto sanctificationis fiue perfectionis. Nihil fanctificauit Lex. Ergo nullis viribus praedita, & inutilis est. Quod si enim vis & vtilitas Legis fuisset aliqua profecto fuisset ea ad sanctificationem. Sed adscita) E diuerso veram fanctificationis caussam subijcit, quam vocat introductione spei melioris. Hoc nomine spei melioris intelligit Euangelium Christi,quod Legi successit & in eius locum introductum est. Ab effecto autem suo sic vocat Euangelium: nam Euangelium spem gignit meliorem. Per quam) Descriptio quaedam huius spei ab effecto suo, per eam enim appropinquamus Deo, diruta quasi iam maceria Legis, & ceremoniarum, quae nostrum ad Deum aditum quasi intercluferunt, obfueruntque quo minus ad eum appropinquaremus.Eph.2.16.Col.2.14.
units.tr: 19 For the law made nothing perfect) The reason why the commandment is powerless and useless is drawn from the effect of sanctification, or perfection. The law sanctified nothing. Therefore it is powerless and useless. For if the law had any power or usefulness, it would certainly have been so for sanctification. But there is a bringing in of a better hope) On the other side he states the true cause of sanctification, which he calls the introduction of a better hope. By this name of a better hope he means the gospel of Christ, which succeeded the law and was introduced in its place. He calls the gospel this from its effect, for the gospel begets a better hope. By which) A description of this hope from its effect: for through it we draw near to God, the wall of the law and of the ceremonies, which had as it were shut us off and stood in the way of our approach to him, now being broken down. Ephesians 2:16; Colossians 2:14.

units.la: 20 Et quatenus non absque iureiurando superinducta est.
units.tr: 20 And inasmuch as it was not without an oath.

units.la: 21 Nam illi quidem, citra iuriurandum Sacerdotes fatisfunt: hic vero cum iureiurando per eum qui dixit ei, iurauit Dominus, & non paenitebit eum, Tu es Sacerdos in aeternum secundum ordinem Melchisedec.
units.tr: 21 For those indeed became priests without an oath, but this one with an oath, by him who said to him, The Lord has sworn, and will not repent, Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek.

units.la: 22 Tanto potior est foederis sponsor Iesus.
units.tr: 22 By so much more is Jesus the surety of a better covenant.

units.la: 23 Et illi quidem plures sacerdotes, quod quod mors prohibere eos permanere:
units.tr: 23 And indeed there were many priests, because death prevented them from continuing.

units.la: 24. At iste propterea quod in æternum manet, perpetuum habet Sacerdotium.
units.tr: 24 But he, because he abides for ever, has a priesthood that does not pass away.

units.la: 25 Unde & feruare prorsus potest eos qui per ipsum accedunt ad Deum, semper viuens, vt interpellet pro eis.
units.tr: 25 Wherefore he is also able completely to save those who come to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them.

units.la: 26 Talis enim nos decebat Pontifex sanctus, innocens, impollutus, segregatus a peccatoribus, & sublimior cælis factus.
units.tr: 26 For such a high priest was fitting for us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens.

units.la: 27 Cui non sit quotidie necesse, quemadmodum illis pontificibus, prius pro peccatis propriis victimas offerre, deinde pro peccatis populi: hoc enim fecit semel quum seipsum obtulit.
units.tr: 27 who does not need daily, as those high priests did, first to offer sacrifices for his own sins and then for the sins of the people; for this he did once for all when he offered himself.

units.la: 28 Lex enim homines constituit Pontifices infirmos: at sermo iurisiurandi post Legem conceptí, Filium constituit qui in æternum est sanctificatus.
units.tr: 28 For the law appoints men as high priests who are weak, but the word of the oath, which came after the law, appoints the Son, who has been made perfect for ever.

units.la: Et quatenus non) Hactenus hoc capite, de Melchisedeco Christi typo, & eius descriptione primum, deinde præstantia, de sacerdotio legali quod abolitum sit: de Lege ipsa, totoque legali ministerio, quod sit abrogata. Nunc agitur de Christo ipso, cuius typus erat Melchisedec: eiusque præstantia & excellentia per comparationem cum Leuiticis sacerdotibus ostenditur. Propositio igitur ostendenda est ista, Iesus Christus præstantior Sacerdos est, quam fuerunt sacerdotes Leuitici. Argumentum primum sumptum est a præstantia fœderis illius, cuius est sponsor Iesus, in hanc formam. Iesus factus est potioris fœderis sponsor. Ergo præstantior est sacerdotibus Leuiticis. Enthymematis hujus antecedens habetur vers.22. Consequens autem subticetur hoc loco, & intelligedum relinquitur:Enthymematis autem antecedens sic probat. Factus est Iesus Sacerdos non absque iurejurando. Ergo factus est sponsor potioris fœderis. Enthymematis hujus antecedens habetur versu 20. Consequens autem versu 22. Sequela sic patet. Qui factus est Sacerdos, non simplici nudoque verbo,sed adhibito iurejurando, necesse est is respectu potioris præstantiorisque fœderis factus sit Sacerdos. Nam vbi Sacerdos, ibi fœdus cujus fœderis sponsor est Sacerdos. Sponsor fœderis vocatur Iesus, quia spondendo pro nobis, & satisfaciendo sanguine suo pro peccatis nostris, effecit vt nos in gratiam rediremus cum Deo Patre, procurauitque nobis nouum fœdus, quod gratiæ vocant. Duo enim sponsori Christo facieнda erant. Primum oportuit eum in se transferre debitum nostrum, pro eoque iustitiæ Patris satisfacere. Deinde oportuit eum procurare atque promereri nobis nouam gratiam, hoc est, fœdus nouum, quo suturum erat vt denuo Dei amici & quasi confœderati euaderemus. Vtrumque hoc præstitit Christus sponsor per sacrificium & crucem suam.
units.tr: And inasmuch as it was not) So far in this chapter we have treated Melchizedek as the type of Christ: first his description, then his superiority, and that the Levitical priesthood has been abolished; and the law itself and the whole legal ministry have been abrogated. Now the subject is Christ himself, whose type Melchizedek was, and his pre-eminence and excellence are shown by comparison with the Levitical priests. The proposition to be shown, then, is this: Jesus Christ is a more excellent priest than the Levitical priests were. The first argument is drawn from the pre-eminence of that covenant of which Jesus is the surety, in this form: Jesus has been made the surety of a better covenant; therefore he is more excellent than the Levitical priests. The antecedent of this enthymeme is found in verse 22; the consequent is left unstated here and is to be understood. The antecedent of the enthymeme is proved thus: Jesus was made priest not without an oath; therefore he has been made surety of a better covenant. The antecedent of this enthymeme is found in verse 20, and the consequent in verse 22. The sequence is plain thus: he who was made priest not by a simple and bare word, but with an oath added, must necessarily have been made priest with respect to a better and more excellent covenant. For where there is a priest, there is a covenant, of which the priest is the surety. Jesus is called the surety of the covenant because, by undertaking for us, and by satisfying God the Father with his blood for our sins, he has brought it about that we are restored to favour with God the Father, and he has procured for us a new covenant, which they call of grace. For two things had to be done by Christ as surety. First, he had to take our debt upon himself and satisfy the justice of the Father on its account. Second, he had to procure and merit for us a new grace, that is, a new covenant, by which we were to become again the friends and, as it were, the confederates of God. Christ as surety has accomplished both of these through his sacrifice and his cross.

units.la: 21 Namilli) Ostendit quod dixit proximè, ex dissimili comparatione Christi Sacerdotis & sacerdotum Leuiticorum: illi quidem citra jusiurandum sacerdotes facti sunt, hic vero cū jurejurando. Protasis vera esse conspicitur ex libris Mosis, vbi agitur de ordinatione Aaronis, & aliorum sacerdotum Leuiticorum, in quibus nihil legitur de iurejurando in ijs ordinandis adhibito: Quare nullum fuit. Per eum qui) Apodosin probat adduͤcto in medium Scripturæ testimonio illo quod habetur Psal. 110.4.
units.tr: 21 For the Levitical priests, indeed, were made priests without an oath, but this one with an oath. Namely, he shows what he said just before, from the unlike comparison of Christ the priest and the Levitical priests. The protasis is seen to be true from the books of Moses, where the ordination of Aaron and the other Levitical priests is described; in these there is nothing read about an oath being used in ordaining them. Therefore there was none. Through him who: he proves the apodosis by bringing forward the testimony of Scripture found in Psalm 110.4.

units.la: 23 Et illi) Secundum argumentum præstantiæ sacerdotis Christi, à perpetuitate sacerdotii Christi, quæ comparatè tractatur hoc modo. Leuitici facti sunt sacerdotes plures, hoc est, non perpetui, sed alij alijs succeedentes. At iste perpetuum habet Sacerdotium. Ergo hic illis præstantior. Quod mors) Ratio est cur Leuitici Sacerdotes plures sint facti, à morte qua impedita est perpetuitas in sacerdotio. Loquitur Apostolus de summis sacerdotibus, siue Pontificibus, non autem de vulgo sacerdotum Leuiticorum. In genere autem summorum sacerdotum vnus tantum erat vno tempore, non plures, ex præscripto Legis diuinæ: Quamobrem pluralitas hoc loco successiua intelligenda est.
units.tr: 23 And they: the second argument for the excellence of Christ the priest, drawn from the perpetuity of Christ's priesthood, which is treated comparatively in this way. The Levitical priests were made many, that is, not perpetual, but succeeding one another. But this one has a perpetual priesthood. Therefore he is more excellent than they. Because death: this is the reason why the Levitical priests were made many, since perpetuity in the priesthood was hindered by death. The Apostle speaks of the chief priests, or high priests, not of the common body of Levitical priests. Now in the order of chief priests there was only one at a time, not several, according to the prescription of the divine Law; therefore the plurality here must be understood as successive.

units.la: 24 At iste propterea) Ratio est cur perpetuum sit sacerdotium Christi, ab ipsius æternitate, siue duratione æterna: Manet in æternum. Ergo perpetuum habet sacerdotium, non successiuum, quale habuerunt summi sacerdotes Leuitici, qui morti fuerunt obnoxij. Nota igitur, Christum nullum habere in terris successorem in sacerdotio suo; neque debere hoc nomen vsurpari in Ecclesia Christiana post Christum, qui sacerdotali muneri, quod positum erat in victimis & sacrificijs offerendis, finem imposuit. Sumus quidem nos omnes quicunque in nomine Christi baptizati sumus, certo quodam modo sacerdotes, vt & Reges, & Prophetæ: unde Petrus regale sacerdotium nos vocat. 1. Epist. 2. 9. verum post Christum nullum est iIIiusmodi in Ecclesia speciale aliquod munus & officium.
units.tr: 24 But this one, because of this: this is the reason why the priesthood of Christ is perpetual, from his eternity, or eternal duration: he remains for ever. Therefore he has a perpetual priesthood, not a successive one, such as the Levitical chief priests had, who were subject to death. Note, then, that Christ has no successor on earth in his priesthood; and that this name ought not to be claimed in the Christian Church after Christ, who put an end to the priestly office, which consisted in offering victims and sacrifices. We indeed, all who have been baptized in the name of Christ, are in a certain manner priests, as also kings and prophets; whence Peter calls us a royal priesthood (1 Pet. 2.9). But after Christ there is no special office or function of this kind in the Church.

units.la: Unde & seruare) Tertium est argumentum præstantiæ Christi, quod consequens est & effectum æternæ illius ipsius vitæ & durationis, cujus meminit proxime: Sacerdos Christus prorsus, & ( vt sic dicam ) finaliter potest eos seruare qui per ipsum accedunt ad Deum, nempe per fidem. At Leuitici sacerdotes id non potuerunt. Ergo hic ijs præstantior est.
units.tr: Whence also to save: the third argument for the excellence of Christ, which follows from and is the effect of that eternal life and duration of his of which he spoke just before: Christ the priest is wholly, and (so to speak) finally, able to save those who come to God through him, namely through faith. But the Levitical priests could not do this. Therefore he is more excellent than they.

units.la: Semper viuens) Ratio est cur prorsus seruet, quia semper viuit. Vt interpellet) Ratio est sequelæ, quia viuendo interpellat & intercedit apud Deum pro fidelibus. Sequitur ergo, quod si semper viuat, prorsus & perfecte seruet credentes: Non enim in coelis otiosus & inefficax est, verum munus Pontificis exercet, interpellando siue intercedendo odore illo sacrificij ipsius perpetuo. Vnde 1. Ioan. 2.1. postquàm eum aduocatum nostrum vocauit, continuo addidit, ipsum propitiationem esse pro peccatis nostris, hoc est, sacrificium propitiatorium. Sequitur ergo eum intercedere etiam in cœlis, virtute perpetua sacrificij illius propitiatorij, quod semel est oblatum in terris.
units.tr: Always living: this is the reason why he saves completely, because he always lives. That he may intercede: this is the reason for the consequence, because by living he intercedes and makes intercession before God for believers. It follows, therefore, that if he always lives, he saves believers wholly and perfectly; for he is not idle and ineffective in heaven, but exercises the office of high priest, interceding by the perpetual fragrance of his sacrifice. Hence in 1 John 2.1, after calling him our advocate, he at once added that he himself is the propitiation for our sins, that is, a propitiatory sacrifice. It follows, then, that he intercedes even in heaven, by the perpetual virtue of that propitiatory sacrifice which was once offered on earth.

units.la: 16 Talis enim) Argumentum quartum praestantiæ Christi, à qualitate ipsius, quam explicat varijs, ijsque eximijs particularibus qualitatibus & conditionibus induĉtis, quibus omnibus differt à Leuiticis Pontificibus. Pontifex est pius, innocens, impollutus &c. Ex his quæ inducte sunt qualitatibus, quædam ad personam pertinent, nimirum quæ hoc versu continentur, quædam vero ad officium, nimirum quæ habentur versu sequenti. Primum hoc loco propositio quædam est in genere qualitatis quæ requirebatur in Pontifice nostro. Talis, inquit, nos decebat Pontifex, hoc est, hæc qualitas & conditio in Pontifice nostro requirebatur. Deinde sequitur explicatio generalis propositionis siue qualitatis illius quæ in genere proposita est. Pius) Prima qualitas, quæ respicit Deum. Innocens) Secunda quæ respicit proximum. Impollutus) Tertia quæ respicit ipsius personam. Nam quo ad personam sine macula, & labe est. Segregatus) Quarta quæ eadem videtur esse cum superiori, si nisi quod comparatè proposita sit, sacta nimirum cum peccatoribus comparatione.Nam cum segregatum dicit à peccatoribus, fcnfi s est ac fi dixisset, non talem eum esse quales sunt peccatores, hoc est, impollutum & immundum. Sublimior cœlis) Quinta est qualitas, quæ & ipsa quoque respicit personam, estenim personæ dignitas, excellentia, & sublimitas, quæ comparatione cœlorum ipsorum explicatur.
units.tr: 16 For such a one: the fourth argument for the excellence of Christ, from his quality, which he explains by introducing various and distinguished particular qualities and conditions, in all of which he differs from the Levitical high priests. The high priest is pious, innocent, undefiled, etc. Of the qualities introduced, some pertain to the person, namely those contained in this verse; others pertain to the office, namely those found in the following verse. First, in this place, there is a certain proposition in general concerning the quality which was required in our high priest. "Such," he says, "became us as high priest," that is, this quality and condition was required in our high priest. Then follows a general explanation of that proposition or quality which was set forth in general. Holy: the first quality, which regards God. Innocent: the second, which regards our neighbour. Undefiled: the third, which regards his person itself; for as to his person he is without spot and stain. Separate: the fourth, which seems to be the same as the previous one, except that it is set forth comparatively, namely by comparison with sinners; for when he says separate from sinners, the sense is as if he had said that he is not such as sinners are, that is, defiled and unclean. Higher than the heavens: the fifth quality, which also regards the person; for it is the dignity, excellence, and sublimity of the person, which is explained by comparison with the heavens themselves.

units.la: 27 Cui non fit)Sexta conditio fiue qualitas, non est ei imposita necessitas offerendi quotidie : hæc qualitas ad officium & munus sacerdotij pertinet. Quemadmodum illis) hoc est, quemadmodum necesse fuit Pontificibus, quos ex lege oportuit quotidie offerre sacrificia. In hac conditione fiue qualitate expressè coparatus est cumLeuiticis sacerdotibus,idq; indiffimilii in superioribus non nisi intellectè. Prius propeccatu) Septima est conditio: non necesse habet vt prius offerat victimas pro peccatis suis,deinde pro peccatis populi. Et in hac quoque coparatur cum Leuiticis Pontificibus expressè. Nam Leuiticos Pontifices oportuit primus pro peccatis suis,deinde pro peccatis populi victimas offerre. In summa itaque argumentatio est.Pontifex noster pius est,innocens &c. At tales non fuerunt pontifices Leuitici : Ergo hic noster illis præftatior est Pontifex. Id enim) Ratio cur non necesse fit vt quotidie offerat Christus:Semel id fecit,h. e.semel obtulit:Ergo non est necesse quotidie id faciat.Cum semetipsum) Ratio est vt videtur iequelæ, Quia femel id fecit cū femetipsū obtulit: vnde sequitur non necesse esse vt quotidie id faciat,quum semetipsum quotidie offerre non possit. Christus enim sæpius mori non potest. Rom. 6. 10. Nam quod mortuus est peccato, mortuus est semel.quod autem viuit,viuit Deo.
units.tr: 27 Who has no need: the sixth condition or quality: it is not imposed on him as a necessity to offer daily; this quality pertains to the office and function of the priesthood. As those: that is, as it was necessary for the high priests, who by the Law had to offer sacrifices daily. In this condition or quality he is expressly compared with the Levitical priests, and that in a dissimilar way; in the preceding verses he is compared only by implication. First for his own sins: this is the seventh condition: he does not need first to offer victims for his own sins, and then for the sins of the people. In this also he is expressly compared with the Levitical high priests; for the Levitical high priests had to offer victims first for their own sins, then for the sins of the people. In sum, then, the argument is this: our high priest is pious, innocent, etc.; but such were not the Levitical high priests; therefore our high priest is more excellent than they. For this he did: the reason why it is not necessary for Christ to offer daily: he did this once, that is, he offered once; therefore it is not necessary that he do this daily. When he offered himself: this is, as it seems, the reason for the consequence: because he did this once, when he offered himself; whence it follows that it is not necessary that he do it daily, since he cannot offer himself daily. For Christ cannot die often (Rom. 6.10): for in that he died to sin, he died once; but in that he lives, he lives to God.

units.la: 28 Lex enim) Hæc ratio est cur non sit necesse Christum pro peccatis proprijs priùs victimas offerre, deinde pro peccatis populi. Sumpta est à natura & conditione ipsius. Filius est in æternum sanctificatus, hoc est, non est infirmus aut peccator. Vnde non necesse habuit, vt priùs pro peccatis proprijs offerret victimas:illustratur hæc Christi conditio,à dissimili Pontificum Leuiticorum conditione, qui infirmi & peccatores erant. Notandum quod non dicat simpliciter Pontifices Leuiticos infirmos fuisse, verùm dicat legem constituisse homines Pontifices infirmos: neque dicat simpliciter Christum fuisse in æternum sanctificatum, sed dicat, Legem iurisiurandi constituisse filium qui in æternum est sanctificatus:qua quidem re innuit, non tantùm dissimiles esse Pontifices illos Leuiticos & Christum,in natura & conditione sua, sed etiam in ratione vocationis: Nam Leuitici Pontifices vocati sunt per legem,Christus autem vocatus est per sermonem iurisiurandi, quæ vocationis ratio dignior & præstantior est.
units.tr: 28 For the law: this is the reason why it is not necessary for Christ to offer victims first for his own sins and then for the sins of the people. It is taken from his nature and condition: the Son is sanctified for ever, that is, he is not weak or a sinner. Whence he had no need to offer victims first for his own sins. This condition of Christ is illustrated by the unlike condition of the Levitical high priests, who were weak and sinners. It should be noted that he does not simply say that the Levitical high priests were weak, but says that the law constituted men as high priests who were weak; nor does he simply say that Christ was sanctified for ever, but says that the word of the oath, which came after the law, constituted the Son who is sanctified for ever; by which he hints that they are not only unlike, Christ and those Levitical high priests, in their nature and condition, but also in the manner of their calling. For the Levitical high priests were called through the law, but Christ was called through the word of the oath, which manner of calling is more worthy and excellent.

units.la: Argumentum Capitis octavi.
units.tr: Argument of Chapter eight.

units.la: Hoc capite comprehesa sunt præsentis instituti, hoc est, præstantiæ Christi Pontificis, duo argumenta. Primum a versu 1. ad versum 6. Secundum a versu 6. ad finem usque.
units.tr: In this chapter are comprised the two arguments of the present purpose, that is, of the excellence of Christ the high priest. The first runs from verse 1 to verse 6; the second from verse 6 to the end.

units.la: CAPVT. VIII.
units.tr: CAPVT. VIII.

units.la: 1 Caeterum eorum quæ dicimus hæc summa est, Talem nos habere Pontificem qui consedit ad dextram throni maiestatis illius in cœlis.
units.tr: 1 Now the sum of what we say is this: we have such a high priest, who has sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens.

units.la: 2 Sanctuarij minister, ac veri illius tabernaculi quod fixit Dominus & non homo.
units.tr: 2 A minister of the sanctuary and of the true tabernacle, which the Lord pitched and not man.

units.la: 3 Omnis enim Pontifex ad offerenda dona & victimas constituitur: Unde necesse fuit hunc quoque habere quod offerret.
units.tr: 3 For every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices. Hence it was necessary that this one also should have something to offer.

units.la: 4 Nam si esset in terra, nec Sacerdos quidem esset, manentibus illis sacerdotibus qui secundum legem offerunt dona.
units.tr: 4 For if he were on earth, he would not be a priest at all, since there are those priests who offer gifts according to the law.

units.la: 5 Ut qui exemplari & umbra deserviunt rerum cœlestium, sicut divinitus dictum est Moysi quum esset absoluturus tabernaculum, Vide enim, inquit, ut facias omnia ad exemplar quod ostensum est tibi in monte.
units.tr: 5 who serve a copy and shadow of heavenly things, as it was divinely spoken to Moses when he was about to finish the tabernacle: "See," he says, "that you make all things according to the pattern that was shown you on the mountain."

units.la: Caeterum eorum) Principio hujus capitis est argumentum præstantiæ Christi Pontificis quintum, sumptum etiam ab ipsius qualitate. Argumento præmissa est præfatiuncula, qua ipsum commendatur nobis tanquam ςφαλαιον quoddam, hoc est, argumentum princeps ac primarium.Talem nos habere)Generalis quædam propositio est qualitatis Pontificis Christi, vt capite superiori, verf.26. Qui consedit) Explicatio est qualitatis Christi in genere propositæ, per inductionem siue enumerationem partium aliquot ipsius. Prima est, quod sedet ad dexteram Dei. Non dicit dexteram Dei, verum dexteram Throni maiestatis illius. His omnibus verbis amplificat sessionem illam Christi. Vide Heb.1.3. Sessio quidem hæc Pontificis est, sed regalis, nam sacerdotium Christi regale est, vt eorum qui in Christo sunt. 1.Pet.2.9.
units.tr: Caeterum eorum) At the beginning of this chapter comes the fifth argument for the excellence of Christ our High Priest, taken also from his very quality. The argument is prefaced by a short introduction, by which he is commended to us as a [κεφάλαιον], that is, as the chief and principal argument. Such a one we have) This is a general proposition about the quality of Christ the High Priest, as in the previous chapter, verse 26. Who has sat down) This is an explanation of Christ's quality, proposed in general, by the enumeration or listing of some of its parts. The first is that he sits at the right hand of God. He does not say the right hand of God, but the right hand of the throne of that Majesty. By all these words he magnifies that session of Christ. See Heb. 1.3. This session belongs to the priest, but it is a royal session, for the priesthood of Christ is royal, as is that of those who are in Christ. 1 Pet. 2.9.

units.la: 2 Sanctuarij minister) Secunda Christi Pontificis qualitas siue conditio, Minister est Sanctuarij, hoc est, cœli altissimi, cuius typus erat sanctum sanctorum, quod ministrum habebat Pontificem Leviticum, Hebr.9.12. Per proprium sanguinem ingressus est semel in sacrarium: vt enim Pontifex typicus minister fuit sacrarij, siue sanctuarij terreni: ita Pontifex Christus minister est sanctuarij cœlestis. Ac veri illius) Tertia qualitas Christi: Minister est non quidem typici & umbratilis, sed veri Tabernaculi. Nam verum hoc loco umbratili & typico opponitur. Tabernaculi nomine intelligit corporis sui Tabernaculum, cuius minister fuit Christus in eo Patri offerendo pro peccatis nostris. Ministerium hoc Tabernaculi, hoc est, corporis sui, sequitur ministerium Sanctuarij, & cum eo coniunctum est necessario:
units.tr: 2 A minister of the sanctuary) The second quality or condition of Christ the High Priest: he is the minister of the sanctuary, that is, of the highest heaven, whose type was the holy of holies, which had a Levitical high priest as its minister, Heb. 9.12. "Through his own blood he entered once into the sanctuary." For as the typical high priest was the minister of the earthly sanctuary, so Christ the High Priest is the minister of the heavenly sanctuary. And of the true) The third quality of Christ: he is the minister not of a typical and shadowy tabernacle, but of the true tabernacle. For here "true" is opposed to "shadowy" and "typical". By the name tabernacle he means the tabernacle of his own body, of which Christ was the minister when he offered it to the Father for our sins. This ministry of the tabernacle, that is, of his body, follows the ministry of the sanctuary and is necessarily joined with it:

units.la: H
units.tr: H

units.la: Nam non potest Christus minister esse sanctuarij cœlestis, nisi minister patiter ut corporis sui tanquam sacrificij. Non enim erat vetus ac typicus Pontifex minister sanctuarij terrestris, nisi qua ratione fuerat simul minister sacrificij. Ergo non potest Christus minister esse cœlestis sanctuarij, nisi idem sit minister alicuius sacrificij, hoc est, corporis sui: Quod fixit Dominus) Descriptio quædam est veri Tabernaculi. Est enim Tabernaculum sixum, non ab homine, hoc est, non operatione hominis, sed à Domino, hoc est, arcana & secreta Spiritus sancti operatione. Nam Christus conceptus est ex Spiritu sancto. Eodem sensu dicitur Tabernaculum non manufactum, id est, Tabernaculum non huius structuræ. Cap.9.v.11.
units.tr: For Christ cannot be the minister of the heavenly sanctuary unless he is also the minister of his own body as a sacrifice. For the old and typical high priest was not the minister of the earthly sanctuary except on the ground that he was at the same time the minister of a sacrifice. Therefore Christ cannot be the minister of the heavenly sanctuary unless he is likewise the minister of some sacrifice, that is, of his own body. Which the Lord pitched) This is a certain description of the true tabernacle. For the tabernacle is pitched not by man, that is, not by human work, but by the Lord, that is, by the hidden and secret operation of the Holy Spirit. For Christ was conceived of the Holy Spirit. In the same sense the tabernacle is called "not made with hands", that is, a tabernacle not of this construction. Chap. 9 v. 11.

units.la: 3 Omnis enim Pontifex) Explicatio quædam est qualitatis proximæ de ministerio Tabernaculi corporis Christi. Docet autem necesse fuisse vt ipse haberet quod offerret. Argumentum est à genere ipso, & ab officio & munere Pontificis in genere. Omnis Pontifex ad osserenda dona & victimas constituitur, Ergo necesse fuit hunc quoque habere aliquid quod offerret. Habere autem non potuit aliquid, nisi corpus suum. Ergo necessarió fuit minister Tabernaculi corporis suiipsius. Quòd autem necesse fuit vt haberet Tabernaculum corporis sui quod offerret, ex eo apparet, quod cum cùm Pontifex sit, non typicus, quales erant illi veteres Leuitici, sed verus, oportèat eum habere sacrificia quæ offerret, non typica, h.e. victimas, verùm corpus suum ipsius, quod illis omnibus typicis est adumbratum.
units.tr: 3 For every high priest) This is an explanation of the nearer quality concerning the ministry of the tabernacle of Christ's body. It teaches that it was necessary for him to have something to offer. The argument is drawn from the genus itself, and from the office and function of the high priest in general. Every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices. Therefore it was necessary that this one also should have something to offer. But he could have nothing except his own body. Therefore he was necessarily the minister of the tabernacle of his own body. That it was necessary for him to have the tabernacle of his body to offer, appears from this: since he is a high priest not typical, like those old Levitical priests, but a true one, he must have sacrifices to offer which are not typical, that is, victims, but his own body, which was shadowed forth by all those typical things.

units.la: 4 Nam si esset) Explicat quod dixit de sessione illius ad dexteram Dei, docetque necessariò eum considere in cœlis ad dexteram Dei, hoc argumento. Si esset in terra ne sacerdos quidem esset, hoc est, si ei permanendum esset ac viuendum in terris his, non posset esse sacerdos, quod absurdum est. Ergo non absre dixi, eumconsedisse ad dexteram Dei. Manentibus) Probat connexione proximè præcedentem, nempe quod si esset in terra, non posset sacerdos esse. Si esset in terra, manerent adhuc sacerdotes Leuitici, manentibus autem sacerdotibus Leuiticis ne sacerdos quidem esset Christus. Ergo si esset in terra ne sacerdos quidem esset.
units.tr: 4 For if he were) He explains what he said about his session at the right hand of God, and teaches that he necessarily sits in the heavens at the right hand of God, by this argument: if he were on earth, he would not even be a priest, that is, if he had to remain and live on these earthly things, he could not be a priest, which is absurd. Therefore it was not without reason that I said he has sat down at the right hand of God. Since there are) He proves it by the connection with what immediately precedes, namely that if he were on earth he could not be a priest. If he were on earth, the Levitical priests would still remain, and while the Levitical priests remain, Christ would not even be a priest. Therefore if he were on earth he would not even be a priest.

units.la: 5 Vt qui exemplari) Probat assumptionem proximi syllogismi: nempe, quod si manerent sacerdotes Leuitici, ne sacerdos quidem esset Christus, ex eo quòd Leuitici sacerdotes exemplaria quædam sunt & vmbræ rerum cœlestium, sicut nimirum ad imaginem & similitudinem rerum cœlestium. Argumentatio est: Leuitici sacerdotes sunt exemplaria & vmbræ rerum cœlestium. Ergo manentibus ijs non esset sacerdos Christus. Sequela nititur propositioni quæ intelligitur: nempe non vnà eōdemque in loco consistere res cœlestes cum vmbra sua. Deseruire exemplari & vmbræ nihil aliud esse videtur, quàm exemplar & vmbram esse. Exemplar hoc loco est subindicatio quædam in græco est ὑποδείγμα, non τυπὸς. Sicut diuinitus) Ratio est, cur Leuitici sacerdotes exemplaria sint & vmbræ rerum cœlestium, ab oraculo siue testimonio Dei quod habetur Exod.25. 40. Est autem de Tabernaculo eiúsque structura. Hoc autem oraculo mandat Deus Mosi, vt faciat omnia ad typum & exemplar, quod ostensum est ei in monte. Ergo voluit Deus Tabernaculum efformari ad typum qui in monte ostensus est: ac proinde hypodigma esse & vmbram rei cœlestis, ac spiritualis, hoc est, typi illius qui ostensus est in monte. Hoc mandatum speciale de Tabernaculo Apostolus in genere intelligi vult de ijs omnibus qui sub lege erant, & ad genus ipsum accommodari. Vnde hoc Dei oraculum siue mandatum de Tabernaculo accommodat ad Leuiticos sacerdotes hoc loco, ex eoque probat eos exemplaria & vmbras esse rerum cœlestium. Atque hæc de argumento quinto præstantiæ Christi. Altera autem comparationis dissimilis pars, de Leuiticis sacerdotibus, suppre-ssa est: quæ sic supplevi poterit. At non erant tales Leuitici, nempe qualis hic Pontifex noster. Ergo hic iis præstantior est.
units.tr: 5 who serve) He proves the assumption of the immediately preceding syllogism: namely, that if the Levitical priests remained, Christ would not even be a priest, because the Levitical priests are certain copies and shadows of heavenly things, that is, made after the likeness and image of heavenly things. The argument is this: the Levitical priests are copies and shadows of heavenly things. Therefore, while they remain, Christ would not be a priest. The inference rests on a proposition which is understood, namely that heavenly things do not exist in the same place together with their shadow. To serve a copy and shadow seems to be nothing other than to be a copy and shadow. Here "copy" is a hint, in Greek [ὑπόδειγμα], not [τύπος]. As it was divinely spoken) This is the reason why the Levitical priests are copies and shadows of heavenly things, taken from the oracle or testimony of God found in Exod. 25. 40. It concerns the tabernacle and its structure. In this oracle God commands Moses to make all things according to the type and pattern that was shown him on the mountain. Therefore God willed the tabernacle to be fashioned after the type shown on the mountain, and so it is a copy and shadow of a heavenly and spiritual thing, that is, of that type which was shown on the mountain. The Apostle wishes this special command about the tabernacle to be understood in general of all those who were under the law, and to be applied to the kind itself. Hence he applies this oracle or command of God about the tabernacle to the Levitical priests in this place, and from it proves that they are copies and shadows of heavenly things. And so much for the fifth argument for the excellence of Christ. The other part of the dissimilar comparison, concerning the Levitical priests, is suppressed; it can be supplied thus: But the Levitical priests were not such as our High Priest here, namely of such a kind. Therefore he is more excellent than they.

units.la: {*} Sicut diuinitus] (sic)
units.tr: {*} Sicut diuinitus] (sic)

units.la: 6 At nunc noster ille Pontifex eo excellentius ministerium sortitus est, quo prastantioris est foederis intercessor quod prastantioribus promissis sancitum est,
units.tr: 6 But now that our High Priest has obtained a more excellent ministry, by as much as he is the mediator of a better covenant, which is enacted on better promises,

units.la: 7 Nam si prius illud talis fuisset vt nihil in ea possit requiri, haudquaquam fuisset secundo quasitus locus.
units.tr: 7 For if that first covenant had been such that nothing could be found fault with in it, there would by no means have been sought a place for a second.

units.la: 8 Nam increpans eos, inquit, Ecce, dies venient, dicit Dominus, quam pangam cum domo Israel & cum domo Iuda fœdus nouum.
units.tr: 8 For finding fault with them, he says: "Behold, the days come, says the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah.

units.la: 6 Non secundum fœdus quod feci cum patribus ipsorum, quo die prehendi manum ipsorum vt educerem eos ex Ægypto: nam ipsi non persisterunt in illo meo fœdere, & ego despexi eos, dicit Dominus.
units.tr: 9 Not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers, on the day I took them by the hand to lead them out of Egypt; for they did not continue in my covenant, and I disregarded them, says the Lord.

units.la: 10 Quamobrem hoc est fœdus quod paciscar domui Israel post dies illos, dicit Dominus: Indam Leges meas menti eorum, & cordi eorum inscribam: & ero ipsis Deus, & ipsi erunt mihi populus.
units.tr: 10 For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: I will put my laws into their mind, and write them on their hearts, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.

units.la: 11 Neque docebunt singuli proximum suum, & singulí fratrem suum, dicentes, Cognosce Dominum, nam omnes cognoscent me, ab eo qui pufillus fuerit inter eos, ad eum usque qui magnus fuerit inter eos.
units.tr: 11 Neither shall they teach every one his neighbour, and every one his brother, saying, Know the Lord: for they shall all know me, from the least of them unto the greatest of them.

units.la: 12 Ero enim propitius iniquitatibus eorum & peccatis eorum: & iniquitatum ipsorum non recordabor amplius.
units.tr: 12 For I will be merciful to their iniquities, and their sins will I remember no more.

units.la: 13 Dum nouum dicit antiquauit prius: porro quod antiquatur ac senescit prope est vt euanescat.
units.tr: 13 In that he saith, A new covenant, he hath made the first old. Now that which decayeth and waxeth old is ready to vanish away.

units.la: At nunc noster) Argumentum prastantiæ sacerdotis Christi textum, idem re cum primo, quod fuit capite superiori. verf. 20. & deinceps. Sumptum est a praestantia foederis in hanc formam. Praestantioris est foederis intercessor: Ergo ministerium eius excellentius est, siue praestantior est Sacerdos. Primo loco est consequens, secundo antecedens. Quod praestantioribus) Ratio praestantiae foederis a promissionibus, quibus ipsum constat, h.e. ab ipsa foederis materia. De his promissionibus praestationibus videbimus postea, in allato (quod sequitur) Ieremiae testimonio. Hic obserua mentione fieri duorum foederum: veteris & noui. Veteris foederis nomine, non foedus legale tantum, quod conditione habuit operum legalium, neq; gratuitum tantum, quod cum foedere legali obscure propositum fuit, verum nomine veteris foederis intelligo utrumque, & legale, & gratuitum; Legale cuius expressa mentio facta est: Gratuitu cuius non nisi obscure meminit vetus Scriptura. Quod autem veteris foederis nomine utrumque, & legale, & gratuitum, accipiendum sit, vel ex eo apparet, quod hoc loco veteri foederi tribuat intercessores, h.e. Leuiticos sacerdotes, qui totidem Christi fuerunt typi. Intercessor autem proprie est gratuitr foederis. Est quidem etiam foederis legalis: quia in repetendo foedere legali inimicitiae erant inter Deum & populum: vbi autem inimicitiae ibi intercessione opus est. Atque ideo Galat. 3. 19. dicitur Iex data esse per manum μεσίτου, Mediatoris, nempe Mosis. Hoc autem loco, quod dicitur fancitū esse nouum foedus praestantioribus promissis, habetur ratio potissimum veteris foederis, quia legale est. Nam praestantiores sunt promissiones foederis gratuiti, quàm sunt Legales.
units.tr: But now hath he obtained) The argument for the excellence of Christ's priesthood is, in substance, the same as the first argument in the previous chapter, verse 20 and following. It is drawn from the excellence of the covenant, in this form: he is the mediator of a more excellent covenant; therefore his ministry is more excellent, or his priesthood is more excellent. The first clause is the consequence and the second the antecedent. Which was established upon better promises) This is the reason for the excellence of the covenant, taken from the promises on which it rests, that is, from the very matter of the covenant. We shall see these promises later, in the prophecy of Jeremiah quoted here. Note that the author mentions two covenants, the old and the new. By the name of the old covenant I understand not only the legal covenant, which had the condition of legal works, nor only the gratuitous covenant, which was set forth obscurely alongside the legal one, but both together, the legal and the gratuitous. The old Scripture names the legal covenant expressly, and mentions the gratuitous one only obscurely. That the name of the old covenant must be taken in both senses is clear from the fact that here the author assigns to the old covenant mediators, that is, the Levitical priests, who were all types of Christ. A mediator, however, properly belongs to the gratuitous covenant. Yet he belongs to the legal covenant too, since in renewing the legal covenant there was enmity between God and the people, and where there is enmity there is need of a mediator. Hence Galatians 3:19 says that the law was given by the hand of a mediator [μεσίτου], namely Moses. In this passage, when it is said that the new covenant was established on better promises, the reference is chiefly to the old covenant as legal, for the promises of the gratuitous covenant are more excellent than those of the legal one.

units.la: 7 Nam fiprius) Occupatio. At vetus foedus tale fuit, vt nihil in eo posset requiri. Refpondet, fi tale fuisset vt nihil in eo posset requiri, haud quaquam fuisset fecundo quaesitus locus. Similis occupatio fuit cap. 7. verf. 11.
units.tr: 7 For if that first) This is an objection. The old covenant was such that nothing could be found fault with in it. The author replies: if it had been such that nothing could be found fault with, a second place would by no means have been sought. A similar objection occurred in chapter 7, verse 11.

units.la: 8 Nam incusans) Assumptionis intelleƈt ratio est à testimonio Prophetæ, vel Dei potius. Ierem. 31. 31. & deinceps: quo quidem probat fecundo foederi quæsitum esse locum. Testimonium hoc Prophetæ continet promissionem noui foederis conjunƈtam cum accusatione populi ob violatum foedus illud vetus, ideo ait, incusans eos. Ecce dies) Propositio est noui foederis pangendi: siue præfatio est, in qua proponit Dominus, se nouum foedus cum populo suo iƈturum.
units.tr: 8 For finding fault) The reason for the minor premise is taken from the testimony of the prophet, or rather of God. Jeremiah 31:31 and following; by this testimony the author proves that a place was sought for a second covenant. The words of the prophet contain a promise of a new covenant joined with an accusation of the people for having broken that old covenant, which is why he says finding fault with them. Behold, the days come) This is the proposition concerning the making of the new covenant; or it is the preface, in which the Lord announces that he will make a new covenant with his people.

units.la: 9 Non fecundum) Illustrat quod dixit de nouo foedere pangendo, à diuersitate siue dissimilitudine veteris foederis, cuius hic descriptio quædam habetur, petita ab ijs quibuscum iƈtu est, à patribus nempe; deinde à tempore quo iƈtum est, nempe quo die prehendi &c. Loquitur itaque de foedere eo quod iƈtum est cum populo, ex monte Sina per Mosen, inter Deum & populum, Mediatorem. Fuit quidem illud fœdus legale, sed non sine obscura aliqua significatione fœderis gratuiti. Nam ipsi non) Ratio dissimilitudinis siue diuersitatis proximæ, à facto, partim populi, partim Dei, Factum populi est violatio veteris fœderis: facta Dei est reiectio Dei, qua populum suum despexit.
units.tr: 9 Not according to the covenant) He illustrates what he said about making the new covenant by the difference, or unlikeness, of the old covenant. A description of the old covenant is given here, drawn first from the persons with whom it was made, namely the fathers; then from the time when it was made, namely the day when God took them by the hand, and so on. He speaks, therefore, of the covenant that was made with the people through Moses on Mount Sinai, between God and the people, with a mediator. That covenant was indeed legal, yet not without some obscure indication of the gratuitous covenant. For they continued not) This is the reason for the nearest unlikeness or difference, drawn from what was done partly by the people and partly by God. The people's act was the violation of the old covenant; God's act was the rejection of God, by which he despised his people.

units.la: 10 Quamobrem hoc est) Hactenus præfatio fuit, qua præparatus est populus ad accipiendum & audiendum promissionem noui fœderis. Priusquam autem verba ipsa promissionis subiiciat, rursus præfatiuncula quadam populum suum præparat, & attentionem captat. Indam legis meas) Sequitur ipsum nouum fœdus quod promittit. Est autem his verbis prima in nouo fœdere promissio. Promissio autem est Regenerationis, quæ reipsa nihil aliud est quàm legis Dei inscriptio, in mente primum, deinde in corde. Inscribitur autem Lex Dei in mente, quum mens renouatur ad imaginem Dei, quæ est in sapientia & cognitione. Vide Coloss. 3.10. Inscribitur autem Lex Dei cordi, quum ipsum renouatur ad imaginem Dei, secundum iustitiam & sanctimoniam veram. Eph.4.24. Non est quod hic colligant Aduersarij diferimen & differentiam Legis & Euangelij. Quasi vero lex inscribatur tabulis, vel lapideis, vel chartaceis: Euangelium vero tabulis cordis carneis: quum hic sermo sit de ipsa Lege, siue Decalogo, quem prædicit Propheta inscribendum demùm cordi, quum priùs inscriptus fuerit tabulis lapideis. Vide similem locum.2.Corinth.3.1. & deinceps.
