Et ero ipsis Deus) Secunda promissio est in nouo foedere pangendo:promittit (vt sic dicam) confœderationem,qua fiet,vt ipse sit Deus eorum, ij verò sint populus eius: hæc enim confœderatio est inter Deum & hominem virtute fœderis, alter alterius est quasi possessio quædam: Deus est hominis possessio quædam, & homo rursus Dei: verùm hoc discrimine: homo possidet Deum, vt aliquid se superius & excellentius, Deus autem hominem, vt aliquid inferius & ipsi subseruiens,hoc enim populi nomen significat.Talis itaque est confœderatio inter Deum & populum suum, qualis est inter Principem & subditos,Dominum & seruos.
units.tr: 10 For this is the covenant) So far this has been a preface, by which the people were prepared to receive and hear the promise of the new covenant. Before he sets out the very words of the promise, he again prepares his people with a short introduction and wins their attention. I will put my laws) Now follows the new covenant itself, which he promises. The first promise in the new covenant is in these words, and it is a promise of regeneration, which in reality is nothing other than the writing of God's law, first in the mind and then in the heart. The law of God is written in the mind when the mind is renewed after the image of God, which consists in wisdom and knowledge; see Colossians 3:10. The law of God is written in the heart when the heart is renewed after the image of God, in true righteousness and holiness; Ephesians 4:24. There is no reason for the adversaries to draw from this a distinction and difference between Law and Gospel, as if the law were written on tablets of stone, or of wax, or of paper, and the gospel on the fleshy tablets of the heart. Here the subject is the law itself, or the Decalogue, which the prophet foretells is to be written at last on the heart, after it was first written on stone tablets. See a similar passage, 2 Corinthians 3:1 and following. And I will be to them a God) The second promise in the making of the new covenant: it promises, so to speak, a mutual bond, by which he himself will be their God and they will be his people. For this bond between God and man, by the force of the covenant, makes each a kind of possession of the other: God is a certain possession of man, and man again of God. Yet there is this difference: man possesses God as something higher and more excellent, whereas God possesses man as something lower that serves him; for this is what the name people signifies. Such, then, is the bond between God and his people as is between a prince and his subjects, a lord and his servants.

units.la: Neque docebunt)Tertia promissio: Erunt omnes Θεοδίδακτοι, doctia Deo, vide Ioan.6. 45.Sic tractatur. Primùm negat docendos homines aliorum hominum opera: deinde reddit eius rationem,ab extraordinaria scientia & cognitione Dei, qua omnes sunt imbuendi fine discrimine, pusilli æquè atque magni, hoc est, omnes erunt Θεοδίδακτοι, ac proinde non opus erit doctoribus hominibus. Quod quidem non est accipiendum absolutè & simpliciter, quasi in Ecclesia Christi nulli futuri sint homines qui sunt docturi & adducturi alios ad cognitionem Dei in Christo. Nam Christus postquàm ascendit in cœlos, dedit alios quidę Apostolos, alios verò Prophetas, alios autem Euangelistas, alios autem Pastores & Doctores. Eph.4.11.verùm accipiendū est coparate, sicta nimirū cū veteri illa Ecclesia coparatione quæ magna ex parte habebat homines Doctores, quia ante Christi exh. bitionem, & in cœlos ascensionem, minor erat in hominibus Spiritus sancti efficacia: Nondum erat Spiritus sanctus, quia Iesus nondum erat glorificatus. Ioan.7.29. De complemento hujus promissionis, lege. 1. Thes.4.9. Ipsi namq; diuinitus doeti estis vt diligatis alij alios. & 1. Ioan. 2. 20. At vos vnctionem habetis à Sancto illo profecta, & nois omnia. & v.27 Sed vnctio quam vos accepistis à Deo, manet in vobis, nec necesse habetis vt quisquam doceat vos &c.
units.tr: Neither shall they teach) The third promise: all will be taught of God [Θεοδίδακτοι]; see John 6:45. The passage is handled thus. First he denies that men need to be taught by the work of other men; then he gives the reason, drawn from the extraordinary knowledge and acquaintance with God in which all, without distinction, the least as much as the greatest, are to be instructed. That is, all will be taught of God, and therefore there will be no need of human teachers. This is not to be taken absolutely and simply, as if in the Church of Christ there would be no men who are to teach and lead others to the knowledge of God in Christ. For after Christ ascended into heaven, he gave some apostles, some prophets, some evangelists, and some pastors and teachers; Ephesians 4:11. It must rather be taken comparatively, in comparison with the old Church, which had for the most part human teachers, because before the manifestation of Christ and his ascension into heaven the efficacy of the Holy Spirit among men was less. The Holy Spirit was not yet, because Jesus was not yet glorified; John 7:39. For the fulfilment of this promise, read 1 Thessalonians 4:9: For ye yourselves are taught of God to love one another; and 1 John 2:20: But ye have an unction from the Holy One, and ye know all things; and verse 27: But the anointing which ye have received of him abideth in you, and ye need not that any man teach you, and so on.

units.la: 12 Ero enim propitium) Quarta promissio, nempe remissionis peccatorum.
units.tr: 12 For I will be merciful) The fourth promise, namely the remission of sins.

units.la: 13 Dum nouum dicit ) Hoc consectarium est quod infert Author ex verbis Prophetæ, nempe ijs quæ habentur versu 8. (cum domo Iuda fœdus nouum.) Ex eo enim quod Propheta fœdus nouum dixerit fœdus hoc posterius, infert fœdus illud prius eadem opera antiquatum fuisse, ac consenuisse. Ex quo rursus infert & alterum consectarium. Quod si antiquatum fuit ac consenuit, sequitur tum prope fuisse vt euanesceret: quod enim antiquatur ac senescit vergit ad interitum.
units.tr: 13 In that he saith) This is the corollary that the author draws from the words of the prophet, namely those in verse 8 (with the house of Judah a new covenant). From the prophet's calling the latter covenant new, he infers that the former was by the same token made old and grown obsolete. From this he draws a further corollary: if it has been made old and has grown obsolete, it follows that it was then near to vanishing away, for what is becoming old and waxing aged tends toward destruction.

units.la: Argumentum Capitis noni.
units.tr: The argument of the ninth chapter.

units.la: Hoc capite habemus primum argumentum præstantiæ Christi Pontificis septimum, à pluribus Christi prærogatiuis sumptum, ad versum vsque 13. Quo loco digressio est ad versum vsque 14. Vbi redit ad argumentum institutum, & illas Christi prærogatiuas, quas ad finem capitis persequitur.
units.tr: In this chapter we have the first argument for the excellence of Christ as high priest, the seventh, taken from several of Christ's prerogatives, running to verse 13. There is a digression at this point, up to verse 14, where he returns to the argument under way and pursues, to the end of the chapter, those prerogatives of Christ.

units.la: CAPVT IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER 9.

units.la: 1 Habuit igitur prius fœdus etiam constitutos religionis ritus, & sanctuarium mundanum.
units.tr: 1 Then indeed the first covenant also had ordinances of divine worship and a worldly sanctuary.

units.la: 2 Tabernaculum enim constructum fuit: prius quidem in quo erant candelabrum, & mensa: & propositi panes, quod Sancta vocant.
units.tr: 2 For a tabernacle was made: the first part, in which were the lampstand, the table, and the showbread, which is called the holy place.

units.la: 3 Post medium autem velum erat Tabernaculum quod vocant Sancta sanctorum:
units.tr: 3 And behind the second veil was the tabernacle called the Holy of Holies,

units.la: 4 Aureum habens thuribulum, & Arcam fœderis vndique circumtectam auro: in qua urna aurea habens manna, & virga Aaron quæ germinauit, & Tabulæ fœderis:
units.tr: 4 which had the golden censer, and the ark of the covenant overlaid on every side with gold, in which were the golden pot holding the manna, Aaron's rod that budded, and the tables of the covenant;

units.la: 5 Supra hanc autem Cherubin gloriosi obumbrantes propitiatorium: de quibus non est nunc dicendum singulatim.
units.tr: 5 and above it the glorious cherubim overshadowing the mercy seat, of which we cannot now speak in detail.

units.la: 6 His vero ita ordinatis, in prius quidem Tabernaculum quouis tempore ingrediuntur Sacerdotes ritus cheuntes.
units.tr: 6 Now when these things had been so arranged, the priests always went into the first tabernacle, performing the rites of worship.

units.la: 7 In secundum autem, semel quotannis solus Pontifex, non sine sanguine, quem offert pro seipso & pro populi erratis.
units.tr: 7 But into the second, only the high priest went, once a year, not without blood, which he offered for himself and for the errors of the people.

units.la: 8 Hoc declarante spiritu sanĉto, nondum patefactam furiffe Iiam ad Sacrarium, priore Tabernaculo adhuc consistente.
units.tr: 8 The Holy Spirit signifying this, that the way into the sanctuary was not yet made manifest while the first tabernacle still stood.

units.la: 9 Quod erat exemplar pro tempore illo prasenti, quo dona sacrificiaque offeruntur, qua non possunt conscientia sanctificare cultorem.
units.tr: 9 This was a figure for the present time, in which gifts and sacrifices are offered, which cannot make the worshipper perfect in conscience.

units.la: 10 In cibis duntaxat & potionibus, & diversis ablutionibus ac ritibus carnalibus, usque ad tempus correctionis imposita.
units.tr: 10 They stood only in meats and drinks, and various washings and carnal ordinances, imposed until the time of correction.

units.la: 11 Adveniens autem Christus Pontifex suturorum bonorum, per maius & perfectius Tabernaculum, non manu factum, id est, non huius struturae.
units.tr: 11 But Christ, coming as high priest of the good things to come, entered through a greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands, that is, not of this building.

units.la: 12 Neque per sanguinem hircorum & vitulorum sed per proprium sanguinem ingressus est semel in sacrarium, aeternam redemptionem nactus.
units.tr: 12 Neither by the blood of goats and calves, but by his own blood, he entered once into the sanctuary, having obtained eternal redemption.

units.la: Habuit igitur) Transit hoc loco ad Argumentum praestantiae Christi septimum. Agit itaque de foedere illo priore ac vetere: ac primum ipsum describit ex adiunctis duobus: priori, constitutis religionis ritibus, hoc est, constitutionibus de ritibus & ceremoniis: posteriori, loco ubi illi ritus peragi solebant, nempe in Sanctuario: quod mundanum ideo vocat, ut distinguat a coelesti illo in quod ingressus est Christus: mundanum est terrestre & caducum.
units.tr: Had therefore) He passes at this point to the seventh argument for the excellence of Christ. He therefore treats of that former and old covenant, and first describes it by two adjuncts: the first, the ordinances of worship established, that is, the regulations about the rites and ceremonies; the second, the place where those rites were usually performed, namely the sanctuary, which he calls worldly in order to distinguish it from the heavenly one into which Christ entered; for the worldly is the earthly and transitory.

units.la: 2 Tabernaculum) Καὶ ὑγιής duo illa foederis sive Tabernaculi adiuncta explicat. Primum itaque de Tabernaculo agit quam praecedenti versu αγιον vocavit. Tabernaculi est obscura quaedam distributio in prius & pofterius. Prius describitur hoc versu, primum ex instrumentis sacris, deinde ex rebus sacris, tertiò ex nomine suo.Lucerna)Primum instrumentum Lucerna, λυχνία siue λυχνοῦχος fuit qui ad latus Sancti Meridionale collocatus est. Mensa) Secundum instrumentum Mensa, quæ ad latus Sancti Septentrionale collocatus erat. Et propofitipanes) Hæc res sacra est quæ mensæ erat imposita, videlicet panes propositionis, qui quidem panes dispositi fuerunt feni duobus ordinibus. Leuit. 14.6. Quodfanctia) Hoc nomen est prioris Tabernaculi partis.
units.tr: 2 Tabernacle) He explains the two adjuncts of the covenant or tabernacle, the Greek "and" [καί] joining them. He treats first of the tabernacle, which in the previous verse he called the holy place [ἅγιον]. There is a somewhat unclear division of the tabernacle into a first and a second part. The first is described in this verse: first from its sacred furnishings, then from its sacred objects, and thirdly from its name. Lampstand) The first furnishing is the lampstand, [λυχνία] or lampstand-bearer [λυχνοῦχος], placed on the south side of the Holy Place. Table) The second furnishing is the table, placed on the north side. And the showbread) This is the sacred object placed on the table, namely the bread of the presentation, which was set out in two rows of six. Lev. 24.6. Which is called) This is the name of the first part of the tabernacle.

units.la: 3 Post medium) Periphrasis quædam posterioris Tabernaculi, Dixisset enim, Posterius vero Tebernaculum erat quod vocant, &c. verum pro eo dixit post medium velum erat Tabernaculum quod vocant, &c. ponens pro Tabernaculo posteriori Tabernaculum situm post medium velum. Medium dicit velum respectu primi, quo sanctum distinguebatur ab atrio populi. Vide Exod. 26.33.36. Describitur Tabernaculum posterius, primum à nomine suo, vocant enim illud Sancta sanctorum.
units.tr: 3 After the second) A periphrasis for the second part of the tabernacle. He could have said, "The second tabernacle was that which is called," etc., but instead he says, "after the second veil was the tabernacle which is called," etc., putting for the second tabernacle the tabernacle situated behind the second veil. He calls the veil "second" with respect to the first, by which the holy place was separated from the court of the people. See Exod. 26.33, 36. The second tabernacle is described first by its name, for it is called the Holy of Holies.

units.la: 4 aureum habens) Secunda pars defcriptionis, ab instrumentis sacris duobus, quorum primum erat thuribulum, altare suffitus, quod extra velum coram arca positum fuisse videtur. Exod. 30.6. & deinceps. Nam illic expresse dicitur thymaterium ponendum esse ante velum: deinde præcipitur vt quotidie suffitus adoleatur, id quod fieri non potuisset fi intra velum fuisset collocatum, quippe intra quod semel tantum in anno ingredi licebat. Et arcam) Hoc fecundum est instrumentum sacrum quod rursus describitur, primum ex ornatu suo, tectorio aureo : deinde ex rebus fcris, quæ in arca erant, vrna aurea habente mana,virga Aaronis qu̅ germinauit,& tabulis fœderis, e quibus tabulæ fœderis, proprie loquendo, in arca seu intra arcam reconditæ fuerunt: Virga autem Aaronis, itemque manna in vrna reconditum coram arca, reposita fuerunt, vt liquet ex 1.Reg.8.9. Exod.16.34.35. Numeri 17.25.
units.tr: 4 Which had the golden) The second part of the description is from two sacred furnishings, the first of which was the golden censer, the altar of incense, which seems to have been placed outside the veil in front of the ark. Exod. 30.6 and following: for there it is expressly said that the altar of incense is to be placed before the veil; and then it is commanded that incense be burned on it every day, which could not have been done if it had been placed within the veil, into which it was permitted to enter only once a year. And the ark) This is the second sacred furnishing, which is again described, first from its ornament, the gold overlay, and then from the sacred objects in the ark: the golden pot holding the manna, Aaron's rod that budded, and the tables of the covenant. Of these, the tables of the covenant were properly placed within the ark, while Aaron's rod and the manna in the pot were stored before the ark, as is clear from 1 Kings 8.9, Exod. 16.34-35, and Num. 17.25.

units.la: 5 Supra hanc autem) Descripta jam est arca abijs quæ dicta sunt fuisse in ipla arca nempe vrna &c. Nunc describitur ab ijs quæ dicuntur fuisse supra arcam, nempe Cherubinis qui operculo arcæ in duabus oris e regione insistentes, alis ad fe inuicem conuersis operculum obumbrabunt, inter quas alas gloria Iehouæ, id est, Iehouah gloriosus residebat,& consulentibus responsa dabat. Vide Exod.25. 18. & deinceps 1. Reg. 6. 27. Gloriosi) Defcriptio est Cherubinorum. primum ab adjuncta gloria, deinde ab officio : propitiatorium erat operculum arcæ. De quibus.) Reijcit ab hoc loco & tempore accuratiorem singulorum istorum explicationem. His autem ita) Hactenus de Sanctuario mundano siue Tabernaculo, h. e. de loco, in quo ritus peragi solebant. Nunc de ipsis ritibus, h. e. de altero prioris foederis adjungitur. His verbis transitio quaedam est, quasi dicat, atque haec hactenus quae ad Tabernaculum pertinent a nobis ita ordinata sunt & disposita. Nunc dicendum est secundo loco de ritibus, qui peragi solebat in Tabernaculo.
units.tr: 5 Above it) The ark has now been described by what was said to be inside it, namely the pot and so on. Now it is described by what is said to be above the ark: the cherubim, who stood facing each other at the two ends of the ark's cover, and with their wings turned toward each other overshadowed the cover; between those wings the glory of Jehovah, that is, the glorious Jehovah, dwelt, and gave answers to those who consulted him. See Exod. 25.18 and following; 1 Kings 6.27. Glorious) This is a description of the cherubim, first from the glory attached to them, then from their office; the mercy seat was the cover of the ark. Of which) He sets aside a more exact explanation of each of these things for this place and time. Now these things having been so) Thus far he has spoken of the worldly sanctuary or tabernacle, that is, of the place where the rites were usually performed. Now he adds, as the second item, the rites themselves, that is, the other element of the former covenant. These words make a kind of transition, as if he said: "Thus far those things which pertain to the tabernacle have been so arranged and disposed by us. Now we must speak, secondly, of the rites which were performed in the tabernacle."

units.la: 6 In prius quidem) Primo loco agit de ritibus, qui peragebantur in Tabernaculo priori fiue sancto: vbi haec tria habes. Primum sunt personae quae ingrediebantur prius Tabernaculum & ritus obibant: Personae erant Sacerdotes in genere, tam princeps sacerdotum, quam sacerdotum vulgus. Deinde mentio fit temporis quo ingrediebantur, & obibant ritus sacerdotes. Tempus est in genere quodcunque & quotidianum. Tertio habes de ritibus. Ritus erant in genere quicunque, h. e. oblationes omnis generis & preces. Atque ideo vtitur generali verbo rituum, eo significans ritus cujuscunque generis.
units.tr: 6 In the first) First he treats of the rites performed in the first or holy tabernacle, where you have three things. First, the persons who entered the first tabernacle and performed the rites: these were the priests in general, both the chief priest and the common priests. Next, mention is made of the time when the priests entered and performed the rites: the time is in general whatever time and daily. Thirdly, you have the rites. The rites were in general of every kind, that is, offerings of every sort and prayers. And so he uses the general word "rites," meaning rites of every kind.

units.la: 7 In secundum autem) Hic agit de ritibus qui peragebantur in secundo Tabernaculo, siue Sancto sanctorum, vbi primum habes de persona, quae ritus peragebat, nempe Pontifice solo: deinde habes de tempore quo ingrediebatur in Sanctum sanctorum, & peragebat ritus: tempus est vnum tantum, & vnus dies anni cujusque: tertio habes de ipso ritu qui perragebatur semel quotannis, à Pontifice solo: Ritus erat speciales, nempe oblatio sanguinis, subaudi vituli & hirci, in peluim excepti. Vide Levit. 16. 2. & deinceps. Quarto habes ritus siue oblationis finem ac vsum: erat autem oblatio sanguinis, primùm pro ipso Pontifice: pro se enim offerebat sanguinem vituli: deinde pro peccatis populi, pro quibus erat oblatio sanguinis hirci.
units.tr: 7 But into the second) Here he treats of the rites performed in the second tabernacle, or Holy of Holies, where first you have the person who performed the rites, namely the high priest alone; next, the time when he entered the Holy of Holies and performed the rites: the time is only one, one day of each year; thirdly, you have the rite itself, which was performed once a year by the high priest alone. The rite was a special one, namely the offering of blood, understood of the calf and the goat, received in a basin. See Lev. 16.2 and following. Fourthly, you have the end and use of the rite or offering: the offering of blood was first for the high priest himself, for he offered the blood of the calf for himself; then for the sins of the people, for which the blood of the goat was offered.

units.la: 8 Hoc declarante.) Sequitur expositio ritus huius speciali, quem obibat solus Pontifex, semel duntaxat quotannis, idque non solùm pro populi peccatis, sed etiam pro suis. Expositionem hanc confirmat à Spiritus sancti testimonio. Nam idem ille Spiritus qui ritus instituit, idem, inquam, rituum à seinstitutorum, & circumstantium omnium quae cum ritibus coniunctae sunt, interpres est & expositor. Expositio autem & declaratio proximi ritus, & circumstantium eius est, quòd priore Tabernaculo adhuc consistente; in quo ritus proximus aliique peragebantur, nondum patef facta fuerit via ad Sacrarium. Id quod indicabatur, partim ex persona solius Pontificis, cui, aliis omnibus exclusis, soli permissum fuerat vt ingrederetur Sanctum sanctorum, in eoque obiret hunc oblationis ritum: partim ex tempore, quod vnicum erat tantum in vno anno: partim ex ipsa oblatione, quae fuit sanguinis cantum typici: partim denique ex oblationis fine, qui erat, vt oblatio fieret,non tantum propopuli peccatis, verum etiam pro peccatis Pontificis ipsius. Hæc omnia indicabant nondum patefactam fuisse viam ad Sacrarium,nempe verum,quod cælum est.
units.tr: 8 The Holy Spirit signifying) There follows an explanation of this special rite, which the high priest alone performed, once only a year, and that not only for the sins of the people but also for his own. He confirms this explanation from the testimony of the Holy Spirit. For that same Spirit who instituted the rites is, I say, the interpreter and expositor of the rites themselves, and of all their circumstances connected with them. The explanation and declaration of this particular rite and its circumstances is that, while the former tabernacle still stood, in which this rite and others were performed, the way into the sanctuary had not yet been made manifest. This was indicated partly by the person of the high priest alone, to whom, all others being excluded, alone it was permitted to enter the Holy of Holies and perform this rite of offering there; partly by the time, which was unique, only one in the year; partly by the offering itself, which was of blood only, and typical; partly finally by the purpose of the offering, which was that the offering be made not only for the sins of the people, but also for the sins of the high priest himself. All these things indicated that the way into the sanctuary, namely the true one, which is heaven, had not yet been made manifest.

units.la: Quod erat) Occupatio: dici potuit:Quis igitur erat vsus prioris illius Tabernaculi?Re spodet Tabernaculum illud prius fuisse παραβολὴ,similitudinem, hoc est,exemplar seu typum,videlicet alterius Tabernaculi, quod nimirum est ipsum Christi corpus.Atque hoc primum est quo extenuat Tabernaculum illud vetus: alterum est à tempore cui inseruiebat.Tempus erat illud præsens, non quod suturum erat in aduentu Christi. Tertium quo extenuat illud vetus Tabernaculum,est à donis & sacrificiis quæ in eo offerebantur, pro tempore illo præsenti:eiusmodi autem erant ea,quæ non poterant conscientia sanctificare cultorem, h.e.abolere malam conscientiam, quæ est peccatorum commissorum.
units.tr: Which was) Occupatio: someone might ask, "What, then, was the use of that earlier tabernacle?" He answers that the earlier tabernacle was a parable [παραβολὴ], a likeness, that is, an example or type of another tabernacle, namely Christ's own body. This is the first way in which he diminishes that old tabernacle. The second is from the time it served. That time was the present time, not the time that was to come at Christ's coming. The third way in which he diminishes the old tabernacle is from the gifts and sacrifices offered in it for that present time. These were the kind that could not sanctify the worshipper in conscience, that is, do away with the evil conscience that comes from sins committed.

units.la: Incibis) Probat illa dona sacrificiáque, quæ in Tabernaculo offerebantur, non potuisse sanctificare conscientia cultoré, à natura ipsa,& genere earum rerum, quæ donabantur & sacrificabantur:.Erant autem carnales res & externæ, vtpote cibi, potiones, diuersæ ablutiones, ac omninò ritus huiusmodi. Vsque ad tempus) Altera ratio est, cur non poterant sanctificare conscientia cultores rem:quia vt erant carnalia tantum, ita erant temporaria tantum,imposita (subaudi) oneris instar, vsque ad tempus correctionis, hoc est, tempus aduentus Christi,in quo hęc omnia erant corrigenda,hoc est, aboleda, ingrediente nimirum in locum typorum & vmbrarum ipso corpore,quod est Christus.
units.tr: In foods) He proves that those gifts and sacrifices offered in the tabernacle could not sanctify the worshipper in conscience, by reason of their very nature and kind, since they were the things that were given and sacrificed. These were carnal and external things, such as foods, drinks, various washings, and altogether rites of this sort. Until the time) This is the second reason why they could not sanctify the worshipper in conscience. Since they were only carnal, they were also only temporary, laid on as a kind of burden (understand: "until the time") until the time of correction, that is, the time of Christ's coming, when all these things were to be corrected, that is, abolished, since the body itself, which is Christ, was entering into the place of the types and shadows.

units.la: II. Adueniens autem) Hic reuertitur ad institutam comparationem noui Pontificis cū veteri illo.Propositio fuit v.7.de veteri Pontifice, hic assumptio est de nouo. In hanc formā redigitur argumentatio. Vetus Pontifex semel quotannis solus,idq; non fine sanguine, quę offerebat etiam pro suis peccatis, in facrarū terrestre ingrediebatur. At Christus Pōtifex, nimirum futurorū bonorū,in aduetu suo,per maius Tabernaculū, & per sanguine proprium,ingressus est semel in sacrarium cœleste, eóq; facto nactus est nobis Redēptionem æterna. Sequitur ergo Christum præstantiore esse Pontificem illo veteri. Argumentum est excellentiæ siue præstantiæ Christi septimū. Sumptum est à multis prærogatiuis, quibus Christus veterem illum Pōtificem exuperat.
units.tr: II. But coming) Here he returns to the comparison he set up between the new High Priest and that old one. The proposition, in verse 7, was about the old High Priest; here the assumption is about the new one. The argument is reduced to this form: The old High Priest, once a year, alone, and not without blood, which he offered also for his own sins, entered the earthly sanctuary. But Christ, the High Priest of good things to come, by his coming, through a greater tabernacle and through his own blood, entered once into the heavenly sanctuary, and having done so, obtained for us eternal redemption. It follows, therefore, that Christ is a higher priest than that old one. This is the seventh argument, for the excellence or superiority of Christ. It is drawn from the many prerogatives by which Christ surpasses that old High Priest.

units.la: Pontifex futurorum) Non simpliciter Pontificem nominat,sed addit bona illa,siue benedictiones spirituales,quarum est Pontifex, h.e. quas Pontificatu suo nobis acquirit. Hoc adiectum est ad maiorem Pontificatus Christi commendationem: futura bona vocat, quia tum um futura erant, cum erat vetus Pontifex, quasi dicat, bonorum quæ non erant præsentia um quum erat vetus Pontifex, sed tantum suura: Cœperunt autem esse postquàm iam adienit Christus Pontifex.Per maius) Prima præ- rogatiua Christi Pontificis. Ingressus est per maius & perfectius Tabernaculum, quàm fuit illud vetus per quod ingressus est Pontifex vetus.Non manufactum) Hæc verba rationem continent, cur maius & perfectius vocatum sit hoc Tabernaculum. Est autem ab ejus structura, siue à modo ac ratione, qua factum & exstructum est.Non est factum manu, subaudi hominum, h. e. illa hominum opera, sed factum est manu & operatione ipsius Dei, per Spiritum suum sanctum:intelligit autem Christi corpus siue humanam naturam.
units.tr: High Priest of good things to come) He does not simply call him High Priest, but adds the good things, or spiritual blessings, of which he is High Priest, that is, those which he acquires for us by his priesthood. This is added to commend Christ's priesthood more highly. He calls them good things to come because they were still to come when the old High Priest was in office. It is as if he said: they were not yet present good things at the time of the old High Priest, but only future ones. They began to exist after Christ the High Priest had come. Through a greater) The first prerogative of Christ the High Priest. He entered through a greater and more perfect tabernacle than that old one through which the old High Priest entered. Not made with hands) These words give the reason why this tabernacle is called greater and more perfect. It is so from its structure, or from the manner and method by which it was made and built. It was not made by hand, understand "of men," that is, not by human works, but was made by the hand and working of God himself, through his Holy Spirit. He means Christ's body, or human nature.

units.la: 12 Neque per sanguinem) Hæc secunda prærogatiua est Christi Pontificis, qua excellit veterem. Cernitur autem hæc prærogatiua in sacrificio quod Christus obtulit. Semel) Tertia est prærogatiua. Vetus Pontifex semel quotannis ingressus est Sanctum sanctorum. At Christus semel tantum omnino ingressus est cœlum. In sacrarium) Quarta prærogatiua à loco in quem ingressus est Christus, sacrario cœlesti, quod καθ' ἑαυτὸν hoc loco (vt etiam supra versu 8.) simpliciter sacrarium vocatum est. Æternam) Hæc quinta est prærogatiua. Vetus Pontifex sua oblatione non potuit san{E}ificare conscientia cultorem. At Christus suo sacrificio æternam redemptionem est nactus.
units.tr: 12 Nor by the blood) This is the second prerogative of Christ the High Priest, by which he excels the old one. This prerogative is seen in the sacrifice that Christ offered. Once) The third prerogative. The old High Priest entered the Holy of Holies once a year. But Christ entered heaven only once, at all. Into the sanctuary) The fourth prerogative, from the place into which Christ entered, the heavenly sanctuary, which in this passage (as also in verse 8) is simply called the sanctuary [kath' heauton: καθ' ἑαυτὸν]. Eternal) This is the fifth prerogative. The old High Priest, by his offering, could not sanctify the worshipper in conscience. But Christ, by his sacrifice, obtained eternal redemption.

units.la: 13 Nam si sanguis taurorum & hircorum, & cinis iuuencæ aspergens inquinatos, sanctificat ad carnis puritatem?
units.tr: 13 For if the blood of bulls and goats, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkling the unclean, sanctify to the cleanness of the flesh?

units.la: 14 Quanto magis sanguis Christi, qui per spiritum æternum seipsum obtulit inculpatum Deo, purgabit conscientiam vestram à mortuis operibus, ad seruiendum Deo viuo.
units.tr: 14 How much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God?

units.la: 15 Itaque ob id noui Fœderis Mediator est, vt morte intercedente ad redemptionem earum prævaricationum quæ fuerant sub priore Testamento, qui vocati erant, promissam æternam hæreditatem acciperent.
units.tr: 15 And therefore he is the Mediator of a new covenant, so that, death having intervened for the redemption of those transgressions that were under the former testament, those who were called might receive the promised eternal inheritance.

units.la: 16 Nam vbi Testamentum est, mors intercedat necesse est testatoris.
units.tr: 16 For where there is a testament, the death of the testator must necessarily intervene.

units.la: 17 Testamentum enim in mortuis ratum est: quandoquidem nondum valet quum viuit testator.
units.tr: 17 For a testament is confirmed over the dead, since it has no force while the testator lives.

units.la: 18 Vnde ne prius quidem illud absque sanguine dedicatum fuit.
units.tr: 18 Hence not even the first was dedicated without blood.

units.la: 19 Quum enim Moses omnia mandata secundum Legem recitasset toti populo, sumpto sanguine vitulorum & hircorum, cum aqua & lana coccina & hyssopo, simul & ipsum librum & totum populum aspersit.
units.tr: 19 For when Moses had recited all the commandments according to the Law to the whole people, he took the blood of calves and goats, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people.

units.la: 20 Dicens Hic est sanguis Testamenti quod mandauit vobis Deus.
units.tr: 20 Saying, This is the blood of the testament which God has commanded you.

units.la: 21 Insuper autem & Tabernaculum, & omnia vasa sacrorum sanguine similiter aspersit.
units.tr: 21 Moreover, he likewise sprinkled the tabernacle and all the vessels of the sacred service with blood.

units.la: 12 Et omnia fere secundum Legem sanguine purificantur: & absque sanguinis effusione non fit remissio.
units.tr: 22 And almost all things are purified by blood according to the Law, and without shedding of blood there is no remission.

units.la: 13 Itaque necesse fuit exemplaria quidem eorum quae sunt in cœlis, hisce rebus purificari, ipsa autem cœlestia potioribus quam haec sunt victimis.
units.tr: 23 Therefore it was necessary that the copies of the things in the heavens be purified with these things, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these.

units.la: Nam si sanguis.) Digressio est a praesenti instituto, in quo probat proximam Christi Pontificis praerogatiuam. Argumentum sumptum est a minori comparatione efficaciae sanguinis taurorum, & hircorum &c. ad sanctificandum exterius carnem, & efficaciae sanguinis Christi, ad purgandam interius conscientiam. Argumenti forma est. Si sanguis taurorum & hircorum &c. sanctificat ad carnis puritatem, quanto magis sanguis Christi &c. purgabit conscientiam &c. At primum, Ergo secundum. Sanguis taurorum) Vide Leuit. 16. Cinis Iuuencae) Vide Numer. 19. verf. 4. & deinceps: vbi leges cinerem Iuuencae combustae, aqua miscetum fuisse, eaque aqua inquinatos fuisse aspersos. Ad carnem) Hic seorsim capit umbras a rebus ipsis adumbratis.
units.tr: If the blood.) This is a digression from the present line of argument, in which he proves the next prerogative of Christ the High Priest. The argument is drawn from a lesser comparison: the efficacy of the blood of bulls and goats, etc., in sanctifying the flesh outwardly, with the efficacy of Christ's blood in purging the conscience inwardly. The form of the argument is this: If the blood of bulls and goats, etc., sanctifies to the cleanness of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, etc., purge the conscience, etc. But the first is true; therefore the second. The blood of bulls) See Leviticus 16. The ashes of a heifer) See Numbers 19:4 and following, where you will read that the ashes of the burnt heifer were mixed with water, and the unclean were sprinkled with that water. To the flesh) Here he takes the shadows separately from the realities they foreshadowed.

units.la: 14 Quanto magis) Apodosis comparationis. Qui per Spiritum) Hic duo argumenta inferuntur, quibus probat efficaciam sanguinis Christi ad purgandas conscientias. Primum argumentum est a principali offerente illum sanguinem, nempe Spiritu aeterno, hoc est, æterna Christi Deitate, quæ in offerendo Christum primas habuit partes. Christus quidem Sacerdos fuit, seseque obtulit, fateor, vt Deus & homo, verùm Deitatis primæ erant partes. Inculpatum Deo) Hoc alterum argumentum est, à sanctitate humanæ naturæ, quæ à Deitate oblata est Deo. Oblatus quidem est totus Christus Deus & homo. verùm humanæ naturæ proprie & præcipue oblatio est facta. Quemadmodum natura quæ obtulit diuina fuit præcipue ac proprie. Purgabit) Purgare conscientiam, hoc loco est abolere peccata quæ malam efficiunt conscientiam. A mortuis) Hic est quasi terminus a quo procedit purgatio, opera nimirum mortua, hoc est, peccata: quæ ideo mortua dicuntur, quod mortem peccantis gignant. Nam finis & stipendia peccati mors. Rom. 6. 21. 23. Ad seruiendum) Hic terminus est ad quem procedit purgatio, nempe opera viua & bona quæ posita sunt in eo vt seruiatur Deo viuo. Deus ideo viuus dicitur, non tantum quia ipse viuit, verùm etiam quia eos qui ipsi seruiunt viuificat, quemadmodum peccata morte assiciunt seruos suos.
units.tr: 14 How much more) The apodosis of the comparison. Who through the Spirit) Here two arguments are brought in, by which he proves the efficacy of Christ's blood to purge consciences. The first argument is from the principal offerer of that blood, namely the eternal Spirit, that is, the eternal Deity of Christ, which had the chief part in the offering of Christ. Christ indeed was the priest, and offered himself, I grant, as God and man, but the chief part belonged to the Deity. Without spot to God) This is the second argument, from the holiness of the human nature, which was offered to God by the Deity. Indeed, the whole Christ, God and man, was offered, but the offering was made properly and principally in the human nature, just as the nature that offered was principally and properly divine. Will purge) To purge the conscience, in this place, is to abolish the sins which make the conscience evil. From dead) This is, as it were, the starting point from which the purging proceeds, namely dead works, that is, sins. They are called dead because they produce the death of the sinner. For the end and wages of sin is death. Rom. 6:21, 23. To serve) This is the end to which the purging proceeds, namely living and good works, which are done so as to serve the living God. God is called living not only because he himself lives, but also because he gives life to those who serve him, just as sins bring death upon their servants.

units.la: 25 Itaque ob id) Malim retinere propriam significationem particulæ vt legatur, Et, vel, atque ob id. Habetur enim hoc versu alterum argumentum, quo probat Christum Pontificem nactum nobis æternam redemptionem.
units.tr: 25 Therefore on this account) I would prefer to keep the proper meaning of the particle, so that it reads "And, or, and on this account." For in this verse there is a second argument by which he proves that Christ the High Priest has obtained eternal redemption for us.

units.la: Sumptum est à fine cur sit Christus Mediator noui foederis siue Testamenti. Finis est, vt accipiamus promissam illam æternam hæreditatem, h.e. vt nos in æternum redimat. Media per quæ hæreditas ista à Mediatore fœderis ad nos peruenit, hæc sunt. Primum intercedit mors Mediatoris siue sponsoris. Deinde sequitur vocatio efficax: hanc excipit redemptio præuaricationum, h.e. remissio peccatorum. Remissionem peccatorum denique sequitur hæreditas, siue g'orificatio. Quæ fuerant) Remissionem peculiariter tribuit peccatis quæ commissa erant sub veteri Testamento, ea re significans, non fuisse eam veteris Testamenti efficaciam ad eas abolenda: verum toto veteris Testamenti tempore Deum ea præterijsse & tolerasse, aduentu autem Christi & noui Testamenti, quod ad remissionem peccatorum efficax est, iam ea plane remisisse & abolevisse. Vide Rom.3.25.26. Promissionem) h.e. hæreditatem promissam. Sic promissionis nomen accipit Apostolus Rom.4.13.
units.tr: The argument is drawn from the end for which Christ is the Mediator of the new covenant or testament. The end is that we should receive the promised eternal inheritance, that is, that he should redeem us for ever. The means by which this inheritance comes to us from the Mediator of the covenant are these. First, the death of the Mediator or surety intervenes. Then comes effectual calling. This is followed by redemption from transgressions, that is, the remission of sins. Finally, the remission of sins is followed by the inheritance, or glorification. Which had been) He attributes remission specifically to the sins committed under the Old Testament, thereby signifying that the Old Testament had no power to abolish them. Rather, throughout the whole period of the Old Testament God passed over and tolerated those sins, but with the coming of Christ and the New Testament, which is effective for the remission of sins, he has now plainly remitted and abolished them. See Rom. 3.25, 26. The promise) that is, the promised inheritance. In this sense the Apostle uses the word promise, Rom. 4.13.

units.la: 16 Nam [Ibi Testamentum]) Probat non nisi morte intercedente, Christum Mediatorem esse noui foederis seu Testamenti. Argumentum est à natura Testamenti, quæ necessario postulat Testatoris mortem intercedentem, siue argumentum est à necessario Testamenti adiuncto, quod est intercedens mors Testatoris. Sequitur ergo ad hoc vt sit Christus Mediator noui Testamenti, fiue quod idem est, nouum testamentum fit Christi Testamentum, necesse esse vt Christi mors intercedat.
units.tr: 16 For where a testament [is]) He proves that Christ is the Mediator of the new covenant or testament only if his death intervenes. The argument is from the nature of a testament, which necessarily requires the intervening death of the testator. Or the argument is from what necessarily belongs to a testament, namely the intervening death of the testator. It follows, therefore, that for Christ to be the Mediator of the new testament, or, which is the same thing, for the new testament to become Christ's testament, the death of Christ must necessarily intervene.

units.la: 17 Testamentum enim) Probat mortem intercedentem necessarium esse Testamenti ad iunctum, ab effecto quodam mortis, quod in eo cernitur, vt ratum faciat Testamentum, in hanc formam. Mors testatoris est quæ ratum facit testamentum. Ergo vbi testamentum, ibi mors intercedat necesse est: alioqui enim sine morte testatoris ratum esse testamentum non potest. Quandoquidem) Probat hoc mortis Testatoris effectum, à contrario vitæ testatoris effecto. Testator dum viuit non valet neq; ratum est eius Testamentum. Ergo mortuo demum testatore valet, & ratum est eius Testamentum.
units.tr: 17 For a testament) He proves that the intervening death is a necessary adjunct of a testament, from a certain effect of death which is seen in it, namely that it makes the testament valid. The argument runs thus: the death of the testator is what makes a testament valid. Therefore, wherever there is a testament, the death must necessarily intervene; for without the death of the testator a testament cannot be valid. Since) He proves this effect of the testator's death from the contrary effect of the testator's life. While the testator lives, his testament has no force and is not valid. Therefore only when the testator is dead does it take effect and become valid.

units.la: 18 Vnde ne prius) Hoc alterum argumentum est, quo probat, non nisi intercedente morte Christum esse Mediatorem noui fœderis, siue Testamenti Sumptum est à similitudine veteris Testamenti, quod & ipsum Deo non est dedicatum absque sanguine. Quamobrem nouum etiam Testamentum necessariò postulat sanguinem Mediatoris.
units.tr: 18 Whence not even the first) This is a second argument, by which he proves that Christ is the Mediator of the new covenant or testament only if death intervenes. It is drawn from the likeness to the Old Testament, which was likewise not dedicated to God without blood. For this reason the new testament too necessarily requires the blood of the Mediator.

units.la: 19 Cùm enim) Probat ex effectis aliquot Mosis depromptis ex libro Exod. 24. vetus Testamentum absque sanguine dedicatū, & Deo consecratum, non fuisse. Primum Mosis essectum fuit, quo sumpto sanguine vitulorum & hircorum &c.simul & librum, & totum populum aspersit. Hoc effectum Moses circumscribitur suo tempore, nempe postquàm Moíes omnia mandata &c.Mandata secundum legem intelligit, mandata illa quæ in lege Dei erant comprehensa. Cum aqua) Harum rerum non quidem fit expressa mentio Exo. 24. unde hæc recitantur, verùm istas tanquam ordinariè adhibitas tum quoque fuisse, colligitur ex alijs locis, ubi ista diserte præcipiuntur. Librum) nempe fœderis. Totum populum) Id est, duodecim statuas, quas illic erexerat ad repræsentandum duodecim Tribus Israelis. Quemadmodum per altare repræsentabatur Deus fœdus cum illis contrahens.
units.tr: 19 For when) From several effects of Moses, taken from Exodus 24, he proves that the Old Testament was not dedicated and consecrated to God without blood. The first effect of Moses was this: taking the blood of calves and goats, etc., he sprinkled both the book and the whole people. Moses' action is set in its time, namely after Moses had recounted all the commandments, etc. By the commandments he means those commandments which were contained in the law of God. With water) Indeed, these things are not expressly mentioned in Exod. 24, from which they are recited; but that these were also customarily used at that time is gathered from other places where they are explicitly commanded. The book) namely of the covenant. The whole people) that is, the twelve pillars which he had erected there to represent the twelve tribes of Israel, just as the altar represented God, who made the covenant with them.

units.la: 20 Dicens hic est) Hoc est verbum cum signo conjunctum, quo signum sive ritus externus explicatus est à Mose. In Sacramento enim duo sunt, signum visibile & verbum audibile. Hic est sanguis) Sensus est, hic sanguis quem habeo in crateribus, est sanguis Testamenti. Explicat enim Moses vsum illius sanguinis quæ habebat in crateribus, populum quoque aspergebat.
units.tr: 20 Saying, This is) This is the word joined to the sign, by which Moses explained the sign or external rite. For in a sacrament there are two things, a visible sign and an audible word. This is the blood) The sense is: this blood which I have in the bowls is the blood of the testament. For Moses explains the use of that blood which he had in the bowls, and with which he also sprinkled the people.

units.la: 21 Insuper autem) Pergit in effectis Moisis. Vt librum & populum totum, sic Tabernaculum & omnia vasa sacri ministerij sanguine aspersit.
units.tr: 21 Moreover) He goes on with the effects of Moses. Just as he sprinkled the book and the whole people, so he sprinkled the tabernacle and all the vessels of the sacred ministry with blood.

units.la: 22 Et omnia) Inductionis compendium est. Secundum legem) id est, legalia, sive ad legem pertinentia, h.e. ad vetus testamentum, quod hic Lex appellatur. Et absque) Vt proximè docuit ipsum vetus Testamentum non fuisse consecratum Deo sine sanguine; ita hic docet vetus Testamentum impletum non fuisse absque sanguinis effusione. Implebatur autem vetus Testamentum, cum peccata populi remissa fuerunt, quorum in ipso foedere remissio erat promissa. Ergo ut foedus ipsum non erat ictum sine sanguine, ita neque impletum erat sine sanguine. Sic res se habet in novo foedere, in quo, & propter sanguinem Christi pacificitur nobiscum Deus novum foedus, & propter eundem illum sanguinem foedus illud ictum implet & exequitur in nobis justificandis & seruandis.
units.tr: 22 And almost all things) This is a summary of the induction. According to the law) that is, legal things, or things pertaining to the law, that is, to the Old Testament, which is here called the Law. And without) As he has just taught that the Old Testament itself was not consecrated to God without blood, so here he teaches that the Old Testament was not fulfilled without the shedding of blood. Now the Old Testament was fulfilled when the sins of the people were remitted, and the remission of these had been promised in the covenant itself. Therefore, just as the covenant itself was not struck without blood, so neither was it fulfilled without blood. So it is in the new covenant: God makes peace with us through the new covenant on account of the blood of Christ, and on account of that same blood he fulfils and executes that covenant once struck, in justifying and preserving us.

units.la: Itaque necesse) Concludit necessitatem mortis Mediatoris novi foederis, quam probandam suscepit verf. 16. Conclusio illustrata est per dissimilitudinem umbrarum, & figurarum, ac si dixisset: Quamobrem ut necesse fuit umbras rerum coelestium purificari & dedicari rebus istiusmodi carnalibus, ut sanguine vitulorum & hircorum: ita necesse fuit resipsas coeleştes in novo foedere purificari sanguine Mediatoris Christi. Victimas appellat quamen una fuerit Christi victima, fortassis propter unius illius victimae multiplicem usum, in purgandis multis rebus coelestibus & spiritualibus.
units.tr: Therefore it is necessary) He draws the conclusion concerning the necessity of the death of the Mediator of the new covenant, which he undertook to prove in verse 16. The conclusion is illustrated by the contrast between shadows and figures, as if he had said: therefore, just as it was necessary for the shadows of heavenly things to be purified and dedicated with carnal things of this kind, such as the blood of calves and goats, so it was necessary for the heavenly things themselves to be purified in the new covenant with the blood of Christ the Mediator. He calls them sacrifices, although Christ was one sacrifice, perhaps because of the manifold use of that one sacrifice in purifying many heavenly and spiritual things.

units.la: 24. Non enim in manufactum sacrarium ingressus est Christus, quod sit exemplar vero sacrario respondens, sed in ipsum cælum, vt appareat nunc in conspectu Dei pro nobis.
units.tr: 24 For Christ has not entered into a sanctuary made with hands, which is a figure of the true, but into heaven itself, that he may now appear in the presence of God for us.

units.la: 25 Neque vt sæpe offerat semetipsum, sicut Pontifex ingreditur in sacrarium quotannis cum sanguine alieno.
units.tr: 25 Nor that he should offer himself often, as the high priest enters into the sanctuary every year with blood not his own.

units.la: 26 (Alioquin oportuit eum sæpe pati à condito mundo) sed nunc semel in consummatione seculorum, ad abolendum peccatum, per immolationem suiipsius patefactus est.
units.tr: 26 (For then he would have had to suffer often since the foundation of the world); but now once, in the end of the ages, he has been manifested to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.

units.la: 27 Et sicut illud statutum est hominibus semel mori, postea iudicium.
units.tr: 27 And as it is appointed to men once to die, and after this the judgment;

units.la: 28 Ita & Christus semel oblatus est multorum peccata tollere, altera vice absque peccato conspicietur iis qui ipsum expectant ad salutem.
units.tr: 28 So also Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, without sin, to those who wait for him unto salvation.

units.la: Non enim in) Hactenus digressio fuit. Nunc reuertitur ad institutam comparationem Pontificis Christi, & veteris Pontificis: & ad prærogatiuas illas Christi Pontificis, de quibus versibus 11. & 12. Occasio arrepta est ex proximis verbis, quibus dixit Christum potiorem esse victimam omnibus victimis illis Legalibus. Hinc de præstantia Christi Pontificis agit. Primo autem repetit prærogatiuam illam quæ fuit supra ver. 12. eaque eum præfert veteri Pontifici. Vetus Pontifex ingrediebatur sacrarium manufactum, quod exemplar dumtaxat fuit vero sacrario respondens. At Christus nouus Pontifex, non ingressus est in manufactum sacrarium &c. sed in ipsum cælum &c.Vt appareat) Ingressus Christi in cælum à fine suo commendatur, qui est vt apud Deum interpellet pro nobis. Rom. 8. 38. 1. Ioan. 2. 1.
units.tr: For not into) Up to this point there has been a digression. Now he returns to the comparison of Christ the high priest with the old high priest, which he had begun, and to those prerogatives of Christ the high priest mentioned in verses 11 and 12. The occasion is taken from the words immediately preceding, in which he said that Christ is a better sacrifice than all those legal sacrifices. Hence he treats of the excellence of Christ the high priest. First, he repeats that prerogative which was mentioned above in verse 12, and by it he sets Christ above the old high priest. The old high priest entered a sanctuary made with hands, which was only a figure corresponding to the true sanctuary. But Christ, the new high priest, did not enter a sanctuary made with hands, etc., but heaven itself, etc. That he may appear) The entry of Christ into heaven is commended by its end, which is that he may intercede with God for us. Rom. 8.34; 1 John 2.1.

units.la: 25 Neque vt sæpe) Hoc versu habes repetitam secundam & tertiam prærogatiuam: de quibus supra versu 12. quibus ipsis superat veterem illum Pontificem. Vetus Pontifex ingressus est in Sacrarium cum sanguine alieno. At Christus semetipsum obtulit. Vetus Pontifex sæpe obtulit, nempe quotannis. At Christus, non sæpe, sed semel tantum obtulit.
units.tr: 25 Nor that he should often) In this verse you have the second and third prerogatives repeated, which were mentioned above in verse 12, and by which he surpasses that old high priest. The old high priest entered the sanctuary with the blood of another. But Christ offered himself. The old high priest offered often, namely every year. But Christ offered himself not often, but only once.

units.la: 26 Alioqui oportuisset) Probat Christum non sæpe fuisse offerendum semetipsum, ab absurdo, eoque duplici. Primum est quia si oportuisset eum sæpe se offerre, oportuisset eum non modo sæpe passum esse, sed etiam sæpe passum esse à condito mundo. In hanc formam. Si oportuisset Christum sæpe offerre semetipsum, oportuisset eum sæpe passum & mortuum suisse à condito mundo: At hoc est absurdum. Ergo &c. Sequela propositionis sic ostenditur. Primum quia offerri Christum, est pati & mori. Deinde quia si vnica Christi oblatio semel facta suo tempore non sufficiat ad redemptionem omnium peccatorum inde à condito mundo, præteritorum, præsentium, & futurorum, sed oportuisset eum sæpe offerri, ob secto initium mortis ipsius petendum fuisset à condito mundo, quo nimirum tempore cœpit peccatum. Nam si sæpe fieri debeat oblatio pro peccato, certe necesse est incipiat oblatio
units.tr: 26 For otherwise he would have had to) He proves that Christ was not to offer himself often, by a reductio ad absurdum, and this a twofold one. The first is this: if he had had to offer himself often, he would have had to suffer and die not only often but often since the foundation of the world. The argument runs thus: if Christ had had to offer himself often, he would have had to suffer and die often since the foundation of the world; but this is absurd; therefore, etc. The consequence of the premise is shown thus. First, because to be offered is for Christ to suffer and die. Second, because if the single offering of Christ, once made at its time, does not suffice for the redemption of all sins from the foundation of the world, past, present and future, but he had to be offered often, then the beginning of his death would have had to be sought from the foundation of the world, at which time sin certainly began. For if the offering for sin must be made often, it is certainly necessary that the offering begin

units.la: latio Iatiq; quo tempore primum peccatum coepit & commissum elt. Sed nunc) Correctio quaedam est, qua pronunciat Christum, non saepe, sed semel passum esse, non a condito mundo passum, sed in consummatione seculorum, h. e post quam venit plenum illud tempus, a Patre scilicet constitutum. Gal. 4. 4. Ad abolendum) Hic finis cur Christus semel fit passus tantum, idque in consummatione seculorum. Est autem ad abolendum peccatum, in genere omnium temporum, praeteriti, praesentis, futuri.
units.tr: ...the time when sin first began and was committed. But now) This is a corrective, by which he declares that Christ suffered not often, but once, and not from the foundation of the world, but in the consummation of the ages, that is, after that fullness of time came, appointed by the Father. Gal. 4.4. To abolish) This is the end for which Christ suffered only once, and that in the consummation of the ages. It is for the abolishing of sin, in the whole range of times: past, present and future.

units.la: 27 Et sicut) Vt videtur occurrit scandalo passionis Christi, ex eo quod oblationem istam semel factam ingens Christi gloria consecuta sit, ostendens fecunda vice absq; peccato conspiciendum esse, i.e. cum gloria, vtpote gloriosi mundi Iudicem. Illustratur haec sententia similitudine sumpta ab hominibus, quorum morte non iteratam, sed semel factam, idq; ex Dei instituto, sequitur iudicium. Generale illud iudicium videtur intelligere in quo Iesus Christus futurus est Iudex. Sic & Christus, post oblationem ipsius factam, conspicietur gloriosus ille Iudex, ad salutem ipsorum qui illum expectant ad judicium illud venturum. Multorum peccata) Innuit efficaciam vnicae oblationis Christi semel factae. Nam vnica illa oblatio efficax est ad tollenda, non vnius tantum, sed multorum peccata. Absque peccato) Nempe quod ipsi, cum oblatus est in cruce, imputatum est. Nam qui non nouit peccatum, pro nobis peccatum factus est, vt nos efficeremur Iustitia Dei in eo. 2.Cor.5.21. Peccato imputato dicitur Christus mortuus fuisse semel.
units.tr: 27 And as) It seems he meets the scandal of Christ's passion, namely that the offering, made once, was followed by the great glory of Christ, showing that he is to be seen, on the second occasion, without sin, that is, with glory, as the judge of the glorious world. This sentence is illustrated by a comparison taken from men, for whom, by God's appointment, death is not repeated but comes once, and is followed by judgment. He seems to mean that general judgment in which Jesus Christ is to be the Judge. So also Christ, after his offering has been made, will be seen as that glorious Judge, for the salvation of those who await him as he comes to that judgment. The sins of many) He hints at the efficacy of the one offering of Christ, made once. For that one offering is effective for taking away the sins not of one alone, but of many. Apart from sin) Namely, that sin which was imputed to him when he was offered on the cross. For "him who knew no sin he made to be sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in him," 2 Cor. 5.21. With sin imputed, Christ is said to have died once.

units.la: Argumentum Capitis decimi.
units.tr: Argument of the Tenth Chapter.

units.la: Hoc capite primum alijs duobus argumentis offendit Christum non saepius offerendum, sed vnicam eius oblationem sufficere, ad verf. 19. Deinde redit ad instlitutam exhortationem, ad perseuerantiam in fide: eiusque argumenta duo adducit, nonum & decimum, ad verf. 36 usque 16. Tertio vndecimum est exhortationis argumentum, in quo immoratur ad verf. 32. Postremo dehortatur ab Apostasia, argumento sumpto ab afflictionibus, quas iam ante perpessi sunt pro fide, ad finem capitis. Vbi obiter etiam inferuntur argumenta exhortationis principalis duo, duodecimum & decimumtertium.
units.tr: In this chapter he first shows, by two other arguments, up to verse 19, that Christ is not to be offered more often, but that his one offering is sufficient. Then he returns to the exhortation set out earlier, to perseverance in faith, and brings forward two arguments for it, the ninth and the tenth, up to verse 36 and verse 16. Third, there is the eleventh argument of exhortation, which he dwells on up to verse 32. Lastly, he dissuades from apostasy by an argument taken from the afflictions which they have already endured for the faith, to the end of the chapter. Where, in passing, the two arguments of the principal exhortation are also introduced, the twelfth and the thirteenth.

units.la: CAPVT X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: 1 Lex enim vmbram habens futurorum bonorum, non expressam formam rerum, ijs hostiis quas singulis annis eadem continenter offerunt, nunquam potest accedentes perficere.
units.tr: 1 For the law, having a shadow of the good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never with those sacrifices which they offer continually year by year make the comers thereunto perfect.

units.la: 2 Alioqui desiissent offerri, propterea quod sacrificantes semel purgati, nullorum peccatorum amplius conscientiam habuissent.
units.tr: 2 For then would they not have ceased to be offered? because that the worshippers once purged should have had no more conscience of sins.

units.la: 3 At in ipsis fit repetita mentio peccatorum quotannis.
units.tr: 3 But in those sacrifices there is a remembrance again made of sins every year.

units.la: 4 Non enim potest sanguis taurorum & hircorum auferre peccata.
units.tr: 4 For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins.

units.la: 5 Quapropter ingrediens mundum, dicit Sacrificium & oblationem noluisti, corpus autem aptasti mihi.
units.tr: 5 Wherefore when he cometh into the world, he saith, Sacrifice and offering thou wouldest not, but a body hast thou prepared me.

units.la: 6 Holocautomata & hostiam pro peccato non approbasti.
units.tr: 6 In burnt offerings and sacrifices for sin thou hast had no pleasure.

units.la: 7 Tunc dixi, Ecce adsum (in capite libri scriptum est de me) ut faciam, Deus, voluntatem tuam.
units.tr: 7 Then said I, Lo, I come (in the volume of the book it is written of me) to do thy will, O God.

units.la: 8 Quum superius dixisset, Sacrificium & oblationem, & holocautomata, & hostiam pro peccatis noluisti, neque approbasti (quae iuxta Legem osseruntur)
units.tr: 8 When he said above, Sacrifice and offering and burnt offerings and offerings for sin thou wouldest not, neither hadst pleasure therein (which are offered by the law);

units.la: 9 Tunc dixit Ecce adsum ut faciam, Deus, voluntatem tuam. Tollit primus ut postremus statuat.
units.tr: 9 Then said he, Lo, I come to do thy will, O God. He taketh away the first, that he may establish the second.

units.la: 10 Qua voluntate sanctificati sumus, per oblationem corporis Iesu Christi semel factam.
units.tr: 10 By which will we are sanctified, through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.

units.la: 11 Omnis igitur Sacerdos adstat quotidie operans, & eadem saepius offerens hostias, quae nunquam possunt auferre peccata.
units.tr: 11 And every priest standeth daily ministering and offering oftentimes the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins.

units.la: 12 Hic vero una pro peccatis oblata victima, in perpetuum consedit ad dextram Dei.
units.tr: 12 But this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God;

units.la: 13 Id quod superest expectans, donec inimici ipsius scabellum pedum eius fiant.
units.tr: 13 From henceforth expecting till his enemies be made his footstool.

units.la: 14 Unica enim oblatione consecravit in perpetuum eos qui sanctificantur.
units.tr: 14 For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.

units.la: 15 Testificatur autem hoc nobis, & ipse Spiritus sanctus: nam postea quam praedixit,
units.tr: 15 Whereof the Holy Ghost also is a witness to us: for after that he had said before,

units.la: 16 Hoc est foedus quod pactus cum eis post dies illos, dicit Dominus, indam leges meas cordibus eorum, & eorum mentibus eas inscribam.
units.tr: 16 This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, saith the Lord; I will put my laws into their hearts, and in their minds will I write them;

units.la: 17 Et peccatorum atque iniquitatum ipsorum non recordabor amplius.
units.tr: 17 And their sins and iniquities will I remember no more.

units.la: 18 Porro ubi est horum remissio, non est amplius oblatio pro peccato.
units.tr: 18 Now where remission of these is, there is no more offering for sin.

units.la: Lex enim umbram) Sequitur argumentum secundum, quo ostendit Christum non saepe offerendum fuisse, sed unicam ejus oblationem sufficere: in hanc formam. Per oblationem corporis Iesu Christi semel factam sanctificamur. Ergo non opus est saepe iterum ipsum osserat. Argumentum est ab effecto unicae illius oblationis, nempe perfectione & sanctificatione nostri. Integer syllogismus hic est. Si unica Christi oblatio semel facta sanctificet, non opus est ut ipse saepius se offerat. At primum, Ergo secundum. Syllogismi hujus propositio non est in textu expressa: assumptio habetur postea, vers. 10. Conclusio intelligenda relinquitur. Illustratio assumptionis a dissimili efsecto sacrificiorum legalium praecedit ab initio capitis, ad vers. 10. Dissimilitudo haec est, Sacrificia legalia saepius oblata non sanctificant. At oblatio Christi semel facta sanctificat. Protasis dissimilitudinis de legalibus sacrificiis ostenditur pluribus argumentis. Primum habetur versu primo, a natura eorum quae lege continentur. Sunt tantum umbra & rudis quaedam delineatio futurorum bonorum, non autem expressa imago rerum ipsarum coloribus depicta, picta: Argumenti forma est. Lex tantum vmbram obtinet, &c. Lex ergo & legalia sacrificia, quæ singulis annis continenter offeruntur à Pontifice, nunquam possunt accedentes sanctificare.
units.tr: For the law (having a shadow) There follows the second argument, by which he shows that Christ did not need to be offered often, but that his one offering suffices. In this form: we are sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ made once. Therefore there is no need for him to offer himself again and again. The argument is drawn from the effect of that one offering, namely our perfection and sanctification. This is a complete syllogism. If the one offering of Christ, once made, sanctifies, there is no need that he offer himself more often. But the first holds; therefore the second. The proposition of this syllogism is not expressed in the text; the assumption is given afterwards, at verse 10. The conclusion is left to be understood. An illustration of the assumption, from the dissimilar effect of the legal sacrifices, comes before it, from the beginning of the chapter down to verse 10. The dissimilarity is this: legal sacrifices offered often do not sanctify; but the offering of Christ, made once, does sanctify. The protasis of this dissimilarity, concerning the legal sacrifices, is shown by several arguments. The first is in verse 1, drawn from the nature of the things contained in the law. They are only a shadow and a rough outline of good things to come, not the true image of the things themselves painted in their own colours. The form of the argument is: the law has only a shadow, etc. Therefore the law and the legal sacrifices, which are offered continually year by year by the high priest, can never sanctify those who come.

units.la: 2 Alioqui nonne) Secundum argumentum. Si sacrificia legalia per se sanctificassent, anno desiisset offerri? Atqui non desierunt offerri: Ergo non sanctificârunt. Propterea quod) Probat connexionem, facta semel bona conscientia non amplius opus est oblatione. At si sancti ficassent legalia sacrificia fecissent bona conscientiâ. Ergo si sanctificassent desijssent offerri. Argumetum sumptum est à natura sanctificationis, quæ nihil aliud est, quàm conscientiæ purgatio, abolitio malæ conscientiæ, quæ est ipsa peccatorum conscientia, & effectio bonæ conscientiæ.Qui sacrificassent) Cultores vocat cap.9.v.9. vbi dicit sacrificia illa non posse sanctificare conscientia cultorem.
units.tr: 2 Otherwise would they not) The second argument. If the legal sacrifices had sanctified by themselves, would they not have ceased to be offered after a year? But they did not cease to be offered; therefore they did not sanctify. Because that) This proves the connection: once a good conscience is made, there is no longer any need for offering. But if the legal sacrifices had sanctified, they would have made a good conscience. Therefore, if they had sanctified, they would have ceased to be offered. The argument is taken from the nature of sanctification, which is nothing other than the purging of the conscience, the removal of a bad conscience (which is the very consciousness of sins), and the making of a good conscience. Those who offered) He calls them worshippers, as in chapter 9, verse 9, where he says that those sacrifices could not make the worshipper perfect in conscience.

units.la: 3 Atqui in) Argumentū tertium à cōiuncta fiue adiuncta cū anniuersariis illis sacrificiis legalibus, omnium superiorū peccatorū mētione repetita. Quoties enim oblatio facta est, totics mentio facta est superiorum peccatorum. Sequitur ergo non habuisse sacrificia illa vim sanctificandi & abolendi peccata: si enim iam expiata erant peccata illa quorsum repetebantur, h.e. si per priora sacrificia expiata & abolita erant, quorsum cum postea rioribus sacrificiis repetita eorum mentio fiebat? De his vide Leuit. 16.
units.tr: 3 But in) The third argument, drawn from the remembrance of all previous sins which is renewed together with those annual legal sacrifices. For as often as an offering was made, so often was mention made of earlier sins. It follows, then, that those sacrifices did not have the power of sanctifying and taking away sins. For if those sins had already been expiated, why were they repeated? That is, if they had been expiated and taken away by the earlier sacrifices, why was mention of them made again with the later sacrifices? On these things see Leviticus 16.

units.la: 4 Non enim potest) Argumentum quartum ab impotentia sanguinis taurorū & hircorū. Oblationes illæ legales erant sanguinis tantum bestiarum. Atqui sanguis bestiarum non potest auferre peccata. Ergo oblationes illæ non possunt sanctificare. Sanctificare & auferre peccata, idem sunt hoc loco. Observa toto hoc loco, figuras siue typos seorsim considerari à rebus ipsis figuratis.
units.tr: 4 For it is not) The fourth argument, from the powerlessness of the blood of bulls and goats. Those legal offerings were only the blood of beasts. But the blood of beasts cannot take away sins; therefore those offerings cannot sanctify. To sanctify and to take away sins are the same thing in this place. Observe throughout this passage that the types or figures are considered apart from the realities they represent.

units.la: 5 Quapropter) Ex proxima demonstratione, qua ostensum est legalia sacrificia nō sanctificare, infert sublata esse ea, vt voluntas Dei de Christi sacrificio statueretur & ponerētur: In hanc sententiam primum affert verba Psalmistæ de Christo loquentis. Psalm. 40. ad versum vsque 8. Deinde ea verba interpretatur, ad versum 10. Ingrediens mundum) id est, Dei Filius, quo tempore homo factus est. Dicit) Introducitur à Psalmista Dei Filius pronuntians sublata esse à Patre suo sacrificia legalia. Nā hic est sensus huius loci, ad versum vsque septimum: vt Apostolus ipse interpretatur verf. 9. quum dicit Tollit primum. In hanc sententiam sunt omnia quę dicuntur duobus his versibus, excepto hoc quod inseritur de corpore ipsi aptato, quibus verbis receditur à vocibus iis, quæ habentur illo Psalmo: Nam illic habetur, (Aures perforasti mihi) pro quo hic legiturCorpus aptasti mihi.) Sed sensus est plane idem. Nam vtrobique intelligitur Filiurn Dei formatum esse ad summum obsequium & obedientiam Patris sui. Hoc enim significatur phrasi illa, quæ habetur in Psalmo de aurium perforatione, quæ signum erat seruitutis perpetuæ. Hoc quoque ipsum significatur aptatione ista corporis, h. e. naturæ humanæ aptatæ Deitati Filij Dei, quo factum est, vt formam serui acceperit, ad hoc vt sese submitteret Patri, & obediens fieret ad mortem, mortem autem crucis. Quæ alij afferunt ad locorum duorum conciliationem, ego hic prætereo.
units.tr: 5 Wherefore) From the immediately preceding demonstration, by which it has been shown that the legal sacrifices do not sanctify, he infers that they were removed so that God's will concerning Christ's sacrifice might be established and set in place. To this purpose he first brings the words of the Psalmist speaking of Christ, Psalm 40, down to verse 8, and then he interprets those words in verse 10. When he cometh into the world) that is, the Son of God, at the time when he was made man. He saith) The Son of God is introduced by the Psalmist, pronouncing that the legal sacrifices were removed by his Father. For this is the sense of this passage, down to the seventh verse, as the Apostle himself interprets in verse 9, when he says, "He taketh away the first." All that is said in these two verses is to this same sense, except what is inserted about the body prepared for him, in which words there is a departure from the terms found in that Psalm. For there it reads, "Mine ears hast thou opened," where here it reads "a body hast thou prepared me." Yet the sense is plainly the same. For in both places it is understood that the Son of God was fashioned for the highest obedience and submission to his Father. This is signified by that phrase in the Psalm about the piercing of the ears, which was a sign of perpetual servitude. This same thing is also signified by that preparation of the body, that is, of human nature fitted to the divinity of the Son of God, by which it came about that he took the form of a servant, so that he might submit himself to the Father and become obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Other things which others bring forward to reconcile the two passages I pass over here.

units.la: 7 Tunc dixi)His verbis habes finem, cur sublata sint sacrificia legalia: nempe vt locus esset voluntati Dei de Filio suo Christo, ipsiusque sacrificio. Hic enim profitetur Filius promptitudinem suam ad sese offerendum & moriendum, ex Patris sui voluntate. In capite) h. e. in volumine veteris Testamenti, vel librorum Mosis, quorum volumen dictum est κεφαλίς metaphorice à specie, eò quòd coiuolutum & complicatum libri corpus (vt libri quidem fuerunt veteres) quasi opus capitatum est. Porrò his verbis contineri videtur argumentum obedientiæ Christi quam hoc loco ipse prædicat. Argumentum est, quia sic de eo in veteri Testamento scriptum est. Sequitur ergo necessario ipsi faciendum esse quod vult Deus Pater, vt constet Scripturæ sacræ sua veritas, & Deus iustificetur in sermonibus suis. Rom. 3. 4.
units.tr: 7 Then said I) In these words you have the reason why the legal sacrifices were removed: namely, so that there might be room for the will of God concerning his Son Christ, and his sacrifice. For here the Son declares his readiness to offer and to die himself, in accordance with his Father's will. In the head) that is, in the volume of the Old Testament, or of the books of Moses, whose volume was called metaphorically by its shape [kephalis, κεφαλίς], because the body of the book, rolled up and folded (as ancient books were), is like a headed thing. Moreover, in these words the argument for Christ's obedience, which he proclaims in this place, seems to be contained. The argument is: because it is so written of him in the Old Testament. It follows necessarily that he must do what God the Father wills, so that the truth of Holy Scripture may stand and God may be justified in his words. Romans 3:4.

units.la: 8 Quum Iuftrius) Sermonem hunc Christi qui habetur Psal. 40. Apostolus exponit de abolitione sacrificiorum legalium, & constitutione obedientiæ & sacrificij Christi. Nam priora Christi verba significant (interprete Apostolo) sublata esse sacrificia legalia: posteriora vero, quibus dicit, Ecce adsum &c. significat Christi sacrificium statutum.
units.tr: 8 When he said above) The Apostle explains this saying of Christ, found in Psalm 40, as concerning the abolition of the legal sacrifices and the establishment of Christ's obedience and sacrifice. For Christ's earlier words signify (the Apostle interpreting) that the legal sacrifices were removed; but the later words, in which he says, "Lo, I come," etc., signify that Christ's sacrifice was established.

units.la: 10 Qua Voluntate) Hactenus fuit illustratio assumptionis syllogismi, qui huius loci est, à dissimilitudine legalium sacrificiorum. Nunc autem habetur ipsa assumptio, siue dissimilitudinis apodosis. Nam dissimilitudinis membra hæc sunt. Legalia sacrificia sæpius oblata non sanctificant, Christi vero oblatio semel facta sanctificat. Notandum quod sanctificationis hoc effectum tribuat primum voluntati Dei, tanquam causæ, deinde oblationi corporis Christi, quia oblatio corporis Christi fuit ex Dei voluntate. Iure igitur effectum oblationis Christi adscribitur Dei Patris voluntati, ut ipsi cum Filio suo sit gloria sanctificationis nostræ.
units.tr: 10 By that will) So far has been the illustration of the assumption of the syllogism, which concerns the dissimilarity of the legal sacrifices. Now, however, the assumption itself appears, or the apodosis of the dissimilarity. For the members of the dissimilarity are these: legal sacrifices, though offered often, do not sanctify; but the offering of Christ, made once, does sanctify. It should be noted that he attributes this effect of sanctification first to the will of God as its cause, and then to the offering of the body of Christ, because the offering of Christ's body was made by the will of God. Rightly, therefore, the effect of Christ's offering is ascribed to the will of God the Father, so that the glory of our sanctification may belong to him together with his Son.

units.la: 11 Omnis igitur Sacerdos) Hic repetit integram dissimilitudinem: Protasis dissimilitudinis de hostijs legalibus habetur hoc versu 11. Apodosis vero tribus sequentibus. Qua nunquam) Hoc idem est cum eo quod dixit vers.
units.tr: 11 Therefore every priest) Here he repeats the whole dissimilarity. The protasis of the dissimilarity concerning the legal victims is found in this verse 11, but the apodosis in the three following verses. Which never) This is the same as what he said in verse 1.

units.la: 1. Nunquam possunt sanctificare seu perfi-cere. cere. Nam perfectionis quæ effectum est oblationis Christi, pars quædam est peccati abolitio, siue remissio. In hac itaque parte totum intelligitur.
units.tr: 1. They can never sanctify or perfect. For part of that perfection which is the effect of Christ's offering is the abolition, or remission, of sin. In this part, therefore, the whole is understood.

units.la: 12 Hic vero) Apodosis dissimilitudinis quæ syllogismi assumptio est. Sedet ad dexteram) Iusta dissimilitudo postulabat vt diceretur, Christus vnica pro peccatis victima oblata, in perpetuum durante, sanctificat nos: verum pro sanctificatione potuit sessionem Christi ad dexteram Patris, quæ sanctificationis nostri consequens est, & necessario eam antegredientem præsupponit. Nam tum demum cœpit Christus sedere ad dexteram Dei, & gloriam suam adeptus est, quum victima sua semel oblata, suos sanctificasset ac perfecisset.
