He does not say simply that God called himself their God, but that he was not ashamed to be called their God, by which is signified that God in some measure humbled himself to them by this very fact that he wished to be called their God. For he had prepared) The reason for the consequence: he wished to be called their God because he had prepared a city for them. Therefore this very title of God bears witness that they desired another city, namely the heavenly one. For he means by a city having foundations that which was mentioned above at verse 10, which God had from eternity prepared for them. Hence at Matthew 25:34 it is called the kingdom prepared for the elect from the foundation of the world.

units.la: 17 Abraham quam)Tertium effectum fidei Abrahami. Cum a Deo tentaretur & exploraretur, per fidem obtulit Isaacum. Dicitur Abrahamus Isaacum obtulisse, quia etsi non reipsa & facto, tamen intentione & proposito eum obtulit, & Isaacus Abrahami proposito erat iam mortuus & occisus.Vnigenitum)Amplificatio effecti huius Abrahami, quod obtulerit eum quem vnigenitum, quod maius est quam si filium tantum obtulisset. Is qui promissiones) Secunda amplificatio a persona offerentis: is ipse obtulit Isaacum, qui promissiones acceperat.
units.tr: 17 Abraham, when) The third effect of Abraham's faith. When he was tested and proved by God, he offered Isaac through faith. Abraham is said to have offered Isaac, because although not in deed and fact, yet he offered him in intention and purpose, and Isaac was already dead and slain in Abraham's purpose. His only begotten) An amplification of this effect of Abraham, that he offered the one whom he called his only begotten, which is greater than if he had offered only a son. He who had received the promises) A second amplification, from the person of the one offering: he himself offered Isaac, who had received the promises.

units.la: 18 Ad quem dictum)Tertia amplificatio a promissione ipsa, quae non fuit generalis, de quocunque filio ex Abrahamo genito, aut gignendo, sed specialis de Isaaco nominatim: vt ostenditur recitatis promissionis verbis. In Isaac vocabitur tibi semen. Genef.21.12.
units.tr: 18 To whom it was said) A third amplification, from the promise itself, which was not general, concerning whatever son was born or would be born to Abraham, but special, concerning Isaac by name, as is shown by the words of the promise recited: In Isaac shall your seed be called (Genesis 21:12).

units.la: 19 Quum illud) Causam oftedit; quae mouit Abrahamum vt offerret filium suum Isaacum. Causa fuit consideratio potentiae Dei, qua vel ex mortuis excitare potuit Isaacum, eumque viuificare. Nisi enim perpendisset (secum) Deum posse Isaacum mortuum viuificare, vt in eo semen vocaretur, nequaquam eum obtulisset. Fundamentum igitur tantae in Abrahamo fidei, fuit potentia Dei, de qua fuit persuasus. Idem fundamentum fidei Abrahami habes etiam Rom. 4. 17. vbi dicitur credidisse Deo viuificanti mortuos, & vocanti ea quæ non sunt tanquam sint: & ibidem verf. 10. 21 aduersus promissionem Dei non disceptauit infidelitate, sed robustus factus est fide tributa gloria Deo, ac plene persuasum habes, προπεφορηθεις, eum quod promiserat posse etiam facere. Πληροφορία hæc potentiæ diuinæ hominem ita sustentat, vt etiam summas difficultates, quæ promissionibus Dei videntur esse prorsus contrariæ, earumque impletionem impedire, facile superet. Vnde etiam) Euentus fidei quæ Dei illa potentia nitebatur: recepit eum similitudine quadam quasi a mortuis excitatum. Neque enim vera fuit Isaaci mors, sed similitudinaria (mortuus enim est mete & proposito Abraham mi) eóque etiam similitudine quadam a mortuis resurrexit. Hæc autem similitudinaria mors & resurrectio Isaaci, typus fuit veræ mortis & resurrectionis Christi.
units.tr: 19 Since that) He shows the cause that moved Abraham to offer his son Isaac. The cause was the consideration of the power of God, by which he could raise Isaac even from the dead and give him life again. For unless he had weighed in himself that God could make the dead Isaac alive, so that in him a seed would be called, he would by no means have offered him. The foundation, then, of so great a faith in Abraham was the power of God, of which he was persuaded. You have the same foundation of Abraham's faith also at Romans 4:17, where it is said that he believed God, who gives life to the dead and calls those things which are not as though they were; and in the same place, verse 19–21, he did not waver through unbelief against the promise of God, but was made strong in faith, giving glory to God, and was fully persuaded [προπεφορηθεις] that what he had promised he was also able to do. This full assurance [πληροφορία] of divine power sustains a man in such a way that he easily overcomes even the greatest difficulties, which seem entirely contrary to the promises of God and to their fulfilment. Whence also) The outcome of the faith which rested on that power of God: he received him back by a certain likeness, as though raised from the dead. For Isaac's death was not real, but a likeness of death (for he was dead in the mind and purpose of Abraham), and by a certain likeness he also rose again from the dead. This likeness of death and resurrection in Isaac was a type of the true death and resurrection of Christ.

units.la: 20 Per fidem) Secundum particulare exemplum fidei Patrum, qui fuerunt ante exitum populi ex Ægypto, est Isaaci. Isaacus benedixit duobus filiis, Iacobo & Esauo, Iacobum Esauo præponit, quia ius primogenituræ pertinebat ad Iacobum, qui propterea primam accepit benedictionem, eamque non rem temporalium tantum, sed etiam spiritualium. um.Efau fecundam accepit benedictionem, rerum temporalium tantum, non spiritualiu. Benedictio haec vtraq; processit ex fide, qua Iaac tanquam propheta Dei credidit haec ita esse sutura quemadmodum praedicebat. Ergo pertinet hoc effectum ad illustrandu generale illud fidei effectum primum, quod commune est cuiusq; fidei, & hic ad extraordinariam fidem qualis fuit Prophetarum, extenditur.
units.tr: 20 By faith) The second particular example of the faith of the fathers, who lived before the exodus of the people from Egypt, is that of Isaac. Isaac blessed his two sons, Jacob and Esau, and he set Jacob before Esau, because the right of the firstborn belonged to Jacob, who therefore received the first blessing, and that not only of temporal but also of spiritual things. Esau received the second blessing, of temporal things only, not of spiritual. Both blessings proceeded from faith, by which Isaac, as a prophet of God, believed that these things would be just as he foretold. Therefore this effect pertains to illustrating that general first effect of faith, which is common to every faith, and here it is extended to extraordinary faith, such as that of the prophets.

units.la: 21 Per fidem Iacob) Tertium particulare exemplum fidei Patrum, ante exitum populi ex Aegypto, est Iacobi, qui per fidem (extraordinariam intellige qualis fuit Prophetarum) moriens benedixit duobus filijs Iosephi, Ephraim & Manasse. Nota igitur, ne ipsam quidem mortem imminentem impedire operationem Spiritus sancti per fidem. Et adorauit) Alterum effectum fidei Iacobi. Per fidem adorauit Deum post prolatam benedictionem, vt eam Deus effectam redderet. Baculo innixus) Situs adorantis notatur, ex Genes. 47. 31. vbi in Hebraeo dicitur adorasse ad cervical lecti: quum hic dicatur adorasse baculo innixus, prout etiam locum illum Genesis verterunt septuaginta interpretes, sed vtrumque coniunctim erat verum. Nam senex Iacob benedicturus filiis Iosephi, surrexit e lecto, & baculum manu prehendit quo se fustineret, absoluta autem benedictione inclinauit se ad cervical lecti, vt interea aliqua ex parte etiam [illegible, ~3 letters]tiam baculo inniteretur. Hebraea autem vox quae hic habetur, variatis punctis, vel ceruical, vel baculum significat.
units.tr: Through faith Jacob) The third particular example of the faith of the Fathers, before the people's departure from Egypt, is that of Jacob, who, by faith (understand the extraordinary faith such as the Prophets had), blessed the two sons of Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh, as he was dying. Note, then, that not even impending death itself hinders the operation of the Holy Spirit through faith. And worshipped) The second effect of Jacob's faith. Through faith he worshipped God after pronouncing the blessing, so that God would make it effective. Leaning on his staff) The posture of the worshipper is noted, from Genesis 47:31, where the Hebrew says that he worshipped at the head of the bed. Here it says he worshipped leaning on his staff, as the Seventy also rendered that passage; but both were true together. For the aged Jacob, about to bless Joseph's sons, rose from the bed and took his staff in his hand to support himself; but when the blessing was finished he bowed himself toward the head of the bed, so that in the meantime he also leaned in some part on his staff [illegible]. The Hebrew word found here, with the vowel points varied, means either "head of the bed" or "staff".

units.la: Per fidem Iosephi) Quartum exemplum particulare fidei Patrum ante exitum populi ex Ægypto, est Iosephi: primum effectum fidei Iosephi est, quod meminit de egressione filiorum Israel ex Ægypto. Pertinet hoc ad illustrandum generale illud fidei effectum primum.
units.tr: Through faith Joseph) The fourth particular example of the faith of the Fathers before the people's departure from Egypt is that of Joseph. The first effect of Joseph's faith is that he made mention of the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt. This serves to illustrate that general first effect of faith.

units.la: Deque ossibus) Secundum effectum fidei Iosephi: mandauit de ossibus suis, vt perferrentur in terram Canaan: oritur ex primo effectu, quo certo persuasus fuit Iosephus filios Israelis terram Canaan possessuros.
units.tr: And concerning his bones) The second effect of Joseph's faith: he gave command concerning his bones, that they should be carried to the land of Canaan. This arises from the first effect, by which Joseph was firmly persuaded that the children of Israel would possess the land of Canaan.

units.la: Per fidem Moses) Sequitur tertia classis effectorum fidei particularium, Patrum qui fuerunt ab exitu populi ex Ægypto vsque ad introitum in terram promissam, initio sumpto à Mose qui populum ex Ægypto eduxit. Verum effectis fidei Mosis praemittit effecta fidei parentum Mosis, quibus transit quodammodo ad effecta Mosis ipsius. Effecta fidei parentum Mosis duo sunt, καὶ ὑπερῶν proposita. Primum enim effectum in fine versus est internum in corde: non timuerunt iniustum & impium Pharaonis edictum, quo mandauerat vt omnes filij qui nascerentur Israelitis in riuum proiicerentur: Fides enim timorem expulerat. Secundum effectum (de quo initio versus) ex hoc priori sequitur, externum nimirum ipsorum factum in occultando Mose per tres menses.Quod viderent) Causa impellens parentes Mosis ad eum occultandum, venustas pueruli extraordinaria (fuit enim diuinitus venustus. Act. 7.20.) quæ adjuuans fuit causa illius fidei, qua occultarunt Mosem: fides enim ipsa, qua diuina inspiratione præuiderunt puerulum illum fore liberatorem populi, fuit causa principalis.
units.tr: Through faith Moses) There follows the third class of the particular effects of faith, of those Fathers who lived from the departure of the people from Egypt until their entry into the promised land, beginning with Moses, who led the people out of Egypt. But before the effects of Moses' own faith, the author sets down the effects of the faith of Moses' parents, by which he passes in some way to the effects of Moses himself. The effects of the faith of Moses' parents are two, set forth as above. The first effect, at the end of the verse, is internal, in the heart: they did not fear the unjust and impious edict of Pharaoh, by which he had commanded that every son born to the Israelites be cast into the river; for faith had driven out fear. The second effect (mentioned at the beginning of the verse) follows from this first, namely their external act of hiding Moses for three months. That they saw) The cause that moved Moses' parents to hide him was the extraordinary beauty of the little child (for he was divinely beautiful, Acts 7:20), which helped as a cause of that faith by which they hid Moses. But the faith itself, by which through divine inspiration they foresaw that the little child would be the deliverer of the people, was the principal cause.

units.la: 14 Per fidem) Sequuntur particularia effecta fidei Mosis ipsius: Primum est, quod jam grandis natu renuit vocari filius filiæ Pharaonis.
units.tr: 14 Through faith) There follow the particular effects of the faith of Moses himself. The first is that, now grown up, he refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter.

units.la: 15 Potius eligens) Fundamentum affert hujus effecti, cur renuerit Moses vocari filius-filiæ Pharaonis, quod est electio Mosis factum hoc præcedens, qua ex duobus propositis alterum eligit. Duo hæc erant Mosi proposita, vel ut malis afficeretur cum populo Dei, vel ut temporarijs commodis peccati frueretur. Ex his duobus eligit Moses potius ut malis afficeretur cum populo Dei, electionem hanc sequitur factum, renuit vocari filius filiæ Pharaonis. Temporariis commodis) Peccato tribuit commoda sua: nam ministrat hominibus honores, dignitates, opes, &c. quibus tanquam illecebris Diabolus ad peccandum sollicitat: verum hæc omnia commoda temporaria sunt: nam interea dum his commodis fruitur homo, peccatum eum præcipitat in inferos, & mortem æternam affert: nam finis peccati mors. Rom. 6.23.
units.tr: 15 Choosing rather) The author gives the ground of this effect, why Moses refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter: it is the choice of Moses, a deed preceding this, by which from two options he chose one. These two were set before Moses: either to be afflicted with the people of God, or to enjoy the temporary advantages of sin. From these two Moses chose rather to be afflicted with the people of God; this choice is followed by the deed, that he refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter. Temporary advantages) He attributes to sin its advantages: for it provides men with honours, dignities, wealth, and so on, with which the Devil entices men to sin as with allurements. But all these advantages are temporary: for while a man enjoys these advantages, sin casts him down into hell and brings eternal death, for the end of sin is death (Romans 6:23).

units.la: Maiores arbitratus) Ratio & fundamentum electionis huius:neque enim temere elegit Moses sed praecedente mentis iudicio & arbitrio. Propositis enim duobus illis de quibus dictum, primum de propositis mens iudicat, & resoluit in alteram partem, maiores nimirum esse diuitias probrum Christi, & afflictiones cum populo ipsius, quam Ægyptiorum thesauros. Mentis iudicium sequitur voluntatis electio, eligit potius probrum Christi, & malis affligi cum Ecclesia ipsius, quam temporaria peccati commoda: electionem postremo sequitur actio. Probrum Christi vocat diuitias maiores quam Ægyptiorum thesauros, quo quidem significat, nihil in hoc mundo gloriosius esse, nihil magis honorificum & pluris faciendum, quam Christi probrum & crucem, quae vel omnia regum terrenorum diademata facile exuperat. Unde solet Paulus hoc titulo, tanquam imprimis gloriosa ornare; quod fit captivus Iesu Christi. Ephes. 3.1. Philem. 1. & Gal. 6.14. omnem aliam gloriandi materiam abominatur praeter crucem Christi.Intuebatur enim) Fundamentum est resolutionis huius, quod monuit Moses ut maiores arbitratus sit diuitias probrum Christi, quam Ægyptiorum thesauros. Non temere mens in iudicando resoluit in alteram partem, sed in deliberando intuebatur in praemij largitionem: Deus enim largitur praemia ijs qui ipsum requirunt. supra vers. 6. Praemium autem hic
units.tr: Esteeming greater) The reason and ground of this choice: Moses did not choose rashly, but by a prior judgment and decision of the mind. For when those two options of which we have spoken were set before him, the mind first judges between them and resolves in favour of the one part, namely that the reproach of Christ is greater riches than the treasures of Egypt, and to be afflicted with his people. The judgment of the mind is followed by the choice of the will: he chooses the reproach of Christ and to be afflicted with his Church rather than the temporary advantages of sin; finally, the choice is followed by the action. He calls the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt, which indeed means that nothing in this world is more glorious, nothing more honourable and to be valued more highly, than the reproach and cross of Christ, which easily surpasses all the diadems of earthly kings. Hence Paul is accustomed to adorn himself with this title, as something especially glorious: that he is a prisoner of Jesus Christ (Ephesians 3:1; Philemon 1; and Galatians 6:14, where he abhors every other ground of boasting except the cross of Christ). For he looked) The ground of this resolution is what Moses was warned of, that he esteemed the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt. The mind does not resolve rashly in judging to one side, but in deliberating it looked to the bestowal of the reward: for God bestows rewards on those who seek him (see above, verse 6). The reward, moreover, here

units.la: {26} ... tribuitur afflictionibus Mosis pro Christo, tanquam totidem testimonijs fidei ex qua fluxerunt. Itaque impropria est loquutio, quapræmium non ascribitur fidei, & merito Christi fidem apprehenso, h. e. caussæ: sed effectui eius, ut non fit quod Papistæ in huiusmodi loquutionibus meritu suorum operum quærant.
units.tr: {26} ... is given to the afflictions of Moses for Christ, as so many testimonies of the faith from which they flowed. Therefore the expression is improper when the reward is ascribed not to faith, which lays hold on the merit of Christ, that is, to the cause, but to its effect; so that it is not, as the Papists in such expressions seek the merit of their own works.

units.la: 27 Per fidem reliquit) Alterum effectum fidei Mosis: per fidem reliquit Ægyptum, postquam renuisset vocari filius filiæ Pharaonis: ita effecta fidei in Mose incrementa capiunt. Nihil timens) Externum hoc fidei effectum ostendit ab interno cordis effecto promanasse: nam fides primum reformat cor, illúdq; ab affectibus vitiosis repurgat, ut hic in Mose expellit timorem iræ iniustæ Regis: deinde reformat etiam externas actiones. Nam Ut qui) Hanc Mosis fortitudine in nihil timedo iram Regis, resoluit in altius fundamentum, visionem nimiū Dei inuisibilis. Pertinet igitur hoc ad illustrandum generale fidei effectum primum, Demonstrat ea quæ non videntur. Nota igitur effecta fidei non esse temeraria, sed solidis niti fundamentis. Primum vidit Moses eu qui est inuisibilis. Hinc factu est ut forti animo fuerit, & nihil timuerit iram Regis: contempta Regis ira relinquit Ægyptum. Nota deinde, non est vere fortis animus nisi illius solum hominis qui videt Deum. Nam fortitudinis causa est visio Dei.
units.tr: 27 Through faith he left) The second effect of Moses' faith: through faith he left Egypt, after he had refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter; thus the effects of faith grow in Moses. Not fearing) This external effect of faith shows that it sprang from the internal effect of the heart: for faith first reforms the heart and cleanses it from vicious affections, as here in Moses it drives out the fear of the unjust anger of the king; then it also reforms the external actions. For as one who) This fortitude of Moses in not fearing the king's anger is traced to a deeper foundation, the vision of the invisible God. This therefore serves to illustrate the general first effect of faith: it shows the things that are not seen. Note, then, that the effects of faith are not rash, but rest on solid foundations. First Moses saw him who is invisible. Hence it came about that he had a brave spirit and did not fear the king's anger: having despised the king's wrath, he left Egypt. Note further that a spirit is truly brave only in the man who sees God; for the cause of fortitude is the vision of God.

units.la: 28 Per fidem) Effectum aliud fidei particulare Mosis
units.tr: 28 Through faith) Another particular effect of the faith of Moses

units.la: Mosis simul & populi, peregit pascha & effufione sanguinis.Nam Moses & populus exDei mandato obferuarunt pascha,ante liberatione ex Ægypto, & acceptum paruæ pecudis per singulas domos cæsæ sanguinem imposuerunt duobus postibus & superliminari portæ domus cujusque Israelitarum, quo sanguine conspeƈto transiuit Iehoua præter portam illam, nec passus est interfeƈorem,(qui primogenita Ægyptiorum occidebat) ingredi domos ipsorum. Vnde finis effeƈi huius Mosis & populi hic adijcitur, ne angelus qui perimebat primogenita,ipsos tangeret. Vide Exod.12. Nota igitur quanta fuerit vis in typo, in fanguine Agni, ad feruandum Israelitas, ne Angelus interfeƈtor ipsos vel tangeret, nedum perimeret: quanto major vis ad feruandum est in ipso Christi sanguine pro nobis in cruce effuso.
units.tr: Moses and the people together kept the Passover by the shedding of blood. For Moses and the people, by God's command, observed the Passover before their liberation from Egypt. Taking the blood of a young animal of the flock, slaughtered in each household, they put it on the two door-posts and the lintel of the door of each Israelite's house. When Jehovah saw this blood, he passed over that door and did not allow the destroyer (who killed the firstborn of the Egyptians) to enter their houses. Hence the purpose of this effect of Moses and the people is added here: that the angel who killed the firstborn should not touch them. See Exod. 12. Note, then, how great was the power in the type, in the blood of the lamb, to keep the Israelites so that the destroying angel might not even touch them, much less kill them. How much greater is the power to preserve us in the very blood of Christ, poured out for us on the cross.

units.la: 29 Per fidem transierunt) Aliud effeƈum fidei Mosis & populi. Per fidem salui transierunt mare rubrum, veluti per siccam terram. Fides enim ipsorum in Christum aquas cohibuit & sustinuit, ne in ipsos irruerent. Cuius fasto) Amplificatio huius fidei Mosis & populi, qua mare rubrum transierunt,à contrario penitus euentu in Ægyptijs, qui sine fide eundem transitum tentantes aquis absorpti sunt.
units.tr: 29 Through faith they passed through) Another effect of the faith of Moses and the people. Through faith they crossed the Red Sea safely, as if over dry land. For their faith in Christ held back the waters and kept them up, so that they did not fall upon them. Of which (the Egyptians attempting) ...) This is an amplification of the faith of Moses and the people, by which they crossed the Red Sea, set against the completely opposite outcome among the Egyptians, who, attempting the same crossing without faith, were swallowed up by the waters.

units.la: 30 Per fidem mœnia) Quarta classis effeƈorum fidei particularium, eorum Patrum qui fuerunt ab introitu populi in terram promissam tempore Iudicum & Regum, vsque ad tempus Machabæorum. Primum hoc effectum fidei, est Iosuæ & populi, qui crediderunt verbo Dei promittentis fore, vt postquam septem diebus circuiffent Ierichuntem cum septem sacerdotibus clangentibus buccinis arietinis, & die septimo eam circuiffent septies, conciderent ejus mœnia. Huic promissioni crediderunt Iosua, & populus, & juxta præscriptum Dei circuiuerunt mœnia Ierichuntis septem dies. Vnde secutus est euentus a Deo prædictus, conciderunt mœnia Ciuitatis. Vide Iosuæ 6.
units.tr: 30 Through faith the walls) The fourth class of particular effects of faith, of those fathers who lived from the entry of the people into the promised land, in the time of the Judges and Kings, down to the time of the Maccabees. The first effect of faith here is that of Joshua and the people, who believed the word of God promising that, after they had gone round Jericho for seven days with seven priests blowing ram's-horn trumpets, and on the seventh day had gone round it seven times, its walls would fall. Joshua and the people believed this promise, and according to God's prescription they went round the walls of Jericho for seven days. Hence followed the outcome foretold by God: the walls of the city fell. See Josh. 6.

units.la: 31 Per fidem Rahab) Secundum particulare effectum fidei, Rahab meretricis. Obiectum fidei Rahab, fuit verbum Dei, quo promisit Israelitas possessuros terram Canaan. Huic credidit Rahab, vt ipsa profiteretur Iosuæ 2.9. Hinc factum est vt seruaretur & non perierit, pereuntibus reliquis incolis Ierichuntis, qui verbo huic non crediderant & obedierant. Iis quinon) Significat cautam perditionis Ierichuntinorum fuisse infidelitatem, qua non obedierunt Dei verbo. Quum pacifice) Fidem illam Rahab meretricis illustrat suo opere: neque enim fuit fidesotiosa, sed per charitatem agens. Nam pacifice, hoc est, pacato & benevolo animo, exploratores Israelitarum hospitio excepit, eòsque dimisit incolumes, quod veræ in ipsa fidei testimonium fuit, & eam vera fide coram Deo justificatam esse hominibus testabatur. Vnde dicit Iacobus eam ex operibus justificatam esse, hoc est, ex operibus suis hominibus ostendisse, se fide vera, non mortua & operum experte, coram Deo esse justificatam. Iacob. 2. 2 5.
units.tr: 31 Through faith Rahab) The second particular effect of faith, that of Rahab the harlot. The object of Rahab's faith was the word of God, by which he promised that the Israelites would possess the land of Canaan. Rahab believed this, as she declared in Josh. 2.9. Hence it came about that she was saved and did not perish, while the remaining inhabitants of Jericho perished, who had not believed and obeyed this word. Those who did not) This indicates that the cause of the destruction of the people of Jericho was their unbelief, by which they did not obey God's word. When peaceably) He illustrates that faith of Rahab the harlot by her work. For her faith was not idle, but working through love. For she received the spies of the Israelites peaceably, that is, with a calm and kindly mind, in hospitality, and let them go unharmed. This was a testimony of true faith in her, and it bore witness to men that she had been justified before God by true faith. Hence James says that she was justified by works, that is, she showed to men by her works that she had been justified before God by a true faith, not a dead faith empty of works. James 2.25.

units.la: Et quid praeterea) Per praeteritionem inducit caetera exempla, quæ sunt hujus classis a Iofua primo Iudice, ad ætatem Machabæorum. Deficiet enim) Ratio praeteritionis: qua significat se breuitatis causa horum omnium Patrum exempla praetermittere: Inducit autem hic nominatim exempla, primum quatuor Iudicum, Gedeonis, Barac, Sampsonis, & Iephthe. Deinde Regis vnius, Dauidis: tertio Simuelis Iudicis, ac Prophetæ: postremo Prophetarum, vt Eliæ, Elifæi, Danielis &c.
units.tr: And what more) By way of omission he introduces the other examples, which belong to this class, from Joshua the first Judge down to the age of the Maccabees. For there will not be enough time) The reason for the omission: by it he signifies that, for the sake of brevity, he passes over the examples of all these fathers. He does, however, name examples here: first, four Judges, Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah. Then one king, David. Third, Samuel the judge and prophet. Last, the prophets, such as Elijah, Elisha, Daniel, and so on.

units.la: Qui per fidem) Vt prius accumulauit personas, ita nunc accumulat personarum effectus ex fide promissionum: Nam fide illa qua crediderunt Dei verbo, siue ordinarie, siue extra ordinem reuelato, hæc omnia effecta producta sunt. Primū effectū est, Per fidem debellarunt regna (adjacentia nimirum) vt Ammonitarum, Edomæorum &c. Exercuerunt) Secundum effectum: exercuerunt iustitiam, vt Barac, Samuel, Dauid, & reliqui fere omnes. Assecuti sunt) Tertium effectum omnibus commune: Assecuti sunt promissiones. Sic Dauid assecutus est regnum promissum. Occluserunt ora) Quartum effectum : Occluserunt per fidem ora leonum, vt Samson. Iudic. 14. 7. Dauid. 1. Sam. 17. 35. Benaja comes Dauidis. 2. Sam. 23. 20. Daniel. Dan. 6. 23. vbi expresse fidei Danielis tributur, quod occlusa sunt ora leonum.
units.tr: Who through faith) As he had heaped up persons before, so now he heaps up the effects of the persons, arising from faith in the promises. For by that faith by which they believed God's word, whether given in the ordinary way or revealed beyond the ordinary way, all these effects were produced. The first effect: through faith they subdued kingdoms, namely the neighbouring ones, such as those of the Ammonites, Edomites, and so on. Worked righteousness) The second effect: they worked righteousness, as did Barak, Samuel, David, and almost all the rest. Obtained) The third effect, common to all: they obtained the promises. So David obtained the promised kingdom. Stopped the mouths) The fourth effect: through faith they stopped the mouths of lions, as Samson did. Judg. 14.7. David, 1 Sam. 17.35. Benaiah, companion of David, 2 Sam. 23.20. Daniel, Dan. 6.23, where it is expressly attributed to the faith of Daniel that the mouths of the lions were shut.

units.la: 34 Extinxerunt vim) Quintum effectum: extinxerunt vim ignis, vt socij Danielis, quorum in ignem injectorum ne pilum quidem capitis ignis exusserat, quamuis viros illos qui ipsos intrudebant interfecissent scintillæ ejus. Dan. 3. 22. 27. Effugerunt) Sextum effectum: Effugerunt aciem gladij, vt Elias quem maxime cupiebat Iezabel gladio occidere. 1. Reg. 19. 2. Validis fastis) Septimum effectum. Validi eiuserunt ex imbecillis, vt Ezechias qui ægrotauit vsque ad mortem, fide sanitatem & valetudinem recuperauit. Effecti sunt) Octauum effectum: robusti effecti sunt in bello, vt Samson, qui maxilla asini percussit mille Philistæos: sic Barac, Iephthe, Dauid, & alij, Exercitus) Nonum effectum: Exercitus exterorum verterunt in fugam, vt Gedeon, Iephthe, & alij plerique.
units.tr: 34 Quenched the violence) The fifth effect: they quenched the violence of fire, as did the companions of Daniel, into whose fire, thrown in, the flame had not burned so much as a hair of their heads, although its sparks had killed the men who threw them in. Dan. 3.22, 27. Escaped) The sixth effect: they escaped the edge of the sword, as Elijah did, whom Jezebel most eagerly wished to kill with the sword. 1 Kings 19.2. Out of weakness) The seventh effect. The weak were made strong, as Hezekiah, who was sick unto death, recovered his health and strength by faith. Were made strong) The eighth effect: they were made mighty in war, as Samson, who struck a thousand Philistines with the jawbone of an ass; so did Barak, Jephthah, David, and others. Armies) The ninth effect: the armies of foreigners they turned to flight, as Gideon, Jephthah, and most of the others did.

units.la: 35 Mulieres acceperunt) Decimum effectum quod mulieribus tributur. Per fidem acceperunt mortuos suos, ex resurrectione vitæ restitutos, vt vidua Sareptana recepit filium suum vitæ restitutum precibus Eliæ. 1. Reg. 17. 22. 23. Sic Sunamitis accepit filium suum vitæ red-ditum. ditum per Elifæum.2.Reg.4.36.37.
units.tr: 35 Women received) The tenth effect, which is attributed to women. Through faith they received their dead, restored to life by a resurrection, as the widow of Zarephath received her son restored to life through the prayers of Elijah. 1 Kings 17.22, 23. So the Shunammite woman received her son given back to life through Elisha. 2 Kings 4.36, 37.

units.la: Alij vero dissenti) Quinta & vltima classis effectorum fidei particularium est earumperfonarum quæ fuerunt temporibus Machabæorum, vsque ad Christum. Breuitatis caussa non distinxit hæc exempla, neque nominauit certas personas,sed suppressis nominibus congessit effecta fidei personarum. Sunt autem hæc effecta passionum magis quàm actionum: quum præcedentia omnia fuerint actionum; vt videas fidem non minus efficacem esse & potentem in patiendo, quàm in agendo. Hæc autem effecta quæ sunt passiones, partim sunt tentationes quæ mortem antecedunt, partim sunt mortis genera quæque crudelissima, partim denique cernuntur in fuga persecutionum miserrima. Tentationum quæ mortem antecedunt, & ad defectionem sollicitant genera aliquot hic inducuntur. Primum est quo distendebantur corpora sanctorum tympanis. Est autem τυμπανον instrumentum quo ita distendebantur sontes cùm erant cædendi, aut examinandi flagris, vt nullam corporis sui partem vel latum vnguem mouere possent; sed sustigantium & pulsantium plagis in omnes partes essent expositi. Hoc tormenti genere, plerique in immani illa Antiochi persecutione excruciati sunt.2. Machab. 6. Neglecta) Amplificatio tormenti huius, quod perpessi sunt fideles nonnulli, quòd propositam ipsis condi-
units.tr: Others, however, were tortured) The fifth and last class of particular effects of faith is that of those persons who lived in the time of the Maccabees, down to Christ. For the sake of brevity he has not distinguished these examples, nor named particular persons, but, omitting the names, he has gathered together the effects of faith in persons. These effects, however, are sufferings rather than actions, since all the preceding ones were actions; so that you may see that faith is no less effective and powerful in suffering than in acting. These effects that are sufferings are partly temptations that precede death, partly kinds of the most cruel death, and partly, finally, are seen in the most wretched flight from persecutions. Several kinds of temptations that precede death and urge toward apostasy are introduced here. The first is that by which the bodies of the saints were stretched on [τύμπανον] racks. A tympanum is an instrument by which the guilty were so stretched when they were to be beaten or examined with whips, so that they could not move any part of their body, not even by the breadth of a nail, but were exposed on every side to the blows of those who beat and struck them. Many were tortured with this kind of torment in that monstrous persecution of Antiochus. 2 Macc. 6.

units.la: Aly vero dissenti: Quinta & vltima classis effectorum. tionem liberationis, si fidem abnegarent, neglexerint, & contempserint: vt de Eliazaro quodam legitur. 2. Machab. 6. 21. & deinceps. Vt potiorem ) Finis propter quem neglecta liberatione acerbissima tormenta patienter sunt perpessi, vt in vltimo illo die resurgeret a mortuis ad vitam aeternam, quam vocat resurrectionem potiorem hac, quae est a morte praesente, cum abnegatione veritatis, & salutis aeternae difpendio. Nota igitur: homini pio & fideli non esse, ne ipsam quidem corporis curam abjiciendam, sed simul prospiciendum esse aeterne, tum corporis, tum animae saluti.
units.tr: Others, however, were tortured: the fifth and last class of effects. ...and when the offered deliverance, if they would deny the faith, was neglected and despised by some faithful men, as is read of a certain Eleazar. 2 Macc. 6.21 ff. In order to obtain a better) The purpose for which, having neglected deliverance, they patiently endured the most bitter torments: that they might rise from the dead at that last day to eternal life, which he calls a better resurrection than that which is from present death, with the denial of the truth and the loss of eternal salvation. Note, therefore: a pious and faithful man must not cast away even the care of the body, but at the same time must provide for the eternal salvation of both body and soul.

units.la: 36 Alij rursus) Secundum genus tentationum, quae mortem antecedunt & ad defectionem sollicitant, ludibria a quibus proceferunt ad flagella. Insuper &c.) Tertium genus siftarum tentationum, vincula & carceres.
units.tr: 36 Others again) The second kind of temptations, which precede death and urge toward apostasy: mockings, from which they proceeded to scourgings. Moreover, etc.) The third kind of these temptations: chains and prisons.

units.la: 37 Lapidati sunt) Secundus ordo passionum continet mortis genera quaeque crudelissima. Cujusmodi hic aliqua enumerantur, 1. lapidati sunt, 2. ferra dilecti sunt, vt de Isaia scribit Hieronymus. 3. cremati sunt & igni traditi. Nam pro ἐπειράσθησαν tentati sunt, legendum videtur ἐπυράσθησαν cremati sunt, quod cum praecedentibus & sequentibus magis videtur congruere. 4. gladio caesi occubuerunt. Oberrauerunt) Tertius ordo passionum: fuga a persecutione miserrima: quae varijs adjunctis incommodis amplificatur: Primum oberrauerunt induti vilibus vestimentis, vtpote ouillis & caprinis pellibus: deinde bonis omnibus ad vitam pertinentibus destituti: tertiò oppressi & omni ex parte male habiti.
units.tr: 37 They were stoned. The second order of sufferings contains the most cruel kinds of death. Some of these are listed here: (1) they were stoned; (2) they were sawn in two, as Jerome writes of Isaiah; (3) they were burned and given over to fire. For ἐπειράσθησαν [they were tempted], it seems that ἐπυράσθησαν [they were burned] should be read, since this fits better with what precedes and follows. (4) They died by the sword. They wandered about. This is the third order of sufferings: flight from persecution, which is made worse by various accompanying hardships. First, they wandered about clothed in mean garments, namely sheepskins and goatskins; second, they were deprived of all the goods that pertain to life; third, they were oppressed and badly treated in every way.

units.la: 38 Quibus indignus)Obiter inferta est ratio, cur sic oberrauerint, & ad deserta loca confugerint, quia ijs indignus erat mundus, hoc est, mali in mundo homines, ideò mundo relicto confugerunt ad loca deserta:Putauit quidem mundus eos se & sua societate indignos: At contrà Deus mundum ijs indignum esse censuit, dum eos à mundo seuocaret. Hac ergo ratione exaggeratur hominum à quibus fugerunt, impietas. In desertis errantes) Secunda amplificatio fugæ sanctorum, à locis in quibus oberrauerunt, quæ hic aliquot inducuntur: vt deserta, montes, speluncæ, cauernæ, quæ ferarum, non hominum, habitationi destinantur.
units.tr: 38 Of whom the world was not worthy. The reason why they wandered in this way and took refuge in deserted places is added in passing: the world was not worthy of them, that is, wicked men in the world. Therefore they withdrew from the world and fled to deserted places. The world indeed thought them unworthy of itself and of its company; but on the contrary, God judged the world unworthy of them, since he called them out of the world. By this reasoning the impiety of the men from whom they fled is heightened. Wandering in the deserts. This is a second heightening of the flight of the saints, from the places in which they wandered, and several of these are mentioned here: deserts, mountains, caves, and caverns, which are destined for the habitation of wild beasts, not of men.

units.la: 39 Atque hi omnes) Amplificatio est, & commendatio fidei eorum, quod quamuis hæc omnia per fidem in promissionem sustinuerint, ac testimonium à Deo adepti sint per fidem, tamen non obtinuerunt promissum, hoc est, non viderunt Christum in carne manifestatum & exhibitum, sed eminùs tantùm venturum conspicati sunt. Cùm dicit eos per fidem test monium adeptos, significat hæc particularia eorum effecta pertinere ad illustrandum fidei effectum generale secundum.
units.tr: 39 And all these. This is a heightening and a commendation of their faith: although they endured all these things through faith, looking to the promise, and obtained a testimony from God through faith, nevertheless they did not obtain the promise, that is, they did not see Christ manifested and exhibited in the flesh, but only caught sight of him as one who would come from afar. When he says that they obtained a testimony through faith, he means that these particular effects of theirs serve to illustrate the second, general effect of faith.

units.la: 40 Quod Deus de nobis) Ratio cur non obtinuerunt promissum: Deus differendo promissum melius quiddam de nobis prouidit. Nam patefactio Christi & ejus aduentus in carne, dilata est in vltima tempora propter nos, in quos (teste Paulo) fines seculorum inciderunt. 1. Corinth. 10. 11. Vnde Petrus dicit, Christum patefactum vltimis temporibus propter nos, qui per eum credimus Deo. 1. Epistol. 1. 20. Ne absque nobis) Si veniffet Christus aetate priscorum illorum Patrum, fuissent illi absque nobis consecrati & glorificati: nos autem fuissemus neglecti: quia exhibito Christo nihil aliud quam finis mundi expectari potest. Ergo noluit Deus eos obtinere promissum, & Christum videre reipsa exhibitum, vt nostrae saluti consuleret ne nos a participatione gloriae excludere-mur.
units.tr: 40 God providing something better for us. The reason why they did not obtain the promise: by deferring the promise, God provided something better for us. For the revelation of Christ and his coming in the flesh was postponed until the last times on our account, upon us (as Paul testifies) the ends of the ages have come. 1 Corinthians 10:11. Hence Peter says that Christ was made manifest in the last times for our sake, who through him believe in God. 1 Peter 1:20. That apart from us. If Christ had come in the age of those earlier Fathers, they would have been made perfect and glorified apart from us, and we would have been neglected; for once Christ has been exhibited, nothing else can be expected but the end of the world. Therefore God did not will that they should obtain the promise and see Christ actually exhibited, so that he might provide for our salvation and not exclude us from a share in the glory.

units.la: Argumentum Capitis duodecimi.
units.tr: Argument of the Twelfth Chapter.

units.la: Hoc capite primum redit ad institutam exhortatione ad perseuerantia in fide, eiusque duo affert argumenta, decimumquartum & decimumquintum ad verf. 3. Deinde speciales aliquot sunt exhortationes, ad patientiam in afflictionibus, ad praeeundum aliis bono exemplo, ad pacem, ad sanctimoniam &c. ad verf. vsque 15. Postremo redit ad exhortationem principalem, eiusque tria adducit argumenta, ad finem capitis.
units.tr: In this chapter the author first returns to the exhortation he has begun, to perseverance in faith, and he brings forward two arguments for it, the fourteenth and fifteenth, at verse 3. Then there are several particular exhortations: to patience in afflictions, to going before others with a good example, to peace, to holiness, and so on, down to verse 15. Finally he returns to the principal exhortation and adduces three arguments for it, at the end of the chapter.

units.la: CAPVT. XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: 1 Proinde nos quoque, quum tanta nos circunstet testium testium nubes, abiecto omni pondere, & peccato adnos circumcingendos proclivi, constanter propositum nobis stadium decurramus.
units.tr: 1 Therefore we also, since so great a cloud of witnesses surrounds us, laying aside every weight and the sin that so easily clings to us, let us run with perseverance the race set before us.

units.la: 2. Intuentes in fidei ducem ac perfectorem Iesum, qui pro sibi proposito gaudio pertulit crucem, ignominia contempta, & ad dexteram throniDei consedit.
units.tr: 2. Looking unto Jesus, the author and finisher of faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God.

units.la: Proinde nos quoque) Post digressionem incommendationem fidei, redit ad institutā exhortationem ad constantiam & perseuerantiam in fide. Estque hoc argumentum exhortationis decimumquartum, à testibus, siue abexemplis credētium, qui perseuerárunt in fide. Accommodat enim ad institutum ea quæin digressione dicta sunt capite superiori. Te-stium nubes) Amplificatio argumenti est, à testiū multitudine, quæ nubis voce intelligitur, qua metaphorice multitudo quasi coagulatasignificatur. Constanter propositum) Exhortatioipsa est metaphoricis verbis expressa. Metaphora est ab iis qui in stadio currūt, Scripturæfamiliaris. vt 1. Cor. 9.24. & deinceps. Heb. 6.18. Nam hominis Christiani vita est quasicursus in stadio, & Christianus homo quasi instadio currit ad metā, & palmam illam supernæ vocationis, experiens ecquo modo peruēniat ad resurrectionem mortuorum. Philip. 3.11. 14. Constanter) Legem currendi præscribit, vt currant per patientiam. Neque enimsatis est currere, sed seruāde sunt leges in cur-
units.tr: Therefore we also) After the digression on the commendation of faith, he returns to the exhortation to steadfastness and perseverance in faith. This is the fourteenth argument of exhortation, drawn from witnesses, that is, from the examples of believers who persevered in faith. For it applies to his purpose what was said in the digression in the previous chapter. A cloud of witnesses) This is an amplification of the argument from the multitude of witnesses, which is understood by the word "cloud," by which a multitude gathered together as it were is metaphorically signified. Let us run with patience the race) The exhortation itself is expressed in metaphorical words. The metaphor is taken from those who run in the stadium, and is familiar in Scripture, as in 1 Cor. 9:24 and following, and Heb. 6:18. For the life of a Christian is as it were a race in the stadium, and the Christian runs as it were in the stadium toward the goal, and the prize of the heavenly calling, and he experiences in what way he may attain to the resurrection of the dead. Phil. 3:11, 14. Steadfastly) He prescribes the law of running, that they run through patience. For it is not enough merely to run, but the rules must be observed in running.

units.la: N rndo. Nő coronatur(inquit Paulus)nisi qui legitimè (hoc est,seruatis certandi legibus) certauerit.Hæc igitur lex est currendi præcipua,vt constanter &cum patientia decurrát, inoffenso pede, præteritis omnibus impedimentis quæ cursum ipsorū remorari possint. Propositum) Stadium vocat propositum, quia vt meta,ita vt stadiū ac via ad metam perueniendi nobis àDeo proponitur.Sic spem propositam dicit.Heb.6.18. Abiectis omni) Modus decurrendi constanter hoc stadium obiecto omni pondere: deindè pondus illud interpretatur peccatum. Neqj enim progressum aliquè in cursu potest facere,qui cum pondere currit: nullum autem pódus est quo impedimur in hoc cursu præter peccatum, quo quidem abiecto facillimus nobis & expeditissimus esset cursus ad metam. Duobus autem modis hoc peccati pódus abjicitur: Primùm quidem dū imponitur quasi humeris Christi, qui volens peccata nostra pertulit in corpore suo super lignum. 1.Pet.2.14. &factus est pro nobis peccatum.2.Corinth.5.21. Deindè dum per Spiritum Christi sanctificamur, &purgantur corda nostra ab inhærente in nobis peccato. Atque hoc quidem modo posteriore non prorsus in hac vita abjicitur peccati pódus:Manét enim aliquæ reliquiæ peccati quamdiu hic sumus: Vnde est grauissima illa Pauli lamentatio: Miser ego homo, quis me eripiet ex isto corpore mortis? Rom. 7* 24. & 2. Corinth. 5. 4. Suspiramus onerati: sed danda nobis est opera vt peccatum indies magis ac magis mortificetur in nobis, vt tandem aliquando prorsus leuati hoc onere ad metam perueniamus. Ad nos circumcingendos) Descriptio quaedam est huius peccati ac ponderis, quod sua natura nos circumcingat, tanquam murus aut maceries quaedam, vndique aditum nobis praecludens ad coelos, & cursum nostrum in hoc stadio impediens, vt nisi eo superato, & dirura quasi hac macerie, propofitu nobis stadium non possimus decurrere.
units.tr: For no one is crowned (says Paul) unless he has striven lawfully (that is, observing the rules of the contest). This, therefore, is the chief rule of running: that one runs steadfastly and with patience, with a foot that does not stumble, all hindrances that could delay their course being set aside. Set before us) He calls the course "set before us" because, as the goal, so also the stadium and the way of attaining the goal is set before us by God. Thus he calls it "the hope set before us," Heb. 6:18. Laying aside every) This is the manner of running steadfastly in this stadium: laying aside every weight. Then he interprets that weight as sin. For no one can make progress in a race who runs with a weight, and there is no weight by which we are hindered in this course except sin; once this is laid aside, the course to the goal would be most easy and most unencumbered for us. This weight of sin is laid aside in two ways. First, indeed, when it is laid upon the shoulders of Christ, who willingly bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Pet. 2:24), and was made sin for us (2 Cor. 5:21). Then, when we are sanctified by the Spirit of Christ and our hearts are cleansed from the sin that dwells in us. Yet in this latter way the weight of sin is not wholly laid aside in this life, for some remnants of sin remain as long as we are here. Hence that most grievous lament of Paul: "Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?" (Rom. 7:24), and 2 Cor. 5:4: "We groan, being burdened." But we must labour that sin be mortified in us more and more each day, so that at last, being wholly relieved of this burden, we may reach the goal. To encompass us) This is a certain description of this sin and weight, which by its nature surrounds us like a wall or some barrier, shutting off access to heaven on every side and hindering our course in this stadium, so that unless we overcome it, and as it were break through this barrier, we cannot run the race set before us.

units.la: 2. Intuentes in fidei) Argumentum exhortationis praecipuae decimumquintum, ab ipsius Christi exemplo, quod maioris est momenti quam reliqua omnia sanctorum exempla. Iesus per mediam crucem & ignominiam decurrit stadium sibi propositum. Ergo intuendum nobis est in eum vt propositum &c. Fide ducem) Descriptio est Christi, ad commendationem personae pertinens, vt eo magis incitemur ad imitandum ipsius exemplum in decurredo hoc stadio. Vocat eum primum ducem fidei, quia praeit nobis viam, & ducit nos in hoc fidei stadio, imo ipse est via qua nobis eundum est ad metam, vt fe appellat Ioan. 14.6. Deinde vocat eum fidei perfectorem, quia finis est fidei noftrae, in quo fides nostra consummaturae perficitur. Duo enim sunt quæ Christum respiciunt, fides & aspectus: fide incedimus in hac vita, ait Apoft.2. Corinth. 7. 7. & eatenus quidem Christus est dux fidei: At in altera vita fides mutabitur in aspectum, quia videbimus eum sicuti est. 1. Ioann. 3. 2. & tum quidem Christus erit fidei nostræ persector. Fides enim, ut & spes, imperfectum quiddam est, & via tantummodo ad perfectionem, eoque non est nobis in ea acquiescendum. Perfectio autem & beatitas nostra est in aspectu. Atque ita Christus perficiet fidem nostram, dum eam mutabit in aspectum. Ergo in decurrendo hoc stadium nobis propositum oportet perpetuo intueri & ob oculos habere Christum, primum quidem ut præcursorem & ducem cursus nostri, præeuntem nobis per crucem & ignominiam: deinde ut finem & perfectionem cursus nostri & laborum nostrorum omnium coronam, quæ posita est in aspectu Christi glorificati, ut nunquam debeat oculus noster, neque in hac vita, neque post hanc vitam in altera illa, à Christo diitrahi. Pertulit crucem) Hæc via est qua præiuit nobis Christus, perferendo nimirum crucem. Ignominia) Docet quomodo hac via præiuerit, contempta videlicet ignominia, nempe crucis, quæ profecto omnium maxima fuit, sive externam illam respicias in morte omnium ignominiosissima, sive internam illam, quam interea in anima, iram Dei & horro-
units.tr: 2. Looking unto Jesus) The fifteenth chief argument of exhortation, from the example of Christ himself, which is of greater weight than all the other examples of the saints. Jesus ran through the midst of the cross and shame the stadium set before him. Therefore we ought to look upon him, that we may run the race set before us, and so on. The leader of faith) This is a description of Christ, pertaining to the commendation of his person, so that we may be the more stirred to imitate his example in running this stadium. He calls him first the leader of faith, because he goes before us on the way and leads us in this stadium of faith; indeed he himself is the way by which we must go to the goal, as he calls himself in John 14:6. Then he calls him the perfecter of faith, because he is the end of our faith, in whom our faith is brought to its completion and perfected. For there are two things that have regard to Christ: faith and sight. We walk by faith in this life, says the Apostle (2 Cor. 5:7), and so far Christ is the leader of faith. But in the other life faith will be changed into sight, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). And then Christ will be the perfecter of our faith. For faith, like hope, is something imperfect, and only a way to perfection, and therefore we are not to rest in it. Our perfection and blessedness, however, lies in sight. Thus Christ will perfect our faith when he changes it into sight. Therefore, in running this race set before us, we must always look upon Christ and keep him before our eyes: first indeed as the forerunner and leader of our course, going before us through the cross and shame; then as the end and perfection of our course and of all our labours, the crown, which is placed in the sight of the glorified Christ, so that our eye may never be drawn away from Christ, neither in this life nor after it in that other life. Endured the cross) This is the way by which Christ went before us, namely by enduring the cross. Despising the shame) He teaches how he went before us in this way: namely, by despising the shame, that is, of the cross, which was surely the greatest of all, whether you regard that outward shame of the most ignominious death, or that inward shame, which in the meantime he felt in his soul, enduring the wrath of God and the horrors

units.la: Pertulit crucem) ... horrores ac cruciatus inferorum perpetiente, sensit: cuius externa illa mortis ignominia fuit tantum testimonium externum. Quæ enim potest esse maior ignominia quàm ea quà reprobi detectis ipsorum peccatis in vltimo die afficientur, quam Scriptura vocat pudorem, & confusionem, eamque æternam. Atque hæc fuit ignominia, quam impositis ipsi peccatis nostris pertulit Christus, sine qua nos ab æterna illa ignominia liberare nunquam potuisset.
units.tr: Endured the cross) ...and the horrors and torments of hell. Its outward shame of death was only an outward testimony of it. For what greater shame can there be than that with which the reprobate, their sins being revealed on the last day, will be afflicted, which Scripture calls shame and confusion, and eternal shame? This was the shame which Christ endured when our sins were laid upon him, and without which he could never have delivered us from that eternal shame.

units.la: Vice sibi propositi) Amplificatio crucis quam pertulit, à contrario gaudio sibi proposito, quo vtpote Deus coæternus cum Patre frui potuisset: vice tamen gaudij huius, sasta quasi permutatione, pertulit crucem. Vide Philip. 2. 6. 7.
units.tr: Instead of the joy set before him) This is an amplification of the cross which he endured, set against the joy set before him, a joy which as God co-eternal with the Father he could have enjoyed; yet instead of this joy, as it were by a sort of exchange, he endured the cross. See Phil. 2:6, 7.

units.la: Cùm esset in forma Dei, non duxit rapinam æqualem esse cum Deo: sed ipse se exinaniuit &c. Vide igitur quantum mali sit in peccato, cui satisfieri non potuit, nisi Christus deposito quasi gaudio, & gloria Deitatis, pro nobis crucem pertulisset, & se exinaniuisset, factus obediens ad mortem, mortem autem crucis. Debet hoc nos mouere ad detestationem peccati,
units.tr: Though he was in the form of God, he did not think it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, and so on. See therefore how great is the evil of sin, which could not be satisfied unless Christ, having as it were laid aside his joy and the glory of the Godhead, had endured the cross for us and emptied himself, having become obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. This ought to move us to detest sin.

units.la: Contempta) Interea dum pateretur, crucem & ignominiam contempsit. At quomodo contempsit eam, cùm legamus in historia Euangelica eum grauissimè tulisse, vt quum quæritur, Eli, Eli, lamma sabachthani. Matth. 27. 46. imò profitetur tristem fuisse animam suam vsque ad mortem. Matth. 26. 38. quomodo igitur ignominiam contempsit? Respondeo contemptum hunc positum esse in eo, quod volés ignominiam crucis subierit, quemadmodum pij mortem contemnunt, non quidem eam irridendo, sed voluntarie subeundo, spe vitæ illius gloriosæ qua fruentur. Causa verò cur Christus mortem tam graviter tulerit, fuit, quia mortuus est peccati nomine. Cum autem quis moritur propter peccatum, nullus potest esse pœnæ modus, sed necesse est pœnam esse infinitam, ut in reprobis qui propter peccata sua morientur. Martyrum nullus mortuus est propter peccata, sed eius tantum causa, qui propter ipsorum peccata mortuus est, eoque certò persuasi erant remissa esse sibi peccata. Vnde internum quod sentiebant animi gaudium absorbebat externum corporis dolorem. Et ad dexteram) Commendatio crucis Christi, ab eventu qui has eius perpessiones insecutus est, qui continet argumentum quo nos excitemur ad ferendam crucem pro Christo. Consedit ad dexteram throni Dei, hoc est, consecutus est summam gloriam. De hac gloria Christi perpessiones insecuta vide Philipp. 2. 9. Quapropter extulit eum Deus in summam sublimitatem, & donauit ei nomen quod est supra omne nomen: &c. Sic & nostras quoque afflictiones consequitur gloria, sed latum est discrimen. Nam Christi afflictiones & perpessiones promeritæ sunt gloriam, quia
units.tr: Despising) Meanwhile, while he was suffering, he despised the cross and the shame. But how did he despise it, when we read in the Gospel history that he took it very grievously, as when he cried, "Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani" (Matt. 27:46); indeed he professes that his soul was sorrowful even unto death (Matt. 26:38)? How then did he despise the shame? I answer that this contempt consists in this: that willingly he underwent the shame of the cross, just as the godly despise death, not by mocking it, but by undergoing it willingly, in hope of that glorious life which they will enjoy. But the reason why Christ took death so grievously was that he died on account of sin. When someone dies on account of sin, there can be no measure of punishment, but the punishment must be infinite, as in the reprobate who die for their sins. No martyr has died for sins, but only for the sake of him who died for their sins, and therefore they were certainly persuaded that their sins were forgiven them. Hence the inward joy which they felt swallowed up the outward pain of the body. And is set down at the right hand) This is a commendation of the cross of Christ, drawn from the outcome that followed his sufferings, which contains the argument by which we are stirred to bear the cross for Christ. He sat down at the right hand of the throne of God, that is, he obtained the highest glory. Concerning this glory which followed Christ's sufferings, see Phil. 2:9: "Wherefore God also has highly exalted him and given him a name which is above every name," and so on. So glory also follows our afflictions, but the difference is great. For the afflictions and sufferings of Christ merited glory, because

units.la: Deus passus est, ideo adhibetur eo loco particula causalis δια, quapropter, (hoc est, propter illam humiliationem vtpote meritoriam) exaltauit eum Deus: Sed afflictiones nostrae non merentur gloriam: Non enim sunt paria quae praesenti tempore perpetimur, suturae gloriae in nobis retegendae. Rom. cap. 8. vers. 18.
units.tr: Because Christ suffered, the causal particle διά [dia] is used in that place, "wherefore": God exalted him on account of that humiliation, which was meritorious. But our afflictions do not merit glory, for "the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us" (Rom. 8.18).

units.la: 3 Reputate igitur quis ille fit qui talem fustinuit a peccatoribus aduersus sese contradictionem, ne animis remissi, fatiscatis.
units.tr: 3 Consider therefore him who endured such contradiction of sinners against himself, lest you grow weary and faint in your minds.

units.la: 4 Nondum ad sanguinem vsque resistitiss, aduersus peccatum decertantes.
units.tr: 4 You have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin.

units.la: 5 Et obliti est exhortationis, quae vobis tanquam filiis loquitur, Fili mi, ne negligito castigationem Domini, neque remissus esto quum ab eo argueris.
units.tr: 5 And you have forgotten the exhortation which speaks to you as to children: "My son, despise not the chastening of the Lord, nor faint when you are rebuked by him."

units.la: 6 Quem enim diligit Dominus castigat, et flagellat quemcunque filium recipit.
units.tr: 6 For whom the Lord loves he chastens, and he scourges every son whom he receives.

units.la: 7 Si castigationem sustinetis, Deus sese vobis offert vt filiis (quis enim est filius quem non castiget pater?
units.tr: 7 If you endure chastening, God deals with you as with sons; for what son is there whom the father does not chasten?

units.la: 8 Quod si estis absque castigatione, cuius participes sunt omnes nempe spuri estis, et non filij.
units.tr: 8 But if you are without chastisement, of which all are partakers, then you are bastards and not sons.

units.la: 9 Deinde corporum nostrorum patres habuimus castigatores, et eos reueriti sumus: an non multo magis subiiciemur patri spirituum, et viuemus?
units.tr: 9 Furthermore, we have had fathers of our flesh who corrected us, and we gave them reverence. Shall we not much more be subject to the Father of spirits, and live?

units.la: 10 Nam illi ad paucos dies prout ipsis videbatur, nos castigabant: hic autem ad commodum nostrum, Ut participes simus sanctimoniæ ipsius.
units.tr: 10 For they chastened us for a few days, as seemed good to them; but he does so for our profit, that we may be partakers of his holiness.

units.la: II Omnis autem castigatio in præsens quidem non videtur esse gaudij sed tristitiæ: at postea fructum tranquillum iustitiæ reddit iis qui per eam fuerint exercitati.
units.tr: 11 Now all chastening for the present seems not to be joyful but grievous; yet afterward it yields the peaceable fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.

units.la: 12 Quapropter manus remissas & genua soluta surrigite.
units.tr: 12 Wherefore lift up the hands that hang down, and the feeble knees;

units.la: 13 Et rectas orbitas facite pedibus vestris, ne quod claudum est abducatur a via, sed ut sanetur potius.
units.tr: 13 And make straight paths for your feet, lest what is lame be turned out of the way, but rather be healed.

units.la: 14 Pacem sectamini cum omnibus, & sanctimoniam, sine qua nemo videbit Dominum.
units.tr: 14 Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no one shall see the Lord;

units.la: 15 Prospicientes nequis deficiat a gratia Dei: neque radix amara suppullulans obturbet, & per hanc inquinentur multi.
units.tr: 15 Looking carefully lest anyone fail of the grace of God; lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and through it many be defiled;

units.la: 16 Nequis fit fornicator, aut profanus, velut Esau, qui unico edulio vendidit suum ius primogeniti.
units.tr: 16 Lest there be any fornicator or profane person, like Esau, who for one meal sold his birthright.

units.la: 17 Scitis enim quum etiam postea, quum vellet hæreditario iure benedictionem assequi: reprobatum fuisse: nam enim reperit pœnitentiæ locum, quamuis cum lachrymis benedictionem illam exquisisset.
units.tr: 17 For you know that afterward, when he wished to obtain the blessing by inheritance, he was rejected; for he found no place for repentance, although he sought that blessing with tears.

units.la: 18 Non enim accessistis ad contrectabilem montem, & incensum ignem, ac turbinem & caliginem, & procellam:
units.tr: 18 For you have not come to a mountain that could be touched, and burning with fire, nor to blackness, and darkness, and tempest,

units.la: 19 Tubaque sonitum & vocem verborum: quam qui audierant, deprecati sunt ne amplius sibi fieret sermo.
units.tr: 19 And the sound of a trumpet, and a voice of words, which those who heard begged should speak to them no more.

units.la: 20 (Non enim ferebant quod imperabatur, si vel Si vel bestia tetigerit montem, lapidabitur, aut iaculo configetur.
units.tr: 20 (For they could not bear what was commanded: "If even a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned, or pierced with a dart.")

units.la: 21 Et Moses (adeo terribile erat visum quod apparebat) dixit, Expavefactus sum ac tremebundus.)
units.tr: 21 And so terrible was the sight that Moses said, "I am exceedingly afraid and trembling.")

units.la: 22 Sed accessistis ad montem Sion, & civitatem Dei viui, Hierusalem caelestem, & myriadas Angelorum.
units.tr: 22 But you have come to Mount Zion, and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to innumerable hosts of angels,

units.la: 23 Conuentum & concionem primogenitorum qui conscripti sunt in caelis: & iudicem omnium Deum, & spiritus iustorum consummatorum.
units.tr: 23 To the general assembly and church of the firstborn, who are enrolled in heaven, and to God the judge of all, and to the spirits of just men made perfect,

units.la: 24 Et ad noui Testamenti mediatorem Iesum, & sanguinem aspersionis, praestantiora loquentem quam loquebatur sanguis Abel.
units.tr: 24 And to Jesus the mediator of the new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood, which speaks better things than the blood of Abel.

units.la: Reputate igitur) Quia Christus stadium sibi propositum per crucem & ignominiam decurrit, & per multas afflictiones gloriam consecutus est, ideo nos quoque exemplo Christi hortatur ad afflictiones fortiter sustinendas, ne animis deficientes fatiscamus, atque it a remouet impedimentum perseuerantiae nostrae, afflictiones & persecutionem, ne propter eas deficiamus. Primum argumentum est ab exemplo afflictionum Christi, quod exaggeratur varijs circumstantijs, ad quarum seriam confideration nos excitat, dum dicit (Reputate) Quo verbo innuit in passione Christi multa nobis esse diligenter consideranda & ponderanda, quae in nullius alterius passione occurrunt: Vt igitur Christi exemplo excitemur ad ferendum patienter afflictiones, oportet penitius inspiciamus omnes circumstantias passionis ipsius. Quis ille) Prima circumstantia est personæ eius qui afflictiones has sustinuit. Quis, id est, quàm dignus, quàm excellens, vtpote Dominus gloriæ. Quàm indignum fit Dominum gloriæ pati, & crucifigi fignificit Paulus quum dicit, Nequaquam Dominum gloriæ crucifixissent. 1.Corinth. 2.8. vbi gloriam Christi, & crucis ignominiam, tanquam res inter fe pugnatiffimas opponit. Quæ enim potest esse consensio inter summam gloriam, & extremam ignominiam? Atque hæc causa etiam est cur temporaria ipsius mors æquiualens fuerit mortì æternæ, quæ peccatoribus debebatur, personæ nimirum dignitas, quod Filius Dei, Dominus gloriæ passus fit in carne.Talem)
units.tr: Consider therefore) Because Christ ran the race set before him through the cross and shame, and attained glory through many afflictions, he therefore also urges us, by Christ's example, to bear afflictions bravely, lest we faint and give way in our minds; and so he removes the hindrance to our perseverance, namely afflictions and persecution, lest we fail on account of them. The first argument is from the example of Christ's afflictions, which is set forth through various circumstances, to whose careful consideration he rouses us when he says Consider. By this word he indicates that in the passion of Christ there are many things to be diligently considered and weighed, which do not occur in the suffering of anyone else. So, to be stirred by Christ's example to bear afflictions patiently, we must look more deeply into all the circumstances of his passion. Who he was) The first circumstance is the person of him who endured these afflictions: who, that is, how worthy, how excellent, namely the Lord of glory. How unfitting it was for the Lord of glory to suffer and be crucified Paul signifies when he says, "They would not have crucified the Lord of glory" (1 Cor. 2.8), where he sets the glory of Christ and the ignominy of the cross against each other as things most opposed. For what agreement can there be between the highest glory and the lowest ignominy? This is also the reason why his temporal death was equal to the eternal death owed to sinners: namely, the dignity of the person, that the Son of God, the Lord of glory, suffered in the flesh. Such)

units.la: Secunda circumstantia est magnitudinis contradictionis, & omninò perpeffionum quas sustinuit: Nam coutradictionis nomine, per fynecdochen speciei intelliguntur omnes perpeffiones & afflictiones Christi. Vt prima circumstantia significat nullam vnquam fuisse tantam personam, ita fecunda circumstantia fubindicat, nullam vnquam fuisse talem & tantam poenam. Itaque ex hoc loco colligendum est, Christum non exterius duntaxat passum in corpore (Nam fi externam tantum passionem respicias, latrones duo qui cum eo crucifixi sunt Iunt æqualem pœnam sustinuerunt. Sed multò magis interius in anima, in qua pertulit cruciatus inferorum, & grauissimum illud pondus iræ Dei, quod necessario ipsi incubuit propter suscepta in se peccata omnium hominum, quæ nisi summa & infinita pœna quæ omnes etiam reproborum cruciatus excederet, expiari non poterant. Atque hæc alia etiam causa est, cur temporaria ipsius mors æternam æquipararit, supplicij nimiùm quòd ad tempus perpessus est atrocitas. A peccatoribus. Tertia circumstantia est personæ persecutorum, erant peccatores, hoc est, homines, non vilissimi tantùm, sed etiam sceleratissimi. Ne animis. Hortationis summa: Ne despondeamus animos & in afflictionibus fatiscamus, sed fortiter eas perferamus, ad hoc vt constanter propositum nobis stadium decurramus.
units.tr: The second circumstance is the magnitude of the contradiction, and of all the sufferings which he endured altogether. For under the name of contradiction, by synecdoche of the species, all the sufferings and afflictions of Christ are understood. As the first circumstance shows that there never was so great a person, so the second suggests that there never was so great and such a punishment. Hence it is to be gathered from this passage that Christ suffered not only outwardly in the body (for if you look only at the external passion, the two robbers who were crucified with him endured an equal punishment), but much more inwardly in the soul, in which he bore the torments of hell and that most heavy weight of God's wrath, which necessarily lay upon him because of the sins of all men that he had taken upon himself. These could not be expiated unless by a supreme and infinite punishment which exceeded even all the torments of the reprobate. This is another reason why his temporal death equalled eternal death: the atrocity of the punishment which he suffered for a time. From sinners.) The third circumstance is the persons of the persecutors: they were sinners, that is, men not only most vile but also most wicked. Lest in your minds.) This is the sum of the exhortation: that we should not lose heart and faint in afflictions, but bear them bravely, so that we may run constantly the race set before us.

units.la: 4 Nondum ad sanguinem. Secundum argumentum à leuiore ad afflictionum, quas hactenus sunt pepessi. Nondum ad mortem vsque sustinuistis afflictiones: ergo pergite eas patienter sustinere. Ad sanguinem (sque) id est, ad mortem sine sanguinis effusionem. Resistere Significat afflictionem positam esse in resistendo, & opponendo. Christus quum afflictus est, dicitur sustinuisse contradictionem. Sic quum affliguntur pij, ijs resistitur & ipsi resistunt, vt non possit afflictio esse sine lusta & oppositione. Ergo dicet quis,
units.tr: 4 You have not yet resisted unto blood.) The second argument is from a lesser to a greater: from the afflictions which you have so far suffered. You have not yet endured afflictions to the point of death; therefore press on to bear them patiently. Unto blood) that is, to death without the shedding of blood. Resisting) signifies that affliction consists in resisting and opposing. When Christ was afflicted, he is said to have endured contradiction. So when the godly are afflicted, they are opposed, and they also oppose, so that affliction cannot exist without struggle and opposition. Therefore someone will say:

units.la: Afflicti non patiuntur voluntarie, quia resistunt? Respondeo eos resistere peccato, non afflictioni: Nam summa voluntate patiuntur afflictionem: etsi interea dum patiuntur, continuò resistunt peccato, & decertant aduersus peccatum. Si enim peccato cederent non paterentur. Si Christus cessisset peccato, non fuisset crucifixus, sed cum crucifixus est illi, luƈta fuit cum peccato. Interea tamen dum aduersus peccatum decertaret, summa voluntate se cruciobtulit. Quia autem non cedunt pij peccato, ideo victores euadunt, etiam in ipsa morte.
units.tr: Do the afflicted not suffer voluntarily, because they resist? I answer that they resist sin, not affliction. For they suffer affliction with the greatest willingness; yet while they suffer, they continually resist sin and struggle against sin. For if they yielded to sin, they would not suffer. If Christ had yielded to sin, he would not have been crucified; but when he was crucified, he was wrestling with sin. Yet while he struggled against sin, he offered himself to the cross with the greatest willingness. And because the godly do not yield to sin, they therefore emerge as victors, even in death itself.

units.la: 5 Et obliti estis) Tertium argumentum ab authoritate & testimonio Solomonis. Prou.3. 13. Testimonio huic praemittitur objurgatio, qua reprehendit eorum obliuione, eamque exaggerat ex eo quod amicè ijs loquatur Sapiēs, eos compellans filios. Nota igitur, ne has ipsas quidem compellationes quibus vtitur Scriptura, otiosas & inutiles esse, sed vnicuique suum inesse pondus. Filii mi) Subijcit ipsum testimonium, in quo dissuadet duo extrema, in quibus solent homines peccare. Primum est ne castigationem Domini omnino negligamus & leuiter praetereamus, sine vlla vitae emendatione, quam respicit Deus in nobis castigandis. Alterum est, ne animo deficiamus: Vult ergo teneri a nobis medium, vt castigationem Domini patienter ferentes, vitam emendemus.
units.tr: 5 And you have forgotten) The third argument is from the authority and testimony of Solomon (Prov. 3.13). This testimony is preceded by a rebuke, in which he reproaches them for forgetting, and he heightens it by the fact that the wise man speaks to them in a friendly way, addressing them as sons. Note, therefore, that even these forms of address which Scripture uses are not idle and useless, but each carries its own weight. My son) He then adds the testimony itself, in which he dissuades from the two extremes into which men are wont to fall. The first is that we should altogether neglect the chastening of the Lord, and pass it over lightly, without any amendment of life, which God looks for in us when he chastens us. The second is that we should lose heart. He therefore wills that we hold to the middle way: bearing the chastening of the Lord patiently, and amending our lives.

units.la: 6 Quem enim diligit) Ratio exhortationis à Sapiente subiecta, à dilectione Domini quæ castigatione illa arguitur. Dominus castigat quem diligit, Ergo &c. Nota castigationes signa esse amoris divini: Nisi enim tuos castigaret Dominus, perirent cum mundo: Cum punimur (inquit Paulus) erudimur, ne cum mundo condemnemur. 1. Corinth. 11. 32. Loquitur autem hic Apostolus, de paternis castigationibus, non autem de pœnis quæ proficiscuntur à Deo Iudice: Nam punit impios tanquam Iudex: At vero suos non punit tanquam Iudex, sed castigat tanquam Pater, non ad interitum, sed ad vitæ emendationem & mortificationem. Ergo significat in afflictionibus attollendos esse animos ad amorem Dei, cuius aspectu acerbitas afflictionis tanta suavitate temperatur, ut in mediis afflictionibus exultemus gaudio ineffabili & glorioso.
units.tr: 6 For whom he loves The reason for the exhortation the Sage adds, drawn from the Lord's love, which is shown by this chastening. The Lord chastens whom he loves; therefore, etc. Note that chastenings are signs of divine love. If the Lord did not chasten you, you would perish with the world. "When we are judged," says Paul, "we are chastened, so that we are not condemned with the world" (1 Cor. 11:32). The Apostle here speaks of fatherly chastenings, not of the punishments that proceed from God as Judge. For he punishes the wicked as a judge, but he does not punish his own as a judge; he chastens them as a Father, not to destruction but to the amendment and mortification of life. So he means that in afflictions our minds must be lifted up to the love of God, by whose sight the bitterness of affliction is tempered with such sweetness that in the midst of afflictions we exult with an unspeakable and glorious joy.

units.la: 7 Si castigationem) Applicat ad Hebræos hoc testimonium, quasi dicat, Si castigationem sustinetis, Deus, ut hic testatur Solomon, se vobis offert ut filijs. Nota: non dicit, si castigamini (ut potulare videbantur Sapientis verba) sed si castigationem sustinetis. Non enim satis est castigari, sed oportet sustinere, hoc est, patienter ferre afflictionem, & ut loquitur Petrus 1. Epist. 5. 6. (submittere nos potenti Dei manui. Qui enim ludatur cum manu Dei, ei sese Deus non offert ut filio. Ergo dilectionem
units.tr: 7 If you endure chastening He applies this testimony to the Hebrews, as if to say: if you endure chastening, God, as Solomon here testifies, offers himself to you as to sons. Note that he does not say "if you are chastened" (as the words of the Sage seemed to be taken), but "if you endure chastening." For it is not enough to be chastened; one must endure, that is, bear affliction patiently, and, as Peter says, "submit ourselves under the mighty hand of God" (1 Pet. 5:6). For he who scorns the hand of God does not offer himself to such a person as a son. Therefore the love of God is not to be measured by afflictions, but by patience in afflictions, without which afflictions profit nothing.

units.la: Dei non oportet metiri ex afflictionibus, sed ex patientia in afflictionibus, sine qua nihil prosunt afflictiones. Quis enim est) Ratio cur castigationem sustinentibus offert ie Deus vt filijs, ab ipso genere. Filius quilibet castigatur a Patre. Ergo hoc ipso quod vos castiget Deus & sustinetis, offert se vobis vt Pater filijs.
units.tr: For what son is there The reason why God offers himself as a Father to those who endure chastening, drawn from the nature of the thing itself: every son is chastened by his father. Therefore, by the very fact that God chastens you and you endure it, he offers himself to you as a Father to sons.

units.la: 8 Quod si estis) Illustratio hujus applicationis a contrario. Qui non castigatur est spurius, & non filius. Ergo &c. Quemadmodum castigatio est signum filij: ita impunitas ista cum quis non castigatur, signum est spurij & nothi.
