In educandis liberis videmus non tantam esse in parentibus spuriorum curam, quanta est filiorum legitimorum: quia non est ea parentum dilectio erga spurios, quae est erga filios legitimè procreatos. Ita Deus spurios, qui non sunt filij, praeterit castigationis expertes, cum intereà filios, quos paterna dilectione prosequitur, castiget. Cuius participes) Obiter subindicat hanc esse communem filiorum conditionem, vt castigationis sint participes, vt si quis renuat castigationem sustinere, eo ipso arguat se non esse filium.
units.tr: 8 But if you are An illustration of this application by the contrary: he who is not chastened is a bastard and not a son. Therefore, etc. Just as chastening is the sign of a son, so impunity is the sign of a bastard and a illegitimate child when someone is not chastened. We see in the bringing up of children that parents do not take as much care of bastards as of legitimate sons, because a parent's love for bastards is not the same as for children lawfully born. Thus God passes over the bastards, who are not sons, free of chastening, while he chastens the sons whom he pursues with fatherly love. Whereof all are partakers He hints in passing that this is the common condition of sons, that they share in chastening; so that if anyone refuses to endure chastening, by that very fact he proves that he is not a son.

units.la: 9 Deinde corporum) Argumentum quartum à minori. Patres corporum nostrorum castigaverunt nos & eos sumus revereti: Annon multò magis subiiciemur Deo, Patri Spirituum? Deum vocat Patrem Spirituum, hoc est, animarum nostrarum, quia Deus immediate animā creat, eamque in corpus infundit: Nam etsi corpora immediate sint ab hominibus gignentibus propagatione naturali, animae tamen non sunt ex traduce, neque a Parentibus procreantur, sed a Deo immediate creantur. Reuerit fumus) hoc est, ijs nos submissimus, castigantibus. Quod si patienter aliquid ab hominibus tolerauimus, qui carnem tantum nostram genuerunt, annon multo magis a Deo, & corporum, & animarum genitore; qui corpora quidem genuit per homines, animam autem immediate? Deus igitur plus habet in nos juris, quam vllus homo, vel hoc ipso, quod Pater sit Spirituum: eoque debemus Deo maiorem reuerentiam, quam cuiquam homini, etiam patri, cui in Deo duntaxat parendum est. Homo non aliud jus, non aliam in nos potestatem, habet, quam a Deo accepit, vt non sit absoluta potestas, nisi Dei filius: eoque etiam reuerentiam debemus, Deo primum ac proprie, homini autem propter Deum. Et Vinemus) Amplificatio subjectionis qua Deo subijcimur, ab effecto consequente. Debemus eo magis Deo subjici, quod reuerentiam & subjectionem erga castigantem nos Deum sequatur vita. Hominum castigatio nunquam affert vitam: at Dei castigatio vitam affert, eamque aeternam.
units.tr: 9 Furthermore, the fathers of our flesh The fourth argument, from the lesser: our fathers of the flesh chastened us, and we revered them. Shall we not much more be subject to God, the Father of spirits? He calls God the Father of spirits, that is, of our souls, because God creates the soul immediately and infuses it into the body. For although bodies are immediately begotten by men through natural propagation, souls are not from traducianism, nor are they procreated by parents, but are created immediately by God. We revered them That is, we submitted ourselves to them when they chastened us. If we have patiently borne something from men, who begot only our flesh, shall we not much more bear it from God, the begetter both of bodies and of souls, who begot bodies indeed through men, but the soul immediately? God therefore has more right over us than any man, by this very fact that he is the Father of spirits; and so we owe God greater reverence than to any man, even a father, to whom obedience is due only in God. Man has no other right, no other power over us, than what he has received from God, so that no power is absolute except that of God's Son; and therefore we owe reverence first and properly to God, and to man only on account of God. And shall we live An amplification of the subjection by which we are subject to God, drawn from the consequent effect: we ought all the more to be subject to God because life follows the reverence and subjection we show to God who chastens us. The chastening of men never brings life, but the chastening of God brings life, and eternal life.

units.la: 10 Nam illi ad) Amplificatio superioris comparationis minorum, a dissimili castigationis modo & fine. Patres castigabant nos prout ipsis videbatur, saepe ex corrupto aliquo asseſtu, non aliquo nostro bono Deus autem nos castigat ad commodum nostrum. Ergo multo magis debemus nos Deo castigati submittere quam Patribus. Αδραυγος) Notatur tempus castigationis, quod mihi quidem commune videtur utriq; castigationi, & Dei, & hominis: nam veterq;, & Deus, & homo, ad paucos dies castigant. Ut enim castigatio paterna brevis est & momentanea tamen, ita etiam illa Dei castigatio momentanea dicitur. 2. Corinth. 4.17. Ut participes) Finis & usus castigationis Dei: Non castigamur propter peccatum, aut peccati nomine: id enim Christi passioni, qui perfecte pro omnibus peccatis nostris satisfecit plurimum derogaret: sed castigationis finis est, ut mortificato in nobis peccato, participes simul functionis Dei.
units.tr: 10 For they indeed An amplification of the earlier comparison of the lesser, from the dissimilar manner and end of chastening. Our fathers chastened us as seemed good to them, often out of some corrupt affection, not for any good of ours; but God chastens us for our profit. Therefore we ought much more to submit ourselves to God when he chastens us than to our fathers. For a moment [παραυτίκα] The time of chastening is noted, which seems to me common to both kinds of chastening, that of God and that of man: for both God and man chasten for a few days. For just as paternal chastening is brief and momentary, so God's chastening too is called momentary (2 Cor. 4:17). That we may be partakers The end and use of God's chastening: we are not chastened on account of sin, or in the name of sin; for that would greatly detract from the passion of Christ, who fully satisfied for all our sins. Rather, the end of chastening is that, sin being mortified in us, we may at the same time share in the holiness of God.

units.la: II Omnis autem) Occupatio. At durum est & insuaue castigari, & tristitiam, non gaudium affert; Respondet concessione primum, deinde correctione: In praesens quidem, h. e. eo tempore quo quis castigatur, non videtur esse gaudij, sed tristitiae. Videtur)Hoc verbo subinnuit castigationem non esse reipsa materiam tristitiae, sed potius gaudij, sed ita videri nobis qui in rebus judicandis fallimur, & quibus multa videntur esse id quod non sunt. Admiranda enim est hominis caecitas, ut quod ipsi bonum est & salutare, saepe videatur perniciosum,cótráque. Non igitur oportet res metiri ex præsenti sensu, sed intuendū est in exitum rei cuiusque.Ut posted)Correctio.Etsi in præsens videtur esse tristitiæ, postea tamen fructū tranquillum reddit,&c.Afflictiones & exercitationes cóparat culturæ: Ager post culturam reddit fructum:Sic nos àDeo exculti per afflictiones fructus producimus. Sumus natura steriles, expertes omnis boni & gratiæ, fœcundi autem mali, similes terræ quæ profert spinas & tribulos, cuius exitus tendit ad exultionem.Heb.6.8.Oportet igitur à Deo excolamur, antequam bonos fructus proferamus. Tranquillum) Hoc epitheto significat contrariam conditionem afflictionum, & fructus afflictionem consequetis. Nam quamdiu affligitur quis, nihil sentit præter agitationē & commotionem perpetuam,cum animi, tum corporis, sed fructus afflictionis tranquillus est,& omnis agitationis expers.Iustitiæ) Fructus hic vocatur Iustitiæ: eodem sensu etiam corona iustitiæ appellatur. 2.Tim.4.8. quam rependit Deus iustis, h.e. iis qui iustitiæ ex animo studēt, vel quæ datur propter iustitiam, non illam quidem inhærentē in nobis, sed iustitiam Christi nobis per fidem imputatam.Rom.5.21. Gratia regnat per iustitiam in vitam æternam.
units.tr: 11 But all chastening An objection. It is hard and unpleasant to be chastened, and it brings sorrow, not joy. He replies first by a concession, then by a correction. For the present, that is, at the time when someone is chastened, it does not seem to be a matter of joy but of sorrow. Seems By this word he hints that chastening is not in fact a matter of sorrow but rather of joy, but that it seems so to us, who are mistaken in judging things and to whom many things appear to be what they are not. For the blindness of man is wonderful, so that what is good and salutary for him often seems harmful, and the reverse. Therefore we must not measure things by present feeling, but look to the outcome of each thing. But afterwards The correction: although for the present it seems a matter of sorrow, afterwards it yields the peaceable fruit, etc. He compares afflictions and trials to cultivation: the field after cultivation yields fruit. So we, cultivated by God through afflictions, bring forth fruit. By nature we are barren, void of all good and of grace, and fruitful only in evil, like the earth that brings forth thorns and thistles, whose end is burning (Heb. 6:8). It is necessary, therefore, that we be cultivated by God before we bring forth good fruit. Peaceable By this epithet he signifies the contrary condition of afflictions, and the fruit that follows affliction. For as long as someone is afflicted, he feels nothing but constant agitation and disturbance, both of mind and of body; but the fruit of affliction is peaceable and free of all agitation. Of righteousness This fruit is called righteousness; in the same sense the crown of righteousness is also named (2 Tim. 4:8), which God renders to the righteous, that is, to those who earnestly pursue righteousness, or which is given on account of righteousness: not indeed the righteousness inherent in us, but the righteousness of Christ imputed to us through faith (Rom. 5:21): "grace reigns through righteousness unto eternal life."

units.la: 12 Quapropter manus) Conclusio est hortationis ad patientiam in afflictionibus, quasi dicat,Ne defpódete animos,sed eos erigite,& vofipfos ad afflictiones perferedas cofirmate. Habes hic imaginem quandam hominis meticulofi,& animum plane despondentis. Manus habet remissas, tremulas, & pendulas. genua soluta,& sese inuicem collidetia,vt de Belthezaro legimus, Dan. 5. 6. Non oportet nos sic afflictionibus consternari, sed animo praefenti alacriter easfuftinere. Estque haec prima exhortatio specialis, sub generali illa ad perseuerantiam comprehensa,ad afflictiones fortiter sustinendas.
units.tr: 12 Wherefore lift up The conclusion of the exhortation to patience in afflictions, as if to say: do not let your spirits sink, but raise them up and strengthen yourselves to bear afflictions. Here you have a picture of a fearful man, whose spirit is wholly despondent: his hands are slack, trembling and hanging down; his knees are loosened and knock together, as we read of Belshazzar (Dan. 5:6). We ought not to be dismayed by afflictions in this way, but to endure them with a ready and present spirit. This is the first special exhortation, comprehended under the general one to perseverance: to endure afflictions bravely.

units.la: 13 Et recta facite)Secunda exhortatio specialis,vt praeant alijs bono exemplo.Nam in stadio decurredo non tantum debemus nosipsos respicere,sed & alios qui nos imitatur. Hec exhortatio,vt & proxime superior,metaphoricis verbis concepta est. Redtas(inquit) facite orbitas pedibus vestris, hoc est, bono exemplo aliis praeite,& inter ambulandū, recto ,iustitiaeque operam date. Ne quod claudum)Finis specialis huius exhortationis, vt consulatur saluti fratrum infirmorum,ne orbitis pedum vestrorum non redtis,hominum (qui alioqui tota vita claudicat)pedes magis luxentur: vt hominis claudi pes, fi ad iter asperum &non redtum offenderit,luxatur amplius,ad ipsius euersionem.Nam in hanc sententia accipiendū videtur verbū ἐκλπέπτειν pro eo quod est luxari, vel diuerti à iusto a-cetacetabulo, & commissura ossium, ac si dixisset: Ne forte si quis iam claudus est ex infirmitate pedum, amplius nouo offendiculo periclitetur, vt salutis iactuam faciat, sed potius vestigiis vestris rectis insistens, sanitatem recuperet. Vt igitur supra versu 1. hortatus est ad currendum: Ita hic modum currendi generaliorem praescribit, vt rectas orbitas faciant: sequentibus autem hortationibus cum pacem, sanctimoniam &c. commendat, particulares explicat currendi modos, sub hoc generali comprehensos.
units.tr: 13 And make straight paths The second special exhortation: that they should go before others with a good example. For in running the race we must look not only to ourselves but also to others who imitate us. This exhortation, like the one immediately before, is conveyed in metaphorical words: "Make straight paths," he says, "for your feet," that is, go before others with a good example, and in walking strive after what is straight and righteous. Lest what is lame The particular purpose of this exhortation: that care be taken for the salvation of weaker brethren, so that the feet of men (who in any case limp all their lives) may not be dislocated by the crooked paths of your feet; just as the foot of a lame man, if it strikes a rough and crooked road, is dislocated further, to his ruin. For in this sense the verb [ἐκτρέπεσθαι] seems to be taken as meaning to be dislocated, or turned out of the proper socket of the hip and the joint of the bones, as if he had said: lest perhaps someone who is already lame from weakness of the feet should be endangered by a new stumbling-block and suffer loss of health, but rather, walking on your straight footsteps, recover soundness. Thus, just as in verse 1 he exhorted us to run, so here he prescribes a more general manner of running, that they make straight paths; and in the following exhortations, when he commends peace, holiness, etc., he explains particular ways of running, comprehended under this general one.

units.la: 14. Pacem sectamini) Tertia specialis exhortatio ad pacem, quę primus est currendi modus specialis. Pacis nomine intelligo non externam tantum illam, quę in externa coniunctione posita est, sed etiam internam quae posita est in coniunctione animorum. Est enim pax vinculum quo animi vniuntur, docente Paulo. Eph. 4.3. Studentes seruare vnitatem Spiritus per vinculum pacis. Cum omnibus) Ostendit cum quibus colenda sit pax, cum omnibus nimirum, h.e. cuiuscunque generis & conditionis hominibus, seruata tamen restrictione quam adijcit Paulus. Rom.12.16. Si fieri potest, quantum in vobis est, cum omnibus hominibus in pace viuentes. Neque enim vera est illa pax, quam cum nonnullis colimus, dum interea discordia nobis cum alijs intercedit. Nam vera pax vbiq; est, & cum omnib. hominibus, nullam cum quoquam dissentionem admittens.Et sanctimoniam)Quarta exhortatio specialis, ad sanctimoniā:quæ fecundus est currendi modus specialis. Sanctimoniæ nomine intelligenda videtur hoc loco,tū in genere vitæ sanctitas, tum etiā in specie castitas; Nam infrà vers.16. scortationem simul & prosanitatem, tanquam sanctimoniæ contrarias, coniungit. Castitas autem peculiariter interdum nomen sanctimoniæ obtinet. vt 1. Thess. 4.4. vbi sanctimoniam definit per abstinentiā à scortatione. Hæc (inquit) est voluntas Dei, nempe sanctificatio vestra,id est, vt abstineatis à scortatione: & castus peculiari modo purus & sanctus dicitur, vt contrà peculiarem quandam impuritatem in scortatione innuit Paulus 1.Cor.6. 18. Qui scortatur in proprium corpus peccat. Sine quā nemo) Ratio hortationis ad sanctimoniam,à summo malo & incommodo, quod sanctimoniæ defectum sequitur. Sine ea nemo videbit Dominum. Nullus enim impuro & polluto homini ad Deum patet aditus.Nam impuritas habitationem Spiritus sanctī, omnemque Dei præsentiam, cùm in corpore, tum in anima, penitus exterminat,vt videri Deus non possit: Cùm contrà sanctimonia Dei præsentiam afferat. Vnde Christus: Beati mundo corde; quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt, Matt.5.8.
units.tr: 14. Follow peace) The third special exhortation, to peace, which is the first special mode of running. By the name of peace I understand not only that external peace which consists in external fellowship, but also the internal peace which consists in the fellowship of souls. For peace is the bond by which souls are united, as Paul teaches: Eph. 4.3, "Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace." With all) He shows with whom peace is to be cultivated: with all, that is, with men of every kind and condition, yet within the restriction that Paul adds: Rom. 12.16, "If it is possible, as far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all men." For that peace is not true which we cultivate with some while meanwhile discord stands between us and others. For true peace is everywhere, and is with all men, admitting no dissension with anyone. And holiness) The fourth special exhortation, to holiness, which is the second special mode of running. By holiness here is to be understood both holiness of life in general and chastity in particular; for below, at verse 16, he joins fornication together with profanity as contraries to holiness. Chastity, moreover, sometimes bears the name of holiness in a special sense, as in 1 Thess. 4.4, where he defines holiness as abstinence from fornication: "This is the will of God, namely your sanctification, that is, that you abstain from fornication." And the chaste person is called, in a peculiar way, pure and holy, just as Paul points to a particular impurity in fornication, 1 Cor. 6.18: "He who commits fornication sins against his own body." Without which no one) The reason for the exhortation to holiness is drawn from the greatest evil and loss that follows the lack of holiness. Without it no one will see the Lord. For no access to God lies open to an impure and polluted man. For impurity utterly drives out the dwelling of the Holy Spirit and all the presence of God, both in body and in soul, so that God cannot be seen; whereas holiness brings the presence of God. Hence Christ: "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God," Matt. 5.8.

units.la: Prospicientes ne quis)Tertius currendi modus specialis, & exhortatio specialis quinta, quæ alios respicit, vt prospiciamus ne quis deficiat à gratia Dei. Sic obseruationem aliorum commendat, vt supra 10. 24. Obseruemus alij alios. Attendendum nobis est etiam ad alios, vt illi vnà nobiscum currant, non autem prolabantur & deficiant. Quartus currendi modus speciali s, & exhortatio sexta, proximum etiam respiciens; vt prospiciamus ne qua suppullulet radix amara, h. e. hæresis, aut aliquid simile, quod sit offensioni, vt Deut. 29. 18. radix proferens cicutam, aut absinthium. Euellenda est huiusmodi amara radix, antequam incipiat pullulare, ne offendiculo sint currentibus alijs. Obturbet) Amarę huic radici duo tribuit effecta, quæ totidem sunt exhortationis argumenta. Primum est conturbatio. Et per hanc) Secundum est inquinatio multorum.
units.tr: Looking carefully lest anyone) The third special mode of running, and the fifth special exhortation, which looks to others: that we take care lest anyone fall short of the grace of God. Thus he commends the watching over of others, as above at 10.24: "Let us consider one another." We must attend also to others, so that they may run together with us and not slip away and fail. The fourth special mode of running, and the sixth exhortation, likewise looks to a neighbour: that we take care lest any bitter root spring up, that is, heresy or something similar which is a stumbling block, as in Deut. 29.18, "a root bearing gall and wormwood." Such a bitter root must be plucked up before it begins to sprout, lest it become a stumbling block to the other runners. Trouble) He ascribes two effects to this bitter root, and these are as many arguments for the exhortation. The first is confusion. And through this) The second is the defiling of many.

units.la: 16 Ne quis fit) Quintus specialis currendi modus, & exhortatio septima, vt prospiciamus ne quis fit scortator aut profanus. Speciem præmittit generi: Nam profanitatis species quædam est fcortatio. Est autem profanus qui Deum eiusque gratiam, sancta denique omnia & religiosa contemnit & irridet. Velut Efau) Dissuadet à profanitate, exemplo Efau, cuius profanitas facto ipsius exponitur, vnico edulio vendidit ius primogeniti. Vide Genesis 25. 30. & deinceps. Ius autem primogeniti positum fuit in duabus prærogatiuis, vna dignitatis qua inter fratres primatum tenebat,& eos sibi subiectos habebat. 2. Chron. 21. 3. Altera roboris, ex dupla portione quae ipsi ex paterna hereditate cedebat. Deut. 21. 17. Vide de hac duplici praerogatiua. Genesis 49. 3. & 1. Chron. 5. 12. Unde etiam primogenitus typus erat Christi primogeniti Dei, qui omnes fratres honore & potentia antecedit. Vendito igitur iure primogeniti, Esau, & recusauit typus esse Christi, eoque Christum contempsit, & haereditatem amisit terrae Canaan, quae typus erat regni coelorum.
units.tr: 16 Lest anyone be) The fifth special mode of running, and the seventh exhortation: that we take care lest anyone become a fornicator or a profane person. He sets the species before the genus, for fornication is a certain kind of profanity. A profane person is one who despises and mocks God and his grace, and in short all holy and religious things. Like Esau) He dissuades from profanity by the example of Esau, whose profanity is set forth by his deed: he sold his birthright for a single meal. See Genesis 25.30 and following. The birthright, moreover, consisted in two prerogatives: one of dignity, by which he held the primacy among his brothers and had them subject to him (2 Chron. 21.3); the other of strength, in the double portion which fell to him from his father's inheritance (Deut. 21.17). See on this double prerogative Genesis 49.3 and 1 Chron. 5.12. Hence the firstborn was also a type of Christ, the firstborn of God, who surpasses all his brothers in honour and power. Therefore Esau, by selling the birthright, both refused to be a type of Christ and so despised Christ, and lost the inheritance of the land of Canaan, which was a type of the kingdom of heaven.

units.la: 17 Scitis enim eum etiam) Offenditur iudicium quo punitum est profanum hoc factum, cum vellet haereditario iure benedictionem asequi, reprobatus est a Deo per Isaacum, & ius primogeniturae, & indignitate, & in dupla portione, datum est Iacobo, cui illud vendiderat. Vide Genesis 27. 35. & deinceps. Non enim reperit) Reprobationem Esau offendit, ex immutabilitate sententiae benedictionis de Iacobo pronunciatae ab Isaaco patre. Non reperit locum poenitentiae patris Isaaci, h. e. non potuit efficere ut Isaacum patrem poeniteret benedictionis quantumuis ex errore in Iacobum collatae, ut sententiam illam benedictionis retractaret; quamuis cum Iachymis benedictionem illam exquisisset, ut benedictionem recuperaret. Vide Genes. 27. 39.
units.tr: 17 For you know that afterwards) The judgement is set forth by which this profane deed was punished: when he wished to obtain the blessing by hereditary right, he was rejected by God through Isaac, and the right of the firstborn, with its dignity and the double portion, was given to Jacob, to whom he had sold it. See Genesis 27.35 and following. For he found no place) He sets forth the rejection of Esau by pointing to the immutability of the sentence of blessing pronounced upon Jacob by his father Isaac. He found no place for repentance in his father Isaac: that is, he could not bring it about that his father Isaac would repent of the blessing conferred upon Jacob through a mistake, so as to revoke that sentence of blessing, although with tears he had sought that blessing in order to recover it. See Gen. 27.39.

units.la: Pronomen αὐτὸν proxime ad μεταγοίας vocem referendum videtur. Est ergo hoc primum dehortationis à profanitate argumentū. Efau profanis tristem & miserabilem profanitatis ἰωσ exitum consecutus est.Ergo cauenda est eius exemplo profanitas.
units.tr: The pronoun him [αὐτὸν] seems to refer most closely to the word for repentance [μετανοίας]. This, then, is the first argument for dissuasion from profanity: Esau, by his profanity, met the sad and wretched end [τέλος] of profanity. Therefore profanity is to be avoided by his example.

units.la: 18 Non enim accessistis) Alterum argumentū dehortationis à profanitate, à præsenti eorum conditione, quam copiose hoc loco describit: Est autem conditio hæc præsens eidem illa quam Paulus paucis verbis expressit. Rom. 6. 14. Peccatum vobis non dominabitur: non enim estis sub lege, sed sub gratia. Argumentum igitur est in hanc formam.Estis sub Euangelio:Ergo non oportet vos profanè viuere. In summa luce non debet quis ambulare ac si in tenebris esset. Interdiu enim composite ambulandum. Nox processit ( inquit Paulus) dies autem propinquat: Abijciamus igitur opera tenebrarum , & induamur habitu qui luci conueniat, vt interdiu composite ambulemus. Rom. 13.12. Habitum autem illum luci conuenientem,interpretatur esse Christum. vers. 14. Sic argumentatur etiam Apostolus. Tit. 2.·12. & deinceps. Illuxit gratia illa Dei salutifera omnibus hominibus, erudiens nos vt abnegata impietate &c. Tractatur hoc argumentum ex diuersis,κατ' ἀρχὴν & Διαν. Contrarium vnum remouetur,alterum ponitur.Remouetur conditio sub lege, vt locus fit conditioni sub gratia & Euangelio.Neq; enim vtraq; cöditio potest simul cósistere in eodé homine.Cöditio hæc sub lege amplificatur à terribili forma legis promulgatæ, quæ legis terrores indicat.Contrestabilem.) Forma promulgatæ legis suis quibusdá partibus exponitur: de quibus vide Exod. 19. Prima pars formæ legis promulgatæ, est in loco ex quo promulgata est Lex,Monte nimirū Sinai. Extenuatur autem hic locus à materia, fuit mons crassæ & terrenæ,eóque cótrestabilis materiæ,qui manib.palpari posset,quo distinguitur hic locus à cœlo, quod manibus cótrečtari non potest. Et incensum) Secúda pars formæ promulgatæ legis, in terri bilibus illis signis,quæ Dei præsentiam in illo monte testabantur,cùm ex eo Lex promulgaretur,vt fuerunt hæc meteora, ignis incensus, turbo,caligo, procella. Deus enim ipse nullo sensu percipi potest, sed per sensibiles istas creaturas se præsente declarat.
units.tr: 18 For you have not come) The second argument for dissuasion from profanity, drawn from their present condition, which he describes at length in this place. This present condition is the same that Paul expressed in few words: Rom. 6.14, "Sin shall not have dominion over you, for you are not under the law but under grace." The argument therefore runs in this form: you are under the Gospel; therefore you ought not to live profanely. In the full light no one ought to walk as if he were in darkness, for one must walk properly by day. "The night is far spent," says Paul, "the day is at hand; let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the armour of light, so that we may walk properly by day," Rom. 13.12. He interprets that garment suited to the light as Christ himself (v. 14). The Apostle argues in the same way: Titus 2.11 and following, "The saving grace of God has appeared to all men, teaching us, denying ungodliness" etc. This argument is treated from different things, from the beginning and from the end. One contrary is removed, the other is put in place. The condition under the law is removed, so that room is made for the condition under grace and the Gospel. For the two conditions cannot exist together in the same man. This condition under the law is amplified by the terrifying form of the law as it was promulgated, which indicates the terrors of the law. Tangible) The form of the promulgated law is explained in its several parts, concerning which see Exod. 19. The first part of the form of the promulgated law lies in the place from which the law was promulgated, namely Mount Sinai. This place is described as to its matter: it was a mountain of thick and earthly substance, and therefore tangible, which could be touched with the hands; by which this place is distinguished from heaven, which cannot be handled with the hands. And kindled) The second part of the form of the promulgated law lies in those terrible signs which testified to God's presence on that mountain when the law was promulgated from it: these were the meteors, the kindled fire, the whirlwind, the darkness, the tempest. For God himself cannot be perceived by any sense, but declares his presence through these sensible creatures.

units.la: 19 Tubaque sonitum) Tertia pars formæ promulgatæ legis, in sonitu tubæ, quo præparabatur populus ad audiendum vocem Dei. Et vocem)Quarta pars est ipsa vox legis promulgatæ, quæ tubæ sonitum est insecuta. Quam qui) Amplificatio vocis huius quæ audita est ex hoc mŏte,ab effećto(in terrore incutiēdo audientibus ) eoque duplici. Primum est in populo:alterū est in Mose ipso, duce populi. Effećtum in populo est: Adeò ad auditam illam vocem exhorruerunt,vt audire eam non sustinuerint sed deprecati sunt ne amplius sibi fieret sermo per ipsum Deum immediate, sed loqueretur per Mosen internuncium. Caussa autem hujus terroris fuit, quod terrore hoc ex terno in lege promulgãnda excitatus est internus conscientiæ terror, quòd exactam illam Dei in lege justitiam (cui nullus hominum satisfacere potest) ferre non possent.
units.tr: 19 And the sound of a trumpet) The third part of the form of the promulgated law lies in the sound of the trumpet, by which the people were prepared to hear the voice of God. And the voice) The fourth part is the voice itself of the promulgated law, which followed the sound of the trumpet. Which those who) An amplification of this voice, which was heard from this mountain, from its effect (in striking terror into the hearers), and that a twofold effect. The first is in the people; the second is in Moses himself, the leader of the people. The effect in the people was this: at the hearing of that voice they shrank back in such terror that they could not endure to hear it, but begged that the word should no longer be spoken to them by God himself immediately, but that he should speak through Moses as intermediary. The cause of this terror was that, from the external terror of the law's promulgation, there was aroused an inward terror of conscience, because they could not bear that exact justice of God in the law (to which no man can satisfy).

units.la: 20 Non enim ferebant Altera causa terroris in populo, à Dei interdicto, quo per Mosen vt internuncium significaucrat Deus, morte afficiendum esse quicquid mõtem tangeret, non homo tantum, sed etiam bestia. Vide Exod 19. 13. idque propter præsentiam sacrosanctæ illius Majestatis Dei, ad quam impuræ & pollutæ creaturæ nullus patet accessus, nisi priùs sanctificetur. Itaque necesse fuit Mosen etiam sanctificari antequam hunc montem attingeret.
units.tr: 20 For they could not bear it. This is the second cause of the people's terror: God's prohibition, which he had made known through Moses as mediator, that whatever touched the mountain should be put to death, whether man or beast. See Exod. 19:13. This was because of the presence of that most holy majesty of God, to which no impure and polluted creature has access unless it is first sanctified. Therefore Moses too had to be sanctified before he could approach this mountain.

units.la: 21 Et Moses) Effectum vocis auditæ in promulgãda lege, in ipso Mose, qui & ipse quoque est exterritus, vt hac voce confessus est: Expauefactus sum ac tremebundus. Hæc quidem Mosis verba non expressè in Scripturis habentur, sed Exod. 19. 19. dicitur Moses, quum populum obuiam Deo è castris eduxisset, totusque mons ille tremeret, locutus esse, antequam Deus plane ad montem Sinai descendisset: quid autem locutus sit, eo loco non explicitur, sed hoc loco afferuntur verba, quibus Moses sono illo tubæ territus de suo terrore conquestus est,& Deus ibi dicitur ipsi refpondiffe voce, hoc est,placidis verbis Mosen, de conseruatione sua agentem, consolatus esse & confirmauisse.Hactenus fuit primum membrum diuersorum.Conditio sub lege,quam ex pressit terribili illa legis promulgatione.
units.tr: 21 And Moses (said): This is the effect of the voice heard in the promulgation of the law, in Moses himself, who was also terrified, so that he confessed with this voice: "I am exceedingly afraid and trembling." These words of Moses are not expressly found in the Scriptures, but Exod. 19:19 says that Moses spoke when he had led the people out of the camp to meet God and the whole mountain was trembling, before God had plainly descended onto Mount Sinai. What he said is not explained in that place, but in this place the words are cited by which Moses, terrified by the sound of the trumpet, complained of his terror, and God is said to have answered him with a voice, that is, to have consoled and confirmed Moses, who was speaking about his own preservation, with gentle words. So far is the first part of the contrast, the condition under the law, which he expressed by that terrible promulgation of the law.

units.la: 22 Sed accessistis) Sequitur conditio sub Euangelio,quæ amplificatur descriptione Ecclesiæ noui Testamenti. Describit eam primum ex variis, ijsque suauissimis appellationibus typicis, quibus locus innuitur: Primum vocatur mons Sion. Monti Sinai ex quo promulgata est lex, ex aduerso opponit montem Sion (qui typus erat cœlorum) ex quo primum personauit Euangelium. Nam primum Christus ipse, deinde ejus Apostoli, perspicuè ex Sione Euangelium promulgarunt, juxta Efaiæ vaticinium.Ief.2.3. Et ciuitatem) Altera loci appellatio: vocatur ciuitas Dei viui, hoc est, cœlestis Hierusalem, quæ per terrestrem illam figurabatur, vt subjecta tertia appellatione interpretatur: His ergo tribus nominibus, vnum eundemque locum significat. Et myriadas) Secunda pars descriptionis Ecclesiæ, à personis variis ijsque præstantissimis, quæ sunt in hoc loco, & ad quas accedimus.Perfonæ primum sunt Angeli, ijque non pauci, sed numero infiniti.Nam myriadas vocat Angelorum, numerum finitum pro infinito exprimens.
units.tr: 22 But you have come (to Mount Sion): Now follows the condition under the Gospel, which is set out by a description of the Church of the New Testament. He describes it first by various and most pleasant typical names, by which the place is indicated. First it is called Mount Sion. Opposed to Mount Sinai, from which the law was promulgated, he sets Mount Sion (which was a type of the heavens), from which the Gospel first sounded forth. For first Christ himself, and then his Apostles, clearly proclaimed the Gospel from Sion, in accordance with the prophecy of Isaiah, Isa. 2:3. And to the city (of the living God): this is the second name of the place: it is called the city of the living God, that is, the heavenly Jerusalem, which was prefigured by that earthly one, as the third name added explains. Thus by these three names he signifies one and the same place. And to the innumerable company (of angels): this is the second part of the description of the Church, drawn from various and most excellent persons who are in this place, and to whom we come. The first persons are the angels, and not a few of them but infinite in number. For he calls them myriads, expressing a finite number for an infinite one.

units.la: Conuentum) Deinde electi omnes quos vocat primogenitos, nec primogenitos tantum, sed concentum & concionem primogenitorum, quo significat immensum eorum numerum: quo autem major electorum numerus eo major felicitas & gloria. Vocantur autem electi primogeniti, per allusionem ad primogenitos in populo Dei, qui habebant, tum dignitatem & authoritatem in reliquam familiam, tum duplam hæreditatis portionem: Ita electi omnes obtinent primum dignitatem cœlestem, cujus typus erat dignitas illa in familijs. Deinde hæreditario possidebunt regnum paratum ipsis à jactis mundi fundamentis. Matth. 25. 34.
units.tr: To the general assembly (and church of the firstborn): Next, all the elect, whom he calls firstborn, and not merely firstborn but the assembly and gathering of the firstborn, by which he signifies their immense number; for the greater the number of the elect, the greater the happiness and glory. The elect are called firstborn by an allusion to the firstborn among the people of God, who had both the dignity and authority over the rest of the family and a double portion of the inheritance. So all the elect obtain the first, heavenly dignity, of which that dignity in families was a type. Then they will possess by inheritance the kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world, Matt. 25:34.

units.la: Qui conscripti) Descriptio est primogenitorum: Conscripti sunt in cœlis, id est, à Deo electi sunt ad vitam æternam. Nam electorum nomina dicuntur scripta esse in cœlis. Luc. 10. 20. & in libro vitæ. Philipp. 4. 3. quibus phrasibus significatur eos æterno illo electionis decreto ad vitam æternam esse ordinatos. Et iudicem Vniuersorum) Tertio in personis, quarum præsentia fruimur in cœlesti illa Hierusalem, numeratur Deus, quem vocat judicem vniuersorum, qui solus justissimo suo judicio afflictionem reddit iis qui fideles afflig-unt, ipsis autem fidelibus relaxationem. 2. Thess. 1. 6. 7. Et spiritus) Quarto loco recenset spiritus justorum consecratorum, hoc est, animas fidelium defunctorum, jam in cœlum receptas.Nam homines qui sunt in Ecclesia, vel sunt adhuc in corpore degentes in terris, quos initio versus vocauit primogenitos: vel depofito hoc corporis Tabernaculo in cœlis triumphat cum Christo, vt sunt spiritus justorum, qui consummati hic dicuntur, hoc est, consummatam & perfectam sanctificationem & gloriam adepti, non quidem fecundum omnes consummationis gradus, sed fecundum aliquos tantum: cum quoad animam præsentes jam sint cum Domino. Consummati igitur sunt, non simpliciter, sed καταˈτι, respectu nostri, qui adhuc aduenæ fumus in corpore, & peregre à Domino absumus.
units.tr: Whose names are written (in heaven): This is a description of the firstborn: they are written in heaven, that is, they have been chosen by God to eternal life. For the names of the elect are said to be written in heaven, Luke 10:20, and in the book of life, Phil. 4:3. By these phrases it is signified that they have been ordained to eternal life by that eternal decree of election. And to God the Judge of all: Third among the persons whose presence we enjoy in that heavenly Jerusalem, God is named, whom he calls the Judge of all, who alone by his most just judgment repays affliction to those who afflict the faithful, and relief to the faithful themselves, 2 Thess. 1:6, 7. And to the spirits (of just men made perfect): Fourthly he reckons the spirits of the sanctified righteous, that is, the souls of the faithful who have died and are now received into heaven. For men who are in the Church are either still living in the body on earth, whom at the beginning of the verse he called firstborn, or, having laid aside this tabernacle of the body, they triumph in heaven with Christ, as are the spirits of the righteous, who are here said to be made perfect, that is, who have obtained a complete and perfect sanctification and glory, not indeed according to all the degrees of perfection, but only according to some: since as regards the soul they are already present with the Lord. They are therefore perfected, not simply, but in a certain respect [κατά τι], with regard to us, who are still strangers in the body and are absent from the Lord as pilgrims.

units.la: 24. Et adnoui) Postremo inter personas recensetur Iesus, noui fœderis Mediator, per quem solum κοινωνίαν habemus cum Angelis, cum primogenitis qui conscripti sunt in cœlo, cum Deo vniuersorum iudice, cum spiritibus deniq; justorum. Nam in eo recolliguntur omnia, tum quæ in cœlis, tum quæ in terris. Ephef. 1. 10. Decitur noui Testamenti Mediator, qui nouum illud Testamentum, quo legauit nobis remissionem peccatorum, justitiam & vitam æternam, fanciuit suo sanguine. Et sanguinem) Cum Christo conjungit ejus sanguinem, quo purgatur conscientia nostra, eumque à Christo feorsim nominat, vt doceat videndum nobis ille vt sanguine hoc aspersi & irrigati fimus: nam alioqui nullum ex Christo beneficium percipipercipere possimus. Ideoque sanguis aspersionis dicitur, quod eo per fidem aperta fidelium corda sanctificentur, & a sordibus peccatorum abluantur, allusione facta ad veterem legem, in qua omnia fere sanguine aspersio mundabantur, supra 9. 22. Praestantiora) Commendat hunc Christi sanguinem ab effecto, quod illustrat comparatione Abelis: Sanguis Christi praestantiora loquitur quam sanguis Abelis. Nam sanguis Abelis loquitur & postulat a Deo vindictam: At sanguis Christi postulat a Deo misericordiam & gratiam. Quanquam non incommode, & tum ad graecum contextum, tum ad sequentem exhortationem magis etiam appositè, locutio haec ad ipsas personas referri possit; quod Christus suo sanguine praestantiora loquatur, quam Abel, qui mortuus adhuc loquitur, supra 11. 4. & vindictam a Deo expescit; cum Christus suo sanguine veniam & remissionem peccatorum postulet.
units.tr: 24 And to Jesus, the mediator of the new covenant: Last among the persons, Jesus, the mediator of the new covenant, is named, through whom alone we have fellowship [κοινωνίαν] with the angels, with the firstborn who are written in heaven, with God the Judge of all, and finally with the spirits of the just. For in him all things are gathered together, both those in heaven and those on earth, Eph. 1:10. He is called the mediator of the new testament, who ratified that new testament, by which he bequeathed to us the remission of sins, righteousness and eternal life, with his own blood. And to the blood (of sprinkling): He joins to Christ his blood, by which our conscience is cleansed, and names it separately from Christ, to teach us that we must see that we have been sprinkled and watered with this blood; for otherwise we could receive no benefit from Christ. Therefore it is called the blood of sprinkling, because by it the hearts of the faithful, opened through faith, are sanctified and washed from the defilement of sins, with an allusion to the old law, in which almost all things were cleansed by the sprinkling of blood, see above 9:22. Speaks better things (than Abel): He commends this blood of Christ from its effect, which he illustrates by a comparison with Abel: the blood of Christ speaks better things than the blood of Abel. For the blood of Abel speaks and demands vengeance from God, but the blood of Christ asks from God mercy and grace. Although it is not inappropriate, and indeed more apposite both to the Greek text and to the following exhortation, that this expression may be referred to the persons themselves, so that Christ by his blood speaks better things than Abel, who being dead still speaks, see above 11:4, and asks vengeance from God, while Christ by his blood asks pardon and remission of sins.

units.la: 25 Videte ne aspernemini eum qui loquitur: nam si illi non effugerunt qui auersabantur eum qui loquebatur Dei nomine in terra, multo magis nos, si eum qui de caelis est auersemur.
units.tr: 25 See that you refuse not him that speaketh. For if they escaped not who refused him that spake on earth, much more shall not we escape, if we turn away from him that speaketh from heaven.

units.la: 26 Cuius vox tunc concussit terram: nunc autem denunciauit, dicens, Adhuc semel ego concutiam non solum terram, sed etiam caelum.
units.tr: 26 Whose voice then shook the earth: but now he hath promised, saying, Yet once more I shake not the earth only, but also heaven.

units.la: 27 Porro illud, Adhuc semel declarat instabilium rerum, vt pote facticiarum, amotione, vt maneant quæ sunt stabilia.
units.tr: 27 And this word, Yet once more, signifies the removal of those things that are shaken, as of things that are made, so that those things which cannot be shaken may remain.

units.la: 18 Quapropter regnum assumentes quod concuti non possit, teneamus gratiam per quam itaque placeamus Deo, vt ei placeamus cum verecundia & reuerentia.
units.tr: 28 Wherefore, receiving a kingdom which cannot be moved, let us hold fast grace, by which we may please God, so that we may please him with reverence and fear.

units.la: 19 Etenim Deus noster consumens ignis est.
units.tr: 29 For our God is a consuming fire.

units.la: Videte ne aspernemini.) Occasione proximorum verborum quibus sanguinis Christi efficacium commendauit, redit ad præcipuam exhortationem ad perseuerantiam: Ne Christum loquentem aspernemur, sed teneamus eius doctrinam. Nam si illi) Argumentum exhortationis decimum sextum, à iudicio quod sequetur eos, qui Christum loquentem aspernantur: iudicium hoc confirmatur duobus argumentis. Primum est à comparatione minorum. Si illi non effugerunt qui Moisen Dei nomine in terris loquentem, auersabantur: quanto magis non effugiemus nos, si Christum è cœlis loquentem aspernemur? Quo enim dignior est persona quæ loquitur, eo magis puniendi sunt qui loquentem auersantur. Simile argumentum vide Heb.1.2.3. & 10.28.29.
units.tr: See that you refuse not.) On the occasion of the preceding words, in which he commended the efficacy of Christ's blood, he returns to the principal exhortation to perseverance: let us not refuse Christ when he speaks, but hold fast to his teaching. For if they) The sixteenth argument of the exhortation, from the judgment which will follow those who refuse Christ when he speaks. This judgment is confirmed by two arguments. The first is from comparison of the lesser: If they did not escape who turned away from Moses when he spoke on earth in the name of God, how much more shall we not escape if we refuse Christ when he speaks from heaven? For the more worthy the person who speaks, the more deserving of punishment are those who turn away from him as he speaks. For a similar argument see Heb. 1:2, 3 and 10:28, 29.

units.la: 26 Cuius vox) Secundum argumentum quo confirmat iudicium eorum, qui Christum loquentem auersantur, est à vi & efficacia vocis Christi loquentis, tam præterita in promulganda lege, quà præsenti in prædicando Euangelio. Cuius vox tunc) Cum promulgaret legem concussit terram, hoc est, homines in terris degentes, gentes, qui lege promulgata admiratione maiestatis ipsius affecti sunt. At nunc (in praedicando Euangelio) non solum concutit terram, hoc est, homines, sed etiam caelum, hoc est, Angelos qui in caelis degunt, qui etiam ipsi in Euangelij praedicatione, in admirationem bonitatis & gratiae Dei abripiuntur, & in mysteria Euangelij desiderant introspicere. 1. Pet. 1. 12.
units.tr: 26 Whose voice) The second argument by which he confirms the judgment of those who turn away from Christ speaking is drawn from the power and efficacy of the voice of Christ speaking, both in the past, in the promulgation of the law, and in the present, in the preaching of the Gospel. Whose voice then) When he promulgated the law, he shook the earth, that is, men living on earth, the nations, who were struck with admiration at his majesty when the law was promulgated. But now (in the preaching of the Gospel) he shakes not only the earth, that is, men, but also heaven, that is, the angels who dwell in heaven, who are themselves also carried away in admiration at the goodness and grace of God in the preaching of the Gospel, and desire to look into the mysteries of the Gospel, 1 Pet. 1:12.

units.la: Cum ergo tanta sit efficacia vocis ipsius, & nunc, & jam olim, non effugietis judicium, si eum loquentem aspernemini. Dicens adhuc ego) Concussionem hanc caelorum & terrae, in Euangelij praedicatione, confirmat testimonio Aggaei Prophetae cap. 2. verf. 7. vbi praedicitur ista caelorum simul & terrae commotio in Euangelio praedicando, quae summam arguit esse majestatem & dignitatem Euangelij. Quanquam non incommode concussio ista intelligi potest de externa illa commotione caeli & terrae, ad vocem Christi exspirantis in cruce, cum tenebris super totam terram inductis Sol obscuratus est, aulaeum Templi fissum est medium, terra mota est, petrae fissae sunt. Matth. 27. 50. 51. & deinceps. Luc. 23. 44. 45.
units.tr: Since, then, the voice of him who speaks is so powerful, both now and in former times, you will not escape judgment if you reject him who speaks. Speaking yet once more: he confirms this shaking of heaven and earth in the preaching of the Gospel by the testimony of the prophet Haggai, chapter 2, verse 7, where this shaking of heaven and earth together in the preaching of the Gospel is foretold, which shows the great majesty and dignity of the Gospel. Yet this shaking may not unsuitably be understood of that outward commotion of heaven and earth at the voice of Christ breathing his last on the cross, when, with darkness brought over the whole earth, the sun was darkened, the veil of the Temple was torn in two, the earth quaked, and the rocks were split. Matt. 27. 50, 51 and following. Luke 23. 44, 45.

units.la: 27 Porro illud adhuc) Interpretatur illud Aggaei testimonium; & ex illis Prophetae verbis (adhuc semel) deducit corollarium, de abrogatione Legis, & aeternitate rerum per ceremonias legis & politiam Mosaicam significatarum, hoc est, sacerdotij, & regni Christi, ut inde aliud institutæ hortationis argumetum eliciat. Cum enim dicit, adhuc, significat non satis esse quòd jam antea concussa esset terra in ferenda lege, sed adhuc oportere legis hujus immutationem esse. Cum autem addit Semel, significat vnicam duntaxat fore illam mutationem, vt quod in locum legis successorum fit, maneat perpetuū & immutabile. Tà σαλευόμενα ea quæ concutiuntur, vocat legem Mosaicam, omnesq; legis ceremonias: & instrumenta quæ legalibus ceremonijs seruiebant, quæ nituntur erant instabilis, & non permanentis. Vt putà fallarum) Ratio instabilitatis istarum rerum, quia institutæ quidem & mandatæ erat à Deo, sed ad certum aliquod tempus, ad aduentum vsque Christi. Galat. 3. 19. Cujus quum typi & vmbræ essent, debebant aduentanti corpori cedere: τὰ μὴ σαλευόμενα, stabilia, vocat ea quæ per instabilia fuerunt significata, & in locum instabilium successerunt, vt est Christus ipse, ejus regnum, & omnia bona quæ consequimur in Christo, vt sunt justificatio, sanctificatio & cœlestis illa hæreditas, quæ omnia necessario æterna manent.
units.tr: 27 Moreover, that passage: he interprets the testimony of Haggai, and from the prophet's words (once more) he draws a corollary concerning the abrogation of the Law and the permanence of the things signified by the ceremonies of the Law and the Mosaic polity, namely the priesthood and the kingdom of Christ, so that he may thence draw out another argument for his exhortation. For when he says yet, he signifies that it is not enough that the earth was already shaken when the Law was given, but that this Law must yet be changed. When he adds once, he signifies that this change will be single only, so that what comes in place of the Law may remain perpetual and unchangeable. He calls the law of Moses and all its ceremonies, and the instruments which served the legal ceremonies, the things that are shaken [τὰ σαλευόμενα], which were unstable and not permanent. As, for example, of the shadows: the reason for the instability of these things is that they were indeed instituted and commanded by God, but for a certain time, until the coming of Christ. Gal. 3. 19. Since they were types and shadows, they had to yield to the body that was coming. He calls stable [τὰ μὴ σαλευόμενα] those things which were signified by the unstable things and succeeded them in their place, such as Christ himself, his kingdom, and all the good things we obtain in Christ, such as justification, sanctification, and that heavenly inheritance, all of which necessarily remain eternal.

units.la: 28 Quapropter regnum) Ex hac conditione Regni Christi, ex interpretatione verborum Prophetæ sumpta, deducit argumentum nouum præcipuæ exhortationis, ad perseuerandum in fide, & gratiam retinendam. Si gratiam tenuerimus, participes erimus regni illius, quod concuti non potest. Ergo &c. Eftq; hoc argumentu exhortationis decimuseptimum. Gratię nomine intelligo fidem ex Dei gratia profectam: metonymia efficientis. Per quam) Descriptio gratiæ siue fidei ab effecto: fides enim non potest esse otiosa in nobis: sed necessario producit hoc effectum, vt seruiamus Deo. Vt ei placeamus) Modus seruiendi Deo praescribitur, primum in genere, vt seruiamus ei ad ipsius voluntatę, & placitum, facientes ex animo quæ vult Deus. Ephes. 6.6. Deinde in specie, cum verecundia & reuerētia. Verecundia est pudor, ex infirmitatis noštræ & indignitatis conscientia. Reuerentia est religiosus metus ex agnitione illius Maiestatis Dei nostri, cui seruimus. Harum proprietatum exemplum habes in Publicano. Luc. 18.13. vt & audaciæ, quæ his opponitur, in Pharisæo.
units.tr: 28 Therefore the kingdom: from this condition of the kingdom of Christ, taken from the interpretation of the prophet's words, he draws a new argument for the chief exhortation, to persevere in faith and to retain grace. If we hold fast to grace, we shall be partakers of that kingdom which cannot be shaken. Therefore, etc. This is the seventeenth argument of exhortation. By the name of grace I understand faith proceeding from the grace of God: a metonymy of the efficient cause. Through which: a description of grace or faith from its effect, for faith cannot be idle in us, but necessarily produces this effect, that we serve God. That we may please him: the manner of serving God is prescribed, first in general, that we serve him according to his will and pleasure, doing from the heart what God wills. Eph. 6. 6. Then in particular, with reverence and godly fear. Reverence is shame, arising from the consciousness of our weakness and unworthiness. Godly fear is religious dread arising from the acknowledgment of the majesty of our God whom we serve. You have an example of these qualities in the Publican. Luke 18. 13. Likewise of the boldness which is opposed to them, in the Pharisee.

units.la: 29 Etenim Deus) Postremum exhortationis argumentum, à natura Dei nostri, est ignis consumens, eoque consumpturus est omnes qui non perseuerantes in fide, ipsi non seruiunt iuxta ipsius placitum. Hoc argumentum mutuatus est ex Mose. Deut. 4.24.
units.tr: 29 For our God: the last argument of exhortation, drawn from the nature of our God, is that he is a consuming fire, and so he will consume all who do not persevere in faith and do not serve him according to his pleasure. He has borrowed this argument from Moses. Deut. 4. 24.

units.la: Argumentum Capitis decimitertij.
units.tr: Argument of Chapter Thirteen.

units.la: Hoc capite primùm sunt speciales paraenefes, quibus hortatur ad officia, maximè quæ ad secundam legis Tabulam pertinent ad versum vsque 18. Deinde commendat Hebræis preces pro se, ad versus vbi epistola hanc
units.tr: In this chapter, first, there are special exhortations, by which he urges them to duties, chiefly those which pertain to the second table of the Law, up to verse 18. Then he commends to the Hebrews prayers for himself, up to the verses where he concludes the epistle

units.la: P precibus primùm, deinde hortatione, postremò aliquot alijs varij argumenti sermonibus concludit.
units.tr: with prayers first, then with exhortation, and finally with several other discourses on various subjects.

units.la: CAPVT XIII
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII

units.la: 1 Fraterna charitas maneat.
units.tr: 1 Let brotherly love remain.

units.la: 2 Hospitalitatis ne sitis immemores: per hanc enim quidam inscij exceperunt Angelos hospitio.
units.tr: 2 Do not forget hospitality, for by it some, unawares, have entertained angels.

units.la: 3 Memores et state Vinctorum tanquam Vna cum illis Vincti: eorum qui malis premuntur, ac si ipsi quoque corpore afflicti essetis.
units.tr: 3 Remember those in bonds, as though bound with them, and those who are ill-treated, as though you yourselves were in the body.

units.la: 4 Honorabile est inter quosuis coniugium et cubile impollutum: scortatores autem et adulteros damnabit Deus.
units.tr: 4 Marriage is honourable among all, and the bed undefiled; but God will judge fornicators and adulterers.

units.la: 5 Sint mores alieni ab auaritia: estote contenti praesentibus, dixit enim ipse, Non te deseram, neq; te derelinquam.
units.tr: 5 Let your manners be free from covetousness; be content with what you have, for he himself has said, I will never leave you nor forsake you.

units.la: 6 Adeò Vt confidenti animo dicamus, Dominus mihi auxiliator: nec timebo quid faciat mihi homo.
units.tr: 6 So that we may say with a confident mind, The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man may do to me.

units.la: 7 Memores estote ductorum Vestrorum, qui loquuti sunt Vobis sermonem Dei: quorum imitamini fidem, considerantes qui fuerit exitus conversationis ipsorum.
units.tr: 7 Remember your leaders, who spoke the word of God to you, whose faith you imitate, considering the outcome of their way of life.

units.la: 8 Iesus Christus heri et hodie idem est, et in secula.
units.tr: 8 Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and for ever.

units.la: 9 Doctrinis Varijs et peregrinis ne circumferimini: bonum enim est gratia confirmari cor, non cibis, quibus nonsunt adiuti qui in ipsis versati sunt.
units.tr: 9 Do not be carried about by various and strange teachings; for it is good that the heart be strengthened by grace, not by foods, by which those who were occupied with them were not helped.

units.la: 10 Habemus altare ex quo non habent ius edendi qui tabernaculo deseruiunt.
units.tr: 10 We have an altar, from which those who serve the tabernacle have no right to eat.

units.la: 11 Quorum enim animalium sanguis infertur pro peccato in sacrarium per Pontificem, horum corpora exuruntur extra castra.
units.tr: 11 For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the sanctuary by the high priest for sin are burned outside the camp.

units.la: 12 Quapropter et Iesus, ut sanctificaret populum per proprium sanguinem, passus est extra portam.
units.tr: 12 Therefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate.

units.la: 13 Exeamus igitur ad eum extra castra, opprobrium eius portantes.
units.tr: 13 Let us go out therefore to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach.

units.la: 14 Non enim habemus hic stabilem civitatem, sed futuram inquirimus.
units.tr: 14 For we have here no lasting city, but we seek the one to come.

units.la: 15 Per ipsum igitur assidue offeramus Deo sacrificium laudis, id est, fructum labiorum confitentium nomini eius.
units.tr: 15 Through him, therefore, let us continually offer to God the sacrifice of praise, that is, the fruit of lips confessing his name.

units.la: 16 Beneficentiae et communicationis ne obliviscimini: talibus enim Victimis delectatur Deus.
units.tr: 16 Do not forget beneficence and fellowship, for with such sacrifices God is pleased.

units.la: 17 Obedite ductoribus vestris, et obsecundate: vigilant enim ipsi pro animabus vestris, tanquam rationem reddituri: ut cum gaudio hoc faciant, et non gementes, id enim est vobis inutile.
units.tr: 17 Obey your leaders and submit to them; for they watch over your souls, as those who must give account, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning, for that would be unprofitable for you.

units.la: Fraterna charitas) Prima speciali s praeceptio qua charitatem commendat, non generatim quamlibet, sed φιλαδελφίαν, sive charitate fraternam, qua tantum prosequendi sunt fratres, et domestici fidei, qui omnes eiusdem Patris filij sunt. Hanc distinguit Petrus a charitate, quam ἀγαπᾶν vocat. 2. Epist. 1. 7.
units.tr: Brotherly love) This is the first special precept, by which he commends love, not love in general, but φιλαδελφία [φιλαδελφία], brotherly love, by which only brothers and members of the household of faith are to be cherished, all of whom are sons of the one Father. Peter distinguishes this from the love that he calls ἀγαπᾶν [ἀγαπᾶν]. 2 Pet. 1.7.

units.la: 2 Hospitalitas) Duobus versibus sequentibus duo præcipiuntur officia, quæ ex charitate fraterna, tanquam propria ipsius effecta, profluunt: Hospitalitas nimirum &συμπαθεια erga vinctos & afflictos, siue eorum recordatio: In his enim potissimum effectis, per illa tempora quæ persecutionibus feruebant (cum sanctorum peregrinationes & exilia, vinculaque & afflictiones frequentes essent) occasio exercendæ charitati, offerebatur. Hoc versu præcipitur hospitalitas. Per hanc enim) Hospitalitatem commendat argumento sumpto ab honore illo singulari, qui Dei beneficio accidit quibusdam qui hospitalitatis erant studiosi, quod nimirum Angelos hospitio exceperint. Inscij) Amplificatur hoc eorum factum ex particulari circumstantia inscientiæ ipsorum, quòd receperint Angelos cùm putarent se homines recipere: Nemo enim tam est inhumanus, qui cognitos Angelos recusaret domo excipere. Intelligit autem de Abrahamo, qui tres Angelos hominum specie ipsi apparentes hospitio excepit. Gen. 18. 2. & deinceps, In his exemplis generalis doctrina includitur: Non casituros suo præmio quicunque hospitalitati operam dederint.
units.tr: 2 Hospitality) In the two following verses two duties are enjoined, which flow from brotherly love as its proper effects: namely hospitality, and sympathy [συμπάθεια] towards prisoners and the afflicted, or the remembering of them. For among these effects, especially in those times when persecutions raged (when the wanderings and exiles of the saints, and their bonds and frequent afflictions, were common), an opportunity of exercising love was offered. In this verse hospitality is enjoined. For by it) He commends hospitality by an argument drawn from the singular honour which, by God's gift, came to certain men who were zealous for hospitality, namely that they entertained angels. Unawares) This deed is magnified by the particular circumstance of their ignorance, that they received angels while thinking they were receiving men. For no one is so inhuman as to refuse to receive into his house angels whom he knows. He means Abraham, who entertained three angels appearing to him in the form of men. Gen. 18.2 and following. In these examples a general doctrine is contained: that those who have devoted themselves to hospitality will not go unrewarded.

units.la: Memores essote) Alterum charitatis officium quod præcipit est συμπαθεια & recordatio vinctorum & afflictorum propter Christum eiusque Euangelium. Modus huius recordationis adiungitur, quòd perinde oporteat nos vinctorum {ctorum} & quomodocunque afflictorum meminisse, ac si vna cum illis effemus vincti & afflicti.Nihil enim est,quod nos ferio misericordiæ sensu magis afficiat,quàm si eorum qui affliguntur personam in nos transferamus. Vt qui ipsi) Ratio præceptionis à communione cum vinctis, & afflictis pro Christo: Estis in eodem cum ipsis corpore,membra nimirum eiusdem corporis cuius Christus est caput: Debet autem inter membra eiusdem corporis esse συμπαθεια, vt si patitur vnum membrum simul doleant omnia membra.1.Corinth.12.26. Itaque græca verba ὡς ἡμεῖς ὄντες ἐν σώματι sic ad verbum transferenda censuerim(vt qui ipsi etiam sitis in corpore.)
units.tr: Remember) The second duty of love which he enjoins is sympathy [συμπάθεια] and the remembrance of prisoners and the afflicted, for the sake of Christ and his gospel. The manner of this remembrance is added: that we ought to remember prisoners and those afflicted in any way just as if we were bound and afflicted together with them. For there is nothing that moves us more with the feeling of mercy than if we transfer into ourselves the person of those who suffer. As being yourselves) The reason for the precept is drawn from communion with those who are bound and afflicted for Christ: you are in the same body, namely members of the same body of which Christ is the head. Now among the members of one body there ought to be sympathy, so that if one member suffers, all the members suffer together. 1 Cor. 12.26. Therefore I have judged that the Greek words ὡς ἡμεῖς ὄντες ἐν σώματι [ὡς ἡμεῖς ὄντες ἐν σώματι] should be rendered word for word thus: "as being yourselves also in the body."

units.la: 4. Honorabile est) Quarta præceptio specia- lis qua coniugium commendat, fornicationem prohibet.
units.tr: 4. Marriage is honourable) This is the fourth special precept, by which he commends marriage and forbids fornication.

units.la: Commendatur coniugium ex duobus adiunctis,primum est τίμιον, hoc est, pretiosum, siue honorabile, non apud homines tantum sed etiam apud Deum, vt quod ab ipso institutum sit & celebratum in paradiso ante hominis lapsum, cùm adhuc esset homo in statu innocentiæ & integritatis. Inter quosuis) hoc est, inter cuiuscunque ordinis, & conditionis homines, vt in nullo hominum genere culpari debeat. Et cubile impollutum) Alterum adiunctum quo commendatur coniugium, quod cubile eius sit impollutum, hoc est, purum & omnis culpæ ac pollutionis expers, vtpote quod à Deo sanctificatum sit, vt quibusuis hominibus eo bona conscientia vti liceat. Scortatores autem) Ratio dehortationis à contraria scortatione & adulterio, est à iudicio Dei. Deus scortatores & adulteros iudicabit, hoc est, damnabit. Iudicium siue damnationem intellige aeternam. Eodem sensu pallim docet Paulus scortatores regni Dei haereditatem nunquam possessuros. 1.Cor.6.9. 10. Gal.5.21.Ephes.5.5.
units.tr: Marriage is commended on the basis of two attributes. The first is τίμιον [τίμιον], that is, precious or honourable, not only among men but also before God, since it was instituted and solemnized by him in paradise before the fall of man, when man was still in a state of innocence and integrity. Among all) that is, among men of every rank and condition, so that it may be blamed in no class of men. And the bed undefiled) The second attribute by which marriage is commended is that its bed is undefiled, that is, pure and free from all guilt and pollution, inasmuch as it has been sanctified by God, so that it is lawful for any men to use it with a good conscience. But fornicators) The reason for dissuading from the opposite, fornication and adultery, is taken from the judgment of God. God will judge, that is, condemn, fornicators and adulterers. By judgment or condemnation understand eternal condemnation. In the same sense Paul often teaches that fornicators will never possess the inheritance of the kingdom of God. 1 Cor. 6.9, 10; Gal. 5.21; Eph. 5.5.

units.la: 5 Sint mores alieni) Quinta praeceptio specialis, quaprohibet auaritiam, contra autem praecipit vt contenti sint praesentibus. Vide 1.Timoth.6. 6. & deinceps. Vbi φιλαργυρία vocat malorum omnium radicem, animum autem iua forte contetum coniungit cum pietate, tanquam eius effectum necessarium. Animi autem praesentibus contenti illustre exemplum in iua persona exhibuit nobis Paulus. Philipp. 4. 11. 12. 13. Dixit enim ipse) Ratio praeceptionis à promissione Dei, quae hic à persona promittentis amplificatur, ipse inquit, hoc est, Dominus, dixit: & proferuntur in medium Dei verba, quibus Iosuam ad vocationem suam alacriter obeundam confirmat. Iosu. cap. 1. verf. 5. haec enim promissio Iosuae tanquam duci populi sui fata, ad totum populum communiter spectabat, & ad omnes pios vocationi suae incumbentes extenditur. Promittit autem Deus his verbis perpetuam præsentiam suam, quæ sola nos præsenti conditione quacunque, & debet, & potest, contentos efficere. Auari animus ne toto quidem mundo contentus est, sed quò plura habet plura appetit. Est enim cupiditas animi humani infinita, eòque nunquam plenè satiari potest, nisi impleatur præsentia Dei, qui solus est infinitus. Argumentum igitur est: Deus iuxta promissionem à se fa &tam perpetuò tibi præsens est. Ergo contentus esto præsentibus, & alienus fis ab auaritia. Auarus Deum non habet præsentem, sed pro Deo habet diuitias, unde Idololatra vocatur. Ephes.cap.5. verf. 5. & auaritia Idololatria. Coloff.3.5.
units.tr: 5 Let your manners be free) This is the fifth special precept, which forbids covetousness, and on the contrary enjoins that they be content with what they have. See 1 Tim. 6.6 and following, where he calls φιλαργυρία [φιλαργυρία] the root of all evils, and joins a contented mind with godliness as its necessary effect. Paul has shown us an illustrious example of a mind content with present things in his own person. Phil. 4.11, 12, 13. For he himself has said) The reason for the precept is drawn from God's promise, which here is magnified by the person of the one promising: he himself, he says, that is, the Lord, has said; and the words of God are brought forward, by which he strengthens Joshua to undertake his calling cheerfully. Josh. 1.5. For this promise to Joshua as leader of his people concerned the whole people in common, and it extends to all the godly who apply themselves to their calling. Now God promises by these words his perpetual presence, which alone ought to make us, and can make us, content in whatever present condition. The covetous mind is not content even with the whole world, but the more it has, the more it desires. For the desire of the human mind is infinite, and so it can never be fully satisfied unless the presence of God, who alone is infinite, fills it. The argument, therefore, is this: according to the promise made by him, God is perpetually present to you. Therefore be content with present things and be free from covetousness. The covetous man does not have God present, but has riches in place of God, whence he is called an idolater. Eph. 5.5; and covetousness is idolatry, Col. 3.5.

units.la: 7 Adeo ut confidetis) Amplificat hac Dei promissionem ab effecto, fide nostra promissione amplectente, & in ea confidenter gloriante. Gloriationis formulam singulis fidelibus præscribit, ex Psal. 118. 6. vbi Propheta fiducia præsentiæ & auxilij Dei se confirmat aduersus quoscunque hominum conatus. Vnde inferri potest generatim, non esse timendum nobis à rebus aduersarijs quibuscunque, multò minus à penuria & egestate.
units.tr: 7 So that we may say with confidence) He magnifies this promise of God by its effect: our faith, embracing the promise, and boldly glorying in it. He prescribes to every believer the formula of this boasting from Ps. 118.6, where the prophet confirms himself by confidence in the presence and help of God against all the attempts of men. Whence it may be inferred in general that we ought not to fear any adverse things whatsoever, much less want and poverty.

units.la: 8 Memores efote) Sexta præceptio specialis, qua commendat ijs memoriam ductorum suorum, & nominatim exprimit, quos ductores intelligat, eos nimirum qui locuti sunt ipsis fer monem Dei. Memoriam hanc definit in quo fit posita,in imitatione videlicet fidei & couersationis ipsorum: Neq; enim nudam hic fidem intelligit, sed (vt ex ratione subiecta perspicuum est) fidem agentem per charitatem, vt loquitur Paulus Galat. 5. 6. & in bona ac sanƈta conuersatione sese exerentem. Considerantes) Argumentum hortationis est à conuersationis duƈtorum fœlici exitu, ad cuius considerationem ipsos excitat, vtpote cuius & ipsi quoque futuri sint participes, si eorum fidem imitetur. Nam similes in fide & conuersatione, necesse est etiam similem exitum obtinere. Iesus Christus) Probat eundem fore eorum exitum, qui fuit duƈtorum, si eorum fidem imitentur, ab immutabili natura Iesu Christi, qui semper idem est, & sibi similis, eoque quemadmodum duƈtorum fidem & conuersationem fœlici exitu compensauit, ita etiam similem ipsorum fidem & conuersationem simili exitu compensaturus est. Hac autem Christi descriptione, non tantum innuitur ipsius immutabilitas, sed & distinƈtione trium temporum præteriti, præsentis & futuri (vt Apoc. 1.8.) æternitas denotatur, quæ duæ sunt proprietates diuinæ naturæ.
units.tr: 8 Remember) This is the sixth special precept, by which he commends to them the remembrance of their leaders, and names expressly who the leaders are whom he means: namely, those who spoke to them the word of God. He defines in what this remembrance consists: in the imitation, of course, of their faith and way of life. For here he does not mean bare faith, but (as is plain from the reason added) faith working through love, as Paul says, Gal. 5.6, and showing itself in a good and holy way of life. Considering) The argument of the exhortation is drawn from the happy outcome of the leaders' way of life, to the consideration of which he rouses them, inasmuch as they too will be partakers of it if they imitate their faith. For those who are alike in faith and way of life must necessarily obtain a similar outcome. Jesus Christ) He proves that their outcome will be the same as that of the leaders if they imitate their faith, from the unchangeable nature of Jesus Christ, who is always the same and like himself; and just as he rewarded the faith and way of life of the leaders with a happy outcome, so he will reward their faith and way of life in like manner with a similar outcome. By this description of Christ, not only his immutability is indicated, but also, by the distinction of the three times, past, present and future (as in Rev. 1.8), his eternity is denoted, which are two properties of the divine nature.

units.la: 9. Doƈtrinis Varijs) Septima præceptio specialis, qua dehortatur à doƈtrinis varijs & peregrinis. Dehortatio expressa est allegoria à nauibus petita, quæ in mari circumferuntur vi ventorum: Doƈtrinis varijs, inquit, ne circumferamini, Qui enim non satis firmi sunt in fide, doctrinis hominum tanquam ventis contrariis huc illuc agitantur. Doctrinas varias & peregrinas vocat quascunque doctrinas, quae vel a Deo nunquam sunt traditae verbo suo, ut sunt hominum traditiones, vel quae erant quidem veteri populo mandatae, sed abrogatae sunt in Christi aduentu, cuiusmodi fuit doctrina caeremoniarum legis quae per Christum abolitae sint. Hae doctrinae variae dicuntur & peregrinae, quod a doctrina Christi variant & a Deo profuis non agnoscantur. Bonum enim est{*}Ratio praeceptionis ab inutilitate, quod hae doctrinae non conducant ad confirmandum cor, & solidam ei consolationem ministrandum, sed oporteat cor confirmari doctrina Euangelij, quam gratiam hic appellat, quia tota est de gratia Dei in Christo Iesu, de reconciliatione nostra cum Deo, & redemptione gratia per ipsius sanguinem nobis parta. Haec solum doctrina vim habet stabiliendi corda, quae alioqui necesse est fluctuare, & quasi vacillare. Gratiae autem opponit cibos, hoc est, doctrinam de ciborum mundorum & immundorum discrimine legali obseruando, hac una specie συντελ omne cultu caeremoniale intelligens. Quibus non sunt) Probat huius doctrinae inutilitatem ab experientia, quod qui in cibis illis versati sunt, hoc est, ciborum discrimen superstitiose retinuerunt, & caeremonijs legalibus pertinaciter adhæserunt, ea re non sunt adjuti.
units.tr: 9. Doctrinis varijs (Heb. 13:9): This is the seventh special precept, by which he dissuades us from various and foreign teachings. The dissuasion is expressed by an allegory taken from ships that are carried about on the sea by the force of the winds: "Do not be carried about," he says, "by various teachings. For those who are not firm enough in faith are tossed here and there by the doctrines of men, as by contrary winds." He calls various and foreign teachings all those doctrines that either were never handed down by God in his Word, such as human traditions, or that were indeed commanded to the old people but have been abrogated at the coming of Christ, of which kind was the doctrine of the ceremonies of the law, which have been abolished through Christ. These teachings are called various and foreign because they differ from the teaching of Christ and are not recognised as coming from God. For it is good (Heb. 13:9): the reason for the precept is drawn from its uselessness, namely that these teachings do not serve to strengthen the heart and to give it solid comfort, but the heart must be strengthened by the doctrine of the Gospel, which he here calls grace, because it is wholly about the grace of God in Christ Jesus, about our reconciliation with God, and about the redemption won for us through his blood. This doctrine alone has the power to stabilise hearts, which otherwise must waver and as it were totter. He sets against grace "foods," that is, the doctrine of observing the legal distinction between clean and unclean foods, understanding by this one kind all ceremonial worship [συντελ]. Which have not profited: he proves the uselessness of this doctrine from experience, because those who have been occupied with those foods, that is, who have superstitiously kept the distinction of foods, and who have stubbornly clung to the legal ceremonies, have not been helped by them.

units.la: 10 Habemus altare) Alterum argumentum dehortationis à doctrina ciborum, omninoque ceremoniarum legis, sumptum à pugna inter Christum & ceremonias legis. Qui tabernaculo deseruiunt, hoc est, obstinatè retinent ceremonias legis, non possunt participes esse Christi. Nam Christus cum ceremonijs consistere non potest. Gal. 5. 2. quia ceremoniæ figurabant Christum venturum, & nondum venisse clamitabant. Ergo non sunt retinendæ ceremoniæ legis. Altaris nomen per metonymiam subiecti positum est pro victima in altari oblata: intelligit autem Christum, qui est Pascha nostrum pro nobis sacrificatum. 1. Corinth. 5. 7. Hunc habent omnes quorum corda gratia sunt constabilita. Edere ex hoc altari, est eius esse participem per fidem, forma loquendi ex lege desumpta: Qui enim sacris operabantur & alfidebant altari (ut loquitur Paulus. 1. Cor. cap. 9. verf. 13.) edebant ex sacrificijs quæ osserebantur.
units.tr: 10 We have an altar: the second argument for dissuading us from the doctrine of foods, and indeed from the whole of the ceremonies of the law, taken from the conflict between Christ and the ceremonies of the law. Those who serve the tabernacle, that is, who obstinately retain the ceremonies of the law, cannot be partakers of Christ. For Christ cannot coexist with the ceremonies (Gal. 5:2), since the ceremonies foreshadowed Christ as coming and kept crying out that he had not yet come. Therefore the ceremonies of the law are not to be retained. The name "altar" is put by metonymy of the subject for the victim offered on the altar, and he means Christ, who as our Passover was sacrificed for us (1 Cor. 5:7). All whose hearts are established by grace have this altar. To eat from this altar is to be a partaker of it through faith, a manner of speaking taken from the law: for those who worked in the sacred things and waited at the altar (as Paul says, 1 Cor. 9:13) ate from the sacrifices that were offered.

units.la: 11 Quorum enim) Antecedentis ratio sumpta à consuetudine ex legis præscripto ferunta, in offerendis sacrificijs expiatorijs, quæ typi erant unici illius expiatorij sacrificij Christi: in hanc formam: Si Leuitæ & Sacerdotes qui tabernaculo deseruiebant, non habebant jus edendi ex illis animalibus, quorum sanguis inferebatur pro peccato in sacrarium per Pontificē (quia eorū corpora tota comburebantur extra castra) profecto nēq; ex Christo jus edendi habent qui tabernaculo deseruiunt. At primum, Ergo secundum. Propositio non est quidem expressè posita, sed pendet ex analogia, quæ est inter typum & rem typo significatā.Quemadmodum enim eorum animalium quæ offerebantur pro peccato, sanguis infereb̄tur in sacrarium per Pontificem: Ita Christi sanguis illatus est in sacrarium illud cœlestē per ipsummet Christum tanquam Pontificem. Deinde quemadmodum eorum animalium corpora comburebantur extra castra: Ita Christus passus est extra portam, vt sequenti versu ostenditur.
