Unde sequitur, Quemadmodum qui tabernaculo deseruiebant, non habebant jus edendi ex illis animalibus, ita neque qui retinent ceremonias legis jus habent edendi ex Christo. Assumptio est hoc versu repetita ex lege Moysis, de sacrificijs pro errore summi sacerdotis & Ecclesiæ. Leuit. 4. 11. 12. & anniuersarijs diei expiationum. Leuit. 16. 27. Generalem legem vide Leuit 6. 23.
units.tr: 11 For the bodies: this is the reason for the preceding verse, taken from the custom that the law prescribed in offering the sin-offerings, which were types of that one expiatory sacrifice of Christ, and it runs thus: If the Levites and priests who served the tabernacle had no right to eat of those animals whose blood was brought into the sanctuary by the high priest for sin (because their bodies were wholly burned outside the camp), then surely those who serve the tabernacle have no right to eat of Christ. But the first is true; therefore the second. The proposition is not expressly stated, but it depends on the analogy between the type and the thing signified by the type. For just as the blood of those animals that were offered for sin was brought into the sanctuary by the high priest, so the blood of Christ was brought into that heavenly sanctuary by Christ himself as high priest. Then, just as the bodies of those animals were burned outside the camp, so Christ suffered outside the gate, as is shown in the following verse. Hence it follows: just as those who served the tabernacle had no right to eat of those animals, so neither do those who retain the ceremonies of the law have a right to eat of Christ. The minor premise is repeated in this verse from the law of Moses, concerning the sacrifices for the error of the high priest and of the Church (Lev. 4:11, 12), and for the annual day of atonement (Lev. 16:27). For the general law see Lev. 6:23.

units.la: 12 Quapropter &c. Accommodatio rei significatæ ad typum, quo res in Christo implendæ præfigurabantur, de qua jam proximè diximus. Christus (vt quod in illorum animalium, quæ offerebantur pro peccato, exuitione extra castra præfiguratum est impleretur) passus est extra portam urbis Hierusalem. Vt sanctifi-caret) Passionem hanc Christi illustrat suo fine. Finis est sanctificatio populi, hoc est, electorum omnium per proprium ipsius sanguinem: Sanctificationis nomine hic intelligo non regenerationem, quæ proprie & immediate fit per Spiritum Christi, sed gratuitam peccatorum remissionem & imputationem justitiæ ipsius, quæ proprie est per ipsius sanguinem quo aspersi inculpati & immaculati sistimur Deo Patri.
units.tr: 12 Therefore, etc.: the application of the thing signified to the type, by which the things to be fulfilled in Christ were foreshadowed, which I have just spoken of. Christ (so that what was foreshadowed in the burning of those animals that were offered for sin outside the camp might be fulfilled) suffered outside the gate of the city of Jerusalem. That he might sanctify: he illustrates this suffering of Christ by its purpose. The purpose is the sanctification of the people, that is, of all the elect, through his own blood. By sanctification here I understand not regeneration, which is properly and immediately effected by the Spirit of Christ, but the gratuitous remission of sins and the imputation of his righteousness, which properly takes place through his blood, by which we, sprinkled and made blameless and spotless, stand before God the Father.

units.la: 13 Exeamus igitur) Octava præceptio speciali, ex proximis verbis; quibus dictum est, Iesum ut sanctificaret populum extra portam passum esse, deducta: Hinc enim sequitur nobis etiam extra castra ad Deum exeundum esse, si sanctificationis per ipsius sanguinem volumus esse participes. Sensus est. Renunciandum nobis esse huic mundo, ut quasi exeamus extra eum, ut Christum sequamur, ferentes ipsius opprobrium. Neque enim Christi sequi possumus, & ipsius crucem ferre, quamdiu corda nostra mundo huic & mundanis affectibus addicta sunt, eoque tum demum eximus ad Christum cum corda nostra & omnes affectus erigimus ad Deum, & a mundo sejungimus, atque interea etiam dum in hoc mundo versamur gerimus nos ut municipes coelorum. Philipp. 3. 20. quod qui faciunt Christum sequuntur, & crucem ipsius ferunt patientissime, imo nè, imò gloriantur in afflictionibus. Rom.5.3.
units.tr: 13 Let us go out therefore: the eighth special precept, drawn from the preceding words, in which it was said that Jesus suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people. For from this it follows that we too must go out to God outside the camp, if we wish to be partakers of the sanctification through his blood. The sense is this: we must renounce this world, so that we go out, as it were, beyond it, in order to follow Christ, bearing his reproach. For we cannot follow Christ and bear his cross as long as our hearts are given over to this world and to worldly affections; we go out to Christ only when we lift up our hearts and all our affections to God and separate ourselves from the world, and meanwhile, even while we dwell in this world, we conduct ourselves as citizens of heaven (Phil. 3:20). Those who do this follow Christ and bear his cross most patiently, nay more, they glory in afflictions (Rom. 5:3).

units.la: 14. Non enim habemus) Ratio præceptionis: Non habemus in hoc mundo ciuitatem stabilem & permanentem, sed eam inquirimus suturam extra hunc mundum in cœlis vbi est Christus. Ergo exeundum nobis est ad eum extra castra: eò enim nobis est eundum vbi est ciuitas nobis stabilis & firma. Ciuitatem futuram vocat fixam illam, stabilem, & æternam, quam vocauit vrbem habentem fundamenta: supra 11. 10. & cœlestem patriam. Ibidem vers.16.
units.tr: 14. For we have no: the reason for the precept. We have in this world no stable and permanent city, but we seek the one that is to come outside this world, in the heavens where Christ is. Therefore we must go out to him outside the camp; for we must go to where the city that is stable and firm for us is. He calls the coming city that fixed, stable and eternal city, which he called the city having foundations (Heb. 11:10), and the heavenly country (Heb. 11:16).

units.la: 15. Per ipsum igitur) Nona præceptio specialis ad sacrificium laudis Deo offerendum, ex præcedentibus deducta. Cùm enim (vt dictum est) passus fit Christus, vt sanctificaret populum, per ipsum assiduè offerendum est Deo sacrificium laudis. Per Christum autem docet offerendum esse hoc sacrificium, quia nullum sacrificium potest Deo gratum & acceptum esse, nisi Christo mediante, & intercedente ipsius sacrificio, in quo, & nosipsi & sacrificia nostra omnia Deo placent. Id est fructum) Interpretatur hoc laudis sacrificium, quod (ab externo organo quo vtitur cor in eo proferendo & exprimendo) vocat fructum labiorum consitentium nomini ejus. Videtur autem respicere ad locum illum Oseæ.14.3. vbi laudes Deo exhibitæ vocantur vituli labiorum.
units.tr: 15. Through him therefore: the ninth special precept, to be offered to God as a sacrifice of praise, deduced from what precedes. For since Christ suffered, as has been said, in order to sanctify the people, through him a sacrifice of praise must be continually offered to God. He teaches that this sacrifice must be offered through Christ, because no sacrifice can be pleasing and acceptable to God except through the mediation of Christ and by the intercession of his sacrifice, in which both we ourselves and all our sacrifices are pleasing to God. That is, the fruit: he explains this sacrifice of praise, which (from the external organ by which the heart is used in uttering and expressing it) he calls the fruit of lips confessing his name. He seems, however, to be looking back to that passage of Hosea (14:2, 3), where the praises offered to God are called the calves of the lips.

units.la: 16. Beneficentia) Decima præceptio specialis, qua aliud sacrificij genus commendat facrificium nimirum beneficentiæ & communicationis facultatum, quas ad fi atrum egentium necessitatem leuandam oportet imperiri : Nam hoc sacrificium ipedat immediate ad proximum, vt prius illud immediate ad Deum spectabat. Talibus enim) Ratio utriusque præceptionis præcedentis, ab oblectatione Dei, qui nunc non typicis illis sacrificijs in lege præscriptis, sed is demum veris sacrificijs, tanquam vnicè sibi gratis, delectatur. Vocem εὐαρεστεῖται male reddidit vetus interpres (promereatur) vt locum aliquem meritis nostris inueniret: neque enim his victimis quicquam possumus apud Deum promereri, aut ipsi nobis acquirere, sed εὐαρεστεῖσθαι dicitur Deus, quatenus hæc officia Deo placent, eique grata sunt & accepta. Hanc genuinam esse hujus vocis signi-ficationem facile animaduerteret qui hunc locum contulerit cum Heb.11.5.6.
units.tr: 16. Beneficence: the tenth special precept, by which he commends another kind of sacrifice, namely the sacrifice of beneficence and of the sharing of goods, which must be employed to relieve the need of the poor. For this sacrifice bears immediately upon the neighbour, as the former bore immediately upon God. For with such sacrifices: the reason for both the preceding precepts, from the delight of God, who now takes delight not in those typical sacrifices prescribed in the law, but finally in true sacrifices, as in those alone that are acceptable to him. The old translator rendered the word εὐαρεστεῖται badly as "is merited," so as to find some place for our merits; for we can merit nothing with God by these victims, nor acquire anything for ourselves, but God is said to be well pleased [εὐαρεστεῖσθαι] inasmuch as these duties please God and are pleasing and acceptable to him. Anyone who compares this passage with Heb. 11:5, 6 will easily notice that this is the genuine meaning of this word.

units.la: 17 Obedite ducibus) Vndecima præceptio specialis, vt ducibus, hoc est, præfloribus, ductoribus, gubernatoribus, obedientiam & submissionem præstemus. Vigilant enim) Præceptionis hujus duas affert rationes, prima est à ducum officio, in quo laborant & præsunt gregi: Vigilant pro grege, & non pro ipsorum corporibus, sed pro animabus, vt salutem consequantur: atque eò magis obligamur ad obedientiam ipsis praestandam. Tanquam rationem) Amplificatio hujus vigilantiæ pro animabus, ab obligatione qua obstringuntur Deo, vtpote obiti hujus officij rationem ei reddituri. Vt cum gaudio) Ratio secunda est à fine obedientiæ ducibus præstitæ: vt hoc quod ipsis incumbit muneris obeant cum gaudio, non cum gemitu, quem necesse est sequi ex gregis inobedientia. Id enim est) Probat non eiie pastori vigilandum pro animabus cum gemitu, quòd hac ratione nihil vtilitatis ex ipsius laboribus redundet ad gregem, qui cûm debuerit esse pastori materia gaudij, vt Pauli exemplo intelligi potest. 1. Thessal. 2. 19. 20. inobedientia sua gemendi occasionem ei præbet.
units.tr: 17 Obey your leaders) The eleventh special precept: that we render obedience and submission to our leaders, that is, to those who go before, guide and govern. For they watch) He gives two reasons for this precept. The first is drawn from the office of leaders, in which they labour and preside over the flock. They watch on behalf of the flock, and not for their own bodies, but for souls, that the flock may attain salvation. For this reason we are all the more bound to render them obedience. As those who must give account) This amplifies the watchfulness on behalf of souls by the obligation with which they are bound to God, since they must render account to him for the discharge of this office. That they may do it with joy) The second reason is drawn from the end of the obedience rendered to leaders: that they may discharge the duty laid upon them with joy, not with groaning, which must follow from the disobedience of the flock. For this is) He proves that a minister should not have to watch over souls with groaning, because in that case nothing of profit from his labours flows back to the flock. Whereas the flock ought to be a matter of joy to the minister, as may be understood from the example of Paul (1 Thess. 2.19, 20), their disobedience gives him occasion for groaning.

units.la: 18 Orate pro nobis: confidimus enim nos bonam conscientiam habere, vt qui in omnibus cupiamus honestè conuersari.
units.tr: 18 Pray for us: for we trust that we have a good conscience, desiring in all things to live honestly.

units.la: 19 Amplius autem ut id faciatis, vt celerius restituar vobis.
units.tr: 19 But I beseech you the more earnestly to do this, that I may be restored to you the sooner.

units.la: Orate pro nobis) Secunda pars capitis, qua commendat Hebræis preces pro se. Confidimus) Causas precum quas vult pro se concipi duas affert, prima est à testimonio bonæ conscientiæ, cujus certum & indubitatum argumentum affert, à studio honestæ conuersationis in tota vita, & rebus omnibus, quod semper sibi adfuisse profitetur.
units.tr: Pray for us) The second part of the chapter, in which he commends to the Hebrews prayers for himself. We trust) He gives two grounds for the prayers he wishes to be offered on his behalf. The first is the testimony of a good conscience, whose certain and indubitable evidence he adduces: his zeal for honest conduct throughout his whole life and in all things, which he professes has always been with him.

units.la: 19 Amplius autem) Secunda causa est, Apostoli liberatio cum ipsorum commodo conjunƈta, vt celeriùs ipsis restituatur ad communem nimirum consolationem percipiendam per mutuam fidem, vt loquitur Paulus. Rom. i. 22. Atque hoc nomine eò magis serio has pro se preces flagitat.
units.tr: 19 But I beseech) The second ground is the apostle's deliverance, joined with their own advantage, that he may be restored to them sooner, namely to receive common consolation through mutual faith, as Paul says (Rom. 1.12). On this account he urges these prayers for himself all the more earnestly.

units.la: 20 Deus Ϝero pacis author, qui magnum illum ouium per sanguinem suum fœderis æterni pastorem, Dominum nostrum Iesum, à mortuis reduxit:
units.tr: 20 Now the God of peace, who brought again from the dead that great shepherd of the sheep, our Lord Jesus, through the blood of the everlasting covenant,

units.la: 21 Perficiat vos in omni opere bono, ad præstandam ipsius voluntatem, efficiens in vobis quod acceptum sit in conspectu suo per Iesum Christum: cui sit gloria in sæcula sæculorum. Amen.
units.tr: 21 make you perfect in every good work to do his will, working in you that which is well pleasing in his sight through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

units.la: 22 Precor autem vos, fratres, sufferte sermonem exhortationis: etenim breuibus scripsi vobis.
units.tr: 22 I beseech you, brethren, bear with the word of exhortation; for I have written to you in few words.

units.la: 23 Scitote fratrem nostrum Timotheum solutum esse, cum quo (si celerius venerit) visam vos.
units.tr: 23 Know that our brother Timothy has been set free, with whom, if he comes shortly, I will see you.

units.la: 24 Salutate omnes duƈtores vestros, & omnes sanƈtos. Salutant vos Itali.
units.tr: 24 Greet all your leaders, and all the saints. Those from Italy greet you.

units.la: 25 Gratia sit cum omnibus vobis. Amen.
units.tr: 25 Grace be with you all. Amen.

units.la: Deus Ϝero pacis) Precatione primùm, deinde hortatione, postremò aliis aliquot sermonibus varij ac multiplicis argumenti, Epistolam concludit. Precatur Deum vt Hebræos perficiat in omni opere bono. Deum autem quem precatur describit ex duobus effeƈtis. Primum effeƈtum est pax. Pacem intellige illam Dei quæ superat omnem intelleƈtum, quæque præsidio est cordibus ac mentibus nostris per Iesum Christum. Philip.4.7. Alterum est excitatio Christi é mortuis,quæ ipsius potentiam adid efficiendum quod precatur luculentiffimè demonstrat.Nâ in hoc effecto Deus admirabilem,suam potentiam maxime exeruit: Vnde Ephef.1.20.dicitur efficacitatem fortis roboris Dei exertam esse in Christo,cùm excitauit eũ ex mortuis. Magnum illum) Iesum à mortuis reductum vocat, tum magnum illum ouium Pastorem, tum Dominum noftrum. Pastor ouium vocatur,quia eues suas pascit; salutari pabulo verbi, eodémq; verbo veluti sceptro,& Spiritu suo,eas regit ad vitam æternam. Magnus ouium Pastor dicitur ad discrimen aliorum Pastorum omniũ quos ipse constituit ministros, vt ei inseruiant in pascendis ouibus,quæ solius sunt Christi.Eodem sensu princeps Pastorum vocatur. 1. Pet. 5. 4. Per sanguinem) Ostendit quo iure Christus fit magnus ille ouium Pastor, quia nimirum sanguine suo eas acquisiuit.Act.20. 28. & animam suam posuit pro ouibus.Ioan. 10.11.Sanguinem hunc vocat fœderis æterni, quia hoc sanguine fancitum est & obfignatum æternum illud fœdus gratiæ, quod absque sanguine Mediatoris cum homine peccatore & fœdifrago percuti nunquâ potuisset. Nam absque sanguinis effusione non fit remissio Heb.9.22.
units.tr: The God of peace) He concludes the epistle first with a prayer, then with exhortation, and finally with several other discourses on various and manifold subjects. He prays that God would make the Hebrews perfect in every good work. He describes the God whom he prays to by two effects. The first effect is peace: understand that peace of God which surpasses all understanding, and which guards our hearts and minds through Jesus Christ (Phil. 4.7). The second is the raising of Christ from the dead, which most clearly shows his power to bring about what he prays for. For in this effect God most especially displayed his admirable power. Hence Ephesians 1.20 says that the working of the strength of his might was exerted in Christ when he raised him from the dead. That great one) He calls Jesus, brought back from the dead, both that great Shepherd of the sheep and our Lord. He is called Shepherd of the sheep because he feeds his sheep with the saving food of the word, and by that same word, as with a sceptre, and by his Spirit, leads them to eternal life. He is called the great Shepherd of the sheep in distinction from all the other shepherds whom he appoints as ministers, to serve him in feeding the sheep, which belong to Christ alone. In the same sense he is called the chief Shepherd (1 Pet. 5.4). Through the blood) He shows by what right Christ is that great Shepherd of the sheep: namely, because he won them by his own blood (Acts 20.28), and laid down his life for the sheep (John 10.11). He calls this blood of the everlasting covenant because by this blood that eternal covenant of grace was confirmed and sealed, which could never have been struck with sinful and covenant-breaking man without the blood of the Mediator. For without the shedding of blood there is no remission (Heb. 9.22).

units.la: 21 Perficiat)Petitio ipsa,qua postulat Hebręis à Deo perfectione, non quidé in vna re aliqua, sed in omni opere bono. Opus autem bonum definit ex præstatione voluntatis Dei patefactæ nobis in ipsius lege, quæ non solum opus ipsum quoad substantiam, sed & operandi modum, & operis finem præcipit, vt nimirum fiat ex cordis sinceritate, & ad Deiglo riam referatur: his enim conditionibus opus bonum definitur. Efficiens) Declarat hanc quam ijs precatur perfectione, à modo quo fit: perficit nos Deus in omni opere bono, dū ipse illud efficit in nobis: Deus est, inquit Paulus, qui efficit in vobis, & vt velitis, & vt efficiatis, pro gratuita sua beneuolentia. Philip. 2.13. Bonum autem opus hic rursum definit, quod fit acceptum in conspectu ipsius. Per Iesum) Efficientiam hanc Patri tribuit per Iesum Christum tanquam Mediatorem: cuius beneficio omnis gratia abundé in nos confertur à Deo. Nisi malis hæc verba cum proximé præcedentibus coniungere, vt opus quod efficit Deus in nobis dicatur acceptum coram eo per Iesum Christum: Neque enim possunt opera nostra, etiam quæ Deus efficit in nobis, Deo esse grata, aut in eius cospectum prodire, nisi sacrificij Christi odore perfusa, quo tota ipsorum imperfectio, quam à nobis tanquā instrumentis in quibus operatur Deus attrahunt, integatur Cuius gloria) Preces suas ad Deum pro Hebræis con-
units.tr: 21 Perficiat) The petition itself, by which he asks God to perfect the Hebrews, is not for some one thing but for every good work. He defines a good work from the performance of God's will made known to us in his law, which prescribes not only the work itself as to its substance but also the manner of doing it and the end of the work: namely, that it be done from sincerity of heart and referred to the glory of God, for a good work is defined by these conditions. Efficiens) He explains by the manner of its coming about the perfection for which he prays: God perfects us in every good work while he himself effects it in us. "It is God," says Paul, "who works in you both to will and to do, for his good pleasure" (Philip. 2.13). Here again he defines a good work as one that is acceptable in God's sight. Per Iesum) He attributes this effecting to the Father through Jesus Christ as Mediator, by whose benefit all grace is poured out upon us abundantly from God. Unless you prefer to join these words with the immediately preceding ones, so that the work God effects in us is said to be acceptable before him through Jesus Christ: for our works, even those which God effects in us, cannot be pleasing to God or come into his sight unless they are steeped in the fragrance of Christ's sacrifice, by which all their imperfection, which they draw from us as the instruments through which God works, is covered over. Cuius gloria) He concludes his prayers for the Hebrews with the glorification of God the Father and Christ.

units.la: {*} Cuius gloria) marginal gloss. conclúdit glorificatione Dei Patris & Christi, vt enim illis optat perfectionem à Deo, ita Deo optat suam gloriam, & eam quidem æternam. Nam vt à gratia Dei omnia illi profluunt quæ pij precantur, ita in Dei gloriam debent redundare. Ex eo, & per eum, & in ipsum sut omnia, ipsi sit gloria in seculà. Rom. 11.36. Atque ex hac optationis formula dicimus concludendas esse preces nostras & petitiones omnes, cum glorificatione nominis Dei illius, à quo omnia petimus, vt vel hoc ipso significemus, nos non tam respicere bonum aliquod hominum, quàm Dei in Christo Iesu gloriam, cuius respectu preces pro hominibus fundimus, ijsque bona omnia à Deo exoptamus.
units.tr: {*} Cuius gloria) marginal gloss. He concludes with the glorifying of God the Father and of Christ. For just as he wishes them perfection from God, so he wishes God his glory, and that an eternal one. For as all that the godly pray for flows to them from the grace of God, so it ought to redound to the glory of God. "From him, and through him, and to him are all things; to him be glory for ever" (Rom. 11.36). From this form of wishing we say that all our prayers and petitions ought to be concluded with the glorification of the name of that God from whom we ask everything, so that by this very thing we signify that we look not so much to some good of men as to the glory of God in Christ Jesus, with respect to which we pour out prayers for men and desire for them every good from God.

units.la: Precor autem) Hebræos ad quos scribit, hortatur vt sermonem exhortationis sufferant, hoc est, æqui boniqueconsulant, eique obtemperent. Hanc Epistolam vocat sermonem exhortationis, quia tota fere occupata est in exhortatione ad retinendam doctrinam quam acceperunt. Etenim) Ratio hortationis à scripti breuitate.
units.tr: Precor autem) He urges the Hebrews, to whom he writes, to bear the word of exhortation, that is, to take it in good part and to obey it. He calls this Epistle a word of exhortation because almost the whole of it is occupied with exhortation to hold fast the doctrine they have received. Etenim) The reason for the exhortation is drawn from the brevity of the writing.

units.la: Scitote Timotheum)Narratio breuis, qua certiores eos facit de Timothei solutione è vinculis, cum quo se etiam ipsos inuisurum spondet, si celeriùs venerit. Hinc facile considerit, & Timotheum, paulò ante hanc Epistolam ad Hebræos missam, vinctum fuisse (de cuius tamen vinculis nihil alibi scriptum legimus, vt quando in vincula inciderit difficile admodum sit diuinare) & Epistolæ huius auctorem liberum fuisse ac suæ potestatis cum hæc scriberet.
units.tr: Know that Timothy) A brief narrative by which he informs them of Timothy's release from prison, with whom he promises to visit them too, if he comes sooner. From this one may readily conclude that Timothy, shortly before this epistle was sent to the Hebrews, had been imprisoned (though we read nothing written elsewhere about his imprisonment, and it is very difficult to guess when he fell into prison), and that the author of this epistle was free and in command of himself when he wrote it.

units.la: 24 Salutate omnes) Paucis complectitur salutationes, primùm (vt sic dicam) rogatas, quibus salutari petit, tum omnes ductores ipsorum & Pastores, tum generatim omnes sanctos: deinde (vt sic dicam) missas ab Italicis fratribus.
units.tr: 24 Salute all those who rule over you and all the saints. Here he sums up the greetings in a few words: first those requested (so to speak), by which he asks that they be greeted; then all their leaders and ministers, and all the saints in general; and then (so to speak) those sent from the brothers in Italy.

units.la: 25 Gratia sit) Hebraeis valedicens comprecatur ijs gratiam, quo nomine intelligo, primum gratuitum Dei fauorem, deinde spirituales in Christo benedictiones, quæ ex gratuito Dei fauore omnes emanant; cuiusmodi sunt remissio peccatorum, iustificatio, sanctificatio, vita denique æterna. Hanc gratiam exoptat omnibus, quia vt sua natura ad omnes pertinet (vt videre est Rom. 5. 15. & deinceps) ita à Pastore non est contrahenda ad certos duntaxat aliquot, sed omnibus & singulis quantum in ipso est, communicanda & exoptanda à Deo, cui in Christo sit omnis gloria. Amen.
units.tr: 25 Grace be with you all. In bidding farewell to the Hebrews he wishes them grace, which I understand in two senses: first, God's free favour, and then the spiritual blessings in Christ that all flow from God's free favour; of this kind are the remission of sins, justification, sanctification, and finally eternal life. He wishes this grace for all, because, as it belongs by its nature to everyone (as is evident from Rom. 5.15 and following), so it is not to be restricted by the minister to certain few, but is to be communicated to and desired from God for all and each, as far as lies in him, to whom in Christ be all glory. Amen.

units.la: TRA-
units.tr: TRACTATE

units.la: TRACTATVS DE IVSTIFICATIONE.
units.tr: A Treatise on Justification.

units.la: VStificationis nomé duobus modis accipitur, physicè (vt sicloquar) & politicè. Physicè acceptū Iustificationis nome significat inhærēte mutatione hominis è qualitate iustitię inhærēte in qualitate institiæ inhęrente. Hoc modo intelligi videtur Iustificationis nomen. Apoc.22. 11. Qui iustus est, iustificeetur adhuc: & iustus vocatur ab inhærente iustitia.1.Ioh.3.7. Qui exercet iustitiam iustus est. Sic accepta Iustificatio nihil aliud est quàm sanctificatio, quæ mutatio quęda est inter terminos contrarios inhærentes: sed de hac acceptione satis. Altera Iustificationis acceptio est qua significat pronúciatione iustitię de aliquo, eámq; à iudice e tribunali. Rom. 8.33. Quis accusabit electos Dei? Deus est qui iustificat. Hæc acceptio cōmunis est, & ijs qui habent iustitiam suam inhærente, & ijs qui inhærentem non habent & suam proprie, verùm alienam: Nam qui in se iustus est, pronunciari potest à Iudice iustus ex inhærente illa iustitia; Sic iustificantur beati Angeli à Deo, nimirùm ex iustitia sua & inhærente, sic iustificatus suisset homo si stetisset in originali illa iustitia. Similiter iustificari dicitur quis, hoc est, pronunciari iustus, à iustitia quæ in ipso non inhæret, sed quæ aliena est, sed tamen ipsius est aliquo pacto: Hoc modo debitor aliquis iustificatur ex iustitia ipsoris, qui ipsius nomine creditori debitu exoluit: sic iustificatur homo peccator ex iustitia & satisfactione Christi mediatoris.
units.tr: The name of justification is used in two ways, physically (so to speak) and politically. Taken physically, the name of justification signifies a change within a man, from inherent unrighteousness to inherent righteousness. Revelation 22:11 seems to use the word in this sense: "He who is righteous, let him be justified still," and a man is called righteous from the righteousness that is inherent in him. 1 John 3:7: "He who does righteousness is righteous." Taken in this sense, justification is nothing other than sanctification, which is a kind of change between inherent contraries. But enough on this sense. The other use of the name of justification signifies a pronouncement of righteousness concerning someone, made by the judge from the tribunal. Romans 8:33: "Who shall accuse God's elect? It is God who justifies." This sense is common both to those who have their righteousness inherent in them and to those who do not have an inherent righteousness of their own but an alien one. For one who is righteous in himself can be pronounced righteous by the judge on account of that inherent righteousness. Thus the blessed angels are justified by God, namely from their own inherent righteousness, and man would have been justified in this way had he stood in that original righteousness. Likewise someone is said to be justified, that is, pronounced righteous, from a righteousness that does not inhere in him but is alien, yet in some way his own. In this way a debtor is justified by the righteousness of his surety, who pays the debt to the creditor in his name. So a sinful man is justified by the righteousness and satisfaction of Christ the Mediator.

units.la: Vt verbum Iustificationis, ita quoque verbum Imputationis commune est. Nam & imputari ei Iustitia dicitur, qui est in se & inhaerenter iustus, & imputari ei iustitia dicitur, qui non habet suam & inhaerentem iustitiam, verum alienam: vt Christi. Quod autem Iustificationis verbum commune sit etiam iis qui suam & inhaerentem habent iustitiam factis conspicitur, vel ex hac phrasi Apostoli, qua dicit homine non iustificari ex operibus legis, sed per fidem Iesu Christi. Rom. 3. 28. Gal. 2. 16. Haec enim locutione, non obscure innuit iustificari, h. e. pronunciari hominem iustum posse ex operibus & iustitia quadam sua, si modo reipsa essent ea opera, non secus atque iustificari dicitur quis per fidem, h.e. per alienam & Christi iustitiam. Imputandi quoque verbum intelligitur commune esse ex verbis Apostoli. Rom. 4. 4. cum dicit, Ei qui operatur merces non imputatur ex gratia, sed ex debito. Quibus verbis significat iustitiam operum, h.e. inhaerentem dici posse imputari, si modo reipsa esset ea iustitia.
units.tr: As the word justification is common, so too is the word imputation. For a person is said to have righteousness imputed to him who is righteous in himself and inherently, and a person is said to have righteousness imputed to him who does not have his own and inherent righteousness but an alien one, as Christ's. That the word justification is also common to those who have their own and inherent righteousness is seen from the works of the apostle, in this phrase, where he says that a man is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ (Romans 3:28; Galatians 2:16). For by this expression he clearly implies that a man could be justified, that is, pronounced righteous, from works and some righteousness of his own, if those works were really there, just as someone is said to be justified through faith, that is, through an alien righteousness, the righteousness of Christ. The word imputation is also understood to be common from the words of the apostle, Romans 4:4, where he says: "To him who works, the reward is not reckoned as a gift but as a debt." By these words he signifies that the righteousness of works, that is, inherent righteousness, can be said to be imputed, if that righteousness were really there.

units.la: Iustificatio hominis qua pronunciatur quis iustus ex aliena, hoc est, Christi iustitia, vt de ea in specie dicamus, hoc ordine procedit, primum est vocatio efficax in qua Deus offert ChristiChristum cum iustitia sua, peccator autem oblatum fide apprehendit. In Vocatione enim efficaci applicatio duplex est, prima est Dei offerentis Christum cum iustitia sua, secunda est hominis peccatoris per fidem oblatū Christum apprehendentis sibique applicantis. Post vocationem efficacem sequitur Iustificatio, qua Deus iustitiam illam Christi fide iam apprehensam in efficaci vocatione peccatori imputat tanquam suam, vel pronunciat eum iustum in illa Christi iustitia, peccator autem imputatam sibi à Deo iustitiam fide recipit. In iustificatione duplex similiter est applicatio, prior est imputatio Dei, posterior est imputatæ à Deo iustitiæ alienæ per fidem peccatoris apprehensio & applicatio. Differunt hæ duæ applicationes quæ in iustificatione sunt à duabus illis quæ fuerunt in Vocatione efficaci. Nam in Vocatione applicatio Dei appellata est oblatio siue omnino vocatio: In Iustificatione vero applicatio Dei appellatur imputatio. Deinde in Vocatione applicatio hominis iustitiæ oblatæ per fidem apprehensio, siue fides in iustitiam oblata, in Iustificatione vero applicatio hominis vocatur fides in iustitiam imputatam. Ex his obseruā duplex esse fidei munus, vnum quidem in Vocatione efficaci, dum Christum vnà cum iustitia sua oblatum recipit: Alterum in Iustificatione, dum Christum cum sua iustitia imputatam recipit. Notandum autem est, quod cum dicitur hominem per fidem iustificari, intelligenda fit ea fides quæ antecedit in Vocatione efficaci, nempe quæ apprehendit Christum oblatum cum iustitia sua. Quod ad fidem quæ in Iustificatione apprehendit imputatam Christi iustitiam per eam magis proprie seruari dicimur. Ephes. 2. 8. Gratia Dei seruati estis per fidem: Salus enim æterna iustificationem sequitur. Atque hæc paucis de ordine quo ad iustificationem peccatorum proceditur à Deo.
units.tr: The justification of a man, by which someone is pronounced righteous from an alien righteousness, that is, the righteousness of Christ (to speak of it in particular), proceeds in this order. First there is effectual calling, in which God offers Christ with his righteousness, and the sinner, having been offered him, apprehends him by faith. For in effectual calling there is a twofold application: the first is God's offering Christ with his righteousness, the second is the sinner's apprehending by faith the Christ who has been offered and applying him to himself. After effectual calling follows justification, in which God imputes to the sinner, as his own, that righteousness of Christ which has already been apprehended by faith in effectual calling, or pronounces him righteous in that righteousness of Christ; and the sinner receives by faith the righteousness imputed to him by God. In justification there is likewise a twofold application: the first is God's imputation, the second is the sinner's apprehension and application by faith of the alien righteousness imputed by God. These two applications in justification differ from the two that were in effectual calling. For in calling, God's application is called an offer, or simply a calling; but in justification God's application is called imputation. Then, in calling, the man's application is the apprehension by faith of the righteousness offered, or faith directed toward the righteousness offered; but in justification the man's application is called faith in the imputed righteousness. From these things I observe that faith has a twofold office: one in effectual calling, when it receives Christ offered together with his righteousness; the other in justification, when it receives Christ with his imputed righteousness. It must be noted that when it is said that a man is justified through faith, that faith must be understood which comes before, in effectual calling, namely the faith which apprehends Christ offered with his righteousness. As for the faith which in justification apprehends the imputed righteousness of Christ, we are said to be kept more properly by it. Ephesians 2:8: "By the grace of God you have been saved through faith." For eternal salvation follows justification. And these few things will suffice on the order by which God proceeds to the justification of sinners.

units.la: Quæritur, annon cum in efficaci Vocatione apprehendatur per fidem Christi iustitia ab illa iustitia iustificatus iam quis dicitur? Respondeo minimè: Nam Iustificatio est sententiæ pronunciatio, in vocatione autem nulla est sententiæ pronunciatio, quare iustificatus dici nequit ex sola vocatione. Atqui cum per fidem ei insit Christi iustitia qui vocatus est, annon ex ea iustitia quæ ipsi inest per fidem denominari saltem iustus potest? Illud equidem non plane negarim reipsa quodammodo, h. e. per fidem iustum esse, iustû dici & appellari posse non dixerim, cum nondum lata & pronunciata de eo fit Iudicis sententia, sententia videlicet illa quæ ex nova quadam gratia existit, nam non nisi ex Dei gratia est quod iam in efficaci vocatione per fidem iustos, Deus iustos esse pronunciet, & imputet ijs alienam iustitiam tanquam suam.
units.tr: It is asked whether, since by faith in effectual calling the righteousness of Christ is apprehended, a man is not already called justified from that righteousness. I answer: by no means. For justification is the pronouncement of a sentence, but in calling there is no pronouncement of a sentence; therefore a man cannot be called justified from calling alone. But since, through faith, the righteousness of Christ is in the one who has been called, can he not at least be called righteous from that righteousness which dwells in him through faith? Indeed I would not altogether deny that he is in some way actually righteous through faith, and I would not say that he cannot be called and named righteous, although the judge's sentence has not yet been passed and pronounced concerning him, that sentence namely which arises from a new grace. For it is only by the grace of God that God pronounces those who are already righteous through faith in effectual calling to be righteous, and imputes to them an alien righteousness as their own.

units.la: Iustificationis causæ sunt quatuor, Efficiens, materialis, formalis, & finalis. Efficiens causa est Deus, Deus is est qui justificat. Rom.8.33. Modi efficiendi quibus dici potest Deus justificare varij sunt. Primùm dicitur Deus iustificare ex operibus,& inhærente iustitia: sic iustificat beatos Angelos, sic iustificasset hominem si in primæua & originali iustitia sterisset. Hùc iustificationis modum, qui est ex operibus legis sectabantur Iudæi. Rom. 9.31.32. Deinde dicitur Deus iustificare ex fide, vel per fidem: Fidei nomine intelligo Christum cum iustitia, siue satisfactione, siue obedientia, siue merito suo fide apprehensum. In hoc igitur modo duo sunt comprehensa. Primùm Christus siue meritu Christi, deinde fides nostra sine qua Christi meritum non applicatur ad nos ad hoc vt efficax fit ad nos justificandos. Nam de merito Christi vt nonnihil paulò altius repetamus, Causa quidem est omnium benedictionũ spiri tualiũ quas in nos cófert Deus, veru alio atq; alio modo: nam Christus cum merito suo est causa æternæ Prædestinationis nostri citra fide nostram, vel præsentem, vel futuram, vel præuisam. Elegit nos in ipso, subaudi Christo. Eph. 1.4. Rursus Christus cum merito suo causa est Vocationis efficacis quæ fit in tempore, verum citra fidem nostram, cum fides in ipsa demum detur, & altera vocationis pars fit. Tertio Christus cum merito suo causa est Iustificationis nostri, verum non fine fide qua in efficaci vocatione ipsum cum merito suo apprehendimus:Denique Christus cum merito suo causa est glorificationis nostri, sed cum fide imputatam illam Christi justitiam apprehendente in luftificatione. Ex his videmus justisicari hominem per Christi meritum tanquam per modum quo Deus eum justificat, verum non fine fide meritum illud oblatum in efficaci vocatione apprehedente. Vnde Apoft. ad Rom. & Gal. modum hunc, qui compositum quiddam est, vnico fidei vocabulo expressit, nonnunquam cum fide Iesum Christum conjungit. Rom. 3. 22. Iustitiam Dei vocat per fidem Iesu Christi. Sic Gal. 2. 16. justificari nos dicit per fide Iesu Christi, & Rom. 3. 25. vocat fidem in ipsius fanguine. Postremo inter modos quibus Deus justificat hominem censetur gratia Dei fiue misericordia. Gratia cum fide optime conuenit, verum inter gratiam & opera summa est diffenfio. Rom. 11. 6. Ephef. 2. 8. 9. Confentiunt igitur ista, Deus justificat ex fide, & Deus justificat ex gratia; Verum quaestio est de ordine, vtra fidesne an gratia prior fit, vtrum fides fit causa gratiae, an veo gratia fit causa fidei? Respondeo fidem praecedere, gratiam autem subsequi, & fidem, hoc est, Christum cum merito suo fide apprehensum in efficaci vocatione causam esse nouae illius gratiae, qua fit vt Deus hominem justificet. Vt de hoc nonnihil
units.tr: There are four causes of justification: efficient, material, formal, and final. The efficient cause is God; it is God who justifies (Romans 8:33). The modes by which God can be said to justify are various. First, God is said to justify from works and inherent righteousness; thus he justifies the blessed angels, and thus he would have justified man had he remained in his original and first righteousness. The Jews pursued this mode of justification, which is from the works of the law (Romans 9:31-32). Next, God is said to justify from faith, or through faith. By the name of faith I understand Christ, together with his righteousness, whether satisfaction, obedience, or merit, apprehended by faith. In this mode, then, two things are included. First, Christ, or the merit of Christ; and then our faith, without which the merit of Christ is not applied to us so that it becomes effective for justifying us. For, to go back a little further concerning the merit of Christ: it is indeed the cause of all the spiritual blessings that God bestows upon us, but in different ways. For Christ, with his merit, is the cause of our eternal predestination, without regard to our faith, whether present, future, or foreseen: "He chose us in him" (Ephesians 1:4), understood, in Christ. Again, Christ with his merit is the cause of effectual calling, which takes place in time, yet without regard to our faith, since faith is given in calling itself and becomes the other part of calling. Third, Christ with his merit is the cause of our justification, yet not without the faith by which in effectual calling we apprehend him with his merit. Finally, Christ with his merit is the cause of our glorification, but with the faith that apprehends in justification the imputed righteousness of Christ. From these things we see that a man is justified by the merit of Christ, as by the means through which God justifies him, but not without faith, which apprehends that merit offered in effectual calling. Hence the Apostle, in Romans and Galatians, expressed this mode, which is a compound thing, by the single word faith, and sometimes joins it with faith in Jesus Christ. Romans 3:22: he calls it the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ. So in Galatians 2:16 he says that we are justified through faith in Jesus Christ, and in Romans 3:25 he speaks of faith in his blood. Finally, among the modes by which God justifies a man, the grace or mercy of God is reckoned. Grace agrees very well with faith, but between grace and works there is the greatest disagreement (Romans 11:6; Ephesians 2:8-9). Therefore these statements agree: God justifies from faith, and God justifies from grace. But the question concerns the order: which is prior, faith or grace; whether faith is the cause of grace, or grace the cause of faith? I answer that faith goes before and grace follows, and that faith, that is, Christ with his merit apprehended by faith in effectual calling, is the cause of that new grace by which God justifies a man. On this point, let us go back a little further.

units.la: [illegible, ~1 letters] nonnihil paulo altius repetamus. Omnis spiritualis benedictio, vt Praedestinatio, Vocatio, Iustificatio, Glorificatio, ex Dei gratia est: gratia autem Dei ex Christo ipsiusque merito est: verbi gratia: In Praedestinatione hominis ad vitam primum est Christus cum suo merito, hinc sequitur gratia Dei, tanquam Christi & meriti ipsius effectum, ex gratia Dei deinde sequitur Praedestinatio. In efficaci Vocatione primum est Christi meritum, deinde est gratia Dei quam sequitur vocatio. Similiter in Iustificatione primum est meritum Christi: quod in efficaci vocatione apprehensum est, deinde est gratia Dei, ex qua rursus sequitur Iustificatio. Sic denique in Glorificatione primum est meritum Christi, quod quidem imputatum in Iustificatione per fidem apprehensum est, deinde est gratia Dei quam sequitur Glorificatio. Hoc autem in his delcrmen est, quod in Praedestinatione & Vocatione meritum Christi solum sine fide nostra causa fit gratiae: In Iustificatione vero & Glorificatione meritum Christi fide apprehensum causa fit gratiae. Ex his quae diximus apparet fidem seu Christum cum merito suo fide apprehensum causam esse gratiae illius qua Deus hominem iustificat: unde Rom. 3. 24. postquam dixit, Iustificantur autem gratis, id est, ejus gratia, continuo addidit per redemptionem factam in Iesu Christo, quibus verbis causam illius gratiae qua justificantur homines designauit,nempè redemptionem Christi fide apprehensam in efficaci vocatione & Rom. 4. 16. Propterea ex fide est hæreditas, vt fit per gratiam, quibus verbis significat vitam æternam:ideo ex fide esse vt locus fit gratiæ,quæ effectum est fidei justitiam Christi imputatam apprehendentis in luftificatione.
units.tr: So that we may say something about this, let us go back a little further. Every spiritual blessing, such as predestination, calling, justification and glorification, comes from the grace of God. The grace of God, however, comes from Christ and from his merit. For example, in the predestination of a man to life, Christ with his merit comes first; from this follows the grace of God, as the effect of Christ and his merit, and from the grace of God predestination then follows. In effectual calling, Christ's merit comes first, then the grace of God, which calling follows. Likewise in justification, Christ's merit comes first, and it is laid hold of in effectual calling; then comes the grace of God, from which justification again follows. Finally, in glorification, Christ's merit comes first, which indeed is imputed and laid hold of by faith in justification; then comes the grace of God, which glorification follows. The difference in these is this: in predestination and calling, Christ's merit alone, without our faith, is the cause of grace; but in justification and glorification, Christ's merit laid hold of by faith is the cause of grace. From what we have said it is clear that faith, or Christ with his merit laid hold of by faith, is the cause of that grace by which God justifies a man. Hence in Romans 3:24, after saying "they are justified freely", that is, by his grace, he at once added "through the redemption that is in Jesus Christ", words by which he pointed out the cause of that grace by which men are justified, namely the redemption of Christ laid hold of by faith in effectual calling. And in Romans 4:16, "therefore it is of faith, that it might be by grace", words by which he signifies eternal life; so it is of faith that there is room for grace, because faith, laying hold of the righteousness of Christ imputed in justification, is what brings it about.

units.la: Hic fi quæras quomodò fieri potest vt meritum Christi, & gratia Dei,fiue gratuitus Dei fauor,qui merito contrarius est, vnà consistat? Nam Christi satisfactio qua satisfecit iustitiæ patris, ipsa est quæ promeretur Dei erga nos gratiam:sin loquaris de nostro ipsorum merito, profecto nostrum meritum & gratia Dei vnà consistere non possunt, sed tota natura sua pugnant. De efficiente justificationis causa hæc hactenus.
units.tr: Here, if you ask how it can be that Christ's merit and the grace of God, or the free favour of God, which is contrary to merit, can stand together, for Christ's satisfaction, by which he satisfied the justice of the Father, is itself what merits God's grace toward us; but if you speak of our own merit, then truly our merit and the grace of God cannot stand together, but are opposed by their whole nature. So far concerning the efficient cause of justification.

units.la: Materia Iustificationis est homo peccator primùm, vnde dicitur Deus justificare impiū. Rom.4.5. deinde credens: Iustitia Dei per fidè Iesu Christi in omnes & super omnes qui credunt. Rom.3.22. Materiæ nomine intelligo subjectum de quo Deus è tribunali suo pronunciat absolutionis sententiam: Sic accepto materiæ vocabulo, Christus dici non potest Iustificationis materia:Iustitiæ quidem materia siue subjectum vocari potest, Iustificationis non item. Hæc de materia,
units.tr: The matter of justification is first the sinner, man, whence God is said to justify the ungodly (Rom. 4:5); then the believer: "the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ, unto all and upon all who believe" (Rom. 3:22). By the name of matter I understand the subject concerning which God pronounces the sentence of absolution from his judgment seat. Taking the word matter in this sense, Christ cannot be called the matter of justification; he can indeed be called the matter or subject of righteousness, but not of justification. So much concerning the matter.

units.la: Forma siue causa formalis Iustificationis est iustitia illa Christi, quæ de credente pronunciatur, & iustificationis motu quasi introducitur in credentem: Formalis enim causa motus cujusque dicitur ea quæ introducitur forma. Verum quidem est eandem illam Christi iustitiam esse quoque efficientem & meritoriam Iustificationis causam, sed efficiens est quatenus in vocatione efficaci oblata fide apprehenditur: Forma autem est quatenus in iustificatione imputata fide apprehenditur. De iustitia Christi tanquam causa formali loquitur Scriptura cum dicit Deum imputare iustitiam absque operibus, Rom. 4. 6. Vocatur iustitia Dei, Rom. 3. 22. & donum iustitiæ. Rom. 5. 17. & iustitia quæ est ex Deo, Philipp. 3. 9. quo loco opponitur iustitia quam nostram vocat, & quam definit iustitiam quæ est ex lege. Iustitia fateor quæ inhæret, ut ea quæ fuit primi hominis, & quæ est Angelorum beatorum, iustitia quoque Dei vocari potest, nam ex Deo est, & Dei donum est, verum Deus specialiter eam iustitiam pro sua habet quæ non inhæret, sed quam ipse ex gratia imputat peccatori. Hactenus de forma. Sequitur nunc ut de fine dicamus: is geminus est, proximus & ultimus: Proximus quidem est salus nostra, ultimus vero ac præcipuus est Dei gloria in illa iustitia sua imputata. Ad declarandam iustitiam suam præsenti tempore. Rom. 3. 26.
units.tr: The form, or formal cause, of justification is that righteousness of Christ which is pronounced concerning the believer, and is, as it were, introduced into the believer by the act of justification; for that which is introduced is called the formal cause of any motion. It is true that this same righteousness of Christ is also the efficient and meritorious cause of justification, but it is efficient insofar as it is laid hold of by faith offered in effectual calling; it is form insofar as it is laid hold of by faith imputed in justification. Scripture speaks of the righteousness of Christ as the formal cause when it says that God imputes righteousness apart from works (Rom. 4:6). It is called the righteousness of God (Rom. 3:22), and the gift of righteousness (Rom. 5:17), and the righteousness which is of God (Phil. 3:9), where it is set against the righteousness which he calls our own and which he defines as the righteousness that is of the law. I admit that the righteousness which inheres, such as that which the first man had, and that which belongs to the blessed angels, can also be called the righteousness of God, for it is from God and is God's gift; yet God specially claims as his own that righteousness which does not inhere, but which he himself imputes to the sinner by grace. So far concerning the form. It follows now that we speak of the end. This is twofold, proximate and ultimate. The proximate end is our salvation; the ultimate and chief end is the glory of God in that righteousness of his which is imputed. "To declare his righteousness at the present time" (Rom. 3:26).

units.la: Quemadmodum enim glorificatur Deus in iustitia, ea, quæ ipsi essentialis est, ita glorificatur in justitia Christi filij sui, quæ ipsa quoque iustitia Dei dicitur.
units.tr: For just as God is glorified in righteousness, that which is essential to him, so he is glorified in the righteousness of Christ his Son, which is also itself called the righteousness of God.

units.la: Iustificationis partes sunt duæ: prior est peccatorum remissio, posterior justitiæ imputatio, vel justificatio proprie dicta. Sciendum est non esse iustos diuersos & numero differentes quasi motus, verum unicum esse quasi motum respectu & numero, habere autem hunc unicum quasi motum diuersas appellationes ratione duorum terminorum, ratione quidem termini a quo vocari peccatorum remissionem, seu absolutionem a peccato, seu non imputationem peccati: ratione vero termini ad quem vocari Iustificationem seu justitiæ imputationem: idem autem re ipsa est & numero motus quo aboletur peccatum, & introducitur justitia: ratione tamen terminorum distingui potest: Quod autem unicus sit numero quasi motus appareat ex Rom. 4.6.7. vbi quod Dauid in Psalmo tuo vocauit remissionem peccatorum, Apostolus eodem sensu vocat imputationem justitiæ.
units.tr: There are two parts of justification: the first is the remission of sins, the second the imputation of righteousness, or justification properly so called. It must be understood that these are not two different motions, differing in number, but one motion, one in respect and in number; this one motion, however, has different names according to its two termini. According to the terminus from which, it is called the remission of sins, or absolution from sin, or non-imputation of sin; but according to the terminus to which, it is called justification, or the imputation of righteousness. In fact, the motion by which sin is taken away and righteousness introduced is one and the same, and one in number, yet it can be distinguished by its termini. That this motion is one in number appears from Romans 4:6–7, where the Apostle, in the same sense, calls the imputation of righteousness what David in the Psalm called the remission of sins.

units.la: Vt igitur de priori Iustificationis parte dicimus, Remissio peccati non est quidem delectio & expunctio peccati e subjecto suo, ita vt iam desinat illud in subjecto inhærere, sed est, qua Deus, cum infit peccatum in subjecto, tamen censet non esse, non imputat ipsum, sed peccatorem habet pro non peccatore. Dum censet nullum peccatū inefle simul aufert peccati reatum, quod est meritum pœnæ, & pœnam ipsam fiue mortem: Ergo in remissione peccatorum tria sunt quæ simul aufert Deus, primùm peccatum ipsum. dum censet illud non inefle, deinde peccati reatum, tertiò pœnam; Ablatio duorum istorum posteriorum, h.e. reatus & pœnæ ex ablatione peccati necessario consequitur. Pars autem ista Iustificationis nomen accipit à peccato qui proprie terminus est à quo procedit motus,& de quo primū est absolutionis sententia: Nam sententia est quoque de reatu & pœna, sed secundo loco.
units.tr: Now, to speak of the first part of justification: the remission of sin is not indeed the removal and erasing of sin from its subject, so that it ceases to inhere in the subject; rather it is that by which God, although sin does inhere in the subject, nevertheless judges that it is not there, does not impute it, and holds the sinner as a non-sinner. While he judges that no sin dwells in him, he at the same time takes away the guilt of sin, which is the desert of punishment, and the punishment itself, namely death. Thus in the remission of sins there are three things which God takes away at once: first the sin itself, insofar as he judges it not to dwell there; then the guilt of sin; and thirdly the punishment. The removal of the last two, that is, the guilt and the punishment, necessarily follows from the removal of sin. This part of justification takes its name from sin, which is properly the terminus from which the motion proceeds, and concerning which the sentence of absolution is first given; for the sentence concerns also the guilt and the punishment, but in second place.

units.la: Nunc de posteriori Iustificationis parte dicamus. Iustificatio proprie dicta, seu justitiæ imputatio non est introductio in subjectum inhærentis alicujus justitiæ, verum est qua Deus censet eum, qui in se peccator est, justum esse in aliena, h.e. Christi justitia per fidem apprehensa, siue qua imputat peccatori Christi justitiam: Hæc enim proportio est inter remissionem peccati & justificationem, quòd quemadmodum in remissione peccati non imputat Deus peccatum, quod tamen inest, ita in justificatione imputat Deus justitiam quæ non inhæret. Iustitiam imputatam sequitur meritum vitæ pariter & vita ipsa: Nam quemadmodum sententia remissionis peccati est de tribus, de peccato, de reatu, & pœnæ merito, ac pœna ipsa, ita sententia justificationis est de tribus,de justitia fiue fatisfactioneChrifti,de merito illius justitiæ fiue satisfactionis,(nam vitæ æternæ meritoria est)denique de ipsa vita. Licet de his omnibus fit Iustificationis sententia, tamen nomen suum sortitur à justitia Christi, quam reliqua duo necessariò consequuntur.
units.tr: Now let us speak of the second part of justification. Justification properly so called, or the imputation of righteousness, is not the introduction into the subject of some righteousness that inheres, but is that by which God judges him who is a sinner in himself to be righteous in another's righteousness, that is, the righteousness of Christ laid hold of by faith, or by which he imputes to the sinner the righteousness of Christ. For this is the parallel between the remission of sin and justification: just as in the remission of sin God does not impute the sin which nevertheless dwells in the man, so in justification God imputes a righteousness which does not inhere. The life of merit follows the imputed righteousness, and life itself likewise: for just as the sentence of the remission of sin concerns three things, sin, the guilt and the merit of punishment, and the punishment itself, so the sentence of justification concerns three things: the righteousness, or satisfaction, of Christ; the merit of that righteousness or satisfaction (for it is meritorious of eternal life); and finally life itself. Although the sentence of justification concerns all of these, it takes its name from the righteousness of Christ, which the other two necessarily follow.

units.la: Executio sententiæ hujus Dei in nobis justificandis tum fit cum per Spiritum suum sanctum nos regenerat, h. e. vitam illam nouam in nobis creat, ad quam jam prius nos justificationis sententia adjudicauit: Ergo executio sententiæ justificationis proprie respicit vitam illam spiritualem & æternam, de qua postremo loco diximus justificationis esse sententiam: Sed de hoc in doctrina regenerationis fusius.
units.tr: The execution of this sentence of God in us who are justified takes place when by his Holy Spirit he regenerates us, that is, creates in us that new life to which the sentence of justification had already previously adjudged us. Thus the execution of the sentence of justification properly regards that spiritual and eternal life, which we mentioned last as the subject of the sentence of justification. But of this more fully in the doctrine of regeneration.

units.la: His ita expositis hanc Iustificationis plenam acrealem, vt vocant, definitionem colligimus, vt sit Iustificatio sententia Dei judicis è tribunali suo pronunciata, qua homini peccatori & credenti ex fide Christi & gratia sua remittit peccata & imputat justitiam suam, ad vitam ipsius hominis æternam, & ad gloriam gratiæ sive justitiæ suæ quam gratis imputat. In hac definitione habes primum ipsa nominis definitione, habes deinde quatuor Iustificationis causas, habes denique duas Iustificationis partes.
units.tr: Having set these things out, we arrive at this full, so-called actual definition of Justification: Justification is the sentence of God the judge, pronounced from his tribunal, by which he remits sins to the sinner who believes, out of faith in Christ and by his grace, and imputes his righteousness, to the eternal life of the man himself and to the glory of his grace or righteousness, which he imputes freely. In this definition you have first the definition of the name itself, then the four causes of Justification, and finally the two parts of Justification.

units.la: Quæritur hoc loco, an Iustificatio perficiatur in hac vita? Respondeo hoc sumpto initio, duo sunt genera beneficiorum Dei in Christo, unum eorum quæ non inhærent, cujusmodi sunt Prædestinatio ab æterno. Iustificatio, Adoptio: Alteī ū eorum quæ inhærent, vt Vocatio & Glorificatio: Hoc commune habent duo hæc beneficiorū genera, quòd non ante manifestatione Christi plena perfeƈtáque sit futura eorum manifestatio & patefaƈtio, non Prædestinationis, non Iustificationis, nō Adoptionis, nō Vocationis, nōGlorificationis. Cœpit quidem eorū in prima Christi manifestatione patefaƈtio, vnde Apost. Rom. 5. 11. Nūc autē patefaƈta est iustitia Dei, &c: verūm nōdum plena est eorū patefaƈtio, vnde 1. Ioh. 3.
units.tr: The question here is whether Justification is perfected in this life. I answer, taking this as the starting point: there are two kinds of benefits of God in Christ. One kind does not inhere, such as Predestination from eternity, Justification and Adoption. The other kind does inhere, such as Vocation and Glorification. These two kinds of benefit have this in common: their manifestation and disclosure were not to be complete and perfect before the full manifestation of Christ, whether of Predestination, Justification, Adoption, Vocation or Glorification. Their disclosure indeed began with the first manifestation of Christ, whence the Apostle says, Rom. 5. 11: "But now the righteousness of God has been revealed," etc. Yet their disclosure is not yet complete, whence 1 John 3. 2: "Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it does not yet appear what we shall be."

units.la: 2. Filij Dei iā sumus, sed nondū apparet quoд erimus. In hoc autē differunt duo hęc beneficiorū genera, quod ea quæ diximus non inhę rentia perficiātur & absoluantur reipsa in hac vita: filij Dei, inquit, nunc sumus: sic iā prædestinati sumus: sic iā iustificati sumus: Ea verò quæ inhærentia esse diximus nō perficiantur suisomnib. gradibus, licèt in hac vita inchoētur. Ex his conspicitur Iustificationem quidē in hac præseti vita perfici atq; absolui reipsa, non autē plenè manifestari. Quæstio est annō in die illo iudicij iustificaturus sit Christ* eos qui inhac vita crediderūt? quòd si ita sit annō in altera demū vita perficieda estIustificatio? Respondeo in die illo iudicij Christus non tā iustificaturus est credentes, quā declaraturus est ex operib. eorū eos in hac vita credidisse & iustificatos fuisse: sic enim iustificandi ver-
units.tr: The difference between these two kinds of benefit is this: the benefits we have called non-inhering are in fact perfected and completed in this life. "We are now the sons of God," he says; so now we are predestined, so now we are justified. But the benefits we have said are inhering are not perfected in all their stages, although they begin in this life. From this it is seen that Justification is indeed perfected and completed in fact in this present life, though not fully manifested. The question is whether Christ, on that day of judgment, will justify those who believed in this life, and if so, whether Justification is to be completed only in another life. I answer: on the day of judgment Christ will not so much justify believers as declare, from their works, that they believed and were justified in this life. For the word "to justify" is sometimes taken in this way, so that to justify means to declare someone justified.

units.la: R bum nonnunquam accipitur, vt fit iustificare declarare iustificatum : sic dixit Iacobus hoc sensu hominem iustificari ex operibus.
units.tr: In this sense James said that a man is justified by works.

units.la: Quaeritur rursus annon petimus quotidie à Deo remissionem peccatorum, h.e. iustificationem? quod si ita fit, an dicemus Iustificationem simul & semel totam perfici in hac vita? Respondeo dum precamur remissionem peccatorum non precamur ipsum beneficium quasi nondum datum, sed precamur incrementum fiduciae nostrae & applicationis beneficij quae fit per fidem & fidei incrementum.
units.tr: Again it is asked: do we not daily ask God for the remission of sins, that is, for justification? If so, shall we say that Justification is wholly perfected all at once in this life? I answer: when we pray for the remission of sins, we do not ask for the benefit itself as though it were not yet given. We ask for an increase of our confidence and of the application of the benefit, which takes place through faith, and for an increase of faith.

units.la: Quaeritur postremo, annon Iustificatio sententia est de vita, vita autem non perficitur nisi in Christi adventu : Ergo Iustificatio non perficitur nisi in Christi demum adventu? Respondeo aliud est perfici sententiam de vita, aliud perfici vitam ipsam : sententia quidem de vita perficitur in hac vita : at vita ipsa non perficitur nisi in ipso Christi adventu. Quamobrem argumentatio haec fallax est & captiosa.
units.tr: Finally it is asked: is not Justification a sentence about life, and does life not come to perfection until Christ's coming? Therefore Justification is not perfected until Christ's coming? I answer: it is one thing for the sentence about life to be perfected, and another for life itself to be perfected. The sentence about life is indeed perfected in this life, but life itself is not perfected until the coming of Christ. Wherefore this argument is fallacious and captious.

units.la: Cum Iustificationis doctrina coniungo doctrinam Adoptionis, de qua principio paulo altius repetito sic erit dicendum: Beneficia Dei quae in Christo conferuntur in tempore sunt Vocatio efficax, Iustificatio, sub qua comprehenditur adoptio, denique Regeneratio sive Glorificatio. Vnumquodque ex his beneficijs constat applicatione Christi & gratiae ipsius , vel in vnoquoque ex his est Christi cum gratia sua quædam applicatio: Applicatio Christi duplex est, prima qua ipse Deus nobis eum applicat, secunda est qua nos applicatum nobis à Deo Christum ipsi deinde nobis applicamus : Ergo prima applicatio est Dei, secunda nostra : Applicatio nostra in genere vocatur fides Christi.Cum Dei applicatio ne semper coniunctus est Spiritus sanctus, per quem ipse operatur in nobis applicationem nostram , vel applicationis nostræ instrumentum,h.e.fidem.
units.tr: Since I join the doctrine of Adoption to the doctrine of Justification, which must be discussed by going back a little further at the start, it will be said thus. The benefits of God conferred in Christ in time are: effectual Vocation; Justification, under which Adoption is comprehended; and finally Regeneration or Glorification. Each of these benefits consists in an application of Christ and his grace, or in each there is a certain application of Christ with his grace to us. The application of Christ is twofold. The first is that by which God himself applies him to us; the second is that by which we, having had Christ applied to us by God, then apply him to ourselves. Therefore the first application is God's, the second is ours. Our application in general is called faith in Christ. With God's application the Holy Spirit is always joined, through whom he himself works in us our application, or the instrument of our application, that is, faith.

units.la: Hæc quæ in genere dicimus primùm de applicatione Dei, deinde nostra, apertiora euadent si viderimus quæ sit vtraque applicatio seorsim in singulis Dei beneficijs.Primùm itaque in Vocatione efficaci est applicatio Dei qua Christum cum vniuersa gratia sua nobis offert in verbo suo, cuius quidem verbi comes est Spiritus sanctus. Applicatio autem nostra est qua fide per verbum & Spiritum sanctum in cordibus nostris accensa Christum cum vniuersa gratia sua oblatum apprehendimus.
units.tr: These things we say in general, first of God's application and then of ours, will become clearer if we see what each application is, taken separately, in each of God's benefits. First, then, in effectual Vocation there is God's application, by which he offers Christ with his whole grace to us in his word, and the Holy Spirit accompanies that word. Our application is that by which, with faith kindled in our hearts through the word and the Holy Spirit, we apprehend Christ offered with his whole grace.

units.la: Deinde in Iustificatione applicatio Dei est qua Christum illum in efficaci vocatione iam applicatum cum gratia sua vniuersa propius ad nos admouet & applicat, imputando nobis ipsum ipsiusque specialem quandam gratiam,nempe iustitiam:Cùm hac Dei imputatione coniunctus est Spiritus sanctus: nostra autem applicatio in Iustificatione est qua nos Christum cum ipsius justitia à Deo imputatum per fidem accensam in cordibus nostris beneficio Spiritus illius Dei apprehendimus. Iustificationi succedit Adoptio. In Adoptione (vt de ea nunc dicamus) applicatio Dei est qua adhuc ad nos propius admouet & applicat Christum tanquam fratrem nostrum, censendo nos primogeniti fui fratres, ac proinde filios suos in eo. Vt enim in Iustificatione applicauit Deus nobis Christum tanquam justum, ita in Adoptione applicat nobis Christum tanquam fratrem primogenitum, qui vlterior quidam est & arctior applicationis & conjunctionis gradus: Cum hac quoque applicatione Dei conjunctus est Spiritus sanctus. In Adoptione applicatio nostra est qua per fide beneficio Spiritus sancti accensam applicamus nobis Christum tanquam fratrem primogenitum, siue(vt sic dicam) filiationem in Christo, quam Deus nobis imputauit. Denique in Regeneratione (vt de ea nonnihil etiam nunc dicamus) primum est applicatio Dei, qua etiamnum Christum ad nos propius admouet, eumque nobiscum conjungit tanquam caput cum corpore: Cum hac quoque applicatione Dei conjunctus est Spiritus sanctus. In hac applicatione conjungit Deus nobiscum Christum primum mortuum ad mortificationem carnis: deinde ex mortuis suscitatum ad viuificationem spiritus. In
units.tr: Then in Justification God's application is that by which he brings Christ, already applied to us in effectual vocation, with his whole grace, nearer to us and applies him, imputing to us Christ himself and his special grace, namely righteousness. The Holy Spirit is joined with this imputation of God. Our application in Justification is that by which, through faith kindled in our hearts by the benefit of that Spirit of God, we apprehend Christ with his righteousness, imputed by God. Adoption follows Justification. In Adoption (to speak of it now) God's application is that by which he brings Christ still nearer to us and applies him to us as our brother, counting us the brothers of his firstborn and therefore his sons in him. For as in Justification God applied Christ to us as righteous, so in Adoption he applies Christ to us as firstborn brother, which is a further and closer degree of application and conjunction. The Holy Spirit is also joined with this application of God. In Adoption our application is that by which, through faith kindled by the benefit of the Holy Spirit, we apply to ourselves Christ as firstborn brother, or (so to speak) sonship in Christ, which God has imputed to us. Finally, in Regeneration (to speak of it a little now also), the first thing is God's application, by which he brings Christ still nearer to us and joins him with us as head with body. The Holy Spirit is also joined with this application of God. In this application God joins Christ with us, first as one put to death for the mortification of the flesh, then as one raised from the dead for the quickening of the spirit.

units.la: Regeneratione deinde applicatio nostra est, qua nos conjunctum nobiscum Christum in morte & in vita sua fide per Spiritum sanctum excitataapprehendimus:Atque in hac applicatione primum Dei, deinde nostra, qua fit vt Christus nobiscum conjungatur tanquam caput cum corpore,cernitur nostri Regeneratio: vna enim eademque opera, & conjungitur Christus nobiscum tanquam caput,& nos regeneramur fiue renouamur:Sed de Regeneratione suo loco erit dicendum. Ex his autem quae diximus videmus quae fit Adoptionis natura,in qua explicanda non est opus vt diutius immoremur.
units.tr: In Regeneration, then, our application is that by which we apprehend by faith, stirred up by the Holy Spirit, Christ joined with us in his death and in his life. In this application, first God's and then ours, by which it comes about that Christ is joined with us as head with body, our regeneration is discerned. For by one and the same work Christ is joined with us as head and we are regenerated or renewed. But regeneration must be discussed in its own place. From what we have said we see the nature of Adoption, and there is no need to linger longer over explaining it.

units.la: Hoc postremo ad superiora adijcimus, Spiritum illum qui datur a Deo dum nobis applicat singula beneficia, nomen sortiri a singulis, cum tamen vnus idemque fit Dei Spiritus:Qui enim in Vocatione datur Spiritus,Spiritus vocationis appellatur: Qui in Iustificatione Spiritus justificationis,qui in Adoptione Spiritus adoptionis,qui denique in Regeneratione,Spiritus regenerationis.
units.tr: Lastly we add to what has gone before that the Spirit who is given by God, while he applies the single benefits to us, takes his name from each of them, although it is one and the same Spirit of God. For the Spirit given in Vocation is called the Spirit of vocation; the Spirit in Justification, the Spirit of justification; the Spirit in Adoption, the Spirit of adoption; and finally the Spirit in Regeneration, the Spirit of regeneration.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: THE END.
